(w) Wider debate needed q

5.23. Some witnesses, who appeared before the Committee, were of the view that the |
present Bill has been brought forward by the Government in a very hasty manner. This is an _ 2
important piece of legislation which aims at bringing about a fundamental change in the field —
of management of higher education and hence it calls for a wider debate, both at the
regional as well as national levels. The Government has not made any serious efforts at
eliciting the opinions of the academicians, the student community, teachers, etc. in this
regard. Many of the students’ and teachers’ associations have called for a more wider
national debate on the subject so that the interests of all the segments of the society are
taken care of before the Bill is enacted by the Parliament.

5.23.1. “The Committee, therefore, feels that in view of the availability of time before
the next elections, the suggested process of consultation may be gone through by the
Ministry of Human Resource Development while, at the same time, considering the
suggestions made by the Committee in the earlier paragraphs. The Committee commends
the adoption of the Bill with the necessary changes”.

MINUTES OF DISSENT

The undersigned are basically in disagreement with the final recommendation of the
report that the Bill may be adopted with ‘the necessary changes’. If the Committee agrees
that the change in policy, signified by the Bill requires wider consultations—even a national
debate—how can the Committee propose the adoption of the Bill when such consultations
are yet to be held and elections are to be declared in a matter of days?

None denies the need for non-Government investment in education, paticularly higher
education; at the same time everyone is agreed that education must be protected from
commercialisation. The-safeguards in the Bill against this are totally inadequate. Moreover,
in the report, there is no indication why non-Government investment in higher education has
to take the form of setting up universities, without means being explored for increasing
private investment in the existing universities in the form of endowments, donations, chairs,
etc. Nor has it been pointed out that except for Annamalai University, which is a special
case, all other universities, initially set up with non-Government funding, had to be
eventually taken over either by the Central or the State Government.

The argument that private individuals or institutions, while investing in education, may
like to-have a greater say in the management is not acceptable because education is not an
area where a promoter or financier with money power should have the greatest say. Even
‘deemed universities’ have to demonstrate academic excellence over a number of years as
institutes of higher studies before they can achieve ‘deemed university’ status. The report
fails even to make any such stipulation in the case of new universities.

The provision of ‘winding up’ the universities is a dangerous one. The promoters may
raise money from the public, give degrees for a few years and then plead inability to run the
university so that the Government would be obliged to wind it up. Apart from students,
scholars engaged in reasearch projects, teachers and non-teaching staff would then be left on
the lurch. The Government may be able to impound the permanent endowment fund, but
this would not be enough to run the university.

Finally, there cannot be any compromise on the position that admission should be on
the basis of merit alone. The S.C. verdict on Unnikrishnan case is about private colleges and
institutes already established in spite of Government policy to the contrary and the verdict
only seeks to curb the evil effects of a fait accompli. But when Government is itself
proposing to sanction new private universities, they cannot start from the same assumption.
Admission on merit, followed by a graded fee structure based on the income of respective
guardians and a calculation of unit cost for the institution, is the only way out. Otherwise,
there is violation of Clauses 38(1) and 46 of the Constitution. Hence, we beg to submit this

note of dissent.

ANNEXURE-I
Press Release
The Private Universities (Establishment and Regulation) Bill, 1995

The Private Universities (Establishment and Regulation) Bill, 1995, as introduced in the
Rajya Sabha on 25th August, 1995, has been referred to the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Human Resource Development, headed by Shri P. Upendra, M.P., for
examination and report.

Education has hitherto been primarily the concern of the Central as well as State
Governments. Of late, considerable interest has been generated in the establishment of self-
financing universities not requiring any financial support from the Government. Such
universities can play a subsidiary but supportive role to the endeavours of the State run
universities in the tertiary education sector. In emerging areas of science and technology,
especially, these universities may provide useful! instructional inputs by making available
additional finances.

Establishment of universities rev sires either a specific or enabling legislation. As the
establishment of such universities would require 3 broadly uniform set of guidelines for
ensuring academic standards, prevention of commercialization and mismanagement, etc.,
enactment of an enabling legislation of genera! applicability is considered expedient. It has,
therefore, been decided to provide for establishment of self-financing private universities in
the country and to regulate their functioning by enacting an enabling law on the subject.

Since the proposed “THE PRIVATE UNIVERSITIES (ESTABLISHMENT AND
REGULATION) BILL. 19957 is of very vitai public importance, the Committee invites

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Forty-second Report of the Committee on the
Demands for Grants (Demand No. 40) of the Department of Indian Systems of Medicine
and Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 1996-97.

2. The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from
the Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, Ministry of Health and
Family Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department on the
said Demands for Grants in its meeting held on 10th August, 1996.

REPORT

The National Health Policy of 1983 envisages the necessity to initiate organised
measures to enable each of the systems of Indian Medicine. i.e., Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,
Yoga and Naturopathy as well as Homoeopathy to develop in accordance with its genius,
and find an appropriate role and place for these different systems in the overall health care
delivery system for the benefit of the people. In order to achieve the said goal, a new
Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to
promote and develop the Indian Systems of Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,
Homoeopathy & Drugless Therapies like Yoga and Naturopathy).

2. The new Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H)
aims at strengthening the educational and research institutions of Indian Systems of
Medicine and Homoeopathy, Drug Standardisation and Quality Control, Cultivation of
Medicinal plants including research, Establishment of Specialised ISM&H Centres, etc.

3. People of our country have faith in the traditional systems especially as the services
provided are generally cheaper and available everywhere and the remedies are known to be
generally free from side-effects. Further, India has a large resource of about 4.06 lakh
practitioners of Indian Systems of Medicine and 1.63 lakh practitioners of Homoeopathy,
whose services need to be fully utilised in the national health care delivery system. There are
about 273 Under-graduate and 43 Post-graduate Colleges of Indian Systems of Medicine and
Homoeopathy producing about 11,796 graduates including diploma holders in Homoeopathy
and 491 Post-graduates every year.

4. The basic concept in all the three Indian Systems relates to maintaining a balance in
the body between different elements of humors, of which the body is made up of. Any
disturbance in the balance leads to disease and the therapy lies in restoring the balance
through use of medicines of natural origin based on herbs and minerals. Yoga and
Naturopahty, which are being practised in the country as a way of living for maintenance of
health have also been included under Indian Systems of Medicine. Yoga is a unique system
which views health in totality, emphasising both the physical and mental well being of
human beings.

5. The Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy have practically grown and
developed in the Indian society on the basis of learning through family traditions and Guru
Shishya Parampara, although a few colleges had come up in the late 19th century and the
earlier part of the 20th century. There was practically no Governmental support to this
system. There were no regulations either, regarding the practice and education standard.
Patients used to approach these indigenous physicians on the basis of faith in their skill,
knowledge and integrity.

6. However, after Independence, Institutions like Central Council of Indian Medicines
and Central Council for Homoeopathy were established to register practitioner in these
Systems and to lay down minimum standards for education. The Central Council of
Research in Ayurveda and Siddha, the Central Council of Unani Medicine, the Central
Council of Research in Homoeopathy and the National Institute of Ayurveda at Jaipur and
the National Institute of Homoeopathy at Calcutta have been set up as apex bodies for
research and teaching. In order to formulate Standards for Drugs, Pharmacopoeia
Committees for each of these Systems were set up and supported by the Pharmacopoeia
Laboratories for Indian Medicine (PLIM) and the Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia Laboratory
(HPL) both located at Ghaziabad, U.P. The Central Council of Indian Medicine (CIM) and

1


the Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH) are responsible for laying down and
maintaining uniform standards of education and regulate the professional practices of the
Practitioners in the field of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy, respectively.

7. The Committee was given to understand that out of the Plan Budget of Rs. 2309
lakhs for the year 1995-96, an amount of Rs. 15 crores has been spent on the establishment
of Central Research Councils and the National Institutes leaving an amount of Rs. 8 crores
(Approx.) for the implementation of various programmes by the Department. For the year
1996-97, the Department has been allocated only 2319 lakhs. The Department had asked for
an allocation of Rs. 29 crores from the Planning Commission at the time of finalisation of
the annual Plan for 1996-97. During the course of the plan discussions, the Planning
Commission had indicated an allocation of Rs. 26 crores to the Department for the year
1996-97. But, unfortunately, the Department has received only Rs. 2319 lakhs allocations for
the current financial year.

The Secretary while explaining the position of financial constraint informed that about
Rs. 15 crores will be spent on salaries and running the 5-6 Councils of Research and
National Institutions. The remaining amount of Rs. 8 crores would be hardly sufficient to
support any sizeable scheme, create infrastructure and strengthen the medical services in the
various parts of the country. Even this small amount of Rs. 8 crores would be further
distributed in the 6 Systems of Ayurveda, Siddha, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani and
Homoeopathy. The Secretary informed that the Department is completely starved of funds
and requires adequate financial support for its survival and expansion.

7.1. The budgetary allocations during the last and the current financial year are as
follows:

7.2. The Budgetary provision for the year 1995-96 for the Department of ISM&H was
Rs. 2309 lakhs which was curtailed to Rs. 2250 lakhs at the RE stage 1995-96 due to
economy measures imposed by the Government. The Committee is of the view that
whenever any cut is made in the allocations due to economy measures, the Department
concerned should be allowed as to where the cut should be made.

7.3. There are some schemes where the Department has not been able to make full
utilisation of the budgetary allocations made during the year 1995-96. For example, a sum of
Rs. 200 lakhs was allocated to National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur at BE 1995-96 which
was ‘slashed down to 170 lakhs at the RE stage due to slow pace of construction in the
Institute. Similarly, the Pharmacopoeia Laboratories for Indian Medicines (PLIM),
Ghaziabad, was allocated a sum of Rs. 40 lakhs in BE 1995-96 which was reduced to Rs. 30
lakhs at the RE stage of 1995-96.The Department could utilise only Rs. 4 lakhs during the
year.The reasons advanced for surrendering Rs. 36 lakhs was due to non-filling up of the


5

vacant posts by the Institute.Thus, out of the total allocation of Rs. 2309 lakhs made in the
Budget Estimates of 1995-96, the Department has spent only Rs.2200 lakhs, thereby
surrendering an amount of Rs. 109 lakhs in the financial year 1995-96. Interestingly, an
amount of Rs. 50 lakhs was diverted from the Department of ISM&H to the Department of
Health during the Financial Year 1995-96. Under utilisation of funds would not lead the
system to success. The Department should plug the loop holes and ensure full utilisation of
funds. Full utilisation will be possible only when physical targets are achieved intime. No,
since a separate Department has been created, the Committee hopes that all out efforts
should be made in this direction.

7.4. The total allocation for the Eighth Five Year Plan for the Department of Indian
Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) was initially fixed at Rs. 88 crores. Out of
this, the amount utilised upto 1995-96 was Rs. 68.96 crores. An additional amount of Rs. 20
crores was approved by the Cabinet for this Department for establishment purposes after its
bifurcation from the Department of Health. The Secretary, Department of ISM&H,
informed the Committee that this enhanced allocation of Rs. 20 crores have not been given
to the Department either in the last year’s budgetary allocations or in the current year’s
allocation, The Committee is rather surprised to note as to why the allocation of Rs. 20
crores have not been given to the Department, particularly when a Cabinet decision has
already been taken in this regard. When the higher outlay was cleared by the Cabinet, there
should be no reason for withholding this amount. The Committee desires that the Planning
Commission should release the funds at RE stage provided the Department assures to utilise
the funds.

7.5. The Committee was given to understand that the Indian Systems of Medicine,
particularly Ayurveda has developed a number of new medicines like Ayush-64 for Malaria,
Ayush-66 for Epilepsy, Ayush-82 for Diabetes and Oil 777 for Psoriasis, etc. These
medicines, the Committee was given to understand, have proved very effective and can play
a meaningful role, particularly in the circumstances when allopathic medicines do not have
permanent remedy to cure many of the diseases like Piles, Polio, Diarrhea, etc. In the case
of Malaria, mosquitoes have become immune to the insecticides being used at present. The
Committee was informed that Ayush-64, an Ayurvedic medicine has proved to be quite
effective in curing the patients from malaria in a period of 7 to 8 days. Thus, many of the
Ayurvedic medicines can play a very vital role to supplement the allopathic medicines. It is
precisely for this reason that people have now started turning towards Ayurvedic and
Homoeopathic Systems of Medicines.

7.6. The potential of Indian Systems of Medicines is very well known. The atmosphere
is encouraging. People have got tired of taking allopathic medicines and they are turning
towards the Indian Systems of Medicine. The treatment and the medicines do not have any
side effects. But this potential and the strengths have not been tapped and exploited fully so
far. We have not been able to mount programmes to harness these systems and convert
them either into treatment facilities or preventive health facilities. A time has come now for
the country to take full advantage of the encouraging atmosphere.

7.17. The Committee is constrained to note that the Students of the Indian Systems of
Medicine are taught on the lines of modern methods. Much stress is not laid on the
traditional system. Further, after completing training under Indian Systems of Medicine, the
physicians practise under allopathic system. This should not be allowed to continue if the
Indian Systems of Medicine are to grow and flourish.


4

NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS

8. The Committee notes that availability of herbs and medicinal plants sufficiently is the
basic ingredient of the Indian systems of medicines. The forest and arid land can be made
better use of by plantation of herbs and medicinal plants. There are as many as 150 plants
on the endangered list. The Committee, feels that in order to maintain the efficacy of
traditional medicines, it is essential to preserve and cultivate the medicinal plants and herbs
by starting plantation on a large scale. The State-Governments should made the land
available for such plantations. This is particularly necessary to check the use of spurious
plants in place of genuine herbs. Unless this problem is checked firmly, the traditional
systems of medicines will become ineffective and people will lose their faith in the System.

POOR QUALITY OF DRUGS

9. The manufacturers of these drugs do not have sophisticated and latest technology for
ensuring meticulous standards required for the preparation of drugs. The Committee was
given to understand that lot of spurious material is being used by the manufacturers of
traditional drugs. There is a strong need to take specific decision by which it would be
possible to determine the quality and standard of drugs being used in the ISM&H. Proper
laboratories and research facilities are required to be created for developing the requisite
standards and carrying out the necessary tests, he added. The pharmacopoeia work in this
sector is still reported to be incomplete due to shortage of funds. The Committee agrees
with the plea made by the Secretary and recommends that the allocation for the Department
should be suitably enhanced at the RE stage. The Department should, however, ensure full
utilisation of the scarce resource placed at its disposal. The 9th Five Year Plan is now under
formulation. The Committee hopes that at least in the 9th Plan a new approach and thrust
would be given to these neglected areas.

NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF AYURVEDA, JAIPUR

10. The National Institute of Ayurveda was established in the year 1976 at Jaipur by the
Government of India in collaboration with the Government of Rajasthan. The Institute was
established to develop high standards of teaching, training and research in all aspects of
Ayurvedic System of Medicine. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the
Institute is suffering from a number of problems. There are no research activities in the
Institute. Many of the posts are lying vacant for years together. Even the post of Director
has been recently filled up after many years. The Institute is not able to cater to the needs
of the students. The Department only is responsible for these problems. No attention has
been given to solve the problems. It was allowed to languish in problems. The Department
should take all out efforts to’ activate the Institute.

10.1. The Committee was constrained to note that the Institute could not utilise the
allocation of Rs. 200 lakhs made to it in the year 1995-96 fully as a sum of Rs. 30 lakhs had
to be surrendered due to slow pace of construction in the Institute. The Committee is of the
firm view that there is no monitoring of the programmes undertaken by the Institute. The
Department should fix a time frame for completing construction work’ and should ensure
completion n of the work as per schedule. If this is done, then there would be no scope for
under utilisation of funds. There should also be a regular monitoring. The Committee
reiterates its earlier recommendations and impress upon the Department for full and proper
utilisation of funds already placed at its disposal.

NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF HOMOEOPATHY, CALCUTTA

11. This is the only Homoeopathy Institute in the country which is run by the Central
Government. Today, many patients are turning towards Homoeopathy due to reasons of low


cost in treatment with little or no side effects. But the Committee is constrained to note that
the National Institute of Homoeopathy, Calcutta is really in a very bad shape as there are
only 10 permanent teachers available with the Institute against the requirement of 64
teachers. There is no permanent Director in the Institute.

11.1. The Secretary, Department of ISM&H informed the Committee that the post of
Director of the National Institute of Homoeopathy has been lying vacant as a result of the
stay order granted by the Calcutta High Court. The Department and the Institute have been
making efforts to have the stay order vacated at the earliest possible. The Secretry, admitted
the fact that many posts in the Institute are lying vacant and the level of facilities is not upto
the mark. The reason advanced by the Secretary for this state of affairs is that the
Governing Body of the Institute has not been meeting regularly as a result of which many of
its problems have been pending since long. The paucity of funds with the Department has
also been cited as one of the reasons for the poor state of affairs of this Institute. In view of
the problems and difficulties explained by the Department, the Committee recommends
suitable enhancement of budgetary allocations to this Institute at the RE stage. However,
the Department has not taken sufficient steps. The Department is responsible for this state
of affairs. The Committee strongly recommends that urgent steps may be taken in this
direction.

NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF YOGA

12. There has been a proposal for quite some time to set up a National Institute for
Yoga. However, this proposal is tied up with the winding up of Viswayathan Yogashram and
Central Research Institute for Yoga. The Committee is constrained to note that just because
government has not been able to arrive at a decision that the NIY could not be set up. The
Committee feels that it is not necessary to set up the NIY in Delhi only. There are places
such as Nasik, Lonawala where Yoga has got good following. Therefore, the proposal may
be considered from this angle.

STRENGTHENING OF RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT

13. There are four Research Councils, viz. Central Council for Research in Ayurveda,
Central Council of Research in Unani Medicine, Central Council for Research in Yoga and
Naturopathy and Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy. These councils initiate aid,
guide, develop and coordinate scientific research in the respective systems.

13.1. The Committee is, however, constrained to note that no research activity worth
the name is carred out by these institutes. The Committee strongly feels the need for
research and development in the medicinal plants within the country rather than importing
them from the multinationals 10 years later. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the
Department to. accelerate and strengthen the pace of research activities. The Committee also
feels that the research activities cannot be ignored due to resource constraints and,
therefore, the Committee recommends that sufficient amount needs to be earmarked to the
Institutes for this purpose.

SIDDHA

14. The Committee feels that very scant attention is being given for the development of
SIDDHA. This is evident from the fact that no separate allocation has been given for
SIDDHA in the budgetary allocations of the Department for 1996-97. Explaining this the
department stated that no separate allocation has been made for SIDDHA because
Ayurveda and Siddha are treated in a composite manner because of their many similarities.
The Central Council for Research in Ayurveda and SIDDHA is also for the same reason a


composite body for both Ayurveda and Siddha, the Department added. The Committee
however, does not agree with this contention of the Department and recommends that
separate allocation should be provided for SIDDHA.

14.1 There has been a proposal with the Government to set-up National Institute of
SIDDHA in Tamil Nadu. The proposal was sent by the State Government of Tamil Nadu.
On this, the Department informed the Committee that land has already been identified and
the construction work would be taken up only in the Ninth Five Year Plan period. The
Committee is constrained to note that the Government is taking unduly long on the proposal
to set up the Institute. Since, it is an important proposal, the Planning Commission and the
Ministry of Finance should take a realistic view and provide necessary funds at the Revised
Estimates stage to enable the Department to go ahead with the proposal during the current
financial year itself.

SETTING UP OF PATENT CELL

15. The Committee was given to understand that some patents were taken out in the
Western countries, particularly U.S.A. on Neem and Turmeric. When the Secretary was
asked to clarify on this, he informed that no patent has been sought for Neem or Haldi as
such it appears that patent of one of the chemicals derived from neem has been obtained in
U.S.A. and similarly, patent from one of the treatments in which Haldi is being used has
been taken out in U.S.A. However, the subject of patents is allocated to the Ministry of
Industry and it is understood that the Department of Industrial Development is challenging
the patent granted in regard to Haldi. Since the Department of ISM&H has a vital stake in
the matter, the Department proposed to set up a patent cell consisting of experts in order to
help Indian Scientists in drafting and obtaining patents as well as for increasing awareness
amongst Indian scientists about the consequences / benefits of patents for motivating them.
This Cell will keep an aye on the application of patents field in different countries to
safeguard the Indian interests. The Secretary also explained that no patent can be sought or
acquired for naturally occurring substances medicinal plant or for treatments / drugs already
mentioned in the classical text. Patent can be sought for new drugs and treatments and the
Department proposed to safeguard this effectively as soon as additional resources are made
available.

15.1 The Committee also understands that some drugs in Ayurveda such as Ayush-64
for Malaria, Ayush-56 for epilepsy, Aysuh-82 for Diabetes, etc. have been patented.
However, the number of such drugs are very few. The Committee is of the view that
effective steps are required to be taken to help scientists in ISM&H in drafting and obtaining
patents. The Committee desires that steps should be taken to set up the Patent Cell at the
earliest. The Committee is also of the view that effective steps are required to be taken to
popularise the medicines which have been found to be effective.

EDUCATIONAL STANDARDS

16. The Committee is constrained to note that the standard of ISM&H education in the
country is very low. This is largely because both the infrastructure and manpower resources
available in the institutes are grossly inadequate. There is no mechanism on the pattern of
University Grants Commission to this sector to improve the status and standard of the
institutions. The problem is compounded because of meagre allocations made. The Central
Council of Indian Medicine and also the Central Council of Homoeopathy are responsible
for laying down and maintaining uniform standard of education in the fields of Ayurveda,
Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy and regulating practice in these sytems. There are about
273 under-graduate and 43 post-graduate colleges of ISM&H producing 11,795 graduates and


7

491 post-graduates respectively every year. There are four national institutes i.e. 1. National
Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur. 2. National Institute of Homoeopathy, Calcutta. 3. National
Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore. 4. National Institute of Naturopathy, Pune. Besides
these, the Government also proposed to set-up National Institute of Yoga and National
Institute of Siddha.

16.1 The Committee is also constrained to note that more than 90 percent institutions
do not have the minimum facilities prescribed. Therefore, the assistance to medical
institutions is a very large area of urgent requirement.

16.2 The Committee feels that the efforts made by Central Councils of Indian medicine
and Homoeopathy are not sufficient enough to maintain and improve the standard of
education for various courses offered in the Institute/Colleges under ISM&H as the
infrastrucutre provided in the colleges is grossly inadequate, out-dated and these require to
be improved. The number of colleges offering under-graduate and post-graduate courses
under the ISM&H should also be increased. The Committee feels that it is urgently
necessary that the facilities and standards of ISM&H Education should be improved without
any delay. Otherwise these Institutions keep on producing substandard graduates who in
turn will continue to remain a liability rather than an asset to these disciplines.

REPORT

1. The Department of Culture plays a vital role in the promotion and dissemination of
art and culture. The aim of the Department is to develop ways and means for instilling basic
values and perceptions in the minds of people, particularly the young. The Department also
undertakes the programme of preservation, encouragement and dissemination of various
manifestations of creative activity, both past and present. The Department is engaged in
excavation, conservation and promotion of ancient monuments and historic sites; administra-
tion of libraries, museums and institutions of anthropology; collection, preservation and
ethnology of national character; catering to institutions and organisations in the areas of
Buddhist and Tibetan Studies; promoting literary, visual and performing arts; observing
centenaries and anniversaries of important personalities and entering into cultural agree-
ments with foreign countries.

1.1 The Department carries out its various programmes through two attached offices,
six subordinate offices and 26 autonomous organisations. The Department of Culture has
been allocated Rs. 203.23 crores which includes 113.76 crores as Plan component and 89.47
crores as non-Plan component. The allocation of funds during the Eighth Five Year Plan to
Department of Culture was Rs. 460 crores which is only 0.19% of the total Plan outlay. The
Committee strongly feels the necessity of increasing the allocation.

1.2 The Revised Estimates (RE) for 1995-96 for the Department of Culture was Rs.
211.27 crores which has been slashed down to Rs. 203.23 crores in the Budget Estimates of
1996-97. Explaining its justification the Department answered the RE of 1995-96 included a
provision of one time grant of Rs. 10 crores to National Gandhi Museum on the occasion of
the 125th Birth Anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi, but the BE for 1996-97 do not include any
such special provision and, hence, the decrease of Rs. 8.04 crores. For the year 1996-97, the
‘Department had asked for an enhanced allocation of Rs. 273.40 crores under Plan
allocation. However, the Planning Commission after assuring an allocation of Rs. 237 crores,
actually approved a Plan outlay of Rs. 113.76 crores only. The Committee is of the view that
the Planning Commission has not taken a realistic view of the conservation of our cultural
heritage, particularly when the nation is going to celebrate its 50th year of Independence.
The Committee recommends allocation of required amount at the RE stage.

1.3 The Committee, in its Tenth and Eighteenth Reports recomended for setting up of
a National Cultural Fund. The Committee was given to understand that a corpus fund with
the Government contribution of Rs. 19.5 crores has been created. On this the Department
clarified that due to resource crunch the amount from Government side was reduced to 19.5
crores from Rs. 100 crores as proposed originally. The fund has, however, not so far been
set up. Clarifying this the Department informed the Committee that the efforts to set up the
fund are maturing. The proposals, as finalised, providing for the setting up of the Fund and
the Scheme to administer it, stand referred to the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Law and
Justice and Planning Commission for concurrence. The Committee strongly recommends that
the Department should vigorously pursue the matter with them for getting it cleared at the
earliest. The Committee desires that the UNESCO should also be approached for additional
funding.


ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA, NEW DELHI

2. The Archaeological Survey of India was set up in 1861. Conservation, preservation
and maintenance of the centrally protected monuments and sites is the prime task of this
organisation. At present, it has 3562 centrally protected monuments, declared to be of
national importance, with more than 5000 structures

2.1 The BE for 1996-97 is Rs. 52.35 crores as against Rs. 50.85 crores in the RE for the
year 1995-96. Commenting on the increase in the budget provision, the Department of
Culture has stated that even this amount falls short of the requirements. It is also a cause for
concern that if sufficient funds are not provided in the Revised Estimate 1996-97, it may be
difficult even to disburse the salary and allowances of the employees besides meeting office
expenses during the current financial year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
sufficient allocation should be made to the ASI, at RE stage.

2.2 The Committee had earlier recommended to expand the network of ASI and to
increase the staff strength. The Department had formed a Committee with the Joint
Director, SIU, Ministry of Finance to assess actual requirement of the staff through the spot
inspection. But this Committee is yet to visit any circle. The Committee feels that there is
virtually no progress in this respect and there is an urgent need for filling up required
number of vacancies at the earlies:.

2.3 The Committee is concerned to note that Taj Mahal remains closed on Monday and
the entry fee for it after 4 P.M. onwards has been increased to Rs. 100/. Regarding entry
fee for the Taj Mahal, the Secretary stated that at present, the Archaeological Survey of
India has been charging only 50 paise per person. However, with effect from Ist September,
1996, the entry fee for Taj Mahal and some other major monuments will be raised to Rs. 5
per person; in respect of comparatively less important monuments, the entry fee was being
revised to Rs. 2 per person, he added. For the purpose of maintenance, the Taj is also being
closed on Mondays. As regards the levy of Rs. 100 for entering the Taj before 9 A.M. and
after 4.00 P.M., Secretary (Culture) clarified that this had been done by the Agra
Development Authority and that State Government is separately apprising the Supreme
Court as to how this money is being utilised for development of Taj Mahal and Agra. The
Committee, however, desires that the Department should take up the matter with the State
Government of U.P. to reduce the levy of Rs. 100 to a reasonable limit.

NATIONAL MUSEUM

3. The Committee is constrained to observe that during the transit of exhibits for
holding exhibitions abroad and also during the course of the exhibitions there, sufficient
protection to art pieces is not taken care of due to which several exhibits are damaged. In its
reply the Department stated that necessary steps are taken for protecting the art objects in
accordance with the guidelines. The Committee feels that instead of original documents,
replicas may be sent in the exhibitions including those meant to be placed at the festivals
abroad. This would ensure the safety and security of the precious and rare exhibits.
INDIAN MUSEUM, CALCUTTA

4. The Indian Museum, established in 1814, is the oldest and the largest institution of
its kind in the country. It houses unique treasures of Indian and foreign art, representing
centuries of cultural ethos and traditions.

4.1 The Indian Museum, Calcutta was allocated Rs. 2 crores on Plan side and Rs. 1.19
crores on non-Plan side in the BE of 1996-97, which remained same as compared to RE of
1995-96. It may be increased at RE stage.


4.2. The Committee has observed that five organisations namely. Botanical, Zoological,
Geological, Anthropological and Archaeological Survey of India are occuping space in the
Indian Museum, Calcutta. The Department stated that there was no possibility of vacating
the space by these organisations in the near future. The Committee, however, desires that
the matter may be pursued vigorously.

SALARJUNG MUSEUM, HYDERABAD

5. It was brought to the notice of the Committee that some important materials and
jewellaries were missing from the Salarjung Museum. The Committee is of the view that
sufficient security measures are not taken by the Museum and Committee recommends that
enough security measures may be taken immediately.

5.1 The Salarjung Museum has undertaken the construction of two additional wings i.e.
Far Eastern Gallery and European Gallary which were supposed to be completed by 31st
May, 1996 and 15th July, 1996, respectively. The Committee is constrained to note that the
construction work has not yet been completed by the scheduled dates. The National Building
Construction Corporation (NBCC) which is doing the construction job there has sought
extention upto 31st December, 1996. The Committee hopes that the construction would be
completed at least by the revised date.

NATIONAL COUNCIL OF SCIENCE MUSEUMS, CALCUTTA

6. The Committee in its 18th Report had recommended for taking necessary steps to
involve ‘Nagarpalikas and Panchayats’ in the NCSM’s new programme for setting up small
size low capital intensive school science centres in underpriviledged schools in rural areas.
The Department has stated that the Nagarapalikas and Panchayats would henceforth be
involved in these activities. The Committee, however, feels that there is no progress in this
regard and concrete steps are required to be taken immediately.

SCHEME FOR PROMOTION AND STRENGTHENING OF REGIONAL AND LOCAL
MUSEUMS

7. The aim of this scheme is to enable establishment of Regional Museums in the
country. The Budgetary provision made during the last year was Rs. 1 crore which remained
the same in the BE for 1996-97. The Committee in its 18th report had recommended that
steps be taken to involve Panchayats and Nagarpalikas in this scheme. The Department
stated in its reply that at the district level, Panchayats and Nagarpalikus are proposed to be
included. The Committee feels that no concrete steps have so far been taken. Hence the
Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation that necessary steps should be taken to
involve the Panchayats and Nagarpalikas in it.

NATIONAL RESEARCH LABORATORY FOR CONSERVATION OF CULTURAI
PROPERTY, LUCKNOW

8. This institute is a subordinate office of the Department of Culture established in 1976
engaged in the conservation of cultural property including monuments and development of
conservation techniques through short-term and long-term research projects. The budgetary
provision for the institution for the year 1996-97 on the Plan side is Rs. 1.10 crores and on
the non-Plan side Rs. 0.55 crores which may be further increased at RE stage.

8.1 The Committee was given to understand that the historical monuments of great
national importance in Lucknow like Imambara, Mosques and other Maqbaras in the -
adjoining areas are in a depleting stage in the absence of proper care and upkeep. Many of
these monuments have their great historical past which needs to be preserved. The
Committee was given to understand that the President of Iran, during his visit to Lucknow,
last year had announed a grant of Rs. 1 crore exclusively for the upkeep and maintenance of
these historical monuments and to preserve the cultural heritage of this great city of


4

Lucknow. Unfortunately, this money has not reached the place yet, with the result that
these monuments are further decaying. The Committee desires that the position with regard
to this external aid may be checked up and the Ministry of Finance be approached for
making budgetary provisions for this purpose at the RE stage. The Government has no right
to withhold any such grant received from an external agency meant for the preservation and
maintenance of historical monuments of great national importance. The amount should be
utilised for the purpose for which it has been given to the Government of India by the
Iranian Government.

8.2 The Committee was also given to understand that an amount of Rs. 11 to Rs. 12
crores was received by Hussainabad Trust for the maintenance, upkeep and preservation of
very good and rare pieces of architecture in this area. There are a number of monuments of
historical importance but they have not so far been declared as monuments of national
importance. These pieces .f rare art and architecture need to be protected and preserved
with the Government's intervention. The residency is also reported to be in very bad shape.
This residency was the centre of attraction during the freedom struggle. Earlier there used to
be a light and sound show which has since been closed. The Committee being distressed to
hear the sad state of affairs, strongly recommends that every effort should be made to
preserve the cultural heritage of these monuments and the grant of Rs. one crore received
from the President of Iran should be utilised for this purpose without any delay.

ANTHROPOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA

9. The allocation in the RE for 1995-96 on its Plan side was Rs. 1.60 crores, which has
been reduced to Rs. 0.98 crores in 1996-97 BE. Commenting on this reduction, the
Department stated that total allocation for the Eighth Five Year Plan for Anthropological
Survey of India was Rs. 6.00 crores out of which Rs. 5.02 crores were already allocated
during the previous 4 years of the Eighth Five Year Plan. Hence it was restricted to Rs. 0.98
crores only for 1996-97. The Committee feels that the amount allocated for this year is too
limited and it would certainly hamper the progress of the working of Anthropological Survey
of India. The Committee feels that there is a need for rational allocations to be made each
year. Anthropoligcal Survey of India has undertaken a project called “People of India”
under which 43 volumes are expected to be brought out. However, only 8 National volumes
and 14 States volumes have been brought out so far. The Committee recommends that the
remaining volumes also should be completed at the earliest. The reduction in the allocation
is also likely to hamper the progress of this project. The Committee, therefore, desires that
the required funds may be restored at the RE stage.

LIBRARIES

10. Outlay for Libraries was Rs. 17.16 crores in the RE for 1995-96, Where as BE of
1996-97 is only Rs. 14.29 crores. The Department stated that the RE for the year 1995-96
included the amount of Rs. 3 crores for the “School-cum-Village Libraries”. The scheme was
not approved by the Finance Ministry. Hence there was no allocation for this scheme
resulting in reduced allocation in 1996-97, the Department added. The Scheme was not
approved by the Ministry of Finance during 1995-96. The matter was referred to the
Planning Commission for evaluation of the existing schemes on Library Services with special
reference to the utility of the scheme of School-cum-Village Libraries. The evaluation is
being processed by the Planning Commission, and the matter is being actively persued, the
Department added. The Committee desires that an early decision is required to be taken in
the matter.

10.1 The Committee in its 18th Report recommended to spread the network of libraries


5

with computer facilities particularly in small towns. The Department stated that Raja Ram-
Mohan Roy Library Foundation had organised a conference of State Library Planning
Convenors in August, 1995 which recommended the networking of Libraries to the District
level Report of the working group on Libraries and Informatics which recommended that all
Libraries should be linked through networks and that the INFLIBNET should be made fully
operational, is under consideration, the Department added. The Committee recommends that a
final view should be taken in the matter at the earliest.

KHUDA BAKSH ORIENTAL PUBLIC LIBRARY, PATNA

10.2 Khuda Baksh Oriental Public Library, Patna is an institution of national importance
which maintains more than 18,000 manuscripts, 95,000 old and rare printed books and over 200
original paintings of Mughal, Rajput, Iranian and Turkish Schools. This Library has instituted a
Khuda Baksh Award to recognise the original creative work done in related fields. The
Committee has been given to understand that the condition of this library is in a bad shape The
preservation and upkeep of manuscripts in it is not properly done. The Committee recommends
that a thorough study be made on the functioning of this library and proper upkeep and
preservation of manuscripts be ensured.

THANJAVUR MAHARAJA SERFOJI’S SARASVATI MAHAL LIBRARY THANJAVUR

10.3 The Thanjavur Maharaja Serfoji’s Sarasvati Mahal Library, is one of the few medieval
libraries that exist in the world, It symbolises a priceless repository of culture and time defying
treasure house of knowledge, built up by the successive dynasties of Nayaks and Marathas of
Thanjavur. The library embodies rich and rare collection of manuscripts on all the features of
art, culture and literature. The Committee has noted the fact that valuable palm leaf
manuscripts containing important information about Siddha medicines are available here. The
Committee recommends that the Department of Culture may take necessary steps to publish
the material in a suitable manner.

NATIONAL LIBRARY, CALCUTTA

11. The Committee is of the view that much attention is not being given on the preservation
work of the Library. The Committee is constrained to note that the Library is starved of funds.
There is also scarcity of staff. The Secretary accepted that inadequate staff, due to 10%
compulsory cut in recruitment, has adversely affected not only the governance but also the
preservation of documents in the Library. The Committee was informed that the recuitment
rules for filling up various posts. in the National Library has since been finalised based on
chottopadhyay Committee’s recommendation and the vacant posts would be filled up shortly.
The Committee is deeply anguished to observe that a Microfilming Equipment bought in
1993-94 has not yet been used due to paucity of staff. The Committee feels that the staff
problem brooks no delay and should be solved immediately, Required funds may be released at

RE stage.
RAJA RAMMOHAN ROY LIBRARY

12. The Committee had earlier recommended for appointment of an Enquiry Committee to
look into the purchasing methodology of this library. The Department informed that the
Enquiry Committee had submitted its report. However, the present methodology of purchase of
books has not been adversely commented upon by this enquiry Committee, the Department
added. The Committee, however, desires that a regular monitoring should be kept on the
activities of this Library.

12.1 The Enquiry Committee has also recommended to spread the Library Movement to
Village Level. The Committee is of the view that this should be expedited immediately.


DELHI PUBLIC LIBRARY

13. The Committee had earlier recommended to spread the network of the Delhi Public
Library in the slum and under-developed areas. The Department stated that the DPL has
not taken up the construction of Library building in Raja Garden, Janak Puri, R.K. Puram,
Patparganj and Ashok Vihar due to non-availability of funds. The M.C.D. and N.D.M.C
had been approached by the authorities of the DPL since 1992 for allotment of suitable
accommodation for setting up libraries in slum and under-developed areas. The Committee
is, however, constrained to note that though the matter has been vigorously pursued by the
then Director and the administration of the DPL, no success has been achieved in this
direction so far. The present authorities of DPL will be meeting the Chief Minister of Delhi
shortly, to discuss the proposals and prospects of DPL, the Department added. The
Committee feels that there is an urgent need to spread the library facilities in the slum and
under developed areas of Delhi. The required funds and accommodation should be made

available at the earliest.

AKADEMIES

14. The Sahitya Akademi, Lalit kala Akademi and Sangeet Natak Akademi have been
allocated in the plan side Rs. 2.75 crores. Rs. 1.70 crores and Rs. 3.10 crores respectively,
Only in case of Sahitya Akademi Rs. 0.25 crores have been increased in the BE of 1996-97
as compared to RE of 1995-96. The Committee feels that this meagre amount is inadequate
for the Akademies. Hence the Committee is of the view that adequate funds may be
allocated. at RE stage.

14.1 The Committee expresses its concern over the misuse of funds and autonomy in the
Lalit Kala Akademi. They have also not implemented the recommendations made by the
Haksar Committee. However, in view of the serious nature of the alleged irregularities in
this Akademi, it has been decided to institute two enquiries into the recent happenings at
Lalit Kala Akademi; one of the equiries will be conducted by Chief Accounts Officer of the
Department and the other from the Vigilance angle by a Director of the Department, the
Secretary added. The Committee recommends that the enquiries may be completed at the
earliest and necessary action taken thereon.

CENTRE FOR CULTURAL RESOURCE AND TRAINING (CCRT)

15. The allocation made on the plan side for 1996-97 is Rs. 3.10 crores and on non-plan
side Rs. 0.84 crores. The Committee in its 18th Report had recommended for opening of
new CCRTs. The Department stated that due to inadequate resources, opening new CCRTs
will be a difficult proposition. The Committee desires that adequate allocations be made for
this purpose. The Department should chalk out a plan for expansion and seek for additional

funds.
ZONAL CULTURAL CENTRES (ZCC)

15.1° The main purpose is to emphasise the Cultural Linkages that extend beyond
territorial and linguistic boundaries. These centres reflect not only the forms and styles of
different States by which they stand but also represent jointly the composite culture of the
country. The Budget allocation for it is Rs. 2.10 crores which was at the same level last year
also. This scheme is in need of funds and the required funds may be given at RE stage. The
Committee was informed by the Department that a Review Committee had been set up
under that Chairmanship of Dr. U.R. Ananthamurthy to review the functioning of the Zonal
Cultural Centres (ZCC) and its report was submitted in January, 1996. The report has been


7

sent to Centres, Secretaries of the Academies and the State Governments falling under the
jurisdiction of respective Zonal Cultural Centres. The comments from many agencies are still
awaited, the Department added. The Committee desires that the Dej.rtment should pursue
the matter vigorously with all agencies for sending their comments at the earliest as all is not
well in the functioning of Zonal Cultural Centres. After the comments are received, the
Department should take action without much loss of time.

ASSISTANCE TO DANCE, DRAMA AND THEATRE ENSEMBLES

15.2 Under this scheme assistance in the form of salary grant, production grant is given to
well established voluntary cultural organisations for promoting the cultural heritage of the
country. The allocation for 1996-97 on the Plan side is Rs. 2.00 crores and non-plan side is
Rs. 0.40 crores. The scheme is suffering from the under-utilisation of funds. During 1993-94
and 1994-95 the funds could not be utilised fully. The Committee strongly recommends that
full utilisation of the funds should be ensured. Lucknow is a large treasure house of art and
culture; particularly Puppet Dances (Kathputli Dance) Marathi Natya Sangeet in
Maharashtra is culturally a rich art form. However, all such art forms are not getting any
kind of encouragement. They need immediate attention for revival.

DISEMINATION OF TRIBAL, FOLK ART AND CULTURE

15.3 The Scheme provides for financial assistance to voluntary cultural organisations,
institutions and individuals both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small projects of about
a year’s duration on preservation, development and dissemination, of tribal/folk arts and
culture. The Committee feels that special attention needs to be paid for the dissemination of
Tribal Folk Art and Cultural especially in the tribal areas of Orissa. Madhya Pradesh,
Andhra Pradesh and other places. There is a provision for constructing a Centre for
promotion of tribal folk arts and Culture in Hyderabad. But there is no significant
concentration of tribal people in and around Hyderabad. Tribals are located in
Vizianagaram, Srikakulam and Koraput. The Committee, therefore feels that a Tribal
Centre should be appropriately set up in those areas where there is concentration of tribal
population. One finds different kinds of cultural patterns among the tribals of Andhra
Pradesh and Orissa. Steps should be taken to preserve and encourage their culture and they
should be integrated with the rest of the population and the dominant culture.

FESTIVAL OF INDIA

>

15.4 The Government of India has organised festivals of India in United Kingdom, USA,
France, CIS (Former USSR), Sweden, Germany, China and Thailand. These festivals have
been quite successful in carrying the message of the country across the seas and have served
as vehicles for disseminating Indian Culture abroad. The allocation for 1996-97 is Rs. 2.20
crores which is at the same level as that of the last year. The Committee feels that proper
utilisation of money needs to be ensured. The Committee also desires that allocation may be
suitably increased. It has come to the notice of the Committee that various exhibits of
bronze and silver are taken abroad in their original forms for Festivals of India. It has also
come to notice of the Committee that the idols of ancient temples are also carried for the
exhibition purpose in the Festivals stating that those idols are not worshipped in the temples
and, therefore have no sacred value. The Committee, however feels that, even though they
do not have sacred value, but they have the archive value and they should not be allowed to
-be carried abroad in original.


SCHEME FOR SETTING UP MUL¥I-PURPOSE CULTURE COMPLEXES

15.5 The objective of the scheme is to provide financial assistance to autonomous bodies set
up by the State Governments for establishment of cultural complexes for improving the
quality of life among youth and students and making them sensitive to what is aesthetically
and morally good in our society. These are also expected to expose the youth to the finest
forms of creative expression and to foster coordinated activities in the States in different
cultural fields, such as music, drama, dance, literature, fine arts, etc. The Budgetary allocation
for the year 1996-97 has been reduced to Rs. 1.50 crores as compared to Rs. 2.00 crores last
year. the Committee desires that the scheme needs to be restored the required funds. The
Committee feels that there should be one Multi-Purpose Centre at each block level under the
roof of which all the activities of human resource development such as cultural, sports,
education, health could be converged. The Committee recommends that a proposal may be
worked out in this direction in tendem with all other Departments of the Ministry.

MEMORIALS AND CENTENARIES

16. The Committee has been given to understand that the former Prime Minister had
announced a grant of Rs. 6.25 crores for Netaji Research Bureau which is situated in the
ancestral house of Netaji. The present Prime Minister also visited Netaji Bhavan and
reiterated that the grant will be given to the Bureau for development and to keep the
archieves in perfect condition. It was a grant of Rs. 12 crores, half of which was to be released
immediately. This is also going to be the Centenary Year of Netaji. The Committee, however,
is constrained to note that nothing has been done so far by the Department in this regard. The
Museum has not received any grant so far. The Committee was astonished to note that the
Secretary, Department of Culture was not aware of the announcements made by the former
and the present Prime Minister of India in this regard. The Committee strongly recommends
that the matter may be taken up with the Ministry of Finance and Prime Minister’s Office
immediately for an early release of the grant without any more delay.

16.1 The Government of India has decided to celebrate birth centenaries of Shri V.K.
Krishna Menon, Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose, Shri Morarji Desai, centenary of Enlighten-
ment of Bhagwan Ramana Maharishi and comemoration of 50 years of India’s Independence.
The Committee observes that the centenaries of National Leaders like Rana Pratap, Mirza
Ghalib Acharya Vinoba Bhave and Surya Kant Nirala and 500 years of Tulsi Das may also be
included in the list.

50TH YEAR OF INDIA’S INDEPENDENCE

16.2 The Committee is glad to note that the Nation will be celebrating its 50th Year of
Independence soon. The Committee has been informed that the Government has decided to
celebrate the occasion in a befitting manner from 15th August, 1997 to 15th August, 1998. The
Department of Culture has been designated as the nodal agency for it. It was also decided to
constitute a National Committee under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister, an
Implementation Committee under the Chairmanship of the Minister of Human Resource
Development and a Cabinet Committee under the Chairmanship of the Home Minister, the
Department added. The Committee desires that this historic occasion should be celebrated in
a befitting manner. It is indeed a pride occasion for the country. The occasion should also be
taken as an opportunity for the cultural renaissance. Our rich cultural heritage, moral values
and ethos should be reflected in the celebrations. The Department should gear itself up and
rise to the occasion to celebrate this great national event in a grand and befitting manner.


CULTURAL AGREEMENTS AND CULTUKAL EXCHANGE PROGRAMME

17. The allocation made for the scheme during 1996-97 is Rs. 0.365 crores. The
Committee has noted that at present the Government of India has cultural agreements with
98 countries, out of which specific biennial / triennial cultural exchange programme have
been entered into with 70 countries. The Committee feels that allocation is not sufficient and
needs to be suitably increased.

INDIRA GANDHI NATIONAL CENTRE FOR ARTS, NEW DELHI

18. The centre was set up in 1987. A sum of Rs. 25 crores was released to the centre as
the initial corpus fund with the stipulation that the centre would run on the interest accruing
from the investment. During the Eighth Plan an additional corpus fund of Rs. 25 crores was
approved. The allocation for 1996-97 is the same, both on Plan side and Non-Plan side, as
that of 1994-95 i.e. Rs. 20 crores on Plan side and Rs. 2 lakhs on Non-Plan side. The
Committee is of the view that the centre is being allotted substantial budgetary allocations
and its activities must commensurate with the sanctioned funds.

NATIONAL POLICY ON CULTURE

19. The Committee had earlier considered the Approach Paper on the National Policy
on Culture and after a detailed and indepth study of the varied aspects of Indian cultural
scene in its 12th Report, recommended early drafting of the final document on National
Policy on Culture.

19.1 The Committee is not happy with the inordinate delay in drafting the National
Policy on Culture. The Secretary informed that the draft of National Cultural Policy was
now ready and was being processed for obtaining approval of the Cabinet. Drafting the
document had not been an easy task, given the complexity of the issues involved, he added.
The Committee is not happy with the reply and recommends early finalisation of the
National Policy on Culture.

19.2 The Secretary (Culture) also informed that the Department of Culture proposed to
create five organised services i.e. :

(a) Indian Archaeological Service;

(b) Indian Archival Service;

(०) Indian Museums. and Arts Service;
(d) Indian Anthropological Service; and
(e) Indian Library Service.

With the constitution of these services, the gap in the demand and supply of trained
professionals in the aforementioned field will be automatically filled up and the prestigious
cultural organisations of the country will have culture managers of highest calibre.
Visualising the necessity of such professionally specialised services, the Committee recom-
mends for finalisation of the proposal.

19.3 The Committee also observes that in the face of cultural invasion by the West,
through electronic media, India has to bring its voice through its great cultural heritage.
Gandhian Philosophy with its voice for non-violence and peace now stands symbiotically


10

| the voice of UNESCO which focusses its attention on “From Culture of War to Culture
of Peace’. In this respect not only is there a need for Preservation of culture but also a need
for ‘Cultural Renaissance’. In this 50th year of Independence, culture should be the centre
of gravity for India’s progress.

REPORT

1, The most pressing problem faced to-day by the country is the rapid growth of
population. The Population of India has risen from 342 million in 1947 to 846.3 million in
1991 and to an estimated 950 million by the end of 1995. The rapid increase in population
has serious implications on the over all socio-economic development of the country.
Visualising this fact the Government of India was the first national Government in the world
to adopt Family Planning Programme on a national basis in 1951. The objective was to
reduce the birth rate and to stabilise the population at a level consistent with the
requirements of the development of the nation.

1.1 While making the presentation, about the activities and achievements of the
Department, the Secretary informed the Committee that from the year 1986, witu the
introduction of universal Immunisation programme, the component of mother and child
health has became very prominent. The Secretary also stated that now the overall
programme is not only on population stabilisation but also on mother and child health.

1.2 The Secretary also informed the Committee that from Ist April, 1996 the approach
towards Family Welfare Programme has been decentralised. Based on this approach, the
health centres in the country have been asked to identify the needs of the population and to
make an assessment of the population residing in the primary health centre areas. The
Secretary further elaborated that while identifying the needs of the population these
instructions will not be carried out in the first year. For the instructions to be carried out
effectively consultations have to be made with the Gram Pardhans, Primary School teachers,
Non-Governmental Organisations who are working in the field level, he added.

1.3 The Secretary also informed the Committee that there should be a convergence of
the field workers of the adult education, a movement of the primary school teachers, the
Anganwadi workers who are in charge of I.C.D.S projects and Auxiliary Nurse Midwives
(ANM) both male and female, so that the programme can be carried out in a better way.

1.4 The Committee agrees that there should be a convergence of the field workers of
the adult education, a movement of the primary school teacl.ers, Anganwadi workers and
auxiliary mid-wife both male and female, so as to ensure the success of the Family Welfare
Programme. The Committee is also of the view that there is a close co-relation between girl
education and small family. The Committee has also noted that the main reason for the
success of Family Welfare Programme in Kerala is mainly due to high literacy rate among
women. The Committee, therefore, also feels that besides, taking steps for terminal Spacing
Methods and Sterilisation methods. Efforts should also be taken for improving girls
education and for this purpose the convergence of some of the programmes in the
Department of Education and Woman and Child Education may be done.

1.5 Further elaborating on the Programme, the Secretary informed the Committee that the
health of mother and the health of child should become the focal point of the whole
programme. He further stated that if women are empowered to take decisions, then
automatically every family would be having a small family.
