1.6 The Total 8th Plan Outlay for the department is Rs. 6500 crores. The outlay in first
year of the 8th Plan period i.e. 1992-93 was Rs. 900 crores while the actual expenditure was
Rs. 1090.40 crores. In 1993-94 the outlay was Rs. 1060 crores while the actual expenditure
amounted to Rs. 1312.62 crores. In 1994-95 the outlay was Rs. 1280 crores while the actual
expenditure was Rs. 1521.85 crores. In the fourth year of the plan period i.e. 1995-96 the
outlay was Rs. 1440 crores, the anticipated expenditure on the programme is likely to be
around Rs. 1768.67 crores, the Committee noted.

1.7 The Committee notes that the allocation to the department, has been reduced from
Rs. 1593.51 crores in B.E. 1995-96 to Rs. 1550 crores during the current year. Out of
Rs. 1550 crores, Rs. 1535 crores, forms plan component and Rs. 15 crores as non-plan
component.

1.8 Commenting about the allocation to the Family Welfare Programme, the Secretary
informed the Committee that the allocation from the Central Governemnt is not to the
extent desired, if we have to maintain the momentum of the whole programme. The
Secretary also informed that the Family Welfare Programme are centrally sponsored
programmes whereas the implementation of it lies with the States.

1.9 Pleading for more funds, the Secretary informed the Committee that a new
Programme named Reproductive Child Health Programme (RCH) which is the new buzz
word for family planning is being started with the assistance from World Bank to the tune of
300 million dollars and it is a client oriented programme and it is likely to be initiated by the
end of this year or in the beginning of next year. He further informed that the European
Commission has also offered 200 million dollars for the programme due to the change of
policy and change of strategy in implementing the programme.

1.10 The department further stated that the Family Welfare Programme is constantly
underfunded over the years which has led to accumulation of arrears payable to the state
Governemts. For the year 1996-97, an Annual Plan of Rs. 2400.63 crores was proposed to
the Planning Commission. However, after Annual Plan discussions, an allocation of Rs.
1700.00 crores was approved for the Programme. The Committee is concerned to note that
this amount has further been reduced to Rs. 1535.00 crores with the condition that this
allocation will absorb external assistance to the level of Rs. 350.00 crores.

1.11 The Committee is constrained to note that the government instead of providing the


3

amount that should have been allocated by the Government of India is replacing it by the
foreign aid component. The Committee feels that this should not happen. The foreign aid
component should be over and above the amount i.e. suppose to have been-provided by the
Government of India. The Committee is of the view that the department does not take any
steps for starting the fresh phase of a programme well in advance before the completion of
the earlier phase. The department should take care of this aspect.

1.12 With this allocation, the department stated that it will not be able to provide funds
to the State Governments even at the level of 1995-96. The department also stated that there
will be additional financial burden on the State Governments/UTs, as arrears due to them
from the Central Governments, are already in backlog.

1.13 The Committee desire that the Planning Commission should take a realistic view of
the Family Welfare Programme keeping in view the alarming growth of population. The
Plan outlay for the department may be raised adequately at the R.E. stage.

1.14 The Committee recommended last year for setting aside at least 3% of the total
public sector outlay for family welfare plans. The department stated that the Planning
Commission has constituted three working groups including a Working Group on Population
Dynamics and Population Stabilisation for the formulation of Ninth Plan. One of the terms
of reference to the working Group is to project the financial requirement for implementation
of Family Welfare Programmes during the Ninth Plan period both plan and non-plan
requirements and Centre-State participation for the funding, the department added. The
Committee hopes that adequate funds would be made available for Family Welfare
Programme in the Ninth Plan.

LACK OF MONITORING MECHANISM

1.15 The Committee regrets to note that the schemes funded by the Central
Government are not properly and effectively implemented by the State Governments. Many
States do not take the Schemes seriously. There is no proper monitoring mechanism either
by the Central Government or by the States for the implementation. The Committee desires
that the Department should take necessary steps to plug the loopholes and to strengthen the
monitoring mechanism for effective implementation of the schemes.

1.16 The Committee feels that in view of the failure of the State in effectively
implementing the various schemes, the Centre besides strengthening the monitoring
mechanism, should also ensure its regular control over them. Too much of decentralisation is
not yielding the desired results.

ACCURACY AND AUTHENTICITY OF DATA

1.17 The Committee was informed by the Secretary that while the rate of growth of
population in the decade of 60s was 2.2 per cent and it was 2.14 in 70s, it has come down to
the level of 1.9 per cent. The. Committee is however, of the view that the system of
evaluation and data collection are very outdated and not foolproof. Different systems are
followed in different states for registering births and deaths. The Committee feels that a
uniform system of evaluating the rate of growth of population should be adopted to arrive at
reliable authentic and accurate figures. .

RURAL FAMILY WELFARE CENTRES

2. Rural Family Welfare Centres are entrusted with the responsibility of implementing
the Family Welfare Programme i.e Planning, mobilization, monitoring, administration and


4

supervision in rural areas. 5435 such centres are working at all block level PHCs and the
number has been stagnant at the same level since 1.4.1980.

2.1 The budget allocation made to these centres in 1996-97 is Rs. 160 crores which is at
the same level as compared to that of last year. The Committee is concerned to note that
the allocation made is not sufficient even to maintain the existing centres and there is no
scope for further expansion of these centres.

2.2 The Rural Family Welfare Centres which are serving the rural poor, should not
starve for funds. The Committee desires that the allocation as required may be made at RE
stage.

2.3 The Rural Family Welfare Centres used to function independently at block level in
the initial stages Later on it was merged with the Primary Health Centres. To a question, as
to why the RFWCs were merged with that of PHCs, the Secretary informed the Committee
that the Rural Family Welfare Centres were sanctioned by the Government of India during
1950's, 1960’s and 1970’s and there used to be one Family Welfare Centre for each Block.
That used to be located at the Block headquarters. After 1980, a decision was taken at the
Central level. The Planning Commission decided that instead of having one Primary Health
Centre for one lakh population, there should be one Primary Health Centre for 30,000
population. The States were asked to implement this. The Secretary further stated that while
doing so, the States felt that the Primary Health Centre would cater to only 30,000
population and each Primary Health Centre can cover all the family planning needs.
Therefore, instead of having two doctors at the block level, one for the Rural Family
Welfare Centre and the other for the Primary Health Centre, both the centres were merged
together. Instead of having one Block Health Centre, the States oxeated four or five PHCs.
In the process, the role of the primary Health Centre got merged into the network, he
added.

2.4 The Committee is constrained to note that the Primary Health Centres located all
over the country are in a very deplorable condition. There are neither doctors nor medicines
in the PHCs. Very old, out dated, equipments are available with the PHCs. In such a
situation it is bound to affect the implementation of Family Welfare Programme. The
Committee, therefore, feels that unless PHCs are strengthened, the future of Family Welfare
Programme will be jeopardised.

RURAL SUB-CENTRES

3. Rural Sub-Centres are the peripheral Health institutions available to the rural
population for the delivery of Health and Family Welfare Services. These centres have been
opened for every 5000 rural population in plain areas and 3000 population in the tribal and
hilly areas. There are at present, 1.31,900 sub-centres functioning in the country out of
which 97757, subcentres are funded by Government of India as per approved pattern and
the rest are funded under Minimum Needs Programme.

3.1 The outlay made for these centre is Rs. 190 crores in the current financial year. The
department stated that the provision is not enough to maintain even the existing sub-centres,
not to talk of further expansion.

3.2 On the question of expansion of the Centres the Secretary informed the Committee
that the most effective person in the system is the auxiliary midwife and there is a need for
having more than one auxiliary midwife in the sub-centre. The Secretary also stated that
there is a need for comprehensive programme for taking care of the mother and the child in
addition to population stabilisation, he further added that if a major programme is taken up
for increasing the number of ANMs there would be more employment for women. He also


stated their approach to the Planning Commission is to build new centres so that more
ANMs can be coopted into the programme to make the programme more successful.

3.3 As the 9th plan is under formulation, the Committee desires that the Department
should: impress upon the Planning Commission to make a substantial allocation for sub-
centres so that more centres could be opened as these centres are peripheral health
institution and they serve the people of rural and tribal area and more number of ANMs
(especially women) could be given employment which in turn will give better results.

3.4 The Committee feels that the staff strength in position in the sub-centres is way
below the actual requirements, which ultimately affects the functioning of the sub-centres.
Moreover, the staff working in the sub-centres are not provided sufficient training to enable
them to provide an efficient service. The Committee desire that the number of Para-Medical
Staff should also be increased and the training should be regularly provided to them.

URBAN FAMILY, WELFARE CENTRES/HEALTH POSTS

4. Urban Family Welfare Centres provide Family Welfare and Maternity Child Health
services in urban areas. At present 1499 centres are functioning of which 208 are run by the
Central Sector. i.e. Ministry of Railways, Defence, Labour, etc.

4.1 An allocation of Rs. 33 crores has been provided for the current financial year and
according to the department expansion will not be possible with this allocation. Therefore,
the department propose to reorganise the existing centres only.

4.2 The Committee is deeply anguished to note that state Governments are not showing
much interest in monitoring the urban family welfare centres. On this the department stated
that the states are monitoring the Urban Family Welfare Cerires with effect from 1.4.1995
and reports have been furnished by the states of Haryana, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Tamil
Nadu, Gujarat, Orissa, Rajasthan and Chandigarh and the rest of the states have not
furnished the reports inspite of repeated reminders. The Committee desires that the
Department should take up the matter at political level.

4.3 Urban revamping scheme introduced to provide imporved service delivery, out reach
services of Primary Health Care, Family Welfare Maternity Services in Urban slum areas
could not be expanded during the last year due to resource crunch.

4.4 The department stated that during 1996-97, an amount of Rs. 32.46 crores was
proposed which included Rs. 4.6 crores for expansion of urban revamping scheme. But only
an amount of Rs. 18 crores has been allocated. The department therefore stated that the
expansion of the scheme is not possible even during the current year.

4.5 The Committee is of the opinion that these centres serve the poorer sections of
society in the urban areas, and the department should initiate steps to expand the scheme
and adequate allocation may be earmarked in future.

INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION (IEC)

5. To provide full and integrated support to the community oriented services for mother
and child health and to encourage adoption of small family norm, IEC activities were re-
oriented during the 8th Plan by carrying the family welfare programme towards the
community.

5.1 The allocation to IEC activities has been raised from Rs. 34.46 crores in 8.8. 1995-
96 to Rs. 44.05 crores this year. Justifying the increase, the department stated that during
the year 1995-96, a plan allocation of Rs. 33.50 crores was provided for IEC activities. Due


RESEARCH AND EVALUATION

to launching of some new schemes such as Swasthya Mela at PHC level, Primary School
Health Check-up Scheme and Target Free Approach and Pulse Polio Programme, the’
Budget Division was requested to enhance the Budget in the RE 1995-96. Consequently, BE
1995-96 was increased from Rs. 33.50 crores to Rs. 34.15 crores in RE 1995-96.

5.2 The Committee is constrained to note that inspite of the introduction of new
schemes only Rs. 43.00 crores has been provided on the plan side even though the
Department proposed Rs. 71.30 crores. In fact, there is no budget outlay on account of four
new schemes as compared to the normal TEC. Budget provision.

5.3 The Committee is surprised to note that without any adequate Budget Provision
under IEC four new important schemes have been launched. In order to effectively
popularise the Family Welfare Programime and also to give added impetus to the new
schemes, the provision to IEC must be adequately raised. The Committee also feels that
specific steps should be taken by the department to popularise the family welfare programme
among the poor and illiterate people.

5.4 The Committee is of the view that IEC activities should be strengthened. For this
purpose, the services of school teachers can be utilised particularly during vacations.

5,5 The Committee feels that the Planning Commission has not taken a realistic view of
the programme and the need for popularising it. The Committee, therefore, strongly
recommends that the allocation as required may be provided at R.E. stage.

DAIS TRAINING '

6. The allocation to this important programme remains at the same level as that of last
year ie. Rs. 12.50 crores. The Committee, in its 8th and 20th Report had strongly
recommended for increase in the allocation to this programme, but the Committee notes
with concern that the allocation has been’ pegged at the same level.

6.1 The National Health policy aims at ensuring 100% deliveries conducted by trained
dais, by 2000 AD. The Department stated that a proposal for a specific dais training
programme has been formulated and approved for implementation and it proposes to train 6
lakh dais during the current year under the programme. The Programme consists of training
one Dai per village in all the districts of the country in a phased manner over 3 period of
three years. | fee

6.2 The programme is being reviewed: from time to time and States whose performance
are not satisfactory are being looked into by deputing officers from the Ministry for problem
sorting and for on the spot analysis, the, Department added.

6.3 The Committee feels that the ‘allocation made for Dais training is not sufficient to
achieve 100% deliveries, through trained hands by the year 2000 A.D. as stated in National
Health Policy and also to train atleast one Dai per 1000 population. There is, therefore, a
need for enhancing the allocation sufficiently.

6.4 Explaining the objective of the Dais Training Programme the Secretary. informed the
Committee that the programme aims at strengthening the various aspects of maternal and
newborn care by improving the knowledge and skill of dais.

6.5 Since the ‘Dais’ are an integral part of rural community and most of them are
involved in the task of delivery, the. Committee feels:that they should be properly trained.
Merely distributing the kits to the dais is a waste of money unless they are properly trained.

-


PB

SPECIAL SCHOOL HEALTH SCHEME FOR PRIMARY SCHOOLS

7. A sum of Rs. 19.50 crores have been allocated for reseaich and evalustien which
includes a provision of Rs. 8 crore to [CMR this year. Explaining the reason for increase in
allocation to ICMR by Rs. 50 lakhs as compared to that of last year, the Department stated
that the family welfare programme is moving towards a paradigm shift and there is a reed
for completing clinical trials and for carrying out basic research on newer contraceptives.

7.1 The Committee is of the view the research activities in the family welfare sector
should be intensified. For carrying out research activities, especially Intra-mural and extra
mural research and for conducting clinical trials to develop newer contraceptives, there is a
need for more funds. The Committee, therefore feels that a suitable increase in the
Provision to Research and Evaluation be made at a later stage.

VILLAGE HEALTH GUIDE SCHEME

8. Village Health Guide Scheme was launched with the objective of training a person
selected by the community for Primary Health Care. It is a 100% centrally sponsored
scheme.

8.1 A provision of Rs. 10 crores has been made in 8.8. 1996-97, which was the same
last year also. The Committee is constrained to note that majority of the States were not in
favour of the continuance of the Scheme: Only the States of Punjab, Maharashtra, West
Bengal, Mizoram and Tripura were in favour of its continuance

8.2 The Department stated that the scheme is not functioning satisfactorily in the
majority of the States and an expert Group was set up to consider the steps for improving
and reviewing the scheme which felt that scheme was not serving any useful purpose and
therefore needed to be scrapped. However, the Department of Health is of the opinion that
the service of the VHGs can be effectively utilised for the delivery of health care for the
rural people and the matter was discussed in the meeting of the Central Council for Health
and Family Welfare in Oct., 1995 and a decision was taken not to introduce the new Village
Health Guide Scheme and in so far as the existing Village Health Guide Scheme is
concerned, it is left to the State Governments to take a decision

8.3 The Department further stated that in pursuance of the above decision and also
keeping in view the recommendations of the expert committee formed for reviewing the
scheme, an amount of Rs. 1.00 crore has been made for the PANCHAYAT SWASTHYA
SEVA SCHEME and the details of the scheme are being worked out by the Department of
Health. Meanwhile, the VHG scheme is continuing in its present form.

8.4 The Department also stated that the Pilot Project being considered under
Department of Health called PANCHAYAT SWASTHYA SEVA SCHEME if extended to
the whole country will cost approximately Rs. 300.00 crores and is as such, untenable. The
exercise of evaluation of school health check-up and the leading role played by primary
school teachers in this is going on and it is possible that using school teachers, may, in fact
become a viable alternative to VHG Scheme.

8.5 The Committee hopes that the recommendations made by the expert Committee
would be taken into consideration while formulating an alternative to the scheme. The
Committee, however, desires that an early decision may be taken in this regard.
STERILISATION BEDS SCHEME

9. For providing facility for tubectomy operations in hospitals run by Goyernment, local
bodies and Voluntary Organisations where such cases could not be admitted due to non-
availability of beds, a maintenance grant of Rs. 3000 per bed per annum is paid to each


8

institution subject to the condition that a minimum 75/60 tubectomy operations per bed are
achieved. The grant has been revised to Rs. 4500 per bed now. At present, 2679 beds are
functioning. An allocation of Rs. two crore has been made this year.

9.1 Commenting on the ptoposal of the United Nations Family Planning Association
(UNFPA) assisted no Scalpel Vasectomy Project and on the steps taken to popularise it the
Department stated that it has been approved by the Project Implementation Committee on
13.6.1996 with a total outlay of Rs. 4.27 crores. Out of this a component of Rs. 1.61 crore
will be spent for publicity campaign and IEC activity which includes advertisement in
national and regional language dailies/through electronic media and also towards production
of IEC material at the central level. The department also stated that other methods on
regional basis will be adopted towards popularising the new method and the perception
knowledge and attitude of the acceptors as also the impact of the method will be assessed
through. an appropriate operational research technique.

9.2 The Committee feels that the Départment should take effective steps to popularise
it among the people in rural, backward and tribal areas by preparing IEC material based on
their requirements. To ensure the family planning programme, a huge success, the
Committee feels the target should be more on men and not women because the women have
no control over their bodies and it is the husband who controls his wife body and decides the
number of children. Therefore, the Committee feels that more money and effort should be
spent on performing vasectomy operations rather than tubectomy.

AREA PROJECTS

10. The Committee is. very deeply anguished to note that the allocation has gone down
considerably from Rs. 250 crores in 1995-96 to Rs. 195 crores in 1996-97. Explaining the
reasons for reduction in allocation, the Secretary stated that it was mainly due to the expiry
of a number of on-going projects and due to the time required for finalising new projects
after negotiations with donor agencies.

10.1 About the new projects proposed to be taken up during the current year the
department stated that Phase-III DANIDA assisted project in Tamil Nadu and ODA
assisted project in Orissa are being taken up and the proposed Reproductive and Child
Health Project could be started only in Jan-Feb., 1997, the Department added. Accordingly,
only nominal provisions are proposed for 1996-97 as expenditure for remaining part of the
year. These projects are being finalised in consultation with the donor agencies and could be
started only in the later part of 1996-97, the Department added.

10.2 The Committee feels that the Department should finalise the Area Projects with
the donor agencies at the earliest and the projects should be extended to the rest of the
State especially in urban slums.

INVOLVEMENT OF VOLUNTARY ORGANISATIONS

11. A provision of Rs. 13.70 crores has been made this year, for voluntary
organisations. Keeping in view the nature and magnitude of population control programme,
the Committee feels that the involvement of NGOs is very essential. The allocation made is
less and there is a need for increase in allocation.

11.1 It has also come to the notice of the Committee that there are a number of fake
NGOs working in this field, therefore, before giving any assistance, the Committee feels that
the track record of NGO’s in the field should be verified, and NGO’s with proven track
record alone should be assisted. -


9

SPECIAL SCHOOL HEALTH SCHEME FOR PRIMARY SCHOOLS

12. With the collaboration of Department of Education a new Scheme for medical check
up of children in Primary Schools for ailments like anaemia, eye problems, night blindness,
oral hygiene and skin problems etc., has been launched. The two major fall out of this
scheme are: (1) Extensive build up of awareness among children and consequently to parents
about various health needs; (2) Basic health check up for children in primary school and
setting up of an effective referral system for cases requiring further treatment.

12.1 A sum of Rs.45 crores has been provided this year for the scheme. Asked about
the response to the new scheme, the Department claimed that Reports from 221 districts out
of about 385 districts in 27 States and UTs have been received upto 8th August, 1996 and
the coverage response has been quite encouraging.

12.2 The Committee was also informed by the Department that five States namely
Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra could not take up
the scheme, the Committee feels that the Department should impress upon these five States
also to implement the scheme at the earliest.

PULSE POLIO IMMUNIZATION (PPI)

13. In order to achieve the National Health Policy goal of eradication of Poliomylitis by
the year 2000 AD a new initiative of Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) was started in 1995-96.
Under this scheme every child below 3 years of age have been given two doses of OPV
vaccine on two specified days i.e. 9th December, 1995 and 20th January, 1996 irrespective of
the status of previous Immunization. The Department claims that the PPI campaign during
1995-96 yielded notable achievements and during the Campaign over 80 million children
were immunised on each, day. This strategy required an unprecedented logistics and social
mobilisation efforts and from the current year, it has been decided to enhance the age group
of below 5 years instead of below 3 years taken during 1995-96. The strategy will be
continued for further 3-4 years, the Department added

13.1 The Department also informed the Committee that it has been decided to
implement the 2nd phase of Pulse Polio Immunization on two days i.e. on 7th December, 96
and 18th January, 1997.

13.2 The Committee was informed that cent percent target was achieved in State/UTs
of Arunchal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Haryana, Jammu and Kashmir, Kerala, Manipur,
Mizoram, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi,
Dadar and Nagar Haveli and Pondicherry. The Committee also notes that coverage in urban
areas was in general lower than in rural areas.

13.3 The Committee feels that the Department should take steps for achievement of
target of 100% in the rest of the States also. The Committee also feels that effective steps
should be taken by the Department to increase the coverage level in urban areas also.
NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY

14. The Draft National Population Policy prepared by the Swaminathan Committee, was
presented to the Parliament in June, 1994. However the final document has not yet been
finalised. The Department stated that consultation with State Governments, UTs and various
organisations on draft was complete and it is being discussed at senior levels of the
Department.

14.1 The Committee desires that the discussions should be completed at the earliest.
The Committee also desires that the Department should try to give the draft a final shape at
an early date, in view of the rapid explosion in the population.

TECHOLOGY MISSION
15. The Committee in its 8th Report suggested creation of a Technology Mission for


10

Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan which account for 40% of the
country’s population and where the progress of family welfare programme is very slow. The
Committee again in its 20th Report urged the Department with the cooperation of the
concerned State Governments to operationalise the Mission by July, 1995. However the
Department could not operationalise it due to resource constraint. The Department further
stated that it propose to implement the Mission through externally assisted project.

15.1 The Secretary informed the Committee that substantial and detailed preliminary
work on it has been done by the Department. On account of constraint of resources, the
Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) adivsed the Department to implement the measures
envisaged under the project through externally assisted projects.

15.2 In view of the country’s rising population and 40% of the population being
accounted for by these States, the Committee feels there is a urgent need to implement this
mission at an early date by the Department and it should also make all out efforts to
mobilise the resources from the external agencies at the earliest.

PRE-NATAL DIAGNOSTIC TECHNIQUES (REGULATION AND PREVENTION OF
MISUSE) ACT, 1994

16. On the question of the status of enforcement of the pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques
(Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1994, the Department stated that the Act came
into force with effect from 1st January, 1996 and the rules under the Act have been notified
on the same day.

16.1 The Committtee recommends that the provisions of the Act should be
implemented in its true spirits to check the instances of termination of female foeticides,
which is a very serious concern.

FREE DISTRIBUTION OF CONVENTIONAL CONTRACEPTIVES

17. The Plan allocation for Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptives has been
slashed from Rs. 109 crores in 1995-96 to Rs. 99 crores in 1996-97. Justifying the reasons for
reduction to such an important programme, the Department stated that the plan allocation
for grant-in-aid to States/UTs for materials and supplies under the scheme has been reduced
by Rs.10 crores and also due to the fact that the targets for Family Planning methods have
been removed with effect from April, 1996 throughout the country.

17.1 The Committee has noted that IUDs and Copper Ts are freely distributed. The
Committee was given to understand that by using them women get infection. When the
Committee sought to know as to whether any survey was made on this, the Secretary
informed that no such survey was conducted. The Committee desires that a survey should be
conducted in this regard.

CHILD SURVIVAL & SAFE MOTHERHOOD PROJECT (CSSM)

18. This programme cgnsists of two components, namely child survival component and
safe motherhood component. Under the child survival component all districts are proposed
to be convered in a phased manner. The Districts covered are supplied with Drug Kit-A.
The Committee is constrained to note that very few districts have been covered under the
programme. Further, wherever the kits are sent, they reach the end users very late. The
Department should look into these issues and ensure that the programme is covered in all
the districts of the country. The Kits should also reach the end users in time.

NEW STRATEGY

19. The goal of the country is “Health for All by 2000 AD”. While certain components
of this goal are reasonably making good progress, others such as population control have not
achieved the desired success. We are far from the Net Reproductive Rate of Unity (NRR-1)


11

and the population keeps on mounting Even though this is the last year of the Eighth Plan
and the Ninth Plan is about to.commence, still, we do not seem to be really making a dent
on the issue of solving the problem. The Committee strongly feels that a well thought
strategy should be adopted and the National Population Policy should be the first attempt in
this direction.

SOCIAL MARKETING OF NIRODH

20. With a view to promote use of Nirodh for spacing, a social Marketing Programme is
being implemented. At present there are three varieties of Nirodh available under the
programme viz, New Lubricated, Deluxe and super Deluxe. A budget provision of Rs. 35
crores has been provided this year. The Secretary informed the Committee that steps are
being taken to involve Public Distribution system for selling Nirodh in order to increase its
outreach to the far flung areas of the country.

20.1 Asked about the poor quality of condoms, being supplied and the sources of
procurement of condoms and about the quality control measures that are being taken, the
Department stated that condoms required by the Department are presently procured from
the following domesitc manufacturers:

1. M/s Hindustan Latex Ltd., Thiruvananthapuram (a Central PSU)
2. M/s London Rubber Co., Madras (Pvt. Sector)

3. M/s TTK Biomed, Bombay (Pvt. Sector)

4. M/s J.K. Chemicals, Bombay (Pvt. Sector)

5. M/s Polar Latex Ltd., Calcutta (Pvt. Sector)

6. M/s Frontline Latex, Bangalore (Pvt. Sector)

20.2 The Department further stated that random samples from lots offered for sale by
manufacturers are drawn by the inspecting Officers designed by the Department and are
tested at laboratories authorised for this purpose to ensure that condoms conform to the
specifications contained in the Schedule ‘R’ of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. It also
stated that two laboratories under the Ministry of Defence located in Thiruvananthapuram
and Madras and one laboratory in the private sector located in Hyderabad are presently
authorised to test condom samples on behalf of the Department. The condoms are accepted
by the Deptt. only after getting satisfactory test reports from these laboratories.

20.3 The Committee feels that the testing mechanism should be further strengthened
and there should be regular monitoring on this. The Committee, has, however, taken note
of the reports appeared in the Newspapers stating about sub-standard quality of condoms.

REPORT 
I. INTRODUCTION 
1.1. The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible 
for implementation of various programmes of national importance like family welfare, 
primary health care, prevention, control and eradication of major diseases which form the 
main plank of our development efforts. Apart from these, the Ministry also takes special 
care for preventing the spread of diseases assuming the dimension of epidemic. The 
Department of Health, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is 
committed to achieve the goal of health for all by the year 2000 A.D. is responsible for 
evolving broad policies for the health sector and provides financial and technical assistance · 
to State Governments in critical areas through the implementation of important health 
programmes. 
1.2. Broadly, the objectives of the Department are to undertake National Health 
Programmes, to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to 
prevent adu.Iteration of food as well as drugs, to provide primary health care at the door 
steps of the people, to take steps for better implementation of health care programmes for 
tribal and other weaker sections of the society and also to collaborate with member countries 
of United Nations and international agencies like WHO, UNICEF, etc. in matters relating 
to health promotion and development, etc. 
1.3. The Department finances a number of health programmes aimed at controlling 
Malaria, Leprosy, Blindness, AIDS, TB, Gunieawarm either on 100 per cent or on 50 per 
cent basis. The Department also finances wholly or substantially autonomous institutions 
engaged in patient care and or research such as All India Institute of Medical Sciences, 
Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research , Chandigarh, All India Institute 
of Speech and Hearing, Mysore, Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi, National 
Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore etc. The Department also assists 
voluntary organisations and institutions substantially such as Indian Red Cross Society, New 
Delhi, Tuberculosis Centre, New Delhi, Lala Ram Swarup TB Hospital, Mehrauli, etc. 
1.4. The health infrastructure comprises of 2,385 Community Health Centres, 1,693 
Primary Health Centres and 1,31,900 Sub-centres. Some of the new programmes initiated 
·during the current financial year by the Department are Urban Hospital Waste 
Management, Setting up of National Illness Assistance Fund and National Blood Transfusion 
Council, Development of Public Private Partnership and Joint Sector Approach and 
Epidemiological Surveillance and Support System, etc. Pilot projects on Diabetes Control, 
Oral Health, Prevention of deafness and hearing impairment, micro nutrient, malnutrition, 
. medical rahabilitation and cardio-vascular diseases have also been initiated. 
1.5. The overall proportion of the Budget to the Health sector has not increased since 
the beginning of the first Plan. The Health Sector including Family Welfare has been getting 
only abo\tt 3 per cent of the total outlays through the successive Five-Year Plans. The 
Working Group for Health Financing set up by the Planning Commission for the 8th Five 
Year Plan had .recommended that the Health Sector allocation should not be less than 5% of 
the total outlay. The Fourth Conference of Central Council of Health and Family Welfart>. 
has recommended that the direct investment by the Government should be raised .to a 
minimum o(S per cent of the GDP and the total investment in health could go up to 10 per 
cent. The World Health Organisation (WHO) also recommended that the public health care 
expenditure should be at least 5 per cent of the GDP if equity and universal coverage is to 
be realised. However, as per the figures available, the total investment on health and family

(ii) National Leprosy Eradication Programme 
5.9. This programme is implemented with the aim to achieve elimination of leprosy by the 
year 2000 A.D. The Government of India have taken World Bank assistance of Rs. 302 crores 
for ensuring early detection and free Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) services to all leprosy cases. 
The progress of the programme, the Committee was given to understand, has been remarkable. 
The prevalence of leprosy has been reduced from the level of 4 million estimated cases in 1981 
to 0.54 million on record by March, 1996. The prevalence rate of leprosy was 57 per 10,000 in 
1981 which has since been reduced to 5.8 per 10,000 population by now. A total of 6.53 million 
patients have been cured with MDT till March, 1996. The implementation of the programme, 
however, appears to be lacking the desired determination and seriousness as the funds allocated 
for the programme have not been utilized fully. For example, during 1995-96,· out of the total 
allqcation of Rs. 30 crores, only Rs. 64.8 crores could be utilized. Again during the current year, 
Rs. 74 crores only have been allocated. Explaning about the under utilisation of funds, the 
Department have stated that this was mainly due to non-finalisation of agreement for supply of 
additiof\al drugs and free supply drugs received from W.H.O. The M.D.T. Scheme was 
sanctioned in about 200 Districts, towards the end of the financial year 1994-95 and the Districts 
took time in establishing the infrastructure and recruiting staff. The Committee recommends 
that the programme should be implemented with added seriousness and be extended in all parts 
of the country. Funds allocated should be utilized fully._ There is also a need for intensified 
health education and public awareness compaigns to remove the social stigma attached with the 
disease. The Department, should take necessary steps in this direction.

VII. NURSING SERVICES 
7. The Committee is of the view that the nursing services need to be strengthened 
further. There is a need for setting up more nursing schools and colleges particularly in rural 
and trib"l areas. · The Secretary during his oral evidence informed the Committee that in 
order to expand the nursing services and nursing education qualitatively and quantitatively in 
the country, State Governments were requested to send proposals. The Committee is, 
however, constrained to note that there is no encouraging response from the States. The 
Secretary has also informed the Committee that in view of lukewarm response from the 
States, a concept proposal has been prepared by the Nursing experts for upgradation of

VIII. AVAILABILITY OF SPURIOUS DRUGS 
8. The Committee is disturbed to note that spurious drugs are freely available in the 
market without any check and monitoring. This has been posing a very serious problem 
resulting in grave health hazard and consequent deaths of innocent persons. The problem of 
manufacture and sale of spurious and fake drugs in man-made and it has to be curbed with a 
firm hand. The Committee is of the firm view that the matter needs to be examined at great 
length. We can't afford to be silent spectator to innocent lives being taken away by anti­
social elements fndulging in ~h e sale of spurious drugs. A comprehensive plan, the 
Committee recommends, should be prepared to check the menace of manufacture, sale and 
supply of spurious and fake drugs. There should be provision for stringent punishments 
against the persons found responsible for spurious drugs. At a time when there are already 
many diseases like AIDS, Malaria, Cancer, etc. afflicting the nation, the country cannot 
afford to have another man-made problem like the one of spurious drugs . The Committee 
also recommends that a legislation should be made to provide for rigorous punishment to 
those who indulge in manufacture, sale and supply of spurious and fake drugs.

smooth and efficient functioning. The Committee strongly recommends that the Department 
should introduce a system and mechanism of foolpro'of monitoring both by the Central and 
State Governments to plug these loopholes so as to put these PHCs in some order.

(ii) Hospital Waste Management 
10.2. Hospital Waste Management (HWM) is one of the burning problems faced by all 
the hospitals and the society at large as of today. There are discussions about infections 
being caused and spread through hospital wastes. The problems has received alarming ' 
situations requiring the intervention of courts. There is need for installation of incinerators 
as hospital wastes are a cause of environmental pollution as well. The Committee is happy to 
note that a separate scheme has been launched by the Department of Health to tackle the 
problem of the hospital wastes confronting the society: The allocation made for this scheme 
is Rs. 10 lakhs. Since Hospital Waste Management is one of the essential component of 
health programmes. The Committee feels, that the allocation for this programme ~hould be 
suitably enhanc,:ed so as to facilitate all the hospitals in the country to install incinerators and 
check the spread of various diseases through this menace.

current year to assist the poor patients in need of specialised medical treatment for major 
life threatening diseases. This Scheme is on the lines suggested by the Committee. The 
Committee desires that efforts should be made to set up the fund as early as possible. The

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS I OBSERVATIONS OF 31ST REPORT 
1. Overcrowding 
Hospitals in or outside Delhi are extremely overcrowded with patients. This is mainly 
due to Jack of adequate medical care facilities and personnel at the PHCs', and the dist·rict 
and sub-district hospitals for providing primary and secondary level of treatment to patients. 
As a result of this, patients from all parts of the country directly approach the hospitals even 
for minor ailments instead of going to the PHCs or the district and sub-district hospitals. 
Another factor, particular to Delhi, is that some patients try to approach many hospitals, 
one after the other, for the same ailment for psychological satisfaction. (Para 4) 
This results in shortage of beds, resulting in two to three patients sharing the .same bed 
in many hospitals. The hospital authorities cannot increase the number of beds due to acute 
shortage of space. The solution to the problem is that the Government should pay 
immediate attention to improve and expand facilities for medical care at the primary and 
secondary ·levels so . that only those patients needing specialist care and attention, ·are 
referred to the tertiary level hospitals located in the Metro cities. The problem could be also 
tackled partly by setting up screening OPDs, with essential testing facilities slightly away 
from the· main hospitals. "Fhe Committee, therefore, recommends that overcrowding may be 
reduced by simultaneous improvement in: · 
(a) the levels of management efficiency in hospitals; 
(b) improvement in peripheral facilities in District and Sub-districts hospitals for 
primary and secondary treatment; and 
(c) organising a functionaf referral sys.tem. (Para 4. 7) 
There is a need to optimise all existing and available physical facilities to control 
overcrowding. The Committee would emphasise the necessity for opening more counters and 
creating space for patients attending OPDs. There is also a need for proper guidance and 
direction to patients approaching the OPDs so that patients dq not have ·to wander from one 
counter to another. This will, to some extent, ease congestion and overcrowding of patients 
at strategic points. There is also an urgent need to reduce the waiting time of the patients at 
various counters keeping in view the patients' convenience. The underlying idea behind this 
proposal should be that the patients visiting OPD do not have to spend more than half a day -
at the hospitals for purpose of consultation/treatment, etc. (Para 4.12) 
2. Referral Character 
The premier institutions like the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) and 
the Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research were set up to promote high 
standards of medical care, training and research. These were originally marked as referral 
hospitals where patients would be referred by other hospitals for a specialised treatment of a 
high ordt!r. These hospital s were n~)t supposed to entertain new patients, with common 
disease:-., which cuuid be trea ted at the ordinary hospitals. In course of time, due to non-

availability of primary health care facilities at the peripheral health centres resulting in inDl!x of 
patients to the metro cities. The premier instituti~ns like AIIMS and PGIMER have lost their 
referral character as they have to attend to all kinds of patients, irrespective of the nature of 
disease. This has prevented specialists to carry out research of the highest order as their 
attention is primarily focussed on the day to day medical problem of ordinary patients. (Para 5) 
The Committee was informed that there was a proposal under consideration with the 
Government to restore to AIIMS and PGIMER their referral character. The Committee would 
like to know the fate of the proposal. The Government should draw a time-bound programme 
to conyert these hospitals into purely referral hospitals and sort out all the related issues I 
problems of strengthening the peripheral medical facilities by providing them adequate finance 
and other resources. (Para 5.3) 
3. Computerisation 
There is an immediate need for providing computers in the hospitals for maintenance of 
patient - related records, and for better coordination between various departments /wings of 
the hospitals. (Para 6) 
4. Duplication of Facilities 
Duplication of specialist services in the hospitals results in non-optimal use of scarce 
resources. This requires proper co-ordination.and redesignation of the hospitals with specialised 
services .. There is a need for greater horizontalliaisoning among the specialists and to evolve a 
scheme for linking a group of smaller hospitals with one major hospital having specialists' 
expertise. For example, neuro-surgery facilities to deal with accident cases could be made 
available in one hospital and a group of smaller hospitals could make use of these services for 
entire region. (Para 7.1) 
Duplication of services, and facilities in hospitals, particularly in view of the constraints of 
space, beds and financial resources, results in wasteful expenditure and, thus, should be avoided 
as far as possible. Every hospital could specialise in a particular area I discipline so that the 
patients know which hospital they should approach for a particular disease/treatment 
(Para 7.2) 
5. Coordination amongst Hospitals 
Duplication of services I facilities cannot be altogether avoided unless there is a proper and 
efficient coordination between various hospitals there should be a close liaison and coordination 
among di.fferent hospitals for making available efficient specialist services to patients. For 
example, Safdarjung Hospital and AIIMS could work with greater coordination between them 
so as to reduce the burden on each other. (Para 8) 
6. More autonomy to Medical Superintendents 
Medical Superintendents of some hospitals have voiced concern about their dependence on 
the Ministry even for day-to -day works needing immediate attention. This results in avoidable 
delay, affecting the efficiency and quality of services rendered by the hospitals. (Para 9) 
The Committee recommends that the Medical Superintendents should'be given more 
autonomy to enable them to discharge their functions more efficiently. The Ministry may 
consider redesignating the posts of Merlical Superintendents of major hospitals as 'Directors' 
with all the concomitant powers. Such redesignation would not have any financial implication as 
the posts of Medical Superintendents of major hospitals have already been upgraded to that of 
Additoinal D.G. of Health. Services, whjch is equivalent to the rank of Additional Secretary to 
the Government of India. (Para 9.1)

7. Maintenance/Repair of Medical Equipment 
Maintenance of sophisticated and costly equipments is very crucial keeping_ in view the 
investments made in their procurement and also the patients' care and convenience. The 
Government should consider running of workshop in Delhi for this purpose where all the 
medical equipments and appliances could be serviced I repaired without delays. (Para 10) 
8. Strengthening of Blood Banks 
The Blood Banks in the Central Government hospitals have no modern facilities and 
equipments commensurate with the nature of services required today. There is an urgent 
need to look into this problem, keeping in view the detection of new and deadly diseases 
like AIDS etc. The Government should provide HIV tests facilities and modern blood banks 
in each hospital where fractionation of .blood into its different components can be done and 
the transfusion of blood is made foolproof. (Para 11) 
9. Poor Performance of Family Welfare 
The Committee found that the infrastructure provided in the Family Welfare Units in 
each hospital was not being put of op-vimum use. Near total Jack of motivation and 
dedication in the staff was also noticed. The Committee is surprised to note the indifferent 
and nonchalant attitude of the Ministry/hospitals in regard to such a high priority aspect of 
our socio-economic development. It, therefore, recommends that family welfare units 
provided in the Central Government hospitals be strengthened and activated immediately. 
(Para 12) 
10. Campaign against AIDS 
The Central Government hospitals, which are supposed to be role models in campaign 
against AIDS, do not appear to be serious about in. The Committee, therefore, feels that 
the Central Government hospitals should launch massive· campaign against the spread of this 
deadly disease. (Para 13) 
11. Establishing ·an epilepsy Centre 
Epilepsy in our country is being treated in Neurological centres of the major hospitals 
where the •facilities available for its treatment are inefficient and unorganised. The 
Committee feels that there is an imperative · need to establish an Epilepsy centre, to begin 
with, in New Delhi. Once this centre is developed, similar centres, either separate or 
branches thereof, should be set up in other parts of the country. (Para 14.1) 
12. Exposure of Doctors to latest Development 
With the advancement of medical science and technology, there is an urgent need for 
doctors/professors to keep pace with the latest medical innovations so as to pass on the 
benefit of these advancements to patient care. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Doctors and Faculty Members should be provided with adequate opportunities to 
undergo training, and refresher courses, from time to time, to improve the quality of 
services. Simultaneously, the technicians/para medical staff handling various sophisticated 
and modern medical equipments should also be given requisite training to facilitate efficient 
handling of these equipruents and bring precision in their work. (Para 15)

Cleanliness and hygienic conditions in various hospitals are of very poor standJr d. 
Choked sewage leaking water pipes, stinking toilets and heaps of garbage lying uncovered in 
various comers of the hospitals could be seen almost in every hospital. The Committee is 
deeply distressed to see such unhygienic conditions and the hospital authorities paying scant 
attention to such an important aspect of medical care. The hospital buildings, including the 
Operation Theatres and the wards, are no better in their upkeep and maintenance. (Para 16) 
One of the reasons cited for this state of affairs is that the CPWD, which is primarily 
responsible for the maintenance of the buildings, is not giving prompt and efficient services 
and they are also not under the direct administrative control of the hospital authorities. The 
hospitals should, therefore, either have their own engineering departments or the CPWD 
unit should be put under the direct administrative control of the respective Medical 
Superintendents to control and supervise the maintenance work. (Pa_ra 16.1) 
14. Shortage of Staff 
The shortage of staff particularly in Group 'C' and 'D' categories, in almost all the 
hospitals has been observed by the Committee. Similar was the position for many posts of 
faculty members and senior doctors which were lying vacant for years together. The problem 
was more prominent in JIPMER, Pondicherry, where no one is willing to go because of the 
distance factor. Similarly, in AIIPMER, Bombay, doctors are reluctant to join mainly 
because of acute shortage of residential accommodation. Unattractive pay-scales have also 
been cited as another reason for doctors not joining the Government institutes. Further, 
while the number of doctors over a period of time, has increased manifold, there is no 
corresponding increase in the staff of Group 'C' and 'D' categories. (Para 17) 
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that shortage of staff in Group 'C' and 
'D' categories should be immediately made good and procedure of filling the higher level 
posts should be reviewed and streamlined to avoid delays in recruitments. (Para 17.2) 
15. Doctors on Prolonged Deputation 
The Committee deprecates the practice of doctonvprofessors going on deputation and 
coming back at the time of promotions, which is against the very ethics of medical 
profession. It, therefore, recommends that the Department should take a serious view in 
these cases and discourage such practices. (Para 18) 
16. Indiscipline in Hospitals 
Complaints of rude behaviour by Doctors and other staff in hospitals are a common 
feature. There is no cordial relationship between the hospital administration and the 
employees either. Irresponsible unionism is very much rampant amongst the employees, 
culminating, quite often, in 'Bandhs' and 'Strikes'. There is no effective grievance redressal 
machinery in the hospitals. While the genuine grievances of the employees should be 
redressed promptly, through the medium of JCMs or other grievance redressal machineries, 
indiscipline resulting in chaotic situations, causing inconvenience to patients, should be 
firmly dealt with. It would be useful to set up a mechanism similar to the JCM in 
Government establishm~nts, in each hospital to redress the grievances of the staff . The role 
and functions of hospital Management Boards ~!so need to be redefined in order to improve 
the effectiveness and cred:bility of these Boards. The services of outside experts in these 
Boards may also be utilised to improve the state of affairs. (Para 19)

17. Lack of Residential Accommodation 
Doctors and nurses are responsible for running the patient care services round the clock 
and are required to come to hospitals at odd hours at short notice. In case they are provided 
residential accommodation nearer the hospitals they would be able to discharge their duties 
more efficiently and promptly. The Committee; therefore, recommends that sufficient 
number of residential units for all categories of employees be provided in the hospital pools 
and the Department should also take up the matter with the Ministry of Urban Affairs and 
Employment to get adequate number of quarters earmarked for the hospital functionaries in 
the nearby Government colonies. There is also a strong-felt need to provide adequate 
hospital accommodation to the resident doctors and nurses, preferably within the campus of 
the hospital itself. Nurses should also be given priority in the Working Women's Hostels 
situated near the hospitals. (Para 20.4) 
The Committee is happy to learn that there is a proposal to construct Delhi Nurses 
Colony in Srinivaspuri for which the possession of land has been taken. There are proposals 
in hand to acquire two acres of land in Rohini. The Committee is, however, distressed to 
note ·that funds for the purpose were not provided by the Ministry of Finance last year and 
recommends that sufficient funds be allocated for this purpose. The Ministry of Health may 
also vigorously pursue the matter of allocation of land at suitable si..:es with the D.D.A. and 
N.O.I.D.A. for construction of residential quarters for the hospital employees. (Paras 20.1 
& 20.3) 
18. Separate CGHS Wings 
The CGHS Wings, presently earmarked and functioning in Safdarjung and Dr. Ram 
Manohar Lohia Hospitals, are not geared enough to cope with the needs of the CGHS 
beneficiaries. At times, the time taken in the CGHS wings is more than the time taken in 
the general OPD's. It is, therefore, recommeded that the procedures for consultation/tests 
etc. in the CGHS wings of the hospitals need to be thoroughly streamlined so as to provide 
prompt and efficient services. (Para 21) 
19. Senior Citizens 
There should be special arrangements in the hospitals for the senior citizens and the 
retired CGHS beneficiaries keeping in view their old age problems. (Para 22) 
20. Geriatrics 
'The Committee recommends that Government should take necessary steps to develop 
geriatrics as specialised subject, and provide sufficient number of specialists and 
infrastructure for opening Geriatric Clinics in all the Central Government hospitals. 
(Para 23) 
21. Provision for Poor Patients 
The Committee has noted that several major invasive procedures, e.g. cardiac surgery 
are far too expensive for the poor people. Therefore, it would suggest the Ministry must 
urgently explore all appropriate sources of funds to assist poor patients coming to AIIMS or 
other Central Government hospitals for specific life threatening illnesses. If a mechanism can 
be set up, such as a National Catastrophic lllness Assistance Fund, then resources can flow 
from all sources, induding private charities and international agencies and organisation. 
Besides, there can be many imaginative methods of requiring both government and private

should explore the possibilities of generating-Sparing more resources for allocation to this

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. The Department of Women and Child Development is engaged in the welfare and
development of Women and Children. The Department is responsible for sefeguarding
certain provisions of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy with
reference to Women and Children.

1.2. The Department in its nodal capacity formulates plans, policies and programmes;
enacts/amends legislations; guides and coordinates the efforts of both Governmental and
non-Governmental organisations working in the field of Women and Child Development.
For a holistic child development, the Department implements the widely acclaimed
programme of Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS). The ICDS provides an
integrated package of services comprising supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health
check-up and pre-school and non-formal education and health and nutrition education for
women.

1.3. The other major schemes implemented by the department includes funding of
Hostels for working women, Support, Training and Employment Programme, scheme of
Training-cum-employment-cum Production Centres (NORAD), Socio-Economic Programme,
the programme of condensed courses of education and vocational training etc. Most of the
programmes of the Department are run through non-Governmental organisations.

1.4. The new policy initiatives taken up by the Department, are setting-up of the
Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, adoption of National Nutrition Policy, setting up of National Creche
Fund and Mahila Samriddhi Yojana and launching the Indira Mahila Yojana. The
Department also propose to launch a comprehensive National Policy for the empowerment
of women.

1.5. The total 8th Plan outlay made for the Department was Rs. 2010 crores. The
foreign aid component during the 8th Plan period upto 1996-97 is about Rs. 556 crores, and
the total expenditure incurred during the period of 1992—96 by the Department is Rs.
2530.41 crores. However, there are certain schemes started in the middle of the 8th Five
Year Plan, for which there was no allocation in the 8th Plan. The number of such schemes is
7 and the amount spent on them upto 1995-96 is about Rs. 153 crores out of the total
expenditure incurred.

1.8. The Committee has noticed under-utilisation of funds by some schemes during the

suffering from this malady. The 8th Plan allocation made for this scheme was Rs. 33.30

more such schemes which are also suffering from this malady. Even though they are all
smaller schemes, their performance cannot just be ignored. These schemes are dealt
separately in this report later.

1.9. The Committee takes a serious note of under-utilisation of scarce resources placed
at the disposal of the Department and impresses upon the need for proper monitoring of the
schemes both by the Central and State Governments in future and ensuring effective
implementation.

1.10. The Committee has noticed proliferation of a number of schemes having identical
activities and objectives. Such a fragmented and un-organised approach results in waste of
scarce resources. The Committee with this view in mind, recommended last year for
revamping and rationalising of schemes by concentrating on important and meaningful
schemes. On this, the Department stated that three schemes namely, the Integrated
Education in Nutrition (JEN), Mass Media Communication (MMC) and Strengthening of
Community Food & Nutrition Extension Units (CFNEU) of Food and Nutrition Board
(FNB) were suggested for amalgamation in the 1996-97 Annual Plan proposals. The
Planning Commission has, however, suggested that these amalgamations may be given effect
from the Ninth Five Year Plan i.e. from 1997-98, the Department added. The Schemes of
Balwadi Nutrition Programme (BNP) and Early Childhood Education (ECE) which have
been non-expanding, are to be phased out and merged into Integrated Child Development
Services when the out-reach of this programme is extended to their areas. The Department
also stated that the Schemes of ‘Short Stay Homes for Women and Girls’ and ‘Education
work for the Prevention of Atrocities against Women’ are to be transferred/shifted to
Central Social Welfare Board beginning from 1997-98 as suggested by the Planning
Commission. The Committee, however, feels that the Early Childhood Education Scheme is
a good scheme and is also utilising the funds fully well. This may not, therefore, be merged.
The Balwadi Nutrition Programme is not utilising the funds fully. This scheme may,
therefore, be looked into. The Committee also feels that immediate steps are required to be
taken to review and revamp all the schemes.

1.11. The Committee observes that the Schemes funded by the Central Government are
not properly and effectively implemented by the States. The State Governments are not
showing much interest in the schemes. The Committee, therefore, desires that the
Department should strengthen its monitoring mechanism and should ensure effective
implementation of the schemes by the States. This is all the more necessary in view of the
