SUMMARY OF OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF 34TH REPORT

1. The Committee feels that it should be our objective to see that every child takes part
in sports and games, and that every parent encourages the child to do so. It should also be
our endeavour to see that as children grow, they do not lose their enthusiasm for sports, nor
do the pressure of studies towards a bright career diminish their interest for participating in
sports and games. (para 31)

2. Our performance in creating a conducive environment for sports should also ensure
that boys and girls with high potential are encouraged to remain active in sports through a
system which offers them due scial recognition and encouragement, as well as financial
benefit. This is very essential, if we are to become competitive internationally as a nation.
(para 31)

3. The Committee emphasises that physical education and sports should be made an
essential and integral part of educational activity in schools and colleges. There is need for
reducing academic burden on the children, particularly at the primary stage, so that they
could spare enough time for sports. (paras 33 & 34)

4. Ideally all the schools and colleges must have physical education teachers/coaches.
Until it is possible, physical education teachers may be provided in each secondary school
and one in a group of primary schools. The Committee feels that unless some financial
support is provided to the schools and colleges specifically for this purpose and for purchase
of simple and basic sports equipments and consumable sports items, this objective would not
be achieved. (para 34)

5. There is also a need to develop at least one sports school, preferably residential, in
each district with the requisite playing facilities and equipments. These schools could
ultimately be developed as Centres of excellence in sports, on the same pattern as is being
done by China and East European countries. (para 35)

6. The University Grants Commission should identify a few colleges, preferably physical
education colleges, which, in addition to giving theoretical knowledge, should encourage
their students to participate in performance sports. The Government should also seriously
think of establishing a sports university to which all the colleges of physical education could
be affiliated. (para 36)

7. The Committee strongly recommends that the functioning of the association of Indian
Universities should be revamped to increase sports activities in the universities and
improving thereby their contribution to sports. The Inter-University Sports Board, which
existed before the Independence, should be revived, so as to supervise sports activities in
our universities and their affiliated colleges. (para 37)

8. Coupled with the absence of sports consciousness and culture in the country, there is
almost total lack of sports infrastructure at the grassroot level all over the country. The
Committee found that the infrastructure, so far created, is mainly confined to the metro
cities, big industrial townships, defence cantonments, etc. and caters to the needs of people
living in the urban areas, whereas 80 per cent of the population, which lives in the villages

10


18

and small towns, is generally deprived of this benefit. The tribal and rural areas, with their
age-old games, are devoid of any sports infrastructure worth the name. (paras 39 & 40)

9. One of the reasons cited for the lack of sports infrastructure in the country is the
non-availability of sufficient funds for the promotion of sports. The amount provided for
sports in the Central Government is less than 0.0001 per cent of the Government’s total
budget. Even taking into consideration the States’ provisions for sports, the percentage of
allocation does not improve either, which shows that sports is not a priority area. (para 41)

10. The Committee feels that Government should plan the development of sports in a
phased manner so that necessary infrastructure is built up over a period of time and scarce
resources earmarked for the purpose are optimally utilised. (para 42)

11. The Committee feels that, as far as possible, there should be a condition regarding
provision of a playfield while granting permission for opening a school or college in rural, as
well as urban areas. Where, however, it is not possible to have a separate playfield in the
urban areas for want of space, a group of schools/colleges could be allowed to use a
cominon playfield at different timings. Surplus land available with different Ministries,
including Railways, Defence, Civil Aviation and Tourism, etc. should be allowed to be used
as playfields. All the Municipal Corporations, Cantonment Boards and Development
Authorities should also be directed to ban the use of playfields for any other purposes.
(para 43)

12. The Committee, while visiting the Regional Centres of Sports Authority of India,
LNCPEs, NIS and the important stadia/sports complexes, found it distressing that barring
the Bangalore, Calcutta and Gandhinagar Regional Centres, the condition of most of the
sports complexes/stadia was far from satisfactory. (para 45)

13. The Committee recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports
should work out a proper plan and schedule for maintenance of these buildings/stadia
constructed at a huge cost. The Department should also introduce a system of regular
monitoring and inspection of these buildings by senior officials so as to ensure their proper
maintenance and upkeep. (para 48)

14. The Committee, during its visit to Lakshmibai National College of Physical
Education, Gwalior, noted that even though it has been made a deemed university, no
Director has been appointed for the Institute so far. The Committee desires that the
Director be appointed to the Institute expeditiously. (para 52)

15. The Government has erected huge and massive sports infrastructure in the metro
cities and big towns. These structures are used only when national or international
tournaments take place. For the rest of the period, they are just lying idle or under-utilised.
Some of them are rented out for cultural programmes and other shows. There is a problem
of their maintenance as well. A plan should be drawn up for utilisation of the infrastructure.
(para 53)

16. The Committee feels that instead of organising the games at the State capitals, many
of the games could be held in other places in the State so that the sports infrastructure is not
concentrated in one particular area. (para 55)

17. Several cases of indisciplined behaviour of many of our sportspersons are reported,
quite often, in the press. Coaches and Managers are scared of reporting against them
because of various reasons. The Committee is of the firm view that the country can ill-afford
to take lightly the instances of indiscipline and lack of sportsmanship, particularly from


12

persons representing the country in international arena. The authorities, the Committee feels,
have to be firm and strict in handling the instances of indiscipline amongst sportspersons and
ensure that such people do not find place in the Indian contingents going abroad for
international tournaments. (paras 58 & 60)

18. The Committee feels that if we really want to promote sports in the country we will
have to make available adequate incentives, good job opportunities and recognition of talent
and achievements. At present, there are very few incentives/rewards for our talented and
outstanding sportspersons. The Central Government, the State Governments and the public
sector undertakings do not offer good job opportunities for our sportspersons. (paras 61 & 62)

19. The Committee feels that there is an urgent need for fixing a percentage of jobs in
each and every organisation for sportspersons. This would definitely prove to be a strong
incentive to take sports as a career, provided all the orgnisations like Banks, Railways,
Airlines, public sector undertakings, etc. meticulously implement the scheme of employment
of sportspersons under this category. At present, there is no mechanism to monitor this aspect
by the Government. (para 63)

20. The Committee feels that in schools and colleges students, who perform well in
sports, may be given some percentage of grace marks in each subject. Similarly, certain
percentage of seats for admission in colleges should be reserved for students who have
excelled in sports. (para 64)

21. The Committee desires that, as an incentive, sportspersons who have participated in
the state, national and international events should be allotted houses or plots by Housing
Boards and Urban Development Authorities on priority basis and at concessional rates. They
may also be given house building loans by Banks and other financial institutions at low
interest. Eminent sportspersons, who, after retirement, intend to start their own industry/
business etc. may be given licenses for the purpose, alongwith bank loans and land, if
necessary. (para 65)

22. The Committee was shocked to learn that till March 1995, only 25 persons were
recruited as sportspersons in the 25 Ministries/Departments of the Government of India
(except in Railways and Defence) and that too in the Group ‘C’ category. (para 67)

23. The Committee feels that there is a lack of will and determination also in
implementing the existing guidelines in employing sportspersons by the government. There is
no provision for promotion of outstanding sportspersons or giving them adequate cash awards
after they win medals and bring laurels to the country. (para 69)

24. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the government should have (i) a
definite policy for recruiting sportspersons in various Ministries/Departments and public
sector undertakings; (ii) effective monitoring to get regular feedback and to ensure proper
implementation of the provisions of the policy, which is virtually non-existent as on date; (iii)
the Department of Sports and Youth Affairs should act as a nodal agency for this purpose;
(iv) the government should also issue clear-cut guidelines to the Union Public Service
Commission for recruiting sportspersons in Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ services also as there are many
sportspersons of international standard having adequate educational qualifications for these
categories of posts. (para 70)

25. The Committee does realise the sportspersons’ concern about not getting adequate
time for practice due to pressure of work in their jobs. In such a situation, the Committee
feels, it is the duty, both of the sportspersons and their employers, to give top most priority to
sports so long as the person is in full form and is in a position to win medals. (para 71)


13

26. The Committee notes that the existing cash awards system is not adequate to give
the much-needed financial support to sportspersons; and that cash awards for juniors and
seniors are highly disproportionate; and that for some sports these are incredibly higher.
(para 72)

27. The amount of cash awards and pension being given to sportspersons by. the
government should be increased substantially so as to make sports more attractive and
lucrative. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Railways and the airlines
operating in the country, both private and the government, should provide free/concessional
tickets to eminent sportspersons. (paras 73 & 75)

28. The Committee also recommends that certain categories of sportspersons should be
given preference in the allotment of soft loans by the banks, petrol and LP gas agencies and
other such incentives/benefits by the government. (para. 76)

29. The Committee recommends that one of the outstanding sportspersons may be
nominated to the Rajya Sabha in recognition of his/her distinguished service to the country.
(para 77)

30. The Committee suggests that the government should ensure that no player or team
is sent abroad for participation in international tournaments unless they are accompanied by
qualified sports medicine doctors alongwith the necessary kits and other aids. (para 78)

31. The Committee was informed that, in some cases, the government is paying only
90% of the fare and the remaining 10% is to be borne by the player himself or herself. The
government should investigate as to why part payment of air fare is being made to players
attending international meets and ensure that such a thing is not repeated in future. (paras
79 & 80)

32. The Committee is of the opinion that training forms the core of good performance
and champions cannot be produced by training the sportspersons just for a few months
before the games. The training system in the country, the Committee feels, leaves much to
be desired. Sports training has to be properly planned and controlled for achieving the best
results. (para 81)

33. The Committee feels that kits should be provided to players and teams well in
advance before they leave for international meets. (para 82)

34. Efforts should be made to ensure that the diet available to sportsmen and women
has the nutritional value necessary to meet the specific requirements of different games and
sports in which they participate. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the government
should immediately raise the amount of diet allowance substantially so that players can get a
rich and nutritious diet. (paras 83 & 84)

35. The Government should evolve a system of proper monitoring and evaluation of the
performance of SAI coaches deployed at various places. Coaches who work hard and show
good results should be suitably rewarded. Simultaneously, those who do not take interest in
sports or fail to give any tangible results need to be dealt with sternly. (para 86)

36. The Committee feels that once a good rapport is established between the coach and
the students, it would not be advisable to disturb such coaches in the overall interest of the
students and the sports. (para 87)

37. Outstanding sportspersons who have represented the country in the international
games and have now retired from active sports, can work as good coaches. The Committee


14

feels that services of such sportspersons would be both beneficial and economical aud it
would also give them the much needed financial help and recognition of their talent. The
Committee desires that this system could be initially tried on an experimental basis which
could be subsequently extended or discontinued depending upon the results. (para 88)

38. The Committee suggests that either the entire control of the SAI coaches should be
given to the state governments who have comparatively better mechanism for their close
monitoring or they may be completely withdrawn. The state governments should be given
full authority for all the service matters of SAI coaches, including their postings and
transfers. (para 89)

39. One of the problems raised by the coaches deployed in the schools was that they did
not have accommodation either in the school premises or anywhere near the school. The
Committee feels that it is a genuine problem which needs to be looked into sympathetically
and government should try to give residential accommodation to these coaches either in the
school premises itself, or just near to their working place so that they could reach the ground
early in the morning. (para 90)

40. The Committee emphasises the need for continuous skill development and
orientation of coaches in view of the rapid changes in the techniques of various games. The
Committee desires that the SAI should identify certain specialised training institutes in
various sports disciplines, both within the country and abroad, so that our coaches could be
deputed for refresher training courses from time to time to upgrade their skills. The
Committee came to know that, at present, there was no policy with regard to training of the
coaches and that only a handful of coaches were repeatedly being sent for foreign exposure.
The Committee expresses its unhappiness over such a state of affairs and recommends that a
uniform policy be evolved for training the coaches without any discrimination. (para 91)

41. The Committee strongly recommends that the practice of making frequent changes
of coaches be avoided and whenever any team or player performs well, the credit should
also be given to the coaches who are basically responsible for their training. (para 92)

42. The Committee feels that government should make arrangements to provide
personal coaches to those sportspersons who have adequate potential and hope of winning
medals at international level. These personal coaches should also accompany the
sportspersons whenever they go abroad to participate in international tournaments. (para 93)

43. A comprehensive plan to upgrade the skills and qualifications of technical officials,
referees and judges in the identified disciplines needs to be taken up as quickly as possible.
(para 95)

44. The various Federations/Associations in the country are alleged to be the weakest
link in the chain of sports management and their functioning has been described as
perfunctory. The selection of teams and players by them is also stated to be lopsided, based
on favouritism, nepotism and arbitrariness. There is no democratic functioning,at all in most
of them. It is also stated that huge amounts of money are spent on the election of office-
bearers. Many Federations/Associations are being headed by people who have nothing to do
with sports. (para 96)

45. Federations must hold their elections regularly and democratically. The first and the
most important task before each national federation is to mobilise its energies and efforts for
obtaining sponsorship and finanical support from various sources. (para 98)

46. It is essential that the national federations organise competitions, tournaments and


championships on a regular basis throughout the sporting season. This can be achieved by
monitoring, guiding and motivating their state/district units. (para 99)

47. The national federations are also responsible for enforcing the rules of the game and
for ensuring the officials who conduct: games, tournaments and competitions are fully
competent and fit for the purpose. The national federations should ensure that the rules
approved by the international federations to. which they are affiliated, are followed in
recognised national championships. (para 100)

48. While it will take some time for federations to become financially independent, and
to organise their work and responsibilities along structures and well regulated lines,
assistance from the Government of India for various purposes may have to continue.
However, government may impose certain conditions with regard to such matters as
democratic functioning, appointment of selection committees, dope testing, age verification
procedure, etc., as are considered necessary to protect our sportspersons from exploitation,
and also to ensure against adverse publicity in India and abroad. (para 102)

49. An important areas of resource mobilisation in which the government can help the
federations greatly is by way of transferring the remaining sum of the advertising revenues
earned by Doordarshan from showing sports programmes to the concerned federations after
deducting its costs. (para 103)

50. The Committee also feels that I.0.A. is not in a position to maintain any effective
control and effect any co-ordination with national sports. federations/associations. The
1.0.A. should reiterate to each federation the importance of making long-term development
planning and also ensuring its implementation. (para 104)

51. There is no coordination or cooperation between various agencies engaged in
promotion of sports. There is no accountability and responsibility for poor performance in
sports in international events. The Committee emphasises the need for clearly demarcating
the duties and responsibilities of each one of the agencies so that accountability could be
fixed for their lapses. (para 105)

52. It is often seen that teams are selected virtually almost on the last day and at times
had reported after the events had already started. The Committee feels that this state of
affairs is highly deplorable and has to be stopped forthwith if we really intend to achieve
medals in the international sports arena. The Committee feels that there is a need for a
long-term planning and selection of teams has to be made much in advance so that players
are aware of their selection and they could concentrate more on sports rather than running
around till the last moment for various clearances. The Committee also desires that once the
teams are selected they should be sent to places of training and also sufficiently in advance
to the venue of the event for proper exposure and acclimatisation to the foreign
environment. (paras 106 & 107)

53. The Committee suggests that each one of the sports organisations should have an
annual calendar of events giving the details of events, their venues and the dates for the
entire year. The Committee also suggests that there should be only one National Calendar of
Events of various disciplines which should be finalised after consulting different agencies
involved in its promotion. This calendar of events should be sent to the Sports Authority of
India (SAI) by the concerned sports federations for consolidation and publication. (para 109)

54. The Committee is happy to know that the sports goods industry had come a long
way in producing good quality equipments which are in great demand and that some of these
have been approved even for Olympic games. The Committee, however, feels that such


16

quality production is confined to a few games like tennis and cricket which are very costly.
India still does not produce good quality and reasonably priced sports items of common use.
The Committee is of the opinion that making sports equipment easily available, upto the
grassroot level at economical cost, is absolutely necessary which would contribute not only to
broad-basing the participation but also creating a mass sports movement in the country. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports should
have a meeting with the representatives of sports goods industry to identify their problems,
which should be sorted out in consultation with the Ministries of Commerce, Finance and
Industry. The Committee also feels that small and cottage industries involved in production
of sports goods should be encouraged so that they can sell their products to local buyers at
reasonable prices. (paras 112, 113 & 114)

55. During its visits to various places, the Committee received a number of complaints
from players and organisers of various sports events that sports, except a few like cricket,
tennis and golf, are not given adequate coverage by the government-owned electronic media,
particularly Doordarshan. (para 115)

56. The Committee is of the opinion that media, particularly Doordarshan, is a potent
and powerful instrument for popularising sports. The Committee, keeping the condition of
sports in the country in view, feels that endeavour should be made to cover live, as far as
possible, or through highlights, all the national championships at senior and junior levels.
The Committee feels that there is a need to increase the equipments and other facilities
available with Doordarshan and AIR so that they do not feel handicapped in covering
important and major sports events. The Committee also emphasises the need for improving
the quality of live coverage and commentaries. Doordarshan and AIR may also play an
effective role in projecting the techniques and style of eminent sportspersons by showing
them in slow motion on the national hook-up. There is also a need for calling eminent
sportspersons in programmes on fitness, yoga, sports and games. (para 119)

57. The Committee is concerned to learn that some of the federations/boards are giving
the telecasting/broadcasting rights to foreign media companies, which is depriving
Doordarshan of an opportunity to earn revenues for its expansion and improvement. The

- Committee notes the suggestion of Director General, Doordarshan, to have a legislation
* declaring some sports as of national importance so that national media would be bound to
cover the important events connected with them, as is being done in Britain. (para 120)

58. The Committee notice that neither the sports psychology nor the sports medicine
was being given any priority in India. The Committee feels that all the organisations working
towards promotion of sports must give due attention and priority to both these disciplines.
The Committee recommends that the services of good sports physiologists, psychologists and
sports medical experts be made available to our players on the ground. There is a need for a
more coordinated effort on the part of coaches, sports scientists and sports medicine doctors
to help sportspersons enhance their performance. Though SAI has made a beginning in this
direction, yet a lot more needs to be done. (paras 122 & 123)

59. In view of the decentralisation. of resources to panchayats, government should
ensure that there is a sports complex in each panchayat. Panchayats should also hold sports
competitions and championships periodically. There is also need for scouting talent at an
early age and select them on scientific basis because it is all the more easier to train the
young ones. Panchayat bodies should take up this responsibility. (para 124)

60. The Committee finds it disappointing that most of the state governments have not
made any concrete plans to streamline the procedure for selection of sportspersons, their


17

coaching and participation in the national events so far. Improper selection of sportspersons,
coupled with lack of modern and rigorous training, results in disastrous performance at the
international level. The Committee, therefore, emphasises the need for streamlining the
entire system of selection of sportspersons and their training so as to achieve the best results.
State governments should be asked to evolve long-term development programmes and also
match them with adequate budget. (para 126)

61. The Committee finds that so far neither the Department of Youth Affairs and
Sports nor the federations have taken any particular interest in the development of sports
among Indian women and whatever distinction women have achieved so far is largely due to
their individual efforts. (para 128)

62. The Committee feels there is a need to give good incentives in the form of cash
awards and medals so as to attract mass participation by women. Many parents would like to
send their daughters to play games but they are hesistant to do so because of security and
safety reasons. The Committee noticed that out of 18 sports hostels of SAI, there is only one
sports-hostel for women and there is no exclusive SPDA hostel for girls. Therefore, the
Committee feels, there is a need for proper planning to develop sport amongst women, by
opening more sports hostels and adopting more sports-oriented girls schools. (para 129)

63. In India, there is a club culture but it’ is restricted only to football, cricket and
wrestling. Club culture can be developed by organising inter-club competitions and by
providing patronage at different levels by government agencies as well as business
establishments. The Committee feels that the club culture needs to be encouraged right from
the panchayat level. The Committee feels that the government should probe into the
workings of the National Sports Club of India. The Committee also desires that the other
sports clubs existing in various parts of the country should throw open their facilities/
infrastructure to sportspersons on concessional basis. (para 135)

64. At present there are about 32 to 34 disciplines in sports on which the country is
spending a lot of money. The Committee feels that due to paucity of funds we should not
spread our scarce resources thinly on each one of the games and it would be desirable to
concentrate on a few selected games and try to bag medals in these games at the
international arena. (para 136) हि

65. The Committee emphasises the need for concentrating on traditional, rural and
tribal sports like kho-kho, archery and kabaddi in which India could always do better than
other countries. (para 138)

66. The Committee also feels that we should not send our teams to international sports
events in the disciplines where we do not have any chance of bagging medals. It would
perhaps be better not to participate than participating and losing in all the games, which
would have a demoralising effect. Before participating in international events, our players
should be given enough exposure at the national level, and if need be, we may invite foreign
teams to India to participate in competitions. (para 139)

67. The Committee feels that lack of funds and budgetary constraints are coming in the
way of development and promotion of sports. The amount earmarked by Government of
India for sports in 1995-96 is only Rs. 68.86 crores, which works out to 0.0001% of the total
budget of the Government. The Committee recommends that, to begin with, atleast 0.5 per
cent of the total budget should be earmarked for sports promotion. (para 144)

68. Members of Parliament are given Rs. 1 crore every year under the MPs’ Local Area
Development Scheme by the Central Government. MLAs are also given special


18

discretionary funds by the respective state governments. A suggestion has come to the
Committee that the MPs and MLAs may be requested to earmark at least one to five per
cent of this money every year for purchasing sports equipments in the schools/colleges in
their respective constituencies. (para 148)

69. The Committee feels that the Government alone cannot deliver the goods. Public
and private sectors’ involvement is necessary in supplementing the governmental efforts. The
Committee, therefore, emphasises the need for a joint and coordinated approach by all the
agencies, including public and private sectors, in pooling their resources to promote sports in
the country. This is particularly necessary in the context of financial constraints, both at the
Central and State levels. (para 149)

70. The Committee recommends that each major industrial house, both in public and
private sectors, should be asked to adopt one sports discipline and they should take the total
responsibility of scouting talent and nurturing the same, including their participation in
various national and international events. On reciprocal basis, the concerned industrial house
should have its nominee in the particular national federation/association. (para 151)

71. Representatives of industrial houses appealed for tax exemption under revenue
expenditure also for scouting talent and training the teams. Such incentives are necessary for
the continued support of industrial houses in sports. The Income-tax Act should, therefore,
be suitably amended so as to give substantial tax exemption to organisations investing in
sports. Special Customs Duty exemption for certain categories of imported sports
equipments is required to be made. Liberalised access to foreign exchange for import of
sports equipment is also called for. (paras 152 & 154)

72. There is a lot of duplication of efforts as various sports control boards, such as
Services, Railways, P & T, Banks and Para-military police forces, Steel plants, Coal-fields
etc., are contibuting in their own way for promotion of sports without any coordination
with each other. Much worse is the lack of cooperation and communication between these
bodies on the one hand and the Sports Authority of India (SAI) and the federations on the
other. The Committee is not happy with this chaotic situation and lack of coordination
among various bodies is resulting in loss of scarce resources and time. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports should take
immediate steps to develop an effective machinery for regular dialogue and coordination
with various organisations so that no effort is duplicated and wastage of time and money
could be avoided. (para 155)

73. The Committee found that very limited sports infrastructure has been provided in
the whole of the North-Eastern region. The region is also denied major sports tournaments
and championships. The Committee, therefore, recommends that governments and SAI, as
well as national sports federations, should concentrate in this sports fertile area, not only for
scouting and nurturing of potential sportspersons and providing adequate and suitable
infrastructure in this region but also for holding more and more competitions. (para 132)

74. The Committee is quite disappointed to learn that we have not been able to, till
now, identify the sportspersons who would represent India in the 1996 Olympics at Atlanta
even though only seven months are left now. The Committee strongly recommends that we
should start selecting our players/teams without further delay not only for Olympics 1996
and Asian Games 1998 but also for Olympics 2000 and prepare them scientifically with a
view to winning medals for the country. (para 156)

75. The Committee feels that unless Sports is also brought under the “Concurrent List”


19

of the Constitution, sports activities in the country cannot be uniformly regulated in an
effective and coordinated manner. (para 157)

76. The Committee also recommends thatthe government should bring forward a
Central legislation, specifying the roles and responsibilities of the SAI, federations/
associations and of the state bodies so that a uniform and common approach could ७९
adopted towards promotion of sports by different agencies. This law should also provide for
an effective regulatory mechanism in the sports arena without impairing the autonomy of
various agencies. Such legislations are already in existence in countries like USA, Germany,
Thailand, Sri Lanka and China. (para 157)

77. The Committee has come to the conclusion that the bureaucratic functioning of the
SAI is proving to be a major obstacle in the free and smooth operation of the regional
centres. The Committee feels that unless these Centres are strengthened, we cannot expect
better results from them. The SAI office in Delhi could be just a coordinating authority and
should concentrate on policy, planning and monitoring. There should be a Sub-regional
centre of SAI in each State, with a Director in charge of it. (para 162)

78. At present there are six Regional Centres at Chandigarh, Delhi, Bangalore,
Calcutta, Imphal and Gandhinagar. The Central Region, which is at present located in
Delhi, should be shifted to Lucknow, as originally contemplated. The North-Eastern region,
comprising eight States including Sikkim, should have two centres, one located at Imphal
and the other at Guwahati/Shillong. The Committee desires that each one of the Regional
Centres should be headed by a Regional Director, with almost full powers. Two Executive
Directors in Delhi could look after the administrative and coordinating works of the
organisation, as well as matters relating to teams. The Secretary, Department of Youth
Affairs and Sports, should not be the Director-General of SAI. Instead, a full-time
Chairman-cum-MD, with good sports background or interest in sports, should be appointed
by the government. (para 163)

79. The SAI governing body shall consist of fifteen members, including the Chairman-
cum-MD, two Executive Directors, seven Regional Directors, on, Financial Advisor and
four non-official Members elected by the General Council. The General Council of SAI,
headed by the Minister of Human Resource Development, shall consist of the Minister of
Sports, the Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Chairman-cum-MD of
SAI, the Financial Advisor, the Executive Directors, Regional Directors and Directors of
SAI sub-centres, representatives of the State Sports Authorities / Sports Council, Joint
Secretary in the Ministry of HRD, five Arjuna Awardees / Olympians, three coaches,
Secretary-General, IOA, five representatives of national sports federations, two
representatives of public sector sports control boards, five sports experts such as sports
journalists and commentators and three Members of Parliament. The number shall not
exceed 100. (para 163)

80. The Committee feels that the National Sports Talent Contest Scheme appears to be
very sound, reaching upto the village or panchayat level. However, in actual practice, it has
achieved very limited results. After ten years of its implementation, the scheme has thrown
up very few outstanding sportspersons. The scheme is now operated only in 44 scheols in the
country. SAI and State Governments do not seem to be paying attention to give adequate
publicity to it.

The Committee, therefore, feels that a wide publicity campaign should be launched
through mass media / local newspapers and also through locally elected bodies, well before
the selection process starts. ‘The Committee also expresses its concern over the
implementation aspect of the scheme, which is fraught with various flaws and loopholes. The
Sports Authority of India should periodically monitor the functioning of each school and also

/


insist on improving the sports infrastructure and boarding / lodging facilities. The
Committee finds that no serious thoughtehas been given to the number of schools to be
adopted which is borne out by the fact that the number of schools adopted is not
commensurate with the number of children selected. Henceforth, preference should be given
under NSTC Scheme to Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodaya Vidyalayas, Sainik Schools and
government boys / girls schools. (paras 169, 170, 171, 172 & 176)

81. Out of 78 SPDA Centres proposed to be set up, only 33 centres have started
functioning so far. The Committee expresses its displeasure over such a tardy progress of the
scheme and strongly urges upon the central as well as the state governments to work in close
tandem with each other in the larger interest of development of sports. As regards the
suggestion of the Tata Consultancy Services to phase out the SPDA scheme, the Committee
is of the view that it is not based on a sound proposition. To wind up the scheme simply on
the pretext of States’ failure is not sound. The SPDA centres should be converted into SAI
Sub-regional Centres in course of time, with additional inputs. (paras 182 & 190)

82. Although the Committee expresses its overall satisfaction with the functioning and
performance of the Special Area Games Scheme as far as archery, hockey and watersports
are concerned, it is constrained to observe that the achievements in other disciplines,
particularly gymnastics and athletics, have not been upto the mark. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that based on the population / concentration of tribal and other
communities, government should try to expand this scheme in the rural and tribal areas and
take all necessary measures to streamline and revamp the scheme. (paras 191 & 192)

83. The Committee recommends that government should review the National Coaching
Scheme to set right shortcomings and streamline the functioning of the scheme at the
earliest. The concept of sports hostel should be reoriented and focussed towards
achievement of excellence at the international level. (para 196)

84. The Committee is also of the view that it is imperative to prioritise disciplines for
sports hostel scheme and select only those games in which India has the potentiality of
achieving results in the international arena. (para 201)

85. The Committee found that the Army Boys Sports Company Scheme is functioning
very efficiently because the overall atmosphere of discipline in the Regimental Centres is
quite conducive for the development of sporting skills amongst children. The Committee is
of the opinion that the amount of Rs. 35 being given for diet per head under this scheme is
quite inadequate and should be increased substantially. During the course of their
interaction with the Committee, representatives of the Services Sports Control Board
expressed a desire to have one school in each Regiment. SAI may have to enlarge the
scheme, accordingly as it is likely to pay better dividends. The Committee recommends that
apart from extending the scheme to other regiments of the army, the scheme should be
extended to the central para-military forces also who are keen to run schools on the same
lines as by army regiments. (paras 203, 204 & 205)

Human Resource Development visited the Indian Museum, Calcutta on 9th October 1996 to
make an on the spot Study and get first hand information about the functioning of the
Indian Museum. A list of Members who visited the Indian Museum Calcutta is enclosed as

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. The Museum, the oldest institution of its kind in Asia was founded in 1814. At
present, it comprises six sections such as Art, Archaeology, Anthropology, Geology,
Zoology and Economic Botany with a number of galleries under each section. Many rare
and unique specimens both Indian and Trans-Indian relating to Humanities and Natural
Seciences are preserved and displayed in the galleries of these sections.

1.2. The Parliamentary Standing Committee was shown to round the Museum many
rare objects of art collection made over the years. The rich repository of,cultural and natural
heritage make the museum responsible to the society to exhibit its wealth from time to time
through various exhibitions for the enjoyment and dissemination of knowledge to the people.

1.3. The Parliamentary Committee was also taken to visit the galleries of the Museum
of its select treasures of antiquities and art objects acquired over a long span of years
between 1836 to 1993. The relic containers of the lord ‘Buddha’ carved in stone and crystal
unearthed at the ancient site of belonging to the Mughal emperors; gold coins issued by
Kanishka, Samudragupta, Kumaragupta-I, Akbar and Jahangir—the great emperors of
India; the delicate Mughal miniatures; illustrated leaves from Shahnama, the miniatures
from Kangra valley, and the paintings by the great masters of Bengal school, viz.
Abanindranath Tagore, Nandalal, Bose and Jamini Roy were on show there.

1.4. Of the decorative art objects a Chinese cup carved in rhino horn, ‘Burmese silver
bowl, Japanese musical instrument, Nepalese lamp-stands and a copper gift umbrella
donated by a ‘Burmese monk to the temple of ‘Bodhgaya are added attractions of this
Museum. Besides, a valuable socio-economic document inscribed on a small piece of stone
from Mahasthangarh, Bangladesh, supposed to be the royal communique of a benevolent
ruler, a hubble bubble in silver filigree—a Orissan craftsmanship, a Tibetan eleven headed
and thousand armed icon of Avalokitesvara as well as the decorative ceramic pots from
Bombay, Jaipur, Multan and Madras adorn this Museum.

1.5. Assembled together from the vast treasures of its Art, Archaelogy and Anthropo-
logy Section the exhibits—a visual feast to the eyes of the art-lovers and connoisseurs, offer
a rare glimpse of the Museum’s exquisite collection acquired through sustained efforts over
the past one hundred and eighty years.

1.6. The Museum Directorate has eight co-ordinating service units such as Education,
Preservation, Publication, Presentation, Photography Medical, Modelling and Library. These
programmes should be intensified and expanded and adequate budget provisions must be
made for this purpose.

II. EXHIBITION OF ART OBJECTS IN ROTATION

2.1. During the visit of the Museum the Committee was informed that only 10 precent
of the vast treasures of its antiquities and art objects have been exhibited presently due to
lack of space. As per norms 40 per cent antiquities and art objects are required to be
exhibited. The Committee, was however, given to understand that there are large number of
art objects which are unique and rare lying in the godowns of the Museum located in the

1

980/ RS/F—3-A


2

basement for want of space. The Committee feels that unless these rare pieces of collection
are properly taken care of and preserved, they may wear out with the passage of time.

2.2. The Committee, therefore, recommends that these objects should be properly
preserved and exhibited in the Museum by rotation so that the life span of these valuable
antiquities and art objects could be enhanced. The Committee also recommends that the
space occupied by the Zoological Survey of India, Botanical Survey of India and
Anthropological Survey of India in the building of Museum should be got vacated, so that
the space meant for Museum could be utilised for the exhibition of the antiquities and art
objects acquired over a long span of time. Even after the vacation of the space by these
Departments if the space is not found to be adequate to display at least 40 per cent of the
collections, then the Government should consider construction of a new building so as to
accommodate the display of at least 40 per cent of the collections available with the
Museum. For the vacating Departments, 1.6. Zoological Survey of India, Botanical Survey of
India and Anthropological Survey of India, some building will have to be constructed to
accommodate them according to their requirement.

Ill. STRENGTHENING OF SECURITY ARRANGEMENT

3. During Committee’s visit to the Museum, the Committee was informed that the
security system of the Museum was periodically examined and up dated with the
introduction of some new measures and revamping of the old systems. On the recommenda-
tion of a high power security committee and intelligence department the entry and exist
points of the galleries were minimised. Vehicular traffic was restricted within the campus and
loopholes at all vulnerable points were plugged. Further, the Museum has, of late,
introduced walkie — talkie system and effective illumination of peripheral areas of the
museum complex as well as replacement of fire extinguishing apparatus in order to
strengthen the security and safety of exhibits. However, the Committee feels that the
security arrangements at the-Museum should be reviewed from time to time and adequate
number of fire extinguisheres may also be provided to take care of any untoward incidents.
The Government should consider installation of close circut T.Vs. at tht appropriate places
inside the premises of the Museum keeping in view the importance of the valuable art
objects displayed in the Museum.

IV. INTERNATIONAL EXHIBITION

4.1 The Committee was also informed that the Museum participates in International
Exhibitions form time to time. Recently the Museum participated in two international
exhibitions in the U.S.A. and Japan. The exhibits were taken from the collection of the
Museum. Two Jaina images carved in stone and bronze were sent to Los Angeles in
connection with the exhibition.

4.2 The Committee is happy to note that such International exhibitions serve as vehicles
for disseminating Indian Culture abroad. However, the Committee is of the opinion that the
various invaluable exhibits of bronze and silver idols which are taken abroad for exhibitions
in their original form invites security and safety risks. This practice should be discouraged
keeping in view the security and safety hazards involved in their transit and transportation.
The Committee feels that only the replicas of such idols should be allowed to be carried out
abroad for exhibitions.


9. INSTALLATION OF AUDIO VISUAL AIDES

5. The Committee notes that in many Museums the world over, particularly in the
advanced countries, there is a system of providing Audio and Visual programmes in each
section of the Museum explaining about the art objects kept in that Section. The Committee
desires that the Govt. may examine the feasibility of introducing the similar system in the
Indian Museum also.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human 
Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, do hereby present this Fifth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants of the 
Department of Education, Ministry of Human Resource Development for the year, 1994-95. 
At its meeting held on 3rd March, 1994 the Committee decided to take up for consideration 
the Demands for Grants relating to the Department of Education , Ministry of Human Resource 
Development (Demand No. 47). 
The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the 
Deptt. of Education; Ministry of Human Resource Development and also heard the Secretary 
(Education) and other Officials of that Deptt. on the said Demands for Grants in its meeting held 
on 23rd & 24th March, 1994. 
The Committee considered the Draft Report in its sittings held on 29th and 31st March, 1994 
and adopted the same on 31st March, 1994.

AN OVERVIEW 
The Ministry of Human Resource Development was set up in 1985 with the objective of 
integrating efforts towards the development of human potential in the areas of Education, 
Women & Child Development, Art, Culture, Youth Affairs & Sports. The Department of 
Education is an important constituent of this Ministry. During 1993-94 a budget provision of 
Rs. 2159.33 crores was made available for education in the Central Sector. This was increased to 
Rs. 2192 crores in the Revised Estimate 1993-94. 
2. There are a large number of subordinate offices and autonomous organisations under the 
Department which are engaged in carrying out the activities and programmes of the Department. 
They include, among others, the Directorate of Adult Education, National Council of 
Educational Research & Training (NCERT), National Institute of Educational Planning & 
Administration (NIEPA), University Grants Commission (UGC), Indian Council of Social 
Science Research (ICSSR), Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS), the Navodaya Vidyalaya 
Samiti (NVS), the Central Board of Secondary Education, the National Book Trust, Indian 
Institutes of Technology and Regional Engineering Colleges. 
3. The National Policy on Education, 1986 has been instrumental in laying down the 
priorities in education at the national level. Elementary Education has been getting the highest 
priority in the educational sector, to accelerate the pace for achieving Universal Elementary 
Education by the end of this Century. The Operation Black Board scheme, launched in 1987-88, 
aims at bringing about significant improvement in the provision of facilities in primary schools. 
This is expected to improve retention of children in primary schools. 
4. The programme of Non-Formal Education aims at bringing education to working children, 
girls and children living in habitations which are not covered by formal schools. NFE is envisaged 
as an alternative strategy for formal education and plays a complementary role in achieving 
Universal Elementary Education by covering drop-outs or those who have not enrolled for one 
reason or the another. 
5. The Adult Education programme provides basic functional educational skills for those who 
could not avail the opportunities for education through formal and non-formal schools. The 
Technology Mission for Literacy, set up in 1988 with the aim of covering the total area, has 
achieved success in the southern, eastern and western regions and the focus has now shifted to 
the Hindi speaking States which have a low percentage of literacy. 
6. The Department is giving serious attention to achieving Education for All, and its 
endeavours towards this end found mention during the "Education for All Summit" of 9 populous 
countries of the world, held in 'New Delhi' in December, 1993. As a result of these endeavours, 
the resource allocation to education is expected to be increased from the existing 3.2% to 6% of 
the GNP from the 9th Plan. 
7. In the school education field, there are 796 Kendriya Vidyalayas, including three 
Vidyalayas in foreign countries. These are opened in areas with a sizeable concentration of 
Central Government employees. 
8. The Navodaya Vidyalayas scheme, launched in 1985, provides good quality education to 
talented children predominantly from rural areas. There are 321 Schools which are residential and 
offer education free of charge for all students. 
9. In the area of Vocational Education, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme was started in 1988 
with the main objective of providing diversification of educational opportunities to enhance 
individual employability. Vocational courses, mainly in the areas of Agriculture, Business & 
Commerce, Engineering & Technology, Health and Para Medical, Humanities and Home 
Science, are introduced at the +2 level in schools selected by the State Governments. So far, 

Vocational Sections have been sanctioned in 5,588 schools creating a capacity for diversification 
of 7.96 lakh students. 
10. The scheme of pre-vocational education has also been launched at the lower secondary 
stage in 1993-94 with the objective of imparting simple marketable skills to students in classes IX 
and X. 
11. The Department of Education has been seeking bilateral and multilateral assistance from 
international agencies so that additional resources may be available for educational programmes. 
Some new projects have been started in the last few years such as Mahila Samakhya Project in 
four States with the assistance of Netherlands; Andhra Pradesh Primary School Project with UK 
assistance; Lok Jumbish Project in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA; Shiksha Karmi Project 
in Rajasthan with the assistance of SIDA and Bihar Education Project with UNICEF assistance. 
12. In the Higher Education Sector, the University Grants Commission is concerned with 
promotion and coordination of university education and determination and maintenance of 
standards of teaching, examination and research in universities. The total number of Universities 
in 1993-94 was 189 with 7938 Colleges and a student enrolment of 48.05 Jakhs. A new Central 
University is also being set up in Tezpur to increase the facilities for higher education in the 
North-Eastern Region. 
13. In the Technical Education field, 5 Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) have been 
established to provide instruction and research in some branches of Engineering and Technology, 
Science and Arts for advancement of learning. These Institutes are imparting education at the 
undergraduate, postgraduate and research level, in addition to sponsoring research and they are 
fully funded by the Central Government. One more liT is proposed to be set up in Assam. 
14. The Regional Engineering Colleges have been set up to enable the country to meet the 
growing requirement of trained technical manpower. There are 17 Regional Engineering Colleges 
which offer First Degree Programmes in Engineering and Technology, out of which 14 have 
facilities for postgraduate and Doctoral programmes and also conduct research. 
REPORT 
15. Human Resource Development is of paramount importance for the progress of the 
country and education is one of the most important components in this regard. Though we are 
committed to achieve the objective of Education for All (EFA) by 2000 but increasing population 
and limited resources at hand are the two obstacles in the way of achieving this goal. 
16. At present, Budget outlay for Education is 3.2% of the (Gross Domestic Product) GDP 
and the Department of Education has assured that from 9th Plan onwards the outlay will be 6% 
of the GDP. 
17. The Committee welcomes the decision of the Government that Education will get an 
allocation of 6% of GDP. The Committee also hopes that there would be reflection of this decision 
in the Budget Estimates of the year 1995-96 and of subsequent years. 
18. Revised Budget Estimates for 1993-94 of the Deptt. of Education is Rs. 2192 crores. There 
has been a 10% increase in the Budget Estimates for 1994-95 over the previous year at Rs. 2423.6 
crores, out of which Rs. 1548.3 crores have been provided for planned expenditure and the rest of 
Rs. 875.3 crores is earmarked for Non-Plan expenditure. 
19. Secondary and Physical Education have been allocated 24.3% of the Budget Estimates of 
Educationl Deptt. and 24.2% of the funds of the Deptt. have been provided for University and 
Higher Education. Elementary and Technical Education have been provided 21.6% and 18% 
respectively of the funds for 1994-95. 
20. The Secretary, Deptt. of Education, in his oral evidence before the Committee has stated 

that the major thrust of the budget is on Elementary Educatiofi) with the objective of achieving 
education for all by 2000, decentralisation of educational administration and review of all these 
programmes quarterly, by a group of Chief Ministers. 
Demands for Grants (1994-95) of the Department of Education 
21. Department of Education is running about a dozen schemes, but the Committee took up 
for consideration only some of the major ones, which have been stated in brief in the following 
paragraphs, alongwith the Committee's observations/recommendations thereon. 
I 
Elementary Education 
22. Article 45 of the Constitution of India provides for free and Compulsory Education for 
all children below the age of 14 years. It was expected that by the year 1995, India would achieve 
Universal Elementary Education. However, there is still 153 million children, as on March, 1991, 
in the age group of 6-14 who are yet to be covered under the scheme. They constitute 18 per 
cent of the total population of the country. The Committee hopes that by the end of this century 
this backlog will be covered and total universal Elementary Education will be achieved. 
23. The Revised Budget Estimate for 1993-94 for Elementary Education is Rs. 443.7 crores. 
In Budget Estimate for, 1994-95, has been given Rs. 523.86 crores for Elementary Education. 
24. While the Committee takes note of this increase in allocation for Elementary Education, it 
feels that in view of the rising prices, the increase in real terms, is not substantial. 
25. The Committee feels that the Deptt. may take steps to decentralise Elementary Education 
and take help of Panchayati Raj institutions for proper monitoring and implementation of the 
Scheme.

26. In the Eighth Plan it has been provided that the Scheme would continue and a third 
teacher and a third room would be added to primary schools wherever enrollment exceeds 100 
students. Thirty per cent of such schools would be covered in the said plan. Besides these, 
Operation Blackboard would cover 10 per cent of upper primary schools during the last two years 
of the Plan.

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Fiftieth Report of the Committee on the Netaji
Bhawan, Calcutta.

2. A Study Group of the Departmental-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development visited Netaji Bhawan, Calcutta on 10th October, 1996 to
have a first-hand information on the activities of Netaji Research Bureau engaged in the task
of study, research and enquiry about Netaji’s life of profound experience and super-human
struggle and all round development of Netaji Bhawan. A list of Members who visited Netaji
Bhawan is enclosed as Annexure.

3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same on the 27th

REPORT

1. NETAJI BHAWAN, Calcutta, the ancestral house of Subhas Chandra Bose was
dedicated to the nation on 23rd January, 1947 by Sarat Chandra Bose. The Netaji Museum,
established in 1961 by Netaji Research Bureau, is a full-fledged biographical museum of vast
material on the life of Netaji collected from all parts of the world. Thi: museum is a store
house of inspiration and enlightenment for the people of this country.

2. Netaji Bhawan, with its traditional pillars and porticos, gives the appearance of a
typical early 20th century Bengali residential house. A marble plague, bearing the name of
IN Bose, Netaji’s father, decorates the front entrance. A fine profile of Netaji’s face draws
the attention of the visitors at the entrance gate. In the main portico stands a replica in red
stone of the stately ILN.A. Martyrs Memorial Column with the I.N.A. motto inscribed on it.

3. On the top floor of the Netaji Bhawan, Netaji’s cot, clock, clothes, shoes and Gita
have been preserved in the room where Netaji used to stay. Netaji's office-room during the
period of his Congress Presidentship is still painted in the hues of the Indian tricolour. His
working-desk, revolving chair, book-almirahs, etc. are preserved in-tact. The Netaji Bhawan
contains a treasure of numerous photographs, documents and articles relating to Netaji’s life.
The uniform donned by Netaji as G.O.C. of the Volunteer Corps at Calcutta in 1928, his
original passport and some rare antiques brought by him from Burma are among the
valuable exhibits. Warm clothings used by Netaji in Europe are kept in a show-case. Postage
stamps printed by Free India Centre, Azad Hind journals and Hindusthani translations of
German military texts are some of the interesting things to be seen.

4. The Freedom Library with marvellous collections of books on India’s Freedom
Struggle forms an integral part of the Museum. Books, periodicals and documents are being
collected to cover the entire freedom movement of India since 1857. The archives of the
Bureau consist of almost all published works of and on Netaji in various languages, a large
collection of letters covering his entire life, an extensive compilation of his speeches and
writing and journals, newspapers and other source material relating to Netaji. A scheme of
publishing Netaji’s work has been taken up by the Netaji Research Bureau with the
assistance of the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of Education,
Government of India and nine such volumes have already been released. The remaining
volumes should also be completed before the commencement of Netaji Centenary Celebra-
tion year, i.e. 1997 which also happens to be the 500 year of India’s Independence or at
least efforts should be made to publish rest of the volumes during the centenary year.

5. Modern microfilm reader has since been installed in the Library and relevant
documents have been obtained in microfilm from other organisations and countries,
particularly from German and Japanese foreign offices. Films and voice and music tapes also
constitute part of the archives. The Bureau has also made one documentary film on Netaji
which was shown to the Committee at the time of its visit. The Committee was informed
that film shows, specially historical documentary on Netaji and the Indian struggle for
freedom are regular feature of the programmes of Netaji Museum.

6. The Committee was also informed that Netaji Research Bureau has, through the
years, planned and executed on scientific lines the all round development of Netaji Bhawan.
The rich museum, library and archives are recognised as the first and one of the best of their
kinds. In short, Netaji Research Bureau has grown up to be an impressive National Institute
of History and Politics.

9SORS — 3


2

7. The Committee was informed that Netaji Research Bureau plans to celebrate Netaji
Subhas Chandra Bose Centenary in a befitting manner. As part of the centenary
celebrations, Netaji Research Bureau plans to create Netaji Museum a unique institution of
international importance as a living and permanent memorial to Netaji Subhas Chandra
Bose. The Institution will consist of a Historical Research Organisation, a research oriented
centre for academics and traditionals in economics, politics, sociology, education, health,
environment, etc. and a broad-based cultural centre. Netaji Bhawan will, thus become a
beaconlight for India’s triumphal entry into the twenty first century.

8. While planning for development and modernisation of Netaji Bhawan Complex, a
total view has been taken of reinforcing and developing the old historical building without
interfering with its traditional character and constructing a contemporary building
complementing the existing structure and in harmony with it. The Complex will become a
unique, structurally attractive and eminently functional place. In brief, the development
programme of Netaji Bhawan Complex will include modernisation of Netaji Museum,
upgradation of Netaji archives, expansion of freedom library and automisation of library
services and other ancilliary works. Netaji Research Bureau expects the Government of
India to wholeheartdly contribute and extend financial support in the fulfilment of the
programme of development for Netaji Centenary.

9. The Parliamentry Committee was given to understand that the former Prime Minister
of India had visited Netaji Bhawan Complex at Calcutta and assured to give financial grant
of Rs. 12 crores (Approx.) for the upgradation and development of Netaji Bhawan. Even
the present Prime Minister, while visiting Netaji Bhawan on 14th July, 1996 reiterated that
the commitments made by the previous Government will be honoured. The Parliamentary
Committee -was, however, distressed to note that despite the commitments made by the two
Prime Ministers, Netaji Museum has not received any financial support from the
Government of India so far. The Committee in its 43rd Report on Demand for Grants
1996-97 had also asked the Department of Culture to act fast in consultation with Ministry of
Finance and Prime Minister Office. It is unfortunate that the Department of Culture has not
moved thus far. The Committee fully supports the developmental plans of Netaji Bhawan
and strongly recommends the Government of India to extend the necessary financial support
as per the commitments already made so that Netaji’s Museum could be developed and
strengthened as a monument of national importance in the year of Centenary celebrations of
Netaji. The Committee strongly recommends that the commitments made by the two P.Ms.
should get reflected in the RE for the year 1996-97 because of the centenary year starting in
January, 1997.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. The origin of the National Library, Calcutta can be traced back to March, 1836
when the Calcutta Public Library was opened to the public at 30, Esplanade Row, Calcutta.
Subsequently the Calcutta Public Library was merged with the Imperial Library and offered
to the public in January, 1903. The National Library came into being in 1948 with the
passing of the Imperial Library (Change of Name) Act 1948.

1.2. The National Library, Calcutta is the biggest library in the country with the
collection of about 2.4 million volumes, besides journals, periodicals and palm-leafs etc. It
was declared as an Institution of National importance as enshrined in Article 62 of the 7th
Schedule of the Union List of the Constitution of India. At present the National Library is
housed in three separate buildings with a separate preservation laboratory, spread over 30
acres of land in the compound namely “Belvedere”, a French name meaning beautiful
garden within the heart of Calcutta City.

1.3. The National Library serves as the permanent repository of all reading and
information material produced in India as well as all printed material written by Indians and
concerning India written by foreigners, wherever published and in whichever language. The
National Library is the recipient of all material published in India, under the Delivery of
Books Act, 1954 as amended in 1956. The Library has an Exchange Programme with 225
institutions in 95 countries under the Cultural Exchange Programme of the Government of
India
II. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES

The following are the basic aims and objectives of the National Library:

(i) Acquisition and conservation of all significant printed material produced in the
country to the exclusion of ephemera; ;

(ii) Collection of printed material concerning the country wherever it is published and
also acquisition of a photographic record of such material that is not available
within the country; ,

(iii) Acquisition and conservation of manuscripts of national importance;

(iv) Planned acquisition of foreign material required by the country;

(v) Rendering of bibliographical and documentation services of retrospective material,
both general and specialised;

(vi) Acting as a referral centre purveying full and accurate knowledge of all sources
and bibliographical information and participation in international bibliographical
activities;

(vii) Provision of photocopying and reprographic services; and

(viii) Acting as the centre for international book exchange and international loan.
गा, ACTIVITIES OF THE NATIONAL LIBRARY

(a) Collection .building and collection organisation programme: This is a major

programme which is looked after by the Acquisition and Processing: Divisions of the Library.

‘ In order to manage different activities, there are separate divisions like, Book Selection

Division for purchase and receipt of English books, English Serials Division, Indian
Language Division etc.

(b) Reader’s Service (including Bibliographic Services Programme: The National Library

2610/ RS/ F—3-A.



2

renders services to its readers from different parts of India and abroad on 362 days in a year.
It is closed on 3 national holidays (26th January, 15th August and 2nd October). Throughout
the year the service sections remain open from 9.00 a.m. to 8.00 p.m. on working days and
from 9.30 a.m. to 6.00 p.m. on holidays. On an average, 1000 readers are served everyday.
The Library acts as the main bibliographic centre of India. The Indian National Bibliography
is published on the basis of the receipts under the Delivery of Books Act. The Library also
shoulders responsibility of current and retrospective bibliography on Indology and other
subjects. The Committee observes that the referral centre which is a part of the bibliographic
services is not sufficiently equipped with the retrieval services such as subject index of
articles published in journals, subject search and bibliographic assistance etc. and necessary
steps are required to be taken in this regard

(c) Conservation of Library Materials Programme: In order to conserve library material,
a small repair unit was started in 1957 which has Preservation Division, Laboratory Division
and Reprography Division. The Committee is of the view that this is inadequate and needs
to be further strengthened.

(d) Modernisation: In order to implement the automation programme, the Library
introduced Anglo American Cataloging Rules, 2 (AACR 2) as the first step towards
modernisation of its operations. This rule is a cataloguing code which is a standardised
cataloguing format and is internationally accepted for automated systems. It has taken up
the standardisation of diagritical marks [special marks attached to alphabets (Roman script)
for transliteration from Indian Scripts] for romanisation of Perso-Arabic scripts through
automation system and has also developed a standardisation chart of diacritical marks for
automated bibliographic services in different languages. The Committee feels that the
Library should complete the computer.cataloguing of books and manuscripts without further
delay.

3.1. The Committee feels that in view of the latest developments in technology brought
out in the Library system all over the world, the National Library, Calcutta should also
adapt itself with the changing needs in order to perform its functions properly and
expeditiously. Hence it should acquire the modern software and communication technology
available in these fields and it should’ establish a site on INTERNET and it may be
connected through INTERNET service with all the leading libraries, educational centers and
research-oriented institutes of the world for a speedy and effective exchange programme.
The Committee is of the view that the Library may also examine a proposal to provide this
facility free to the schools and edcuational institutions which have received the Bibliographic
Data Base Project under MPLADS.

IV. BHASA BHAWAN

4.1. The present accommodation available in the National Library is not able to cope
with the various activities of the labrary including preservation of age old books, other
valuable articles and documentation of various new collections etc. The shortage of space
has adversely affected the functioning of the library. In. order to overcome this problem, a
Master Plan has been sanctioned which includes construction of a massive building called
“Bhasa Bhavan” with most modern facilities matching international standards. It would be
equipped with latest software and communication technology including Closed Circuit
Television (CCTV)

4.2. The foundation stone of ‘Bhasa Bhawan’ was laid on the 7th April, 1989 by late
Shri Rajiv Gandhi, the then Prime Minister of India. Originally the estimated cost of the
project in February 1989 was Rs. 35.34 crores. The Administrative approval and expenditure
sanction for Rs. 41.57 crores was issued by the Department of Culture only in January, 1993

after a gap of four years. The Department has taken unduly long to accord administrative
approval and sanction for the expenditure. This inordinate delay must have resulted in cost
escalation for which the Department of Culture owes an explanation. The Secretary and the
Joint Secretary, Department of Culture were summoned by the Chairman, HRD, on 16th
December, 1996 to clarify the reasons for delay in according the administrative approval for
this expenditure. Even’ they were not in a position to clarify the precise reasons for this

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1. The National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur was established on 7th February, 1976 as
an Autonomous Body under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by taking over the
erstwhile Government Ayurvedic College, Jaipur. The Institute complex is spread over in an
area of 13 acres of land situated within the walled city. The activities of the Institute are
controlled and managed by the following 3 Standing Committees:

1. Governing Body

2. Finance Committee

3. Scientific Advisory Committee.

Il. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES

2. The NIA is an apex Institute of Ayurveda engaged in teaching, research and health

care. The main objectives for which the Institute is established are as follows:

1. To promote the growth and development of Ayurveda;

2. To produce graduates and post-graduates in all branches of Ayurveda;

3. To conduct research on various aspects of Ayurveda;

4. To provide medical care through Ayurvedic System of Medicine to the suffering
humanity;

5. To provide and assist in providing services and facilities of the highest order for
research, evaluation, training, consultation and guidance to Ayurvedic System of
Medicine;

6. To conduct experiments and develop patterns of teaching in under-graduate and
post-graduate education in all branches of Ayurveda.

या. INFRASTRUCTURE

3. The Institute has Academic Block, Hospital Block, Hostels for Boys and Girls,
Animal House, Kitchen Block, Pharmacy etc. The Committee was, however, informed that
the Institute has no facility for residential quarters for Staff, Guest House, Administrative
Block etc. Steps are being taken to have separate Administrative Block, Guest House etc.,
the Committee was informed. An amount of Rs. 50.00 lakhs was sanctioned and
negotiations, in this regard, were being made with the Rajasthan Housing Board, it was
added. The Committee desires that immediate steps may be taken for early finalisation.

IV. EQUIPMENTS
4. Major Equipments and Machineries available with the Institute are:
X-Ray Machines (300 MA & 50 MA);
Ultra Sound Sonography Machine (Supplied by WHO);
Anaesthesia Ventilator-Respiratory Gas Monitor;
Dental Unit with X-Ray Machine;
Medicare 8 Channel Polyrite; and Electric Bhatti etc.
