; 2.6 The Committee is constrained to note that there have been several instances of
vandalism of protected monuments and temples. The Department inits reply stated that for
exercising proper watch and ward on the protected monuments, a proposal had been sent to
the IFD/Department of Culture for the creation of 5000 posts of monuments attendants in
the first phase against an overall requirement of about 11000 additional posts. This issue has
been commented upon by the Committee in its earlier Reports also. Follow-up action taken
by the Department reveals half hearted attempts on its part to improve the situation. The
Committee strongly recommends that the Department should take immediate steps for
creation of 5000 posts of monument attendants and their subsequent filling up.

2.7 The Committee was of the view that all and sundry should not be permitted entry
inside the protected temples. The Department in its reply stated that all Superintending
Archaeologists had been directed to regulate the entry of visitors into the monuments.

Ill. MUSEUM

3.1 Indian Museum Calcutta— The Committee expressed its concern over the issue that
along with the need for expansion of space for increasing the range of display in Indian
Museum, Calcutta, there should also be a simultaneous upgradation of technology as well
and adequate arrangements need to be taken in this regard. The Department in its reply
stated that besides arranging availability of additional space after construction of the annexe
building of the Indian museum, the Museum was also planning due upgradation of the
existing technology, i.e. making the entire building centrally airconditioned, installation of
fideorama, audio playback system and interactive. display methods, particularly in the
scientific sections, installation of wireless close circuit TVs, electronic surveillance system,
infra-red cordoning of the rare and valuable exhibits, installation of elevators, sound and
light projection of some historic phases of Indian art and culture etc. Some of these items
had already been taken care of while planning the galleries. The Museum was well set to
introduce all these arrangements in due time. The Department further clarified. The


5

Committee is constrained to note that only the Planning stage has started and nothing
positive has been achieved. Hence the Committee recommends that the allotted tasks should
be carried out without delay. Proper monitoring and time bound projects need to be
undertaken.

3.2 Salarjung Museum— Expressing its concern over a number of thefts that have taken
place in the Salarjung Museum over the last couple of years, the committee enquired about
the details of action taken by the Government in this regard. The Department in its reply
stated that a Committee of Experts was appointed in 1993, to conduct a physical verification
of the art objects of Salarjung Museum. As the report of the Committee submitted in 1994,
confirmed that a number of art objects‘manuscripts were missing from the Museum, the
Government of India referred the case to CBI. In August 1996, the CBI informed that
during their investigations, they have found that out of 635 art objectsymanuscripts as
reported missing earlier, 326 have since been traced out by the Salarjung Museum
Authorities and are available in the Museum. The CBI found it desirable that the traced 326
items be again examined by the same team of experts which had earlier conducted the
Physical Verification of art objects of Salarjung Museum, so that the traced items could be
excluded from the purview of further investigation by CBI, the Department clarified. The
Expert Committee was accordingly reconstituted in November, 1996. Report of the
Committee submitted in February, 1997 is at present under consideration of the
Department. The Committee expresses its deep concern over a large number of precious art
objectsymanuscripts missing from the museum and recommends the CBI inquiry be further
strengthened and the culprits brought to book . The Committee hopes that appropriate
action on the findings of the Expert Committee would be taken without delay. The
Committee strongly recommends that concerted efforts should be made for further
strengthening the security of Salarjung Museum so that this sort of mishappenings do not
recur in future.

3.3 The Committee was constrained to note that the Salarjung Museum’s building was in
a dilapidated condition and no steps had been taken to have it renovated. The Department
in its reply stated that the construction of the new wing of the Salarjung Museum which was
likely to have been completed by 31st March, 1997 could not be accomplished due to the
indifferent performance by NBCC. The Committee is anguished to note that the
construction of two additional wings i.e. Far Eastern gallery and European gallery supposed
to be completed earlier by 31st May & 15th July, 1996 respectively and further extended to
31st December, 1996 still remains incomplete. The Committee hopes that decision of the
Salarjung Board Museum to interact with other available authorised construction agencies
for accomplishing to his unfinished job would bear fruit and construction of two additional
wings would be completed without delay.

3.4 The Committee desired to know about the steps being taken to professionally
catalogue its collection. The Department in its reply stated that a number of art objects were
catalogued and published from 1979 to 1989, Portfolios in 1987 and thereafter monographs
in 1996. The Committee is constrained to note that the work of cataloguing of all the art
objects in Salarjung Museum still remains incomplete. The Committee therefore
recommends that the Department must take effective steps in this regard.

3.5 The Committee expresses its concern regarding the financial constraints faced by the
Salarjung Museum. The Department in its reply stated that the Salarjung Museum had been
facing financial crunch on Non-Plan side. During 1996-97 against an allocation of Rs. 73.39
lakhs under Non-Plan, an expenditure of Rs. 165.15 lakhs upto February, 1997 was incurred.
For meeting this expenditure on the Non-Plan side, the Salarjung Museum is diverting plan

1520/RS F—4-


6

funds, the Department admitted. Unless additional funds to the tune of Rs. 90-100 lakh
approx. are made in the provision under Non-Plan for the year 1997-98 onwards, these
financial problems will persist. The Committee observes that the reason for this extra
expenditure on Non-Plan side is mainly on account of pensiompensionary benefits to the
retiredtetiring employees of Salarjung Museum and on deployment of Central Industrial
Security Force for the Security of Salarjung Museum. The Committee strongly feels that
additional funds for meeting the entire expenditure under the Non-Plan side have to be
provided for, without which plan funds are bound to be affected. Hence the Committee
recommends that adequate allocations be made at the RE stage.

3.6 National Council of Science Museum (NCSM)—While discussing the budgetary
allocations to the National Council of Science Museum (NCSM), the Committee was
perturbed to note that the plan allocation under BE 1996-97 for National Council of Science
Museum was drastically reduced from Rs. 18 crores at BE 1996-97 to Rs. 14 crores at RE
stage of 1996-97 showing a cut of Rs. 4 crores. The Committee was surprised to note that
the plan allocation for this organisation has further been drastically cut at BE 1997-98 to a
nominal amount of Rs. 5 crores only showing a steep fall of Rs. 9 crores compared to RE of
1996-97 and Rs. 13 crores as compared to BE 1996-97. This is an unprecedented cut of
about 72% compared to BE of Rs. 18 crores for 1996-97.

3.7 The Committee fails to understand how this organisation with 26 Science Centres’
MuseumsParksCorners: functioning under its control, will survive for one year with this
meagre allocation of Rs. 5 crores. The Committee fails to understand the logic of imposing
such a drastic cut on NCSM, particularly when this organisation has been performing an
excellent job of promoting and popularising science all over the country. The Committee
observes that the cuts made in the budgetary allocations to this organisation seems to have
been made arbitrarily and without any rational justification. The Committee is seriously
disturbed about the neglect shown to this organisation which now faces a serious threat to its
very existence. The Committee also gets the impression that the Department is least
bothered about the promotion and popularisation of science through the various museums
functioning under the control of NCSM.

3.8 The Committee was also constrained to note that the Department misled the
Committee by intimating that the National Council of Science Museum was transferred to
them from the Department of Science and Technology in the later half of Seventh Five Year
Plan. The Committee came to know that this organisation was transferred to the
Department of Culture from the Department of Education. The Committee was also misled
on the point that the expenditure of this organisation had never been audited in the past.
During the course of discussions, the Committee came to know that the expenditure of this
organisation were duly audited by the Comptroller & Auditor General of India. Thus the
Department has once again tried to mislead the Committee by giving a totally wrong picture.
There were number of typographical mistakes in the replies to the queries given to the
Committee by the Department. This shows the casual approach of the Department of
Culture in dealing with the Parliamentary Standing Committee. The Committee takes a
serious view of the matter and warns the Department about the consequential effects of
misleading the Committee.

3.9 The Secretary, Department of Culture and the other officers who appeared before
the Committee on 3.4.1997 and again on 19.4.1997 could not give any satisfactory


i

vi

explanation for the imposition of cuts in the budgetary allocation made to this organisation
both at the RE stage 1996-97 as well as at BE 1997-98. The argument given by the
Department that the allocations made to the Deptt. could not be regularised by the
Expenditure Finance Committee does not convince the Committee as it is the primary duty
of the Department to see that the allocations are got timely regularised through EFC by the
nodal Ministry/Department concerned. The Committee was informed that all the
information/dates required by the Expenditure Finance Committee were duly supplied by
NCSM to the Department of Culture well in time. But the Department does not seem to
have taken interest on the whole issue for an unduly long period and resorted to arbitrary
cuts instead of getting the allocation regularised in time through EFC. The Committee has
been left with the impression that the Department of Culture is heavily biased against this
organisation as they have by and large given enhanced budgetary allocations to all the other
organisations barring one or two, irrespective of the fact whether the Expenditure Finance
Committee clearances were obtained or not.

3.10 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the National Council of
Science Museum should be given a realistic allocation of funds immediately at least to the
level of allocation made in 1996-97. Any approval required from Cabinet Committee on
Economic Affairs (CCEA) should be obtained without further delay. The additionality
amount of Rs. 15 crores due from Planning Commission for the Science City Project may
also be made available to NCSM fully. The Committee further recommends that in
consideration of the predominantly educational objectives for which NCSM was set up
initially in 1978 under the Deptt. of Education, this organisation may be transferred back to
the Deptt. of Education under the Ministry of Human Resource Development. The Deptt.
of Culture may also send a detailed report in the matter as promised by them to the
Committee in the meeting held on 19.4.1997.

५. LIBRARIES

4.1 The Committee expresses its concern over the poor progress in the growth of the
e Library Scheme, The Department in its reply stated that the Rural Library Scheme
proposed to be implemented through the Raja Rammohan Roy Library Foundation would
be known as the “Scheme of Financial Assistance for setting up Rural Libraries at the
Panchayat level”. The Programme sought to set up libraries in areas where such facilities
were non-existent and to nurture reading habits among the rural people. The Scheme would
be implemented through the State Govts. on a cost sharing basis (3:1). The Library would
be administered at the Panchayat level by a Committee comprised of the Panchayat Pradhan
and the Block Development Officer in their ex-officio capacities and such other
representatives as the State Govt. may nominate, the Department clarified.

4.2 The Committee enquires about the quantum of funds that will be needed to
establish rural libraries iri all the Panchayats. As the success of this scheme would depend on

, the continued cooperation of the State/Panchayat authorities, it was being launched on a

modest budget of Rs. 15 crore in the 9th plan, with an annual outlay of Rs. 3 crore, the
Department informed. If successful, provision for additional funds would be made for
multiplying the rural library network. The Committee observes that the Rural Library
Scheme is proposed to be implemented through the Raja Rammohan Roy Library
Foundation. However, the budget allocation of 1997-98 for RRRLF in plan i.e. Rs. 5.40
crores is Rs. 3.00 crores less than the demand made by the organisation which was Rs. 8.40
crores. The Committee notes that these 3.00 crores were specifically required by RRRLF for
taking up a scheme for assistance for setting up libraries in Gram Panchayats. The

Committee is of the view that during 1997-98 too. Rural Library Scheme would remain
unimplemented. The Committee therefore strongly recommends that Rs. 3 crores should
definitely be provided to RRRLF at the RE stage.

4.3 The Committee desired to know whether the Raja Rammohan Roy Library
Foundation had the infrastructure to implement this programme. The Department in its
reply stated that the RRRLF has the infrastructure to initiate this programme and administer
it in collaboration with the State Govts. Its monitoring infrastructure will be reviewed after
the scheme has been in operation for a period of 2 years. The Committee is constrained to
know that the scheme of Rural Libraries is yet to be approved by the Planning Commission.

9५. ADVERSE IMPACT OF FOREIGN MEDIA

5. The Committee expresses its concern over the adverse impact of foreign media on
Indian Culture and enquired what steps has the Department of Culture taken to reduce it
through the electronic media and whether the Department of Culture had developed a
strategy for an environment which would provide necessary resistance. The Department in
its reply stated that the strategy to combat the adverse effect of foreign culture through the
electronic media required an integrated approach involving not only the Department of
Culture but also a number of other Ministries and Organisations including more importantly
the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting. In fact the Ministry of I&B alone could have
the direct role in that as it was they ultimately who decide as to what was to be beamed
through the electronic media. The role of this Department would be limited to giving an
input to the media policy that Ministry might formulate in that context. The Department of
Culture was quite alive to this responsibility as the National Policy on Culture which was at
present under formulation is expected to make appropriate recommendations in this regard.

VI. NATIONAL ARCHIVES OF INDIA

6. The Committee expresses its concern over the poor maintenance in the National
Archives. Facilities of public conveniences for visiting scholars also needed improvement.
The Department in its reply stated that apart from having thymal fumigation facilities, the
‘National Archives of India has a vacuum fumigation chamber with a capacity of 300 quc.
feet. The National Archives also has an air-cleaning chamber for making incoming records
dust free. The department further stated that the library of the National Archives of India
had already been transferred to the Annexe building which was centrally air-conditioned.
Facilities such as drinking water, toilets, resting place etc. have been provided to scholars.
The Research room will also be moved to the Annexe building partly, which has better
amenities for Research Scholars including lounge facilities. The Committee appreciates the
efforts being made by the Department in the proper maintenance of the National Archives
and hopes that there would be no let up in these efforts.

VII. NETAJI RESEARCH BUREAU

7. The Committee expresses its concern over corpus grant of Rs. 3 crore only in Netaji
Research Bureau which was yet to be leased, even though there was a commitment from
two previous Prime Ministers to give a sum of Rs. 6.5 crore to it out of the total project cost
of Rs. 12.5 crore. The Department in its reply stated that the idea behind the corpus grant
was to ensure a steady income to the Bureau to enable them to pursue their existing
activities more intensively as also to expand their scope and range in due course and at the

‘moment, there was no ‘proposal to give an additional grant to the NRB. The Committee is

surprised to note that even though two previous Prime Ministers had made commitments in

4


9

this regard Rs. 3 crores corpus grant is yet to be released to NRB. The Committee
recommends that the Rs. 3 crores corpus grant and Rs. 3.5 crores for technology
upgradation of the archives of NRB be released at the RE stage.

' VIII. CENTENARIES

8.1 The Committee desired to know about the initiatives taken by the Government of
India for commemorating in a befitting manner the 400th Death Anniversary of Maharana
Pratap. The Department in its reply stated that a National Committee constituted under the
Chairmanship of the Minister of Human Resource Development has taken a number of
decisions in this regard. Commissioning of a historian by Govt. of India for writing a
biography of Maharana Pratap. Commissioning of a TV film and a serial on Maharana
Pratap by I&B Ministry, preparations of a Master Archaeological plan for excavation at the
places connected with the life of Maharana Pratap by ASI are some of the decisions of this
Committee. A commemorative postal stamp will be issued on 19th January, 1998 the
Department further informed. The Committee appreciates the initiatives taken by the
Department for commemorating in a befitting manner the 400th Death Anniversary of

Maharana Pratap.

8.2 Netaji Centenary— The Committee feels that adequate provision should be there to
assist the Government of Orissa to celebrate Netaji’s centenary at his birth place, Cuttack.
The Department in its reply stated that the Chief Minister of Orissa who attended the
meeting of the national Committee for the celebrations of birth centenary of Netaji Subhash
Chandra Bose on 15th January, 1997 sought the assistance of the Central Government for:

(i) the renovation and development of Netaji’s ancestral house at Cuttack into a
Museum; and

(ii) maintenance of Revenshaw Collegiate School, Cuttack where Netaji studied.

A detailed proposal, bringing out clearly the financial implications, in this regard was
awaited from the State Government, the Department informed. The Committee is of the
view that timely action in the matter is called for.

IX. ZONAL CULTURAL CENTRES(ZCCs)

9. The Com.inittee was of the view that activities of ZCCs have declined in general and
Udaipur in particular. The Department in its reply stated that the activities of the ZCCs had
maintained a steady growth. The seven Zonal Cultural Centres were set up under the 7th
Plan for creative development of Indian Culture in various regions with a thrust on folk art
and to create cultural awareness and participation at the grass root level as would emphasize
and underscore the cultural cohesiveness and unity of India. Besides their normal intrazonal
programmes the ZCCs have taken up 3 new schemes during the 8th Plan, such as National
Cultural Exchange Programmes, setting up of Shilpgram to provide promotional and
marketing facilities to craftsmen. Setting up of documentation centres to record both orally
and visually, vanishing and rare art forms. The Udaipur Centre had been very actively
involved in the National Cultural Exchange Programme and had been the first Zonal
Cultural Centre to set up the Shilpgram at Udaipur, the Department further clarified.

X. TRIBAL AND FOLK ARTS

10. The Committee wanted to know about the reasons for only short-term projects and
not long-term being funded under the scheme for support of Tribal and Folk Art. In its


10

reply the Department stated that the nature of projects was preponderantly such that they
have to be completed within a short time frame. Further, if the project took unduly long
time the benefits from the completion will not accrue to the voluntary organisations and
community. Long term project on tribal and folk art were also undertaken through
subordinate/attached offices of the Department like Anthropological Survey of India and the
Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya, Bhopal, the Department clarified. The Committee feels the
necessity of wider publicity and spread of tribal and folk art. The Committee is therefore, of
the view that more concerted efforts on the part of the Department are required in this

regard.
XI. MULTI-PURPOSE CULTURAL COMPLEXES

11. The Government of India provided one crore to each State for setting up Multi-
purpose Cultural Complexes. The Committee desired to know whether the Government
indicated a priority within the different components of the Project and if anyone from the
Department physically inspected any of these complexes set up by the States. The
Department in its reply stated that these complexes were intended to serve as major
resource centres for each State and their basic infrastructure included any or all of these

i components such as Auditorium, library, museum, exhibition area, gallery, open-air theatre,

recording studios. However, no priority within the various components had been indicated
by the Central Government, and the Officer from the Department of Culture had visited
and inspected some of these complexes under construction, in the different States. The
Committee desires that these should be a proper monitoring mechanism for the successful
completion of such sites and making them functional at the earliest.

| XII. 50TH ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATIONS

12.1 The Committee desired to have the details of various programmes being
formulated for the 50th Anniversary Celebration of India’s Independence. The Department
in its reply stated that an Implementation Committee which met under the Chairmanship of
Minister for Human Resource Development on 50 March, 1997 approved the programmes
such as (a) Curtain Raiser Event to focus on the entire episode of Quit India Movement of
9th August, 1942 (b) Inaugural Event in Main Hall of Parliament on 14.8.97 (Mid-Night)
which would focus on Nehru’s speech ‘A Tryst with Destiny’ Dr. Ambedkar’s speech on
29th November, 1949 when the Constitution of India was adopted and concluding remarks of
Dr. Rajendra Prasad on the same day etc. (c) Programme for 15th August, 1997 which
should essentially be a people’s affair and (d) Programmes from 16.8.1997 to 31.8.1998
which will be planned on the basis of suggestions received from individuals. Voluntary

Organisations, State Governments and Central Ministries and in accordance with the

guidelines given by the National Committee. The Committee is of the view that these
programmes must be celebrated in a befitting manner. In this 5070 year of India’s
Independence Culture should be used in such a way that would create among each individual

' a sense of ‘unity in diversity’ and also a feeling of universal brotherhood.

12.2 The Committee expresses its concern over the steps being taken to involve the
youth and students in these celebrations in particular. The Department in its reply stated
that a separate Advisory Group had been constituted on the themes of ‘Children, Students
Youth, Sports, etc.’ under the Chairmanship of Shri Prakash Ambedkar to suggest
programmes to the Implementation Committee. Besides a grant of Rs. 57.2 lakh had been
given during 1996-97 to the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports for programmes
involving youth and students. That Department would involve Nehru Yuva Kendra


11

Sangathan, National Service Scheme and Bharat Scouts and Guides in the implementation of
various programmes involving youth and students, the Department further clarified. The
Committee feels that this Anniversary should be used in such a way which would create a
positive sense and optimistic outlook among the Indian youth.

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The Department of Women and Child Development is engaged in the Welfare and
Development of Women and Child Development. The Department is responsible for
safeguarding certain provisions of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy
with reference to Women and Children.

1.2 The Department, in its nodal capacity, formulates plans, policies and programmes;
enacts/amends legislations; guides and coordinates the efforts of both Governmental and non-
Governmental organisations, working in the field of Women and Child Development. For a
holistic child development, the Department implements the Integrated Child Development
Services (ICDS). The ICDS provides on integrated package of services comprising
supplementary nutrition, immunisation, health check-up and pre-school dnd non-formal
education and health and nutrition education for women.

1.3 The other major schemes implemented by the Department includes funding of Hostels
for working women, Support, Training and Employment Programme, scheme of Training-cum-
Employment-cum . Production Centres (NORAD), Socio-Economic Programme, the
Programme of Condensed Courses of Education and Vocational Training etc. Most of the
programmes of the Department are run through non-Governmental organisations.

Il. EIGHTH FIVE YEAR PLAN

2.1 The total approved outlay of the Department for 8th Plan is Rs. 2010.00 crores. As
against this, the Plan allocations made during all the annual plans in BE from 1992-93 to 1996-97
was Rs. 3260.16 crores. The actual expenditure made, however, was far ahead of this i.e.
Rs. 3377.91 crores, showing a quantum jump from original plan outlay and allocations made in
BEs. Similarly on non-Plan side also the actual expenditure has exceeded the Budget Estimates
in all the annual plans during the 8th Plan period excepting the year 1995-96 during which year
there was a slight shortfall of Rs. 69 crores.

2.2 The Committee has noted that there was a short fall in the achievement of physical
targets in some of the schemes. In the scheme of (i) Training of Anganwari Workers,
(ii) Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, (iii) Mahila Smariddhi Yojana, (iv) Socio-economic Programmes,
the achievement of physical targets set for 8th Plan was far below. In fact in Mahila Samriddhi
Yojana, the number of accounts opened were only 36.7 per cent of the targets fixed. Reviewing
the performance of the Deptt. and various schemes under the Deptt. the Approach Paper to the
9th Five Year Plan observed that there has been a significant shift in the approach towards the
well-being of women and children from “Welfare during 50s’ to ‘Development during 70s’ and
‘Empowerment during 90s’. It was also felt that human resource development, being one of the
major thrust areas in the 8th Plan, all the developmental efforts were directed to empower both
women and children besides mainstreaming them into the national development on equal
footing alongwith their counterparts. The approach paper also observed that while the main
thrust in respect of children was to ensure their survival, protection and development, with a
special focus on the girl child and adolescent girl, the emphasis in respect of women was to make
them economically independent and self-reliant. The Committee, however, feels that there is a
longway to go to feel that the goals of welfare, development and empowerment of women are
fully achieved. The Government should not be complacent with whatever that has been done/is
being done. The Committee is also constrained to note that the Performance Budget of the
Department does not give the actual picture of the achievements of targets fixed. The
Department should therefore take note of this and given full details in Performance Budget in
future.


Ill. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

3. The Department’s annual plan outlay for 1996-97 was Rs. 847.07 crores. The RE was
also kept at the same level. The Committee was informed that the minimum requirement of
the Deptt. was 936.98 crores leaving a backlog of ‘over Rs. 90 crores for 1997-98. For
1997-98, the Department has been allocated Rs. 900 crores on Plan side and on non-Plan
side Rs. 48.10 crores When the Committee sought to know the views of the Deptt. on the
actual projections made by it for the year 1997-98, it was stated that taking into account the
new initiatives undertaken during the 8th Plan period, the pace of expenditure under various
schemes as also the realistic requirements of funds, the Deptt. had projected the
requirement of funds for 1997-98 at Rs. 3718.74 crores. However, the Deptt. has been
allocated only Rs. 900 crores. it was further stated that the requirement of funds for the
Deptt. just to continue the programmes worked out to be Rs. 1820.52 crores for 1997-98 as
against the absolute minimum requirement of Rs. 936.98 crores during 1996-97. The actual
allocation. however has been pegged at only Rs. 900 crores. The’ Secretary, therefore,
informed the Committee that in the backdrop of the original projection of Rs. 3718.74 crores
this drastic reduction is apprehended to adversely affect almost all the schemes and
programmes of the Department. Even though the projections made by the Department
appear to be a bit exaggerated there is no doubt that the allocation made is far below than
the minimum requirement. The Committee was also given to understand that the committed
liability has not been taken care of resulting in a big handicap for the Department. The
Committee dealt with the committeed liability later in detail. For here, the Committee only
recommends that the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance should make a
realistic assessment of the requirements of the Department and meet the minimum
requirements of the Department.

IV. OBJECTIVES AND APPROACH OF THE 9th PLAN

4.1 The Approach Paper felt that large disparities exist in various social groups
particularly women and children. It was also observed that women and children are the
vulnerable group and for them planned State intervention is required in order to provide
them with adequate opportunities for education and in an attempt to involve them
productively in the development process. With this view the Approach Paper to 9th Plan
made empowerment of women as one of the objectives of the 9th Plan. The Approach Paper
felt that in pursuance of this Objective the plan will ensure to create an enabling
environment with requisite policies and programmes legislative support, exclusive
institutional mechanisms at various levels and adequate financial and’ man power resources
to achieve this objective, according to the Approach Paper to the 9th plan.

4.2 The Approach Paper to 9th Five Year Plan while laying emphasis on empowering
women, under-scored harmonization of various efforts on different fronts i.e. social
economic, legal and political. The Approach Paper also emphasises the need to make
reservation of seats for women in the Parliament and State Legislatures, to fulfil the goal of
education for women equality, to adopt a life cycle approach to women’s health. As regards
child development is concerned, the Approach Paper proposes to take the convention of
child’s rights ratified in 1992 as the guiding principle and would like to review the national
policy for children. In order to promote a community based approach action will be initiated
to decentralise women and child programme involving Panchayati Raj Institutions and local
women’s self-help groups. The Committee feels that the objectives are laudable. However,
unless dedicated efforts are made to achieve these objectives, they will remain mere
objectives only. The Committee hopes that efforts would be made in the right perspective
for better delivery of services to the target groups.


3

V. INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES

5.1 The allocation made for ICDS during 1996-97 was Rs. 681.90 crores and in 1997-98
it is Rs. 733.90. crores. Out of 733.90 crores being provided for 1997-98, 180 crores is.the
externally aided component for ICDS training and ICDS World Bank Projects. The
budgetary suport is only Rs. 553.90 crores.

5.2 The funds for ICDS General including IMY are only Rs. 479.40 crores. The
Secretary stated that for ICDS General the actual projection made for 1997-98 was Rs. 2919
crores against which the allocation made was 467.90 crores excluding for IMY. The
Committee, however, recommends that the budgetary support should be over and above the
external aid component agreed, The Department havé stated that the budget provision
approved for ICDS for 1997-98 is grossly inadequate to sustain the on-going ICDS projects
and the ICDS project in different stages of operationalisation. The Committee was informed
that 505 new ICDS projects became operational during 1996-97 and 1668 projects would start
in 1997-98. This would require an outlay of Rs. 1316.94 crores for ICDS General as against
Rs. 467.90 crores actually provided. When the Committee sought to know the basic
minimum requirement for 1997-98, it was stated that the absic minimum requirement for
ICDS for 1997-98 is Rs. 940 crores.

.5.3 The Committee agrees with the resource constraint being faced by the ICDS. Many
proejcts are required to be operationalised. The Planning Commission should take a realistic
view of the basic requirements of the scheme and make necessary allocations accordingly.

5.4 On the recommendation made by the Committee earlier, the Department
redesigned the plan of introduction of services and the maximum time limit has been
reduced from 18 months to 12 months for the States to operationalise newly sanctioned
ICDS projects. When the Committee sought to know as to whether this is strictly being
adhered to. It was submitted that during February-March, 1996, 1668 new ICDS projects
were sanctioned as per ‘redesigned plan of introduction of services. According to the
Department, all the projects should become operational by March 31, 1997. It was, however,
stated that the process of operationalisation has suffered a set back in view of non-release of
required funds to some of the States because of inadequate provision during last year. The
Committee has already recommended above for increasing the allocation for ICDS. The
Committee, however, recommends that the monitoring mechanism should be strengthened
to ensure operationalisation as per the schedule. The schedule also should be strictly
adhered to.

5.5 The concurrent evaluation of ICDS was piloted by National Council of Applied
Economic Research in 5 States covering 10 blocks of Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, U.P.
West Bengal and Gujarat during August, 1996. The study was completed and the reports
were to be submitted soon. The Committee desires that as soon as the reports are received,
the Department should chalk out the programme of action and initiate action as early as
possible. The Committee desires that the evaluation reports should be examined and similar
concurrent evaluation should be done throughout the country. The Department have also
informed the Committee that they propose to initiate nationwide evaluation of ICDS from
April, 1997 through NCAER. The Committee strongly feels an urgent necessity of this
evaluation so that a clear picture of the impact of ICDS in all the States can be had. The
Department should, therefore, not delay the evaluation and start it as proposed
immediately.

5.6 In regard to filling up the vacant posts of Supervisors for training ICDS

functionaries, the Department have submitted that all the States have requested to fill up the
“vacant posts on priority basis. It was included in the agenda item for discussions in the


4

scheduled’ meeting of the State Secretaries/State Ministers. The Committee is of the view
that training of ICDS functionaries is a basic requirement for efficient functioning of the
ICDS projects. For this purpose, supervisors are required but there are a large number of
vacancies in almost all the States for quite sometime and the States have not been taking
necessary steps in this direction. The Committee strongly recommends that the Department
should initiate action at political level to ensure immediate filling up of the vacant posts.

5.7 Last year, the Committee recommended for enhancing the honorarium of
Anganwadi workers. On this the Department have stated that the proposal was sent to PM’s
office for enhancing the honorarium. Initially the proposal was not acceded to. Thereafter
the Minister for Human Resource Development wrote a letter to the Prime Minister on
February 7, 1997 and to the Finance Minister of February 13, 1997 for reconsideration of the
decision. A formal response from the PMO and the Finance Ministry is awaited, the
Department added. The Committee desires that the Department may pursue the matter
vigorously for an early clearance. As regards the achievement of physical targets under
ICDS projects is concerned, the training of Anganwadi workers has lagged behind. The
Eighth Plan target fixed was 2 lakhs whereas the actual achievement is 1 lakh 69 thousands.
Therefore, the physical target achievement was only 84.5% with a shortfall of 15.5%. This is
required to be corrected.

5.8 As regards the performance of ICDS is concerned, the Secretary informed the
Committee that the impact has been good on girl children attendance in schools. There is a
very significant improvement on ICDS. Immunisation has taken place extremely. well and the
infant mortality rate has gone down wherever ICDS projects are functioning. The
Committee is, however, constrained to note that the impact of ICDS is not satisfactory. The
Secretary herself agreed that more work needs to be done. The Committee feels that
nutrition aspect has to be very well taken care of. Specific target groups should be worked
out and the concentration should be laid on them. The Committee has taken note of
horrifying reports in tribal areas. A large number of children are dying because of the total
resistance power that they have lost. The Committee last year recommended to explore the
possibility to mobilise funds from tribal development authorities for providing supplementary
nutrition to children in vulnerable tribal areas. The Department has stated that the Ministry
of Welfare has responded by stating that there exists no provision in the Ministry’s budget
for providing supplementary nutrition to ICDS beneficiaries. The Committee in fact made
the above recommendation last year to ensure supplementary nutrition to tribal children
with the specific idea that the additional funds that could be provided by the tribal
authorities would be beneficial to cover those areas which are not covered under ICDS. The
Committee, therefore, does not agree with the reply given by Ministry of Welfare. If there is
no scheme now in their Ministry, they should start such a scheme. The Committee also
desires that the monitoring mechanism on the programmes implemented in tribal areas
should be strengthened.

VI. CRECHES AND DAY-CARE CENTRES

6. The. Committee last year recommended that the Department may prepare a
perspective plan showing the requirement of creches and make projection of the 9th Plan for
consideration of the Planning Commission. On this, the Department have stated that they
have estimated that 8 lakh creches are required throughout the country. Against this, the
Department has been able to provide about 14,000 creches only. The Department,
therefore, sent a proposal to the Planning Commission to augment the corpus of the national
creche fund to Rs. 2,000 crores. Accordingly, the Department had proposed for creche fund
of an amount of Rs. 154 crores for 1997-98. Against this the Department was allocated


5

only Rs. 94 lakhs. The Committee is of the view that either the projection made by the
Department is too exaggerated or the allocation made is too paltry. The Committee,
however, keeping in view the requirement of creches to be opened for being used,
particularly by the working section of the society, recommends that the Planning
Commission should make a realistic assessment of the requirement of fund and make
necessary allocation at RE stage.

Vil. BALWADI NUTRITION PROGRAMME AND EARLY CHILDHOOD EDUCATION
PROGRAMME

7. The allocation for both the schemes are the same in 1997-98 as that in BE in 1996-97.
When the Department was asked to explain this, it was stated that the schemes are non-
expanding and the benefits available under them are also available under the scheme of
ICDS. It was further stated that as advised by the Planning Commission, both the schemes
are to be phased out as ICDS has been universalised. A decision has been taken to phase
out w.e.f. 1.4,1998. The Committee only expresses its hope that the activities being
undertaken by these programmes would be adequately taken care of by ICDS in all the
projects.

VIII. WORKING WOMEN HOSTELS

8. Allocations for working women hostels for 1997-98 has been kept at the same level as
that of Rs. 7.75 crores in BE 1996-97. The Committee had been recommending for opening
more working women hostels. During 1996-97, 60 hostels were to be sanctioned with
Rs. 7.75 crores. The Department have stated that about 16 hostels to accommodate 1420
women were sanctioned with an expenditure of Rs. 5.54 crores. The Department anticipated
that the target would be achieved. The Committee, however, is not in a position to believe
that 16 hostels were sanctioned with Rs. 5.5 crores and 44 hostels would be sanctioned with
Rs. 2.21 crores. The Committee desires that proper monitoring should be kept on the
utilisation of the amount and to meet to targets as well. The Department has proposed to
sanction 40 hostels with the same amount mentioned above for 1997-98. The Department
should try to achieve the target. The Committee also desires that whenever there are.
vacancies in the hostels, girl students and non-working women also should be considered.

IX. MAHILA SAMRIDHI YOJNA

9. The allocations for Mahila Samridhi Yojna was reduced from 60 crores in BE 1996-97
to 40 crores for BE in 1997-98. The Department have stated that while finalising annual plan
of the Department in 1997-98, the Planning Commission suggested complete review of the
scheme during 1997-98. According to the Department, this was based on the fact that the
operational cost of implementing the scheme was increasing considerably every year. At the
same time as per the trends in number of accounts opened and number of accounts closed, it
appears that the scheme has reached the saturation point, it was added. Therefore, the
provisional allocation of Rs. 40 crores has been made, it was added, when the exact
operational cost of the implementation of the scheme has been finalised with the
Department of Post, the issue that who should bear the operational costs is still pending, the
Department added. It was further stated that Planning Commission had earlier suggested
that the modalities of the appropriation of operational cost of implementing the scheme
should be sorted out amongst the Ministry of Finance, Department of Women and Child
Development and Department of Posts. The Committee desires that this problem may be
sorted out at the earliest. Similarly, the physical targets fixed for the scheme should also be
achieved and monitoring mechanism should be strengthened in the Department. The Mahila
Samridhi Yojna is facing a severe shortfall on account of achieving physical targets. 6 crores


6

accounts were supposed to have been opened and only 2.2 crores were opened resulting in a
shortfall of 63.3.% of target unachieved. This need to be seriously considered and the
Department should take necessary steps.

X. INDIRA MAHILA YOJNA

10. The Indira Mahila Yojna was expected to be extended to additional 200 blocks
during 1996-97. When the Committee sought to know the progress made in this, the
Department submitted that during 1996-97 the scheme could not be extended to the
additional blocks because Planning Commission had given approval only for implementing
IMY in 200 blocks in 1995-96 on a pilot basis. Planning Commission decided that a view on

' expansion of IMY to additional blocks could be taken after reviewing the programmes in the
pilot block by a joint team of Planning Commission and the Department. The Committee is,
however, constrained to note that the review team has not yet been appointed and the
Department has only made a request to the Planning Commission to suggest the names, As
the scheme has become very popular, the Committee desires that necessary and expeditious
steps should be taken by both Planning Commission and the Department for an early review
of the pilot blocks and for starting of additional blocks immediately. The Department has
also informed the Committee of the following areas of concern for this programme:—

(a) Although an amount of Rs. 6.10 lakhs has been released for every block, there are
many blocks which have not yet received these funds. As a result of this, the blocks societies
are not able to work properly;

(b) Many IMBSs have not been registered;

(c) The State level Steering Committees and District level Coordination Committees
have not met in majority of the States districts. As a result of this; the progress could not be
reviewed/guided and activities like convergence have not taken off anywhere;

(d) It was expected that the IMY blocks will be able to access funds from the existing
sources for the purpose of training and capacity building. So far, this has not happened;

(e) In the absence of a proper protocol for group formation, quality of groups formed
so far are not upto the mark and it is not clear as to how many groups will really sustain on
a long-term basis;

(f) Instructions were issued to expand IMY in the World Bank-ICDS blocks and normal
ICDS blocks. These instructions have not been followed;

(g) The Department of Women and Child Development, GOI has decided to cover the
IMBSs under the on-going schemes of Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, STEP, NORAD and CSWB.
The IMBSs were asked to send the required proposals for assistance under these schemes.
The response from IMBSs has not been encouraging;

h) Besides above, IMY is presently facing following structural probelms:
8 8 9
(i) Proper training methodology for the IMY fuctionaries is not available;

(ii) Proper capacity building under IMY will require substantial trained
manpower at the Anganwadi and block levels. So far, such a manpower could not
be identified properly.

(iii) There are no funds under IMY for the purposes mentioned at (i) and (ii)
above without which the capacity building of implementors and fields level
functionaries cannot be created. This is also likely to affect the sustainability of the
whole process.


10.1 The Committee is of the considered view that all the issues may be properly looked
into and appropriate action may be initiated at the earliest.

XI. RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH

11. Rashtriya Mahila Kosh is facing a lot of shortfall in the achievement of physical
targets under Eighth Plan. The target fixed for Eighth Plan period was 2 lakh women
beneficiaries whereas the achievement made was 1.48 lakhs leaving 26% shortfall on the
achievement. This is not a good sign on the part of the scheme. The Department have stated
that the Rashtriya Mahila Kosh mainly is functioning for facilitation of poor women. For this
purpose it is using the NGOs as it is catalising and channelising agencies. However, the
NGOs have to meet certain eligibility criteria since it is not possible to entrust them with
loans without a firm information regarding their infrastructure and capabilities for receiving
the money from RMK and arranging the identification of the women namely those living
below the poverty line and for disbursing RMK’s money to them through their functionaries.
The Department have, however, also stated that the Indira Mahila Centres to be set up
under Indira Mahila Yojna will fill up a gap between RMK and its borrowers. The
Department, therefore, submitted that a large number of Indira Mahila Kendras would be
able to bridge the gap and ultimately ensure to achieve the targets then. The Committee
desires that the Department should go in for more Indira Mahila Kendras through which it
would be easier to reach out to women.

XII. SHORT STAY HOMES

12. Allocation for short stay homes has been reduced from Rs. 4.82 crores in BE 1996-
97 to 4.75 crores for 1997-98. When the Department was asked to explain the reasons it was
stated that an EFC Memo for revising the financial norms for the short stay homes is already
at the final stage of consideration. Normally, 30 short stay homes are sanctioned every year.
As such it would be difficult to implement the scheme in the manner it has been
implemented so far with the reduced allocations, the Department added. The plan allocation
has been kept at the same level, i.e. 2.75 crores but the non-plan allocation has been
reduced from 2.07 crores to Rs. 2 crores. The Department have stated that actual projection
made was Rs. 30.82 crores for the annual plan for 1997-98 as against which Rs. 2.75 crores
has been allocated. Even though the Planning Commission may not be able to allocate the
projected amount but the amount atleast could have been slightly increased keeping in view
the cost escalation. The Committee desires that Planning Commission should reconsider the
allocation at RE stage.

XIII. WOMEN DEVELOPMENT CORPORATIONS

13. The Department started the revamping of the scheme of Women Development
Corporations to give assistance to States for setting up of State Women Development
corporations in the States. The Committee was given to understand that 18 States/Union
Territory Administrations have set up Women Development Corporations (WDCs). The
Committee desires that the Department may take up with the remaining states also for
setting up WDCs. The Committee is impressed by the activities that are to be taken up by
the WDCs. The Committee trusts that the Corporations would succeed in all their
endeavours which ultimately lead to achieve the goal of empowering women and to provide
them equal status.

XIV. SOCIO-ECONOMIC PROGRAMME

14. Under Socio-economic programme, the actual plan outlay was 25 crores and BE
allocations in all the annual plan periods comes to Rs. 27.75 crores and the actual


8

expenditure made was Rs.38.32 crores. The programme has, ape done very well in
achieving the financial targets. Even though the expenditure is far ahead of the outlay and
allocation, yet the achievement of physical targets is lagging behind. In regard to number of
units, the achievement was only 63.6% and as regards the number of beneficiaries, the
achievement was 84.7%. This discrepancy between overutilisation of funds and the shortfall
in physical targets achievement should be gone into and necessary action should be taken. It
appears that the monitoring of the scheme has not properly been done. The Department
should therefore, take necessary action in this regard.

XV. AWARENESS GENERATION PROGRAMME

“15, The Department informed the Committee that there is a need to review the scheme
and the procedure for implementation. The task of awareness generation is one of the most
important programmes of the Central Social Welfare Board and it is necessary to tone up
the implementation of the scheme. The Committee recommends that the reviewing of the
scheme may be done at the earliest to ensure modifications for better implementation.

XVI. NUTRITION EDUCATION

16.1 The overall allocation for nutrition education has been reduced from Rs. 6.06
crores to Rs. 6.01 crores in the current year as compared to last year. The Department have
stated that the reduction of Rs. 5 lakhs in overall allocation should not effect the schemes
being run. The Department however, informed the Committee that the projection made by
it before the Planning Commission on plan side for the current year for Nutrition Education
was Rs. 10.25 crores as against which the allocation made was Rs. 2.31 crores. The
Committee is of the view that all the schemes under the Nutrition Education are very
smaller ones and there is necessity of marging the schemes into one or two for an efficient
functioning. The Department may examine this aspect and take necessary decision in the
matter. The Committee is, however, happy to note that some of the schemes such as
integrated education under nutrition, mass media communication and strengthening of
community food and nutrition expansion units have been amalgamated under nutrition
education in the 9th Five Year Plan starting with the current year. The Department, as
recommended by the Committee above, may make a review of the remaining schemes as
well.

XVII. GENERAL

17.1 CONVERGENCE: The Committee had earlier recommended convergence of
various related schemes under different Departments/Ministries. On this, the Department
informed the Committee that three meetings have so far been held to identify areas of
convergence, particularly those relating to ICDS. Health and Family Welfare functionaries
and women groups existing under sectorial programmes. The Chief Secretaries of the States
have been addressed jointly by the Secretaries of Family Welfare, Women and Child
Development, Rural Development, Education and Health. The Committee was further
informed that the Department was in the process of collecting State-wise information in
respect of identified areas which shall be used to evolve a comprehensive convergent plan.
The Committee is at least happy that an initiative has been made in the direction of
converging the various schemes. But the efforts of all the Departments and the States should
be ultimately in the direction of bringing various related schemes under one single umbrella
for an efficient functioning and implementation and to ensure delivery of better services to
the beneficiaries. The Committee desires that this process should be completed as early as
possible.

17.2 The Committee has noted that the resources have been spread very thinly on a


के

number of schemes just to show that they have covered the entire area. That is one of the
reasons as to why the physical targets are not being achieved. The Committee does not
attach great importance to universalisation part and such other things. Besides this,
concentration should be laid on the targeted groups where the problem is in its gravest form
and then compare as to how best the results are being achieved.

17.3 Monitoring Mechanism: The approach paper to the Ninth Five Year Plan felt that
more practical approach to the programme formulation, particularly for social sector
programmes was to put the lessons learnt from the experience to the implementation. The
approach papers also felt that inspite of the existence of an elaborate monitoring and
evaluation system, the findings made by the monitoring and evaluation system are not put to
use. The Committee takes a very serious note on this aspect and strongly recommends to the
Department to first strengthen the monitoring mechanism on various schemes and ensure
strict implementation of the findings made by the monitoring agencies. The Committee also
observes with concern that the schemes being taken up by the Central Government are not
properly monitored by the State Governments. Merely handing over the money and getting
report from the State Governments is not going to serve any purpose. The Committee is of
the definite view that the State Governments, where the financial position is bad, divert the
funds, given by the Central Government for a particular scheme to other purposes such as
for giving salaries to the employees of the State Governments, etc. The Committee,
therefore, desires that the Centre should impress upon the States about the need to develop
a mechanism to find out whether the money being given to the States for implementation of
various programmes is utilised for the purpose specified and fix responsibility in case the
purpose is defeated.

17.3 NGOs: There are certain areas where the Adivasis are the worst affected lot. The
Committee is constrained to note that not many NGOs are present in tribal areas. One will
find them mostly in areas where the atmosphere and the living conditions are very good.
They would not like to leave big and smaller cities and go into rural areas. The Adivasis are
mostly located in far-flung areas. The Committee, therefore, desires that NGOs which are
working in adivasi areas should be given encouragement.

17.5 There is no doubt that there are committed and devoted NGOs in the field, but at
the same time, one cannot rule out the possibility of mushroom growth of NGOs which are
merely interested in getting assistance from the Government of India. The Department
should, therefore, strengthen its monitoring mechanism to see whether they are working
properly or not and only those NGOs which have proven track record should be given
assistance.

17.6 Committed Liability: The Committee has noted that the committed liability of the
plan schemes has not been reflected in the budgetary allocations for 1997-98 which is the
first year of the Ninth Plan. The Committed expenditure which is accounted in the
subsequent plan at the termination of the previous plan is taken out from the plan and
becomes a separate committed expenditure. If this is not done, the Departments will be
handicapped by this amount of plan expenditure. The exercise of identifying committed
liability has not been done by any of the Departments for 1997-98. Committee in this
connection has considered the report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance
Commission have observed in this regard as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the out-off date for transfer of committed liability on account_of plan scheme,
the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan Scheme
completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The


10

Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider
providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92”.

17.7 The Committee was also given to understand that the Planning Commission issued
circular to all the Departments dated November 5, 1996 sending therewith guidelines for
classification of expenditure. The Ministries were also requested to make necessary provision
as committed non-plan expenditure for the upkeep of existing assets etc. Accordingly, all the
MinistrieyDepartments were asked to adopt the guidelines while submitting the plan
proposals for Ninth Five Year Plan and annual plan 1997-98. However, the Departments
have not done this exercise. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
Department may complete the exercise at the earliest so that they may not be handicapped
on account of this.

17.8 The Committee is also constrained to note that many Departments have not done
the exercise of identifying committed expenditure and to get it earmarked separately for
several plan periods. Accordingly, committed expenditure on the plan schemes completed in
7th Plan or earlier and the assets created and staff employed in plan schemes has been
continuing on plan side resulting in severe resource crunch for the Departments. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Departments should make a thorough review of
the schemes and identify the committed liability. The Committee is very much surprised that
the guidelines given earlier by the Planning Commission were not followed at all. For this,
responsibility should be fixed.

An Overview 
The Department of Youth Affairs & Sports is comparatively a new Depa ·tment which deals with 
the vital subject :>f youth and promotion of sports. Though both these subjects fall under the P!!rview 
of the States, yet Government of India has a very prominent role to play not only in terms of 
operating its own ~chemes but also for coordinating with State Governments and other agcnc1es. The 
Committee found that on youth side, though there are a large number of schemes, but bulk of the 
budget allocation is for the National Service Schemes (NSS) and Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan 
(NYt<S). National Scrvic.! Scheme (along ,.ith NCC) is the most important scheme fc; voiuntary 
participation by student community in a nation building. It is a low-cost scheme which aims at 
personality development of the students through their involvement in social service, literacy, health, 
and environment, etc. Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan, on the other hand, mainly mobilises rural 
youth and focuses on the activities of the Youth Clubs. Amongst other impo;tant schemes there are 
the schemes for National lnteiration and Adventures. There is some scope for streamlining the 
remaining schemes also. Among the new initiatives, taken in the current year is the preparatior for 
the establishment of Rajiv Gandhi National Institute for Youth Development. 
2. On the Sports side, it is observed that the Department has to coordinate with the State 
Governments as well as sports federations, which are autonomous bodies working for 54 different 
disciplines. The important scheme being operated by the Department are the schemes of Grants to 
Sports Federations, and 'Assistance for creation of Sports Infrastructure. While the development of 
infrastructure is essential, it is felt that there is a tendency to set up large stadia in big towEs and 
cities and since the resources with the Centre, as well as State Governments are limited, creation of 
play-fields and other facilities at the Tchsil level do not get the required attention . The Sports 
Authority of India (SAl) is the executive part of the Department and is main.y concerned with the 
broad-based sports, as well as grooming of talented children It is also responsible for organisation of 
National Camps for participation in major international events. The performance of Indian 
sportspersons at the Olympic Games has been undistinguished and it is necessary that all efforts arc 
made oy various concerned agencies to raise the requisite/International standards. In this connectiOn , 
the Committee welcomes the reported consensus of the State Governments about the introduction of 
Sports and Physical Education as a compulsory subject from sehoul level onwards. 
3 It is observed that the Plan provision for 1993-94 was Rs. 98.10 crores including Rs. 37.19 
crores for Youth and Rs. 60.66 crores for Sports. Whereas. this year, Plan provision is Rs. 94 00 
crores only Rs. 4.10 crores less than the previous year Plan provision. The provision for 1993-94 
includes addition of Rs. 13.10 crores earmarked for preparation for the Asian Games . It is felt that 
Department consists of two important parts 1.e. Yout 1 and Sports, therefore, decrease in the 
allocation will go against thl!ir interest. Therefore, the Committee recommends that allocations may 
accordingly be increased.

Youth Hostels 
The idea behind building youth hostels is to enable youth to experience the diversities of their 
country aud facilitate them to have a glimpse of the glories of the past - a process which promotes 
national integration. But, it is surpising to note that some of the centres of historical and cultural 
importanc:: like Patna, Nalanda, Rajgir, Bodgaya, Panipat, Banaras, Ajmer, Khajuraho etc. have not 
been found suitable for construction of such hostels. The distribution of such hostels is also not 
equitable. J\.lany of the Stutes have been neglected. Therefore, the Committee recommends, that to the 
extent possible there should be distribution of such hostels all over the country and prominent cultural 
centres should not be left out. 
27. In the Department's note it has been admitted that only 37 youth hostels have so far been set up 
whereas the performance budget gives a figure of 34 hostels. As regard the youth hostels under 
construction, the former presents a figure of 31 whereas the latter of 29. The Committee is not in the 
know whether these hostels have actually been constructed or are under construction. 
28. The Commit tee recommends that the final decision regarding transfer of scheme to the States 
should be expedited. 
29. It is astonishing to note that a drlstic cut was made in the Budget estimates for the year 1993-
94 in regard to this scheme, as against the B.E. & R.E. provisions for the year 1992-93. A substantial 
decrease has also been made in the B.E. for the year 1994-95, almost a reduction of Rs. 58 lakhs as 
compared to the R.E. of the year 1993-94. The Committee, therefore, would like to know the reasons 
for the !lame. 
National Discipline Scheme & National Fitness Corps 
30. When the scheme of National Discipline scheme (1'-.TDS) has become a non-entity long ago and 
its instructors have been absorbed in State Government services, it appears to be stranges as to why 
the t'cpartmcnt of Yo11th Affairs & Sports is bearing the expenditure under this Scheme. The 
Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs, in course 0f his oral evidence, said that it is done because of 
a ::ommitmcnt made some 20 years ago. He further conceded that the Department is not even sure as 
to how many instructors and workers are or: the jobs. This allocation is not, in any case, justified and 
the committee, therefore, recommends that urgent necessary steps should be taken to take this 
scheme out of Departm<'nt's purview. 
31. According t"l the background note supplied by the Department, a separate scheme, called 
"National Fitness Corps", rc.Jlaccd the National Discipline Scheme. This Scheme also aims at meeting 
various expenses relating to National Discipline Scheme instructors. As suggested earlier, this scheme 
should also be transferred to the State Governments. 
Assistance tu Youth Clubs 
32. This scheme was started with a view to giving impetus to the youth movement in the country 
and to involve the youth in constructive activities which is being implemented by Nehru Yuva 
Kcndras and state Govts. and U.T. Administrations. It is, undt.mbt,dly, a well conceiv( i scheme 
which may go a long way in shaping the pcrsonai1ty of youth. More and mo. e such clubs need to be 
opened in the rural areas. The Committee is of the view that Government should give priority to the 
expansion of this scheme. The Comr'ittee recommends that proper monitoring be done so that such 
youth clubs continue to function properly. This scheme may be implemented with thr help of suitable 
voluntary organisations also and not merely through Ne!:ru Yuva Kendras. 
33. During the years 1992-93 only 3, youth clubs could be assist~d and during 1993,94 with the help 
of NYK 600 youth clubs were assisted. For this year the Department has set same very ambitious target 

of assiting 2,160 youth clubs with the same budgetary allocations as during the last two years. It is not 
known how this target can be achieved. 
Programme of Training of Youth 
34. This scheme appears to be duplication of the scheme of assistance to voluntary organisations as it 
also aims at imparting vocational education of different kinds to the youth. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that this scheme should be integrated with the above scheme. There has been considerable 
under-utilisation of allocation made under this scheme during the year 1992-93 when a total provision 
under Budget Estimates was 130.00 lakhs and the revised estimates present a figure of only Rs. 45.00 -
lakhs. The Committee is of the view that this scheme should be associated or attached with schools, 
colleges, and youth clubs so that the allocations made for this scheme are properly utilised. This step 
will also ensure community participation which is very important for the successful implementation of 
the scheme. 
Rajiv Gandhi National Institute of Youth Development 
35. National Institute of Youth Development, named after late Shri Rajiv Gandhi, was launched as 
an autonomous body and resource centre for providing training, research, documentation and 
extension services for youth-related activities in the country. It was proposed to allocate a total sum 
of Rs. 4.19 crores during the Eighth Five Year Plan to this Institute. The Committee expresses its 
concern over the fact that during the year 1993-94 only an amount of Rs. 13.00 lakhs could be released 
upto December, 1993 as against the budgetary provision of Rs. 77.00 lakhs. For this year again a 
provision of Rs. 77.00 lakhs has been made. The Committee recommends that there should not be any 
let up in the release of allocations for this scheme and this institute be made operational within the 
stipulated period. 
Youth Development Centres 
36. A centre is proposed to be opened for information, sports, and training, etc. for the rural youth 
in a group of 10 villages to be managed by committees of youths from the constituent villages. This is 
a very good scheme and it should be expanded so as to cover all the villages through out the country. 
But some slackness on the part of Government is visible if the budgetary and revised estimates for the 
year 1993-94 are taken into account. Out of a total allocation of Rs. 50.00 lakhs only Rs. 25.00 lakhs 
could be utilised during the same year. The Committee expresses its disappointment over the slow 
progress of the scheme and recommends that all-out efforts should be made to implement this scheme 
effectively. 

CHAPTER-II 
GAMES AND SPORTS 
37. The Second major component of the Department of Youth Affairs and Sports is games and 
Sports and the Sports Authority of India is the Main organisation. In order to put the infrastructure 
created during ASIAD, 1982 and optimum utilisation and also to preserve and maintain the assets, 
the Sports Authrity of India was created. But now its activities have grown manifold and it has 
undertaken multifarious and wide ranging sports activities so much so that if has emerged as the 
premier body for sports at the national level. Its activities includes development of Sports, nurturing 
of talented persons, promotion of sports in special areas, realisation of the concept of 'sports for all', 
creation of a central pool of sports equipment to be loaned to sports persons efforts to promote sports 
consciousness, promotion of women's sports, rural sports, conducting national coaching camps, etc. 
At present, the Sports Authority of India has six regional centres covering the whole country, two 
sub-centres and training centres and a high altitude Training Centre. 
38. However, the Committee expresses its concern over the deteriorating performance of the country 
in the field of sports and in this connection points out that the hopes generated at the time of setting up 
Sports Authority of India have been belied. This is mainly because of the fact that major share of 
allocation for the Sports Authority of India is spent on establishment, salaries and other miscellaneous 
heads and a modicum of amount is spent on sports promotion and development activities. A 
comparative analysis of the figures for the last three years including the current year, suggests that 
almost one-third of the total amount is spent on establishment and miscellaneous items and a little 
amount is spent on the development of sports:
