39. The Committee recommends that adequate funds be harnessed for sports promotion and 

development activities and also some mechanism should be evolved to make various sports schemes 
result-oriented. Some accountability should also be ensured in this regard so that in case of poor 
performance at the sports events the weak points may be identified and rectified. Year, after year, 
Government comes out with assurances that the country's performance in international sports events 
woul1 improve in future, but nothing happens. The Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs and 
Sports, in his oral evidence tendered blofore the Committl'~ has conceded that performance in sports 
has not been upto the mark for the last many years and expressed his firm resolve to make honest and 
sincere efforts, to draw up programmes by which performance could be improved. 
40. The Committee also expresses its deep concern over the constitution of the generaVgoverning 
body of SAl in which more and more bureaucrats are represented rather than the Sports persons and 
experts. The Committee recommends that professionals be given more representation iu the general 
governing body of SAl. 
The Committee notes with concern the reduction in budget allocation of SAl. As compared to 
the Revised Estimates for the year 1993-94 Plan and Non-Plan alloc:Jtion this year has come down to 
Rs. 3913.00 lakhs from Rs. 4,380.00 lakhs. 
41. Sports Authority of India is ruuning various s .. hemcs and programmes to identify persons in 
different disciplines and trnin them to achieve excellence both at national and international levels 
some of which arc as follows:-
(a) Nationa l Spurts Talent Contest (NSTC) Scheme 
42. The main objectiv~ of the scheme is to identify promising school children in :he age group of 
8-12 years and to provide them with opportunit ies to develop them to be a talented sports p.:!rsons. 
For this, children arc required to undergo various tests awl once thC) qualify they arc reared in SAl 
adoplctl schools which hav~ coaching and specia: infra structure facilities. 
43. But the progre ss made in this scheme, as underlined In the performance budgets of the years 
1993-94 and 1994-95, shows that it is almost negligible. During the year 1993-94 the number of adopted 
children was 1300 and the number as sho\vn in the performllnce Budget for 1994-95 remains the same. 
The number of adopted schoo ls vary from 68 (as in the performance Budget, 1994-95) to 58 (Brief back 
ground note on SAl). Whether the selection team visits the schools or selections are made at a 
particular place where school children are required to cQme and participants is nowhere mentioned. 
The Committee recommends that the network under this programme should be considerably expanded 
in rural, backward and remote areas where there is no consciousness and facilities for sports do not 
exist. 
44. The disciplines such as Badminton, Basketball, Gymnastics, Hockey, Table Tennis and 
Volleyball, chosen for the contest are such in which mostly children with affluent family background 
may excel. The Committee recommend s that traditional and indigenous games like Kabaddr and 
Khokho etc., may also be included in the Jist of disciplines under this scheme. 
(b) Sports Project Development Area (SPDA) Scheme 
45. This scheme aims at providing basic sports facilities to the rural children between the age of 
9-14 years at a centre having linkage with regional centres of SAl whicij covers about 80 to 100 
Development blocks. The progress of this scheme is very slow as out of 78 sanctioned centres only 34 
centres have so far been constituted. Even those centres which have been set up are not working 
satisfactorily . Therefore, the cummitte e urges upon the Government to take necessary corrective steps 
in this regard and also recommends that some sort of surveillance committees be constit uted to look 
after the functioning of these centres. The Committee recommends that effective steps should be taken 
to open all the sanctioned centres and make even distribution of the centres. The allocation has come 
down from Rs.280.00 lakhs during 1993-94 to Rs.250.00 lakhs this year. This decrease in allocation as 
compared to last year may affect the progress and, therefore, the amount should be appropriately 
enhanced. 
There has b~en und er-utilisation of the resources also during the year 1993-94, as around Rs.20 
lakhs remained unutili sed. 

(c) Sports IIo~tel Scheme 
46. The progress of this scheme also appears to be tardy. As against the target of establishing one 
hostel in every Stat< only 18 hostels have so far been constructed. Some States like U.P., Punjab and M.P., 
which have vast potentialities for producing sportsmen, do not have such hostels. Therefore, the 
Committee recomends that construction of youth hostels may be expedited. 
47. Apart from the Sports Authority of India development and promotion of sports is undertaken by 
vajous other or~anisations and bodies. National Sports Federations are such bodies which are getting 
financial assistance for furthering various sports disciplines. For this purpose, sports federations 
undertake such activities as conducting national championships, organising coaching camps, purchasing 
sports equipment, participating in International Tournaments, etc. During the year 1993-94 a total of 
Rs.l480.00 lakhs for plan and Rs80.00 lakhs for non-plan expenditure (which include an additional 
allocation of Rs.1080.00 lakhs for the preparation of Indian Contingent for Asian games)' was given to 
sports :ederations. But, the poor performance of teams in international level games has shown that all is 
not going well with the sports federations. Therefore, the Committee recomends that while doling out such 
huge amounts norms and conditions fixed therefor should be strictly adhered to. There should also be some 
mechanism for monitoring to find out whether the amount is being properly utilised or not. There must also 
be a supervisory body to see that the sports federations functions smoothly. 
48. The Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs & Sports during the course of his oral evidence 
tenderd before the Committee stated that since sports is a State subject no proper check upon sports 
federations could be kept. He further added that plans are also being formulated to ensure that these 
federations are run properly. The Committee strongly recommends that all-out effort should be made by 
Government to tone up the functioning and performance of the Sports Federations. 
Grants for Creation of Sports Infrastructure 
49. This scheme is important for expanding the sports infrastructure in the country. For this purpose 
~:!1ancial assistance is extended to State Governments, Union Territory Administrations, local bodies and 
registered voluntary organisations. 
50. The Committee is unhappy to no~c that more and more sports infrastructure is being 
concentrated in large cities and towns, and small cities ~nd towns arc neglected. The Commitee, therefore, 
rccor:uncnds that efforts should be made to ensure that spor ts infrastructure is spread all over the country 
properly utilised. The Committed deplores that the SAl and the Department of sports have no plans for 
purposeful and regular utilisation of the infrastructure already created. They have also no plans to 
construct multipurpose ! !adia in towns and cities which could be utilised for sports during the day and as 
open air theatres for cultural programmes in the evening and "night. 
General ObservationS! Recommendatio11s 
T!lc Committee made some general recommendations which are as follows: 
(a) Efforts should be made to set up hostels for youths on the lines of working women's hostels in major 
cities and towns. (b) Physical educatio n may be integrated in school curriculum and it should be made 
compulsory. Writte11 examinations on physical education may also be conducted as is being done in 
Maharashtra. Provisi<-.ts should be made to have at least one physical education teacher for every 150 boys 
·•nd girls. Effortc should also be made to provide play grounds in every school. (c) Government should also 
make arrangements to provide sports opportunities to the aged persons. (d) The year 1994 is being 
celebrated as SAARC year for the youth. The Committee, in this connection suggests that all out efforts 
should be made to make it successful, and to awake and mobilise the youth of the country. (e) Government 
has taken some measures to give incentives to the outstanding sports persons. Recently, a new scheme of 
incentive to meritorious sports persons has been introduced under which life long pension would be given to 
them who have won me:lals in important hternational events, but these are not adequate and sufficient. 
Still, a large number of promising sports persons are facing lot of hardships. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that adequate steps should be taken to give encouragement to the outstanding sports persons 
by providing tht:m jobs and also extending financial assistance . 
(f) Corporate and Private Sector is doing commendabl e job in furthering the cause of sports by 

organising and holding tournaments for various disciplines and maintaining sports teams etc. Therefor , 
the Committee recommends that private and corporate sectors may be encouraged to come forward in 
the promotion of sports. •

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1. The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible
for implementation of various programmes of national importance like family welfare,
primary health care, prevention, control and eradication of major diseases which form the
main plank of our development efforts. Apart from these, the Ministry also takes special
care for preventing the spread of diseases assuming the dimension of epidemic. The
Department of Health, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is
committed to achieve the goal of health for all by the year 2000 A.D. is responsible for
evolving broad policies for the health sector and provides financial and technical assistance
to State Governments in critical areas through the implementation of important health
programmes.

1.2. Broadly, the objectives of the Department are to undertake National Health
Programmes, to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to
prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs, to provide primary health care at the door
steps of the people, to take steps for better implementation of health care programmes for
tribal and other weaker sections of the society and also to collaborate with member countries
of United Nations and international agencies like WHO, UNICEF, etc. in matters relating
to health promotion and development.

1.3. The Department finances a number of health programmes aimed at controlling
Malaria, Leprosy, Blindness, AIDS, TB, Gunieawarm either on 100 per cent or on 50 per
cent basis. The Department also finances wholly or substantially autonomous institutions
engaged in patient care and or research such as All India Institute of Medical Sciences,
Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, All India Institute
of Speech and Hearing, Mysore, Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi, National
Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Sciences, Bangalore etc. The Department also assists
voluntary organisations and institutions substantially such as Indian red Cross Society, New
Delhi, Tuberculosis Centre, New Delhi, Lala Ram Swarup TB Hospital, Mehrauli, etc.

1.4. The health infrastructure comprises 2424 Community Health Centres, 21853
Primary Health Centres and 1,32,727 Sub-centres. Some of the new programmes initiated

during all the annual plans period is Rs. 2965.11 crores and the actual expenditure made was
Rs. 3065.11 crores. Thus, the expenditure made a quantum jump from the original plan
outlay and approved annual outlay. At the start of Eight Five Year Plan, there were 81

2.3. The Eighth Plan had envisaged improved access to health for the undeserved and
under privileged segments of the population. This was sought to be achieved mainly through
consolidation and operationalization of the health care infrastructure for optimal
performance, building up appropriate referral sevices with emphasis of primary care and
effective implementation of Natioanl Programmes relating to major public health problems.

2.4. These efforts had a distinct impact on the mortality though morbidity due to
communicable and Non-Communicable diseases had not shown a parallel decline. Crude
Birth Rate (CDR) has declined to 9 in 1995 [Sample Registration System (SRS) 1995
provisional]. An emerging factor is increasing morbidity due to non-communicable diseases

‘2.5. However, the Committee is constrained to note that there remains a shortfall in

and programme for control of Blindness. For example the achievement of physical targets
covered between 60% to 75% only. Similarly the targets achievements in the programme for
control of Blindness also was between 20% to 88%. Financial targets also could not be
achieved fully in these two programmes. The Department is required to make a thorough
review of such schemes to see where the things go wrong for the shortfall and corrective

Ill. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

3.1. The overall proportion of the Budget to the Health sector has not increased since
the beginning of the first Plan. The Health Sector including Family Welfare has been getting
only about 3 per cent of the total outlays through the successive Five Year Plans. The
working Group for Health Financing set up by the Planning Commission for the Eighth Five
Year Plan had recommended that the Health Sector allocation should not be less than 5% of
the total outlay. The Fourth Conference of Central Council of Health and Family Welfare

expenditure should be at least 5 per cent of the GDP if equity and universal coverage is to,
be realised. As per the figures available, the total investment on health and family sector is
1.3% by the Government. The Secretary in his discussion has regretted that there has been\
no substantial step up in the outlay of the health sector of the Ninth Plan.

3.2. The Secretary also mentioned the inadequacy of the outlay especially in view of the
additional services required to be provided under certain recent legal directives. In view of
the already insufficient funds available with the Department on all such legal directives, the
Department should approach Finance Ministry for additional funds over and above the

IV. NINTH FIVE YEAR PLAN—APPROACH

4. According to Approach Paper to Ninth Five Year Plan, new initiative would be made
in the Ninth Plan in the areas which have already been covered in the Eighth Plan. The
focus would, however be on provision of rural health care for all through optimally
functioning of Primary Health Care and Sub-centres as a part of basic minimum services.
For control of communicable diseases major efforts would be made for horizontal integration
of these programmes at the district and below district levels within in the existing frame
work of the Primary Health Care infrastructure. This is expected to address the problem of
lack of key personnel in this programme and their sub-optimal performance. Even as efforts
for improved sanitation continue the strategy during the Ninth Plan will be to strengthen
health surveillance early alert and repid response mechanisms for timely detection to prevent
periodic outbreak of epidemics. For the non-communicable disease, the Ministry does not
contemplate in initiating and supporting separate vertical programme. Experience obtained
from pilot programme launched during Eighth Plan will be utilised towards integrated Non
Communicable Diseases Control Programmes. The Ministry also plafs to initiate an urban
Primary health Organisation to provide basic health services to all inhabitants within 1-2
Kms. of their dwellings. Besides, appropriate referral linkages for optimal utilisation of the
available facilities and increasing involvement of Nagar Palikas is envisaged. It is also
proposed to increase the efficiency of the health systems through creation of a functional
Health Management Information System, multi professional eductation and skill upgradation
of all categories of health workers. The objectives made in the Ninth Plan are very good.
Unless they are translated into action, they remain mere objectives. The Committee is happy
to note that focus is being laid on rural health care. The condition of Primary Health
Centres and Rural Family Welfare Centres is in a very bad shape. With the focus being laid
on them now, the Committee hopes that their condition would at least improve now.

Vv. COMMITTED LIABILITY

5.1. The Committee has noted that the committed liability of the plan schemes has not
been reflected in the budgetary allocations for 1997-98 which is the first year of the Ninth
Plan. The Committed expenditure which is accounted in the subsequent plan at the
termination of the previous plan is taken out from the plan and becomes a separate
committed expenditure. If this is not done, the Departments will be handicapped by this
amount of plan expenditure. The exercise of identifying committed liability has not been
done by any of the Departments for 1997-98. Committee in this connection has considered
the report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance Commission have observed
in this regard as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liabilty on account of plan
scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan
scheme completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The
Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider
providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92”.


4

5.2. The Committee was also given to understand that the Planning Commission issued
circular to all the Departments dated November 5, 1996 sending therewith guidelines for
classification of expenditure. The Ministries were also requested to make necessary provision
as committed non-plan expenditure for the upkeep of existing assets etc. Accordingly, all the
Ministries/Departments were asked to adopt the guidelines while submitting the plan
proposals for Ninth Five Year Plan and annual plan 1997-98. However, the Departments have
not done this exercise. The Committee in this connection heard the views of the Secretary,
Department of Expenditure to clarify the position. He informed the Committee that even
though communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the
committed expenditure in time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under
Demand No.31. The Department may approach the Department of Expenditure for their
share. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Department may complete the exercise at
the earliest so that they may not be handicapped on account of this. The Committee in this
connection also directs the Ministry of Finance to prepare a format and send it to all the
Ministries atleast one year before the termination of the plan period. The Departments should
be asked to identify the committed expenditure and send their proposals to Planning
Commission/Finance Ministry for consideration and approval, six month before the
termination of the plan. The Committee is also constrained to note that many Departments
have not done the exercise of identifying committed expenditure and to get it earmarked
separately for several plan periods. Accordingly, committed expenditure on the plan schemes
completed in 7th Plan or earlier and the assets created and staff employed in plan schemes has
been continuing on plan side resulting in severe resource crunch for the Department. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department, should make a thorough review of
the schemes and identify the committed liability. The Committee is very much surprised that
the guidelines given earlier were not followed at all. For this, responsibility should be fixed.

शा, ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES, NEW DELHI (AIIMS)

7.1, All India Institute of Medical Sciences has been set up by an Act of Parliament in
1956 as a premier institute to conduct experiments and research on various disciplines of
medical services. It has a bed strength of 1589. The Central Government provides 100%
Financial support to the Institute. x


7.2, An allocation of Rs.131 crores, (i.e. Rs.54 crores on plan side and Rs.77 crores on
the Non-Plan side) has been provided during the current year to the institute. The
Committee was given to understand that the equipments used in the institute are obsolete
and should be replaced. The Committee feels that AIIMS is the premier institute of this
country and should be equipped with the latest equipment for which there is a need for huge |
resources. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a one time liberal grant should be
provided to the apex institute for replacement of equipments, so that the patients could|
derive the benefit.

7.3. The Committee notes that some patients go out of the country for some super-
speciality services. The Committee is of the view that there is a need to develop one institute
in the country of international standard, with latest super-speciality facilities and equipments.
The Committee feels that AIIMS is the ideal institute which can be given the necessary fillip
to lift it to world standard.

7.4, The premier institution like AIIMS was set up for promoting high standards of
medical education and training and also for providing comprehensive medical care to the
people. These were originally thought of being only as referral hospital where patients would
be referred from other hospitals for specialised treatment of a higher order. In other words,
Institute would not entertain new patients in the OPDs. However, due to overcrowding and
lack of medical facilities in and around Delhi at various levels, it has lost referral character
and become just like any other hospital working at the District level.

7.5. The critical role that has been assigned to the referral system in National Health
Policy (NHP) deserves emphasis; for the PHC approach is predicated on the proposition that
only 5% of ailments need reach tertiary hospitals and the rest can be treated at primary and
through referral to secondary levels. Only through such an integrally related referral system,
the poorer sections of society, living in rural and remote areas, can get equitable access to
quality medical care and preventive public health measures.

7.6. The Committee is deeply concerned about the deteriorating standards of research
and patient care and this needs to be strengthened.

7.7. An efficient and organised referral system, the Committee feels, can be a good
edifice of a competent medical care available in all the lower level peripheral hospitals. This
means that hospitals and health centres in and around Delhi and also in the States have to
be sustained and simultaneously developed with adequate funds over a period of time, so
that a successful referral system can function in premier hospitals like AIIMS, New Delhi.
After considering various practical difficulties, the Committee is of the view that there must
be a clear objective to make it purely referral hospital by a fixed date, and all necessary
short and medium term problems must be sorted out within a definite timeframe. The
Committee is convinced that this decision brooks no delay and expects that appropriate
mechanism would be developed to achieve this.

X. CANCER RESEARCH

10.1. It is distressing to note that about 7 lakh new cases of cancer occur in the
country every year out of which two-third cases are in advance and incurable stage at the
time of diagnosis. It has been estimated that by the year 2026, cancer deaths in India will
be nearly threefold. The Secretary Department of Health informed the Committee that the
cancer control activities are being carried in the limited way because of the inadequate
resources.

10.2. For cancer research, there is a marginal increase in allocation i.e. from Rs. 18
crores in BE & RE 1996-97 to Rs. 20 crores in BE 1997-98. The Department while
explaining the adequacy of funds stated that the incidence of the Cancer in the country is
increasing as the life expectancy is going up and people are living longer. The most
common cancer amongst men is oral cancer and amongst females, it is cancer of cervix and
breast. The existing facilities for treatment in the country are grossly inadequate. There are
10 Regional Centres in the country which cover less than 10% of the population. Grants
being provided to these Regional Centres are to the extent of Rs. 50 lakhs per year for
developmental work. The cost of equipment and maintenance in the case of cancer
treatment is very high and it is being proposed that the grant to the Regional Centre be
enhanced from Rs. 50 lakhs to Rs. 75 lakhs. The Committee, however, desires that Cancer
diagnostic centres should be opened in all districts and referral centres should be at some
selected places. Necessary funds may therefore be provided for the purpose.

10.3. It has also been stated that providing Cobalt Unit to Medical Colleges and other
institutions for cancer treatment is a big problem. For a population of 1 million, the
requirement would be around 900 such units. At present there are 200 Cobalt Units
functioning in the country. This gap needs to be filled up. Similarly the funds required for
setting up a Department of Oncology in the Government Medical Colleges would be in the
range of Rs. 5 to 6 crores. Only 1.5 crores are provided to the Government Medical
Colleges for setting up Oncology wings. The funds required for providing adequate services


8

will be very large and the slight enhancement of Rs. 2 crores will only partly meet the
demand.

10.4. The Committee, therefore, feels that the marginal increase is grossly insufficient
in view of the growing incidence of cancer. Cancer requires a costly treatment. Majority of
our population affected by Cancer are poor people and they can not afford the treatment.
Government will have to step up its efforts to raise funds.

XII. MEDICAL EDUCATION

12.1. The Committee after considering the relevance of Medical curriculum to the
actual needs of doctors in the Indian conditions, feels that the medical curricula continue to

P. Falciparum variety of malaria in recent years. It has also been stated that intensified

an important cause responsible for high failure rates in development of drug resistant

XVII. NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME

17.1. The Committee is deeply troubled over the quick spread and future dangerous
potential of AIDS disease, which is not only incurable but is also capable of impairing the
defence mechanism of the body. The AIDS control programme was started in 1992. The
major thrust of the programme is towards screening the blood samples of high risk behaviour
groups and surveillance activities. The Secretary, Department of Health informed that till
November, 1996 a total of 2.95 million people had been screened out of whom 50984 were
found to be HIV positive. The number of confirmed cases are 3263. Seen against the fact
that 2.8 million persons had been screened upto June, 1996 and 23147 were found to be HIV


ine

positive, it would appear that between June, 1996 and November, 1996, 1.5 lakh people
were screened out of which 27837 were found to be HIV positive. The Committee draws the
attention of the Government to the false positive cases of HIV. The problem with the HIV
Tests which are being used in our country (ELISA & WESTERN BLOT) is that neither of
the test is specific to HIV. Both the tests react to many other proteins of other diseases. For
example the protein p24 generally accepted to be proof of existence of HIV, is also found in
all the retroviruses which are living in the human body and are not harmful.
Hepatitis 8 & C, Malaria, Papillomavirus warts, glandular fever, tuberculosis, syphillis and
leprosy are some of the few conditions that are capable of producing biological false
positives in ELISA Test. This means that all HIV positive cases will not lead to AIDS. But
once a person is found HIV positive he gets the social stigma. The Department must
therefore find out the incidence of False Positive cases and in that light modify its statistics
of HIV leading to AIDS. The Committee feels that this factor alone will modify the
estimates of the magnitude of the problem.

17.2. The results of the screening indicate that HIV infection has reached almost all
parts of the country. The existing surveillance mechanism is based on 62 HIV testing
laboratories. Designated as surveillance centres, located all over the country. The
Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over improper generation of data from these centres
and its inadequacy to meet rapidly changing trends. The Committee would like the
Department to carefully frame the data which can be generated from these centres keeping
in view the need for study of epidemeological trends, need for follow-up of AIDS cases and
utility data for research.

17.3. The Secretary also informed the Committee that HIV surveillance activities in the
country are being revamped by adopting sentinel surveillance methodology wherein few
selected sentinel sites and population would be screened (instead of a wide geographical
area) for HIV prevalance and trends with the active involvement of State AIDs cells. These
sites would represent not only high risk population groups but also low risks population
groups and data representing rural population. As there is no vaccination against AIDS, it is
of paramount importance to increase awareness among people about the mode of its
transmission, lack of any cure against it and existence of physical means to
prevent it.

17.4, The Committee however reiterates that this survey is not very effective and
foolproof. The Committee desires that the data collection should be strengthened and made
accurate.

17.5 The Committee also reiterates that a survey ‘should be got conducted through an
impartial and reliable agency to have an idea about the exact magnitude of the problem in
all the Metro towns beginning with Calcutta, Mumbai and Delhi.

17.6. The Committee is dismayed to note that allocation under the head National AIDS
Control Organisations has been reduced from Rs. 141 crores in BE 1996-97 to Rs. 100 crores
in RE 1997-98. Justifying the reduction, the Department stated that for 1997-98 the


12

organisation proposed an amount of Rs. 155 crores as per following components of the
programme:—

(Rs. in crores)

Programme Management 25.00

IEC including NGOs 80.00 (including 10
crores for NGOs)

Blood Safety 25.00

STD Control 10.00

Surveillence & Clinical 10.00

Management.
USAID APAC Project. 5.00

Tora: 155.00

17.7. The Department has further stated that against the proposed BE 1997-98, an
allocation of only Rs. 100 crores has been made, based on the total allocation of Rs. 400
crores (external aid component) for the Department in the annual plan 1997-98.

17.8. The Committee is not convinced with the justification in view of the worsening
AIDS scenario in the country, and feels that the provision should be restored to be last year
level.

XVIII. KALA AZAR CONTROL PROGRAMME

18. Kala Azar continues to be endemic in the States of West Bengal and Bihar. In its
last Report the Committee has emphasised the need for better co-ordination with State
Governments for more effective implementation of the Programme. The Committee is
concerned that the number of deaths has increased to 677 in 1996 from 382 in 1994. The
Committee has noted the efforts being made by the Central Government to bring about
more effective implementation on the part of the State Governments especially the
assessment carried out by expert team headed by Dr. A.K. Hati. The Committee would like
the Central Government to arrive at an early decision on the recommendation of the expert
team wherein it has been stated that possibilities of 100% central’ assistance should be
considered for the programme for effective control as the States have not been providing
adequate financial support.

XIX. TYPHOID

19. The Committee is concerned about the serious problem of Typhoid which has now
risen to greater heights than ever before. The Committee recommends that the Government
consider the feasibility of immunisation against Typhoid alongwith the Triple vaccine or
similar such strategy. The Haffkine Institute and the Haffkine Biopharmaceutical
Corporation must take up its earlier activity of manufacturing and supplying Typhoid
vaccine.

XX. EFFECTIVE HEALTH EDUCATION

20.1. The Committee feels that the poeple are not being given correct and factual health
information. There is a need for paying utmost attention for prevention of communicable
disease. The Committee is of the view that the level of knowledge about causes of these


13

diseases and their prevention is very low in the country. When the Department was asked to
make use of all forms of publicity and feed the people with health information, it has been
stated that as a part of IEC activities, Central Health Education Bureau has collaborated
with NFDC for telecasting health spots on Doordarshan. TV spots are also telecast under
various health programmes like National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme.
National Programme for control of Blindness etc. as a part of IEC activity under these
programmes. However, these telecasts are done on payment basis. As the telecasting of
health spots would be costly in the long run, there is need for Doordarshan to provide free
slots for telecasting health related issues. It has also been stated that at present there is no
proposal under consideration for an independent TV channel for community IEC activities
as it is felt that the scheme may not be economically viable.

20.2. The Committee recommends that adequate funds should be made available for IEC
activities as creating correct awareness about the epidemiological aspects of communicable
disease is critical for their prevention and eradication.

20.3. The Committee strongly advocates the need for having an independent TV channel
for community IEC activities in health sector.

XXI. PRIMARY HEALTH CENTRES

21.1. The functioning of Primary Health Centres in the rural areas is a cause of serious
concern for the Committee. As per the norms fixed by the Planning Commission, a Primary
Health Centre would cater 10 about 30,000 population. The Primary Health Centres are in
deplorable condition. There are no doctors not to talk of the other paramedical staff. The
Committee was given to understand that out of 21,853 PHCs, 1,136 PHCs are without
doctors. Even where the doctors have been posted, they are not regular and punctual in
attending to their duties. They do not stay in the villages and there is no provision for their
stay at these centres. Quite often, doctors posted in the Primary Health Centres are
reluctant to join their duties and manage to get their postings changed by using powerful
influences. The Committee feels that there should be exemplary punishment for such cases.
On the other hand, there are doctors who have been languishing in PHCs for years together
in the absence of any rotational transfer policy. There is no transfer policy worth the name
for the doctors in the Primary Helath Centres.

21.2. Often it is observed that there are no medicines available in the Primary Health
Centres. Even where the medicines are available, they are of either sub-standard quality or
date expired. In some of the Primary Health Centres, doctors are reported to be in league
with the private pathologists and recommend for unwarranted investigations so as to mint
money. Funds available for the Primary Health Centres are very meagre.

21.3. As per the norms followed, a Primary Centres should have 15 staff members
including one Medical Officer, one Pharmasist etc. The Committee is, however, constrained
to note that about 16 per cent of the Primary Health Centres do not have Doctors. In these
States in more than 30 per cent P.H.Cs. doctors are not available. The Committee has also
noted that a proposal is under consideration to utilise the services of private doctors through
their visits to the Centres twice or thrice a week. Ultimate goal should be that all the staff
particularly, doctors, should be in position in all P.H.Cs. It has been informed that the
appointments and posting of doctors at Primary Health Centres and Community Health
Centres are made by the State Governments. The Central Government has been impressing


14

upon the State Governments to ensure that all PHCs and CSCs have doctors and other staff
in position. In fact, the Central Council for Health and Family Welfare in a meeting held on
11-13 October, 1995 had passed the following resolution:

“The Council notes with great concern this severe scarcity of doctors in rural areas and
recommends that rural posting for a specific period be made compulsory and also a pre-
requisite before admission to postgraduate course.”

21.4, The Committee entirely agrees with the recommendation made by the Council.
The Committee recommends that out of the rotating internship of one year which is
mandatory after the Final MBBS, six months should be in the rural areas. The Committee
also feels that rural posting for a specific period from one year to five years should be a
precondition for promotions within the Health Services of the State and Centre.

21.5, The Committee feels that the functioning of the Primary Health Centre needs to
be thoroughly reviewed and revamped the malpractices prevailing in these centres should be
removed urgently. Sufficient funds should be made available for efficient functioning of
these centres. There should be regular and constant inspections by the senior doctors so as
to ensure their smooth and efficient functioning. The Committee also reiterates that the
Department should introduce a system and mechanism of foolproof monitoring both by the
Central and State Governments to plug these loopholes so as to put these PHCs in some
order.

21.6. The Committee draws the attention of the Government to the 250 page Report
prepared by the Expert Committee on the Public Health System headed by Shri J.S. Bajaj,
Member, Planning Commission. The Committee would like to know what action has been
taken on the recommendations of the Expert Group.

XXII. MONITORING MECHANISM

22.1. The approach paper to the Ninth Five Year Plan felt that more practical approach
to the programme foumulation, particularly for social sector programmes was to put the
lessons learnt from the experience to the implementation. The approach paper also felt that
in spite of the existence of an elaborate monitoring and evaluation system, the findings made
by the monitoring and evaluation system are not put to use. The Committee takes a very
serious note on this aspect and strongly recommends to the Department to first strengthen
the monitoring mechanism on various schemes and ensure strict implementation of the
findings made by the monitoring agencies. The Committee also observes with concern that
the schemes being taken up by the Central Government are not properly monitored by the
State Governments. Merely handing over the money and getting report from the State
Governments is not going to serve any purpose. The Committee is of the definite view that
thé State Governments, where the financial position is bad, divert the funds, given by the
Central Government for a particular scheme, to other purposes such as for giving salaries to
the employees of the State Government, etc. The Committee, therefore, desires that the
Centre should impress upon the States about the need to develop a mechanism to find out
whether the money being given to the States for implementation of various programmes is
utilised for the purpose specified and fix responsibility in case the purpose is defeated.

22.2 NGOs: There are certain areas where the Adivasis are the worst affected lot. The
Committee is constrained to note that not many NGOs are present in tribal areas. One will
find them mostly in areas where the atmosphere and the living conditions are very good.
They would not like to leave big and smaller cities and go into rural areas. The Adivasis are
mostly located in far-flung areas. The Committee, therefore, desires that NGOs which are
working in adivasi areas should be given encouragement.

+


15

22.3. There is no doubt-that there are committed and devoted NGOs in the field, but at
the same time, one cannot rule out the possibility of mushroom growth of NGOs which are
merely interested in getting assistance from the Government of India. The Department,
should, therefore, strengthen its monitoring mechanism to see whether they are working
properly or not and only those NGOs which have proven track record should be given
assistance.

XXII... GENERAL

23. Keeping in view the significant potential for transmission and spread of diseases like
AIDS etc., the Committee has constituted a Sub-Committee on Dreaded Diseases. In the
first instance, the Sub-Committee has decided to examine AIDS and Hepatitis-B. Another
Sub-Committee to make an indepth study on varios aspects of Drug Control has also been
constituted.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The National Health Policy of 1983 envisaged the necessity to initiate organised
measures to enable each of the systems of Indian Medicine i.e., Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,
Yoga and Naturopathy as well as Homoeopathy to develop in accordance with its genius,
and find an appropriate role and place for these different systems in the overall health care
delivery system for the benefit of the people. In order to achieve the said goal, a new
Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to
promote and develop the Indian Systems of Medicine (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,
Homoeopathy and Drugless Therapies like Yoga and Naturopathy).

1.2 The new Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H)
aims at strengthening the educational and research institutions of Indian Systems of
Medicine and Homoeopathy, Drug Standardisation and quality control, cultivation of
Medicinal plants, including research, establishment of Specialised ISM&H Centres, etc.

1.3 People of our country have faith in the traditional systems especially as the services
provided are generally cheaper and available everywhere and the remedies are known to be
generally free from side-effects. Further, India has a large resource of about 4.06 lakh
practitioners of ISM and 1.68 lakh practitioners of Homoeopathy, whose services need to be
fully utilised in the national health care delivery system. There are about 311 Under-
graduate and 47 Post-graduate Colleges of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy
producing about 13.292 graduates including diploma holders in Homoeopathy and 482 Post-
graduates every year.

1.4 The Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy have practically grown and
developed in the Indian society on the basis of learning through family traditions of Guru
Shishya Parampara, although a few colleges had come up in the late 19th century and the
earlier part of the 20th century. There was practically no Governmental support to this
system. There were no regulations either, regarding the practice and education standard.
Patients used to approach these indigenous physicians on the basis of faith in their skill,
knowledg- and integrity.

1.5 However, after Independence, institutions like Central Council of Indian Medicines
and Central Council for Homoeopathy were established to register practitioners in these
Systems and to lay down minimum standards for education. The Central Council of
Research in Ayurveda and Siddha, the Central Council of Unani Medicine, the Central
Council of Research in Homoeopathy, the National Institute of Ayurveda at Jaipur and the
National Institute of Homoeopathy at Calcutta have been set up as apex bodies for research
and teaching. In order to formulate Standards for Drugs, Pharmacopoeia Committees for
each of these Systems were set up and supported by the Pharmacopoeia Laboratories for
Indian Medicine (PLIM) and the Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia Laboratory (HPL) both
located at Ghaziabad, U.P. The Central Council of Indian Medicine (CIM) and the Central
Council of Homoeopathy (CCH) are responsible for laying down and maintaining uniform
standards of education and regulate the professional practices of the practitioners in the field
of Indian Systems of Medicines and Homoeopathy, respectively.

1

1664/RS F—3-A


Il. EIGHTH FIVE YEAR PLAN

2.1 The Eighth Plan outlay made for ISM&H was Rs. 88 crores. However, the
annual allocations made in all the years of the plan period comes to Rs. 104.44 crores.
The actual expenditure made by the Department is only 92.07 crores. This shows the
seriousness with which ISM&H division earlier and the ISM&H Department now has
been functioning. The Plan allocations made could not be utilised fully during the years
from . 1993-94 to 1996-97. It could utilise the actual allocations fully only in 1992-93.
Unless the Department is very serious in implementing the programmes and improving
the system, it will never be able to strengthen the efficient delivery of services.

2.2 The Department have stated that a comparison of expenditure, vis-a-vis,
allocation for the last two years, i.e. 1995-96, 1996-97 shows that there is a definite
improvement in the utilisation of funds. The Committee, however, is not satisfied with
this. The fact still remains that the full allocation could not be spent even during 1996-97
also. Out of the plan allocation of Rs. 23.19 crores, only Rs. 23.11 crores could be
spent. The Department also lags behind in achieving physical targets in some of the
schemes. Central Research Institute for Yoga could not achieve both physical and
financial targets in any of the years. Similarly, Central Council for Research in Yoga and
Naturopathy could not achieve the financial targets in 1992-93 and 1993-94. The
Department informed the Committee that there is a genuine need for increasing the plan
allocation for ISM&H sector as it has accumulated such deficiencies in almost all the vital
areas which are briefly as under:—

(i) Although there are Central Councils for Research for each of the disciplines and
functioning National Institutes for Ayurveda and Homoeopathy, each of them is
so inadequately provided that these organisations are barely able to maintain
themselves. They need sizeable resources for undertaking meaningful research and
for their continuous improvement.

(ii) The National Institute for Naturopathy at Pune is notionally in existence but it is
operating from only a large residential premises. It has been decided to set up
National Institute of Unani Medicine at Bangalore about 10 years back but
construction and setting up of the Institute has yet to take place.

(iii) The Pharmacopoeial Laboratories are operating from an office building of the
Government of India at Ghaziabad. Land has been allotted for these laboratories
in Ghaziabad. But, for want of resources construction has yet to begin. These
laboratories have a crucial role to play in determination and maintenance of
standards of ISM&H drugs.

(iv) The availability of genuine medicinal plants all over the country is very inadequate
and this is giving rise to spurious materials and their use in drugs. About 150
medicinal plants are already on the endangered list. A large scale initiative for
determination of package of practices for cultivation of medicinal plants and for
their actual large scale cultivation is urgently called for.

(v) There are serious doubts already raised about the quality of ISM&H drugs.
However, the work of determination of pharmacopoeial standards and testing
facilities in the country is substantially incomplete for want of resources. This
needs to be substantially accelerated in the interest of public health.

1664/RS F—3-B


(vi) The standard of ISM&H education in the country is poor. This is largely because
both the infrastructure and manpower resources available in the educational
institutions are grossly inadequate. A substantial step up of financial resources to
these institutions is urgently called for, for improving the standards of ISM&H
education.

2.3 The Committee does not understand as to how the Department and various
organisations created thereunder have been functioning with so many problems afflicting it.
It is a very sorry state of affairs. The whole world is now looking towards the Indian Systems
of Medicine in view of the effectiveness of the medicines and their having no side effects.
But it is unfortunate that our own country has not been able to strengthen our own systems
of medicine. The Committee is, therefore, of the strong view that unless something radical is
done by the Government, the systems cannot be improved and the Indian System of
Medicine will remain as they are now. The Committee also takes strong exception tc
underutilisation of funds as against the allocation made and non-achievement of physical
targets in some of the schemes. The Department will have to strengthen its monitoring
mechanism to ensure better functioning.

Ill. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

3. For the annual plan 1997-98, the Committee was informed that the Department
sought an outlay of Rs. 144.80 crores. However, the actual allocation made was Rs. 35.3
crores. In view of the various deficiencies being faced by the Department, the Committee is
of the firm belief that additional allocations are required to be provided. The Department
also should ensure better and full utilisation of the funds so that they are in a position to ask
for higher allocations in future.

IV. NINTH FIVE YEAR PLAN

4.1 With a view to evolve major thrust areas in the Ninth Five Year Plan the Planning
Commission had constituted a Working Group on Indian System of Medicine and
Homoeopathy to formulate the Ninth Five Year Plan (1997—2002) under the Chairmanship
of then Secretary, Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy. On the
basis of the report of the Working Group, the Department has formulated proposals in the
fields of:

(a) Upgradation of medical education facilities and improving standard of ISM&H
medical education;

(b) Research and development in the field of ISM&H;
(c) Standardisation of drugs of ISM&H and enforcing quality control on ISM&H drugs;
(d) Making available genuine raw materials for the manufacture of ISM&H drugs;

(e) Development of National Institutes in the field of ISM&H and apex institutions for
research and teaching;

(f) Setting up of intellectual property right cells;

(g) Strengthening of pharmacopoeia laboratory for research and testing of ISM&H
drugs.

4.2 The Department has submitted proposals for an outlay of Rs. 1997.85 crores during
the 9th Five Year Plan to the Planning Commission for development and better utilisation of
ISM assistance for achieving the goal ‘Health for All’ by 2000 A.D.


Vv. AYURVEDA

5. The allocation made for Ayurveda was Rs. 19.13 crores in BE last year which was raised
to Rs. 19.93 crores in RE. This has slightly been increased to Rs. 20.25 crores in 1997-98. This
includes provision for (i) National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur which is expected to serve as a
model institute for teaching training, research and patient-care, (ii) Central Council for
Research in Ayurveda and Siddha, and (iii) maintenance and development grants-in-aid to
Institute of P.G. Training and Research, Jamnagar, a constituent of Gujarat Ayurvedic and
Rashtriya Ayurveda Vidyapeeth, New Delhi. The Committee agrees that as in the case of other
system of medicine, Ayurveda also faces lot of resource crunch. Ayurveda is the oldest Indian
systems of medicines and has good qualities of acceptability and no side-effects. But much work
is not being done on the research and manufacturing of medicines. The Committee desires that
the allocation may be increased sufficiently and the research findings be made public proper
publicity should also take place.

Vill. YOGA AND NATUROPATHY

8. For Yoga and Naturopathy, the BE for 1996-97 on the Plan side was Rs. 1.30
crores, which was reduced to Rs. 1.20 crores in the RE 1996-97. However, it has been

the National Institute of Yoga (NIY) by merging the Central Research Institute for Yoga
(CRIY) with the proposed Institute. Accordingly, as against Rs. 35 lakhs provided for


CRIY in BE 1996-97. Rs. 5 lakhs only are provided/proposed for CRIY in RE 1996-97 and
BE 1997-98.

IX. MEDICAL EDUCATION

9.1 The Committee was informed that the Department has taken steps to check the
growth of new sub-standard colleges in the country. It was stated that the Health Ministry
has taken a decision that no new colleges of ISM&H should be started without the prior
approval of Government of India. The Committee also feels that the prior approval of the
concerned council should be taken besides that of Government of India. The Department of
ISM&H will scrutinise the project reports regarding the infrastructure etc. Letters to the
Presidents of CCIM & CCH have been written in this regard.

9.2 Guidelines to establish a new college and also implement the minimum standards of
infrastructure and education in the existing colleges have been formulated by the CCIM.
Government will notify these norms within 2 months after receiving from CCIM & CCH.

9.3 CCIM had made visits to various colleges and decided to stop admission in sub-
standard colleges from the next financial year.

9.4 The Committee strongly recommends that a task force should be formed to identify
these colleges and suggest suitable action against them. The names of defaulting sub-
standard colleges should be published in the regional and National dailies. The Committee
also advocates that the Universities should not give affiliation to these colleges unless they
get permission from respective Central Councils and State Governments.

9.5 The Committee is pained to note that some colleges under ISM & H charge huge
amounts as donation/capitation fee at the time of admission. The Committee strongly feels
that there is urgent need to stop this wrong practice.

X. NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS

10.1 The Committee notes that availability of herbs and medicinal plants sufficiently is
the basic ingredient of the Indian systems of medicines. The forest and arid land can be
made better use of by planation of herbs and medicinal plants. There are as many as 150
plants on the endangered list. The Committee, with the idea that in order to maintain the
efficacy of traditional medicines, recommended last year that it was essential to preserve and
cultivate the medicinal plants and herbs by starting plantation on a large scale. The State-
Governments would also make land available for such plantations. On this the Department
have stated that the existing scheme of financing Government and autonomous institutions
to grow certain species of medicinal plants was modified, in order to lay emphasis on
developing agro techniques for growing of medicinal plants, etc. This scheme has been
approved and Rs. 80.00 lakhs have been reappropriated in the current year. This amount
will be utilised to select institutions having infrastructure and the expertise to develop agro-
techniques for medicinal plants. A proposal is also under examination to establish vanaspati
Vans on 100 acres plot in each state in denuded forest areas throughout the country during
the Ninth Plan, it was added. The Committee desires that early decision may be taken on
the proposal of Vanaspati Vans. It was also stated that a conference of the Health Ministers
from different States was held on 18th February, 1997 and resolutions were passed for
increasing the availability of raw materials utilised in the ISM & H. Some of the steps
recommended are:—

“Listing of medicinal substances, survey and collection of medicinal substances,
their germ plasm, folklore, in situ conservation through protection from


7

exploitation, through cultivation and introduction in natural habitats, cooperative
farming, creation of central aurborems, setting up of vanaspati vans, etc. The plan
provision has also been increased for this purpose. Waste land also will be utilised
for purpose of growing medicinal plants.”

The Committee desires that action Plan may be initiated on the above steps.

XI. POOR QUALITY OF DRUGS

11.1 The manufacturers of the drugs under ISM & H do not have sophisticated and
latest technology for ensuring meticulous standards required for the preparation of drugs.
The Committee was given to understand that lot of spurious material was being used by the
manufacturers of traditional drugs. As regards Standardisation of ISM Drugs the
Department stated that there are Pharmacopeia Committees in individual systems, for
Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy systems. These were set up separately for each.
These Committees lay down the composition and the standards for individual drug. The
Pharmacopoeia Committee for Ayurveda has so far published two volumes of formularies
covering 634 drugs. Unani Formulary has 441 drugs and Siddha formulary has 248 classical
drugs. Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeia Committee has decided standards for 710 drugs in
6 volumes. Out of 634 mentioned in Ayurvedic Formulary of India, standards on
80 single plant origin drugs had been published in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Par-I
(Vol. I). Monographs on 70 single drugs are ready for publication and about 75 drugs are in
pipeline on which work has been done by Pharmacopoeial Laboratory for Indian Medicines,
Ghaziabad.

11.2 The Department, however stated that a large part of the work remains yet to be
done largely because the laboratories to support the work of the Pharmacopoeia Committee
have been weak and inadequate in the past. There is one Pharmacopoeial Laboratory for
Indian Medicines and another Homoeopathic Pharmacopoeial Laboratory both at Ghaziabad
but both are working from rented premises with laboratory equipment and scientists staff
being inadequate at present. These deficiencies are now being attempted to be rectified, it
was added. It was also stated that now Department of ISM & H has decided to complete the
task on remaining medicines within Ninth Five Year Plan. A new Central Scheme for
functioning of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Pharmacopoeia Committees to develop
pharmacopoeial standards for ISM durgs has been formulated and implemented during
1996-97. Accordingly, 17 institutions/Research laboratories have been allotted funds to the
tune of Rs. 60 lakhs for laying down the standards on approximately 170 Ayurveda, Siddha
and Unani Plant origin drugs. For standardisation of remaining Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani
drugs, other 100 institutions/Research laboratories are being identified. The Committee
strongly recommends that all the deficiencies be removed immediately.

11.3 In regard to quality control, the Committee was informed that to safeguard public
health, Government has taken several measures. One important measure is prevention of
sub-standard drugs or adulteration in ISM drugs and maintenance of high standards of
quality in ISM drugs. For this, Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 was enacted and Rules were
made thereunder known as Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. It is a Central legislation. It
regulates the (i) Import (ii) manufacture (iii) sales and distribution and (iv) standards of
Drugs and Cosmetics. The Drugs and Cosmetic Act, 1940 was amended in 1964 (effective
from 8.12.1969) and Chapter IV-A was added in this Act for licensing and quality control of
the manufacturing of ISM Drugs for sale in the market. All necessary provisions of this Act
in Chapter IV-A were further amended in 1982 in which definitions of misbranded/
adulterated and spurious ISM drugs were given and penalty prescribed. To exercise control


8

over drugs of ISM, two drugs organisations are functioning. The first one is the Central
Drugs Standard Control Organisation of the Government of India headed by Drug
Controller General (India) which is responsible for controlling the quality of drugs imported
into the country. The second one is the State Drug control organisation in each State. This
organisation is responsible for exercising quality control over drugs manufactured, sold or
distributed in its territory so as to ensure that people can get ISM drugs of standard quality.
The Drugs Control Cell (ISM) under Department of ISM & H has been set up in May 1992
to assist the Drug Controller General (India) to look after all the work of quality control of
ISM drugs. In addition, statutory Committees/Board as provided under the Drugs and
Cosmetics Act namely, Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani Drugs Technical Advisory Board have
been set up. The Committee is of the view that there should be a separate Drug Controller
for ISM Medicines with sufficient powers.

XII. NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF AYURVEDA, JAIPUR

12. The allocation made for National Institute of Ayurveda for 1997-98 is Rs. 2.00
crores which was the same allocated last year. The Institute has been facing many problems
from several fronts. The Committee visited the Institute and has given a separate report.
The Secretary, during the course of her oral evidence stated that several measures were
taken to re-vitalise the Institute. The Committee would examine the Action Taken Report as
and when received on its report and would give a separate report.

XII. STRENGTHENING OF RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT

13.1 There are four Research Councils, viz. Central Council for Research in Ayurveda,
Central Council of Research in Unani Medicine, Central Council for Research in Yoga and
Naturopathy and Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy. These Councils initiate aid,
guide, develop and coordinate scientific research in the respective systems.

13.2 The Committee is, however, constrained to note that no research activity worth the
name is carried out by these institutions. The Committee strongly feels the need for research
and development in the medicinal plants within the country rather than importing them. The
Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Department to accelerate and strengthen the pace
of research activities. The Committee also feels that the research activities cannot be ignored
due to resource constraints and, recommends that sufficient amount needs to be earmarked
to the Institutes for this purpose. The Committee also feels that the research should be more
field oritented. Further, the infrastructure of the research centres should be adequately
strengthended. Research findings should be given adequate publicity and be made available
to the public.

XIV. SIDDHA

14.1 When the Department was asked to comment as to how long will it take to set up
National Institute of Siddha, it was stated that the matter in regard to size and location of
plot of land on which the National Institute of Siddha (NIS) is to be constructed is still
under finalisation in consultation with the Government of Tamil Nadu. The nature of
participation of Government of Tamil Nadu is under discussion with that Government;
hence a token provision has been made in BE 1997-98 which will be reviewed at RE stage of
1997-98 for enhancing budgetary provision if required.

14.2 If land and funds are available, the NIS will be set up during Ninth Five Year Plan,
it was added.

14.3 The Committee feels that the various problems being faced by Siddha system


9

should be identified early. The Committee looks forward to the development of Siddha and
hopes its allocation would be enhanced suitably. The Committee also hopes that suitable
steps should be taken for setting up of National Institute of Siddha in Tamil Nadu at an
early date.

XV. NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF HOMOEOPATHY, CALCUTTA

This is the only Homoeopathy Institute in the Country which is run by the Central
Government. Many patients are turning forwards Homoeopathy due to low cost of treatment
with little or no side effects. But the Institute has been facing many problems. In view of
this the Committee visited the Institute and gave a separate report. The Committee will
again examine the functioning of the Institute in detail after the Action Taken note is
received. The Institute has got Rs. 1.10 crores which is a repetition of the allocation made
last year. The Committee feels that it needs to be increased.

XVI. PATENT CELL

The Committee was given to understand that a decision has been taken to establish a
patent cell. Provision of Rs. 10 lakhs has been kept in 1997-98 for its establishment. The
Secretary informed the Committee that a Committee to do the preliminary work has been
set up in this regard. The Committee hopes that the preliminary work would be completed
soon.

XVII. INTERNATIONAL CELL

The Committee feels that traditional systems of medicine akin to ISM & H are also
prevalent in other countries particularly China, Japan and Germany etc. It would therefore
be helpful to have international co-operation and coordination in the related systems. hence,
the Department may set up an international cell to look into these issues.

XVII. GENERAL

18.1 Monitoring mechanism : The approach paper to the Ninth Five Year Plan felt that
more practical approach to the programme forumulation, particularly for social sector
programmes was to put the lessons learnt from the experience to the implementation. The
approach papers also felt that in spite of the existence of an elaborate monitoring and
evaluation system, the findings made by the monitoring and evaluation system are not put to
use. The Committee takes a very serious note on this aspect and strongly recommends to the
Department to first strengthen the monitoring mechanism on various schemes and ensure
strict implementation of the findings made by the monitoring agencies. The Committee also
observes with concern that the schemes being taken up by the Central Government are not
properly monitored by the State Governments. Merely handing over the money and getting
report from the State Governments is not going to serve any purpose. The Committee is of
the definite view that the State Governments, where the financial position is bad, divert the
funds, given by the Central Government for a particular schemes, to other purposes such as
for giving salaries to the employees of the State Government, etc. The Committee therefore,
desires that the Centre should impress upon the States about the need to develop a
mechanism to find out whether the money being given to the States for implementation of
various programmes is utilised for the purpose specified and fix responsibility in case the
purpose is defeated.

18.2 NGOs : There are certain areas where the Adivasis are the worst affected lot. The
Committee is constrained to note that not many NGOs are present in tribal areas. One will
find them mostly in areas where the atmosphere and the living conditions are very good.
They would not like to leave big and smaller cities and go into rural areas. The Adivasis are


10

mostly located in far-flung areas. The Committee, therefore, desires that NGOs which are
working in adivasi areas should be given encouragement.

18.3 There is no doubt that there are committed and devoted NGOs in the field, but at
the same time, one cannot rule out the possibility of mushrocm growth of NGOs which are
merely interested in getting assistance from the Government of India. The Deptt. should,
therefore, strengthen its monitoring mechanism to see whether they are working properly or
not and only those NGOs which have proven track record should be given assistance.

XIX. COMMITTED LIABILITY

19.1 The Committee has noted that the committed liability of the plan schemes has not
been reflected in the budgetary allocations for 1997-98 which is the first year of the Ninth
Plan. The Committed expenditure which is accounted in the subsequent plan at the
termination of the previous plan is taken out from the plan and becomes a separete
committed expenditure. If this is not done, the Departments will be handicapped by this
amount of plan expenditure. The exercise of identifying committed liability has not been
done by any of the Departments for 1997-98. Committee in this connection has considered
the report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance Commission have observed
in this regard as under :

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan
scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of
8th Plan scheme completed in the next two financial years would have to be
provided for. The Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning
Commission may consider providing for the maintenance of such schemes till
1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans
of 1990-91 and 1991-92”.

19.2 The Committee was also given to understand that the Planning Commission issued
circular to all the Departments dated November 5, 1996 sending therewith guidelines for
classification of expenditure. The Ministries were also requested to make necessary provision
as committed non-plan expenditure for the upkeep of existing assets etc. Accordingly, all the
Ministries/Departments were asked to adopt the guidelines while submitted the plan
proposals for Ninth Five Year Plan and annual plan 1997-98. However, the Departments
have not done this exercise. The Committee in this connection heard the views of the
Secretary, Department of Expenditure to clarify the position. He informed the Committee
that even though communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not
identify the committed expenditure in time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been
provided under Demand No. 31. The Department may approach the Department of
Expenditure for their share. The Committees, therefore, desires that the Department may
complete the exercise at the earliest so that they may not be handicapped on account of this.

19.3 The Committee is also constrained to note that many Departments have not done
the exercise of identifying committed expenditure and to get it earmarked separately for
several plan periods. Accordingly, committed expenditure on the plan schemes completed in
7th Plan or earlier and the assets created and staff employed in plan schemes has been
continuing on plan side resulting in severe resource crunch for the Department. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make a thorough review of
the schemes and identify the committed liability. The Committee is very much surprised that
the guidelines given earlier were not followed at all. For this, responsibility should be fixed.
