written memoranda have opposed the proposal of restricting the age limit for providing free
compulsory education between 6 to 14 years of age. According to them Article 45 which is
sought to be deleted, was framed by the founding fathers to provide education to children
upto the age of 14 years without mention of a lower limit and deletion of Article 45 without
simultaneously making a provision for the education of children under 6 years will be
tantamount to taking away the rights sought to be given to this age group by the founding
fathers.

7. As regards limiting the age at 14 years also, many representationists expressed the
view that it should be increased from 14 to either 16 or 18. The general feeling was that at the
time of framing of Article 45, the formal certification of school education was at standard 7th
and the founding fathers had set the limits of free and compulsory education for the child
one year beyond the age at which standard 7th could be completed. However in the present
scenario, a child can finish education up to standard 8th within the age of 6-14 years and no
more. The current educational pattern have no formal certification of completion of school
studies until the successful completion of standard 10th. This means that the child who
cannot afford education except when it is free will have to discontinue her/his education
before formal certification. This closes further avenues of learning or employment. It was,
therefore, prayed that the age limit should be increased upto 16 years. On this the Secretary,
Education stated that the Department, after agonising over this issue for a very long time,
thought that though this issue could not be ignored, but while coming to a situation where
it becomes as justiciable fundamental right, what is possibly enforceable is the age-group
i.e., after 6 years when one enters into a formal system. Prior to that, it is very essential, very
necessary, but it is entirely a different evercise and a big problem as to how it can be
converted into a structure, pattern under which it can be enforced as a fundamental right.

8. It was informed by the Department of Education to the Committee that the
Constitutional amendments to make elementary education a Fundamental Right enforceable
against the State and a Fundamental Duty of parents would need to be backed by suitable
statutory measures for making elementary education compulsory. At present there is no
Central Legislation making elementary education compulsory. About having a Central
Legislation, the Secretary stated that the question was debated extensively by the Committee
of Ministers. The Committee of Ministers, after some discussions, came to the conclusion
that in this land of enormous diversity, it would be, perhaps, undesirable to go in for a Central
Legislation which may not be able to take care of the requirements and specific needs of the
States. The consensus was clearly in favour of State legislation, he added.

9. Most of the experts were of the view that the term ‘free’ needs to be clearly defined.
They felt that it should not mean a mere non-payment of fees but should also include one
meal, books notebooks/slates, medical assistance, transport where needed and above all
guaranteed presence of a teacher and a school. The Committee was given to understand that
free education, so far, has been equated with the exemption of tuition fees which is negligible
in the case of students in primary and upper primary schools run by Government and local
bodies, the consensus which emerged was that there should be, at least, free tuition up to the
primary stage, for both boys and girls. If certain States are in a position to provide additional
incentives, they can do it. But in so far as the common understanding is concerned, the
minimum is, up to the primary level, free tuition and free books, he added. As regards the
question of providing free stationery, he clarified that there was no clear consensus.

10. One of the main apprehensions voiced by the eminent educationists was that the
State cannot provide a fundamental right to compulsory education. Only a right to education
can be provided. The wording free and compulsory education is in consonance with the
spirit of directive principles but while shifting this article to the fundamental rights, this
compulsion does not go well with the concept of right. the Secretary Education clarified that
the compulsion more or less, is being looked at as compulsion of the State Government to
provide basic facilities which the Government must provide.

11. Clause (3) of the proposed Article 21 provides that the State shall not make any
law for free and compulsory education under Clause (2), in relation to the educational

institutions not maintained by the State or not receiving aid out of State funds. However,

" strong apprehensions were voiced about clause (3) of the proposed new Article 21A. Many
of the people in the written memoranda and also educational experts in the oral evidence
have expressed displeasure over keeping the private educational institutions outside the
purview of the fundamental right to be given to the children. The Secretary, stated that the
Supreme Court in the Unnikrishnan judgement said that wherever the State is not providing
any aid to any institution, such an institution need not provide free education. The Department
took into account the Supreme Court judgement in the Unnikrishnan case which laid down
that no private institution, can be compelled to provide free services. Therefore, they provided
in the Constitutional amendment that this concept of free education need not be extended to
schools or institutions-which are not aided by the Government, the Secretary added. He,
however, stated that there was no intention, to exclude them from the overall responsibility
to provide education.

12. The total additional financial requirement estimated to be incurred is Rs. 7,200.00
crore per annum in case the fundamental right to elementary education is operationalised.
Some educationists felt that the amount may increase. But they suggested that if all irrelevant
and non-priority wasteful expenditure on elementary education can be done away with, it will
be possible to fulfil the commitment.

13. The eminent Educationists felt that the Bill is silent on the Quality of Education.
They suggested that there should be a reference to quality of education in the Bill. The
Secretary, Education agreed that the quality aspect also has to be seen. Education definitely
must mean quality education and anything less than that should not be called edutation.
Therefore, the emphasis would be through strengthening the teacher education content, the
Secretary stated.

14. The proposed insertion of Article 51A, provides for a fundamental duty of every
citizen who is a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to all children upto
14 years of age. Apprehensions have been expressed by the educationists that compulsion
on parents as a result of this Article. would pose major problem, particularly for those
parents who ostensibly cannot afford to send their children to school. Defaulting parents
would be subject to considerable harassment resulting in widespread resentment among the
general population. The Secretary, Education, on being asked to cotnment on this, informed
the Committee that the Constitutional amendment as such is not talking about penalising the
parents. But there are already certain existing State legislations in different States which do
have penal provision. When this issue came up before the Saikia Committee, they took the
view that the emphasis should be on the motivation of parents. But, in an extreme case,
where there are aberrations, a penalty should be resorted to as a last resort. But, there again,
the Saikia Committee felt that instead of bringing it under the provisions of the Indian Penal
Code, it should be taken to the court of society, the Secretary added.

15. OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

15.1. The Committee welcomes the initiative of the Government to make the right to
free elementary education a Fundamental Right. It is indeed a welcome step. Inspite of a large
number of schemes taken up for universalisation of elementary education since independence,
it is unfortunate that the country is still languishing with a sizeable number of illiterates. The
high drop-out rate has resulted in total disarray in the implementation of the education
programmes. Reasons for high drop-out rates are varied-social, economic, quality, lack of
interest and jack of attraction can be cited as a few examples. It is unfortunate that the drop-
out rate in 1996-97 in class I to V was as high as 39.37%. This explains the state of affairs
obtaining in the country. The Committee hopes that the amendment of the Constitution to
provide free education to children as a fundamental right would motivate both Governmental
as well as non-Governmental sectors to take necessary measures so as to achieve
universalisation of elementary education, the ultimate goal of the country. The Committee
welcomes the spirit behind the amendment and welcomes it in principle.


15.2. However, the Committee feels that in the enthusiasm to provide this fundamental
right, the quality of education should not be ignored. The education that is provided should
be able to create attraction and interest among the children. The Committee understands that
the National Policy on Education makes a reference to ‘education of satisfactory quality’.
Quality is the most important aspect of education which should not be ignored. The Committee
strongly feels that quality aspect has been totally forgotten and children who can afford are
compelled to go to private institutions for better and quality education. There is, therefore, a
necessity of improving the quality. For this, there is an urgent necessity to improve teacher
training. In regard to the point as to whether there should be a reference to ‘Quality’ in the
proposed amendment, the Committee feels it appropriate to leave it to the Government to
either make a reference to quality aspect in the proposed amendment or not. The Committee,
however, strongly recommends that all efforts should be directed towards providing quality
education. Teacher training programmes are not very much oriented for effective utilisation
of human resources. They do not give stress on techniques and activities that make learning
joyful for students. Lack of follow up measures make them forget and not utilise whatever
they had learnt during their pre-service training programmes. Without primary level teaching
or research experience, particularly on rural school, teacher educators are poorly prepared to
educate. Most of the teacher educators imparting training in elementary teacher training
institutions do not have primary level teaching/research experience. This affects the quality
of training imparted by them. The methods of transaction of theory classes of these teacher
educators are generally devoid of active teaching learning approaches. There is no specific
teacher educator preparation programmes. Teacher educators also need continued assistance
for their professional development. The UGC provides assistance for professional
development of teacher educators in teacher training colleges and departments of education
of universities. But such facilities are at present not available for elementary level teacher
educators. The Committee accordingly recommends that teacher training should be given
sufficient importance and emphasis should be laid on improving the training component.

15.3. The Committee takes note of the fact that the words compulsion and enforcement
as proposed in Article 21A do not go with the theme and spirit of the Fundamental Right. A
right is not given in a spirit of enforcement. The Secretary's clarification that the compulsion
is being looked at as compulsion on the part of the State Government, is an acceptable
proposition. But it should be made amply clear in the proposed amendment to clear all
doubts.

15.4. The Committee understands it well that with elementary education becoming a
justiciable Fundamental Right, the possibility of increased litigation cannot be denied. The
citizens wor! # have every right to go the courts of law if their fundamental right is violated.
The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to find out ways and means to face
this challenge.

15.5. The current education pattern has formal certification after the successful
completion of standard 10th only. This, therefore, means that the children who cannot get
education except when it is free, will have to discontinue their studies before formal
certification, thus closing their further avenues of earning and employment. Thus suggestions
received by Committee were either to extend the age-limit upto 16 years or certification may
be issued at the end of Eighth standard. The Committee, however, feels that increasing the
age limit may not be a viable proposition because of enormous resources that are required
and due to other compulsions of the Government. The Members discussed this at length.
Many Members were of the opinion that it would not be appropriate to put such a heavy
burden on the Government. However, a child should be able to receive some sort of certificate
soas to easily get a gainful employment. The Committee, therefore, feels that the Government
may introduce formal certification at the end of standard 8th to enable the children who come
out of the school after 8th to join some gainful employment or pursue some technical vocational
courses with the help of the certificate. Several Members, however, felt that it may not be
advisable to introduce another Public examination.


5

15.6. As regards follow-up legislation, there are divergent views. Some Members of the
Committee felt that there should be a separate central legislation providing for the basic
structure and the details could be made out by the respective States. Whereas the others did
not feel the necessity of a central legislation. The Secretary, stated that the central legislation
may not be able to take care of the requirements and specific needs of the States. After a
thorough discussion in the matter, the Committee feels that the Centre should not leave
everything to the States. The Centre could make one simple legislation with some skeletal
framework which may also indicate the Central share in the financial burden. The details can
be formulated by the respective States according to their requirements. The Central
Government may, therefore, consider working out the necessary legislation.

15.7. Imposition of penalties on parents is one aspect which has agitated the minds of
the Members. The Committee agrees that the penal provision would lead to harassment of
the parents. It is true that the proposed amendment does not talk of any penalty, but many
States in their existing legislations have made penal provisions. Accordingly, the new follow
up legislations may also have similar provisions. After considering the pros and cons of this,
the Committee strongly desires that such penal provisions on the parents should be avoided
in the follow up legislation to be made. The Centre may make necessary provision to this
effect either in the follow up legislation or in the guidelines that may be issued to the States.
The Committee feels that compulsion should be on State Governments to provide for essential
facilities for UEE rather than on the parents, majority of whom are struggling for their survival.

15.8. Providing free education is another important aspect in the proposed Article 21
A(1). On this, the Committee takes note of the fact that the bill does not define free education.
The Committee understands that there is confusion over the provision of free education.
Many States are already providing free education, but the components vary from State to
State. The Committee has noted that there is a general feeling that free education means
exemption from payment of fees. The Members were, however, unanimous that free education
should not confine just to exemption from payment of fees. The Committee desires that free
education should also include various other components such as text-books, stationery,
uniform, one meal and transportation wherever necessary etc. The Government may consider
including all these components in the free education.

15.9. Financial implications is another important aspect of the Bill. In the Financial
memorandum, the Committee has noted that the estimated financial expenditure to implement
the obligation is forty thousand crores rupees every year. The Committee is constrained to
note that the allocations, made to education every year have so far been very insufficient.
From such a situation to go upto Rs. 40,000 crores, in the Ninth Plan is a gigantic task. The
Committee strongly recommends that the required amount should be allocated to achieve
the goal. Unless this is done, a mere constitutional amendment and providing a fundamental
right is not going to serve the purpose. Besides increasing the allocation, Government may
also take steps to reduce unnecessary expenditure to reduce unnecessary burden on the
State's exchequer.

15.10. The Committee feels that financial burden may be shared by both the Centre
and the States. Administrative responsibility should be left to states for implementation
according to their convenience.

15.11. The proposed Article 21A (1) provides that the State shall provide free and
compulsory education to all citizens of the age of six to fourteen years. The Committee
understands that there is a lot of controversy over the restriction of age limit of the children
between 6-14 years of age. It is true that this provision seeks to take away the rights of the
children in the age group 0-6 years. The Committee is, however, aware that an infant's
education in the age group 0-6 is an enormously complicated one. Much of the education
imparted in this age group is non-formal through the mother and it is difficult to standardise
it. It is all the more difficult to make it a justiciable Fundamental Right. The Committee is also
aware that the Departments of Women & Child Development and Family Welfare are already
working to take care of the requirements of the children in this age group. The controversy
in this regard has arisen because Article 45 does not make any mention of age restriction

प,्5॥॥७६॥-+#


whereas Article 21A (1) seeks to restrict the age to 6-14 years. The proposal also includes
deletion of Article 45, As regards deletion of Article 45, the Committee deals with it in the
succeeding paragraph. Coming to Article 21 A(1), the Committee takes note of the fact that
it is propoged to be included in the chapter III, which provides fundamental right. Due to
various practical difficylties, the provision in the present Article may be allowed, providing
for free education to children of 6 to 14 years in the fundamental right. But Directive Principles
should be followed wherever possible.

15,12, Now, the Committee will deal with the proposal to delete Article 45, The
Committee is not convinced by the reply of the Secretary, Education, that this has been done
on the advice of the Law Ministry that after it is made a fundamental right, Article 45 becomes
redundant, The Directive Principles, of which Article 45 is a part, were incorporated in the
Constitution with an objective of seeking to achieve the ideal of a democratic welfare state
set out in the preamble. This also embodies the object of the state. They are directed towards
the ideals of building a true welfare State,

15,13, Therefore the Committee feels that by providing a fundamental right, the very
philosophy of the Constitution which is embodied in the Directive Principle (Article 45)
should not be removed. The purpose of a fundamental right is different from that of the
Directive Principle. The Directive Principle is not merely a moral precept but is a positive
mandate to the State, Article 45 provides a directive on the State to endeavour to provide free
and compulsory education, No conflict should be seen between the Fundamental Right and
Directive Principle, Both are complementary to each other, Similarly, proposed Article 21A
seeks to provide Fundamental right to free and compulsory education to the citizens in the
age group 6-14 at present, However, Article 45 seeks to provide free education to all upto the
age of 14 years without any age restriction, Therefore, Article 45, besides, giving a directive
on the state to provide free education and explain the object and philosophy of the
Constitution, also takes care of the children in the age group 0-6 as well, In view of the
forgoing conclusions, the Committee feels that Article 45 is required to be retained in the
Constitution. The Government may, therefore, reconsider its proposal to delete Article 45,

15.14. Clause (3) of the proposed Article 21(A) prohibits the State from making any
law for free and compulsory education in relation to educational institutions not maintained
by the State or not receiving aid out of state funds. This issue was discussed by the Members
of the Committee at length. The Members were in agreement that even though the so called
private institutions do not receive any financial aid, the children studying in those institutions
should not be deprived of their fundamental right. As regards the interpretation as to whether
the private institutions should provide free education or not, the Committee is aware of the
Supreme Court Judgement given in the Unni Krishnan case. This judgement provides the
rule for application and interpretation. In view of the judgement, it is not necessary to make
aclause in the Constitution. It would be appropriate to leave the interpretation to the courts
instead of making a specific provision in black and white. Some Members, however, felt that
the private institutions which do not get any financial aid, provide quality education. Therefore,
it would be inappropriate to bring such institutions under the purview of free education. Those
members, accordingly, felt that Clause (3) should not be deleted.

15.15. The Committee, however, after a thorough discussion feels that this provision
need not be there. The Committee recommends that clause (3) of the proposed Article 21 (A)
may be deleted. Smt. Hedwig Michael Rego, M.P., a Member of the Committee gave a Minute
of Dissent. It is appended to the report.

15.16. The Committee recommends that the Bill be passed subject to the
recommendations made in the preceding paragraphs.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS

The founding fathers of our Constitution made a provision imposing an obligation,
under article 45 in Part IV relating to the Directive Principles of State Policy, upon the State to
endeavour to provide within a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution,
for free and compulsory education for children up to fourteen years of age. However, this
goal has proved elusive so far. Our inability to achieve this goal 37 years after the target
period has been a cause for serious concern. Reiterating the constitutional directive, the
National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986, as modified in 1992, states that free and compulsory
elementary education of satisfactory quality shall be provided to all children up to the age of
fourteen years before we enter the 21st century. The Supreme Court in its judgment in Unni
Krishnan J.P. vs. State of Andhra Pradesh, A.I.R. 1993 S.C. 2178, has held that children of
this country have a fundamental right to free education until they complete the age of
fourteen years. The Common Minimum Programme of the United Front Government, resolves
to make right to free and compulsory elementary education a fundamental right and to
enforce it through suitable statutory measures.

2. The Committee of Education Ministers which was set up to examine the implications
of the aforesaid resolution have recommended that the Constitution be amended to make the
Right to Free and Compulsory Education from six to fourteen years of age as a fundamental
right and to make a fundamental duty of parents to provide opportunities for education to
their children of this age group. Consequent thereupon, provision in the nature of compulsory
and free education as a Directive Principles of State Policy under article 45 is no more
required. States and Union territories would be required to enact laws for the enforcement of
free and compulsory education within one year from the commencement of the Constitution
(Eighty-third Amendment) Act, 1997.

3. The amendment of the Constitution to provide for compulsory education of children
as a fundamental right would demonstrate the necessary political will and administrative
resolve of the country to achieve Universalisation of elementary education and to eradicate
illiteracy. This historical amendment of the Constitution in the 50th year of our independence
should inspire the Nation to meet the daunting challenge of achieving the goal of education
for all by 2000 AD.

4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The main function of the Department of Education is to evolve educational policy
and also to coordinate and determine standards in higher education, including research. The
Department mainly undertakes the Programmes relating to elementary education, Secondary
education, University and Higher education, adult education and technical education. The
Department also coordinates various programmes of assistance and other activities with
UNESCO and other foreign agencies.

1.2 The literacy rate in the country as per the 1950-51 census was 18%. Female literacy
of just 9% as compared to the male literacy of 27.2% indicated a wide gap between the two.
In comparison to 1950-51 census, the Census Report 1990-91 shows the literacy rate to be
52.2%. The male literacy is reported to be 64% whereas female literacy is 39.4% thereby
indicating that the wide gap between male and female literacy existing in 1950-51 has been
bridged: only marginally by 1990-91. Not only this, the picture is dismal in educationally
backward States. Against the national average of gender gap at 25%, it ranges between
28.41% (Orissa) and 34.55% (Rajasthan). This calls for a serious review of our educational
planning and its implementation both at the Central and State levels.

1.3 The Eighth Five Year Plan (1992—97) had set the target of achieving 100% literacy
among the people of age group of 15 to 35 years. This involved changing the literacy status
of about 100 million people. The sector-wise plan outlay on education during Eighth Five-
Year Plan (Central) was Rs. 7,443 crores out of which Rs. 4148.75 crores was earmarked for
Central Schemes and Rs. 3294.25 crores for Centrally Sponsored Schemes. The sector-wise
plan outlay on education during the Eighth Five Year Plan (States/UTs.) was Rs. 12,156.73
crores. Thus, the total sector-wise plan outlay on education during Eighth-Five Year Plan
(Central + States/UTs.) was almost Rs. 19,600 crores. As against the initial outlay of
Rs. 7443 crores (Centre) for Eighth Five Year Plan, the Actual Expenditure has shown it to
be Rs. 8521.89 crores.

1.4 Social Services Sectors—The Committee is perturbed to note that in almost all the
Social Service Sectors cut in financial terms have been imposed by the Ministry of Finance
which may affect the overall development of the Country including human resources. The
Committee feels that this tendency is not correct. Hence the Committee recommends that
Social Service Sectors must be given its appropriate weightage as compared to other sectors.

1.5 The Ninth Plan (1997—2002) outlay on Education in general estimates it to be
Rs. 78708.75 crores showing a steep rise when compared to Eighth Plan outlay. The
Approach Paper on the Ninth Five Year Plan indicates that apart from carrying out the
directions given by National Policy on Education, 1986 and NPA 1992, and keeping in view
the declaration of education as an aspect of fundamental human right to life, making the
nation fully literate by the year 2005 will be 'a cominitted goal. Around 6% of the GDP will
be earmarked for the education sector by the year 2000 A.D. and 50% of that will be spent
on Elementary Education. Allocation of substantial funds for, imparting technical and
Vocational skills and training coverage of 100 million adults by the year 1998-99 under
National Literacy Mission (NLM) are the special targets. The unfinished task of Universal
Elementary Education (UEE) will be completed with intensive focus on the backward

1


States/districts, the girl child and other disadvantaged population groups, with active
participation of NGOs, the corporate sector and various other groups. Linkages will be
developed between adult education and formal and non-formal education including open
learning. Similarly in Secondary Education the major issue is one of modification and
diversification of curricula so as to provide skill-training through well-structured vocational
courses, planned with community involvement and support, enlisting the Community and
Agricultural Polytechnics in the task. In Higher education the existing infrastructure needs to
be nurtured in order to enhance the country’s competitiveness in the global market.
Additional resources will be generated by involving industry and commerce and through
contribution from community.

1.6 Committed Liability—The Committee in its 56th Report had recommended that the
Department should make a thorough review of the schemes and identify the committed
liability. In this matter, the Committee considered the Report of the Tenth Finance
Commission. The Tenth Finance Commission have observed as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liability on- account of plan
scheme, the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan
scheme completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The
Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may‘ consider
providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92.”

The Committee in this connection heard the views of the Secretary, Department of
Expenditure last year to clarify the position. He informed the Committee that even though
communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the
committed expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under
Demand No. 31. The Secretary also assured that if required more funds for this purpose will
be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the Departments may approach the
Department of Expenditure for their share.

The Committee notes that the Department had proposed under the scheme of
Installation of Mini-Computer Terminal, UGC and NVS an amount of Rs. 0.14, Rs. 27.87
and Rs. 62.70 crores respectively for the acceptance of the Ministry of Finance for 1997-98
onwards under Committed Liability. No response has been received by the Department from
the Ministry of Finance so far.

The Committee views with corfcern that the Finance Ministry has not honoured such
clear cut commitment made before the Parliamentary Committee. As the recommendations
of the Tenth Finance Commission have been accepted by the Government it is the
commitment of the Government too. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department of Education should get the assurance implemented without any delay.

1.7 The total budgetary allocation for the Department for 1997-98 was Rs. 5231.63
crores (Plan: Rs. 4094.13+Non-Plan 1137.50 crores) which was around 3.7% of the GDP.
The Budgetary allocation for 1998-99 is Rs. 7046.82 crores of which Rs.-4244.18 crores is on
Plan side and Rs. 2802.64 crores is on- Non-Plan side. Compared to last year’s Plan
allocation of Rs. 4094.13 crores at BE 1997-98 which was reduced to Rs. 3350.45 crores at
RE 1997-98 due to economy consideration and also under utilisation in some of the schemes,
the Plan allocation for 1998-99 Rs. 4244.18 crores shows a significant increase.

1.8 The Secretary, Department of Education informed the Committee that at present,
the expenditure on education both of the Central Government and the State Governments,


a dint ———

3

if taken together is less than 4% of GDP. Suitable budgetary provisions in the Ninth Plan
period are required if it is to be raised to the tune of 6% GDP by 2000 A.D. Budgetary’
provision for 1998-99 should, therefore, have been Rs. 9,500 crores instead of Rs. 7046.82
crores. :

1.9 While admitting that there was under utilisation of funds and poor track record in a
number of schemes, during 1997-98, the Secretary stated that the Department had to face a
number of hurdles. In pursuance of Ministry of Finance instructions of September 18, 1997,
there was a 5% cut in Plan and Non-Plan Budget and in addition no new expenditure
proposal was cleared by the Government. 85 ३ result only those existing schemes, which
were continuing beyond the Eighth Plan could be funded. Not only this, even any avoidable
augmentation of expenditure on existing schemes/programmes was met by re-appropriation
of saving. There were a number of schemes, which in the opinion of both Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance ought to be discontinued or transferred to the States.
However, there being no final decision funds were not released. Cumulative result of all
these was certain slackening of pace and lesser expenditure than what was envisaged in the
Budget. J

1.10 The Committee understands that ‘a number of Centrally-sponsored Schemes are
being transferred to the States. The Committee feels that the transfer of innovative and
significant schemes such as Vocational Education, Integrated Education for Disabled
Children (IEDC) and Computer Education etc. will prejudicially affect the interest of the
students. The Committee, therefore, recommends that such schemes should not be
transferred except where the State Governments are themselves willing to take over those
schemes and provide necessary funds.

1.11 The Committee drew the attention of the Department towards press reports about
basic changes likely to be made in the National Policy of Education (NPE) 1986. The
Secretary clarified that there was no such move. Policy updation has become due as 5 years
have elapsed after Plan of Action evolved in 1992.

1.12 The Committee expressed its apprehension about reference made by the Finance
Minister in his Budget speech about making Primary Education free and compulsory upto
fifth standard. The \Secrétary clarified that there was a clear constitutional mandate -for
providing Free and Compulsory Elementary Education upto 14 years of age which has been
validated by Supreme Court judgement also. There was no change in the’ commitment.
Government only plans to go about in phases. However, the Committee feels that this goes
against the National Agenda of achieving Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE)
by 2005 A.D. Hence, this has to be achieved within the stipulated time and not just in
phases.

II. ELEMENTARY EDUCATION

2.1 The Department informed the Committee that in pursuance of the National Policy
of Education, 1986 as modified in 1992, concerted efforts were being made by Central/State
Governments to achieve the goal of UEE before we enter the 21st Century. The Centrally-
sponsored schemes of Operation Blackboard, NFE, Teacher Education and externally aided
projects of primary education like DPEP were aimed at supplementing the efforts of States
and UTs for promotion of primary education. The Department further clarified that it had
been amply reflected in the budgetary allocation made for elementary education in. the
Annual Plan for 1998-99 wherein allocation has increased from Rs. 2543.08 crores in 1997-98
to Rs. 2780.03 crores in 1998-99. Moreover, of the total budget of the Department of
Education for 1998-99, 39.45% has been allocated for the elementary education sector.


n

|
|
|

|
|
|

4

However, the Committee finds that like in the previous year, bigger allocation has been
earmarked for Mid-day Meal Scheme and the District Primary Education Programme
(DPEP).

2.2 Operation Blackboard—The Department informed that under ‘Operation
Blackboard’, 5.23 lakh primary. schools and 0.96 lakh upper primary schools have been
provided funds for teaching learning material. About 1.5 lakh posts of additional teachers
for single teacher primary schools, 0.45 lakh posts of additional teachers at the upper
primary stage and 0.56 lakh posts of third teachers have been sanctioned upto 1997-98. The
figures are quite impressive. However, the Committee finds the ground realities to be
entirely different. Either there was a very tardy progress in construction of class rooms or
class rooms already constructed have not yet started functioning. This was the position in
‘most educationally backward States like U.P. and Bihar. Similarly, inspite of fulfilment of
target of appointment of teachers, the Committee finds that teaching community by and
large was reluctant to be posted to rural areas for want of proper facilities. This defeats the
very purpose of Operation Blackboard Scheme. The Committee firmly believes that those
posted in rural areas must join their duties and the Government concerned should make all
out efforts to solve the problems of such teachers during their posting in rural areas.
Department’s stand that successful implementation of Operation Blackboard Scheme was
entirely the responsibility of State Governments was not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee recommends that a Joint Monitoring Cell comprising of both State and Central
Government representatives and local MLAs/MPs should be evolved to effectively supervise
the implementation of Operation Blackboard Scheme.

2.3 Residential Primary Schools in Rural Areas—The Committee observed that there
were variations in allocation for this scheme. It was Rs. 25 crores in the BE of 1997-98
reduced to a meagre amount of Rs. 1 crore in its RE stage and now stepped up to Rs. 24
crores in BE 1998-99. The Department in its reply clarified that in pursuance of the
instruction of the Ministry of Finance dated September 18, 1997 to defer all new schemes to
the next financial year, the scheme was not taken up for implementation in 1997-98.
However, the deferred allocation i.e. Rs. 24 crores is now reflected in the BE of 1998-99.
Expressing its concern over such drastic cut by the Ministry of Finance, the Committee feels
that once the Parliament has approved the allocations, any cut in the allocations of various
schemes at a subsequent. stage by the Ministry of Finance should be brought to the notice of
Parliament.

2.4 On a specific query about the fate of the feasibility study to be conducted by
NCERT, the Department informed the Committee that in view of the uncertainty regarding
the age group of children to be covered under the Scheme, NCERT has not been in a
position to proceed with the feasibility study in 1997-98. The Committee recommends that
immediate steps should be initiated for resolving this issue so that the scheme of Residential
Primary Schools in rural areas can be started during the current year.

2.5 Teachers Training Programme—There was a provision of Rs. 159 crores in BE of
1997-98 for the Teacher Training Programme which was reduced to only Rs. 89.50 crores at
its RE stage. However, the BE of 1998-99 again proposes it for Rs. 159 crores. When asked
to clarify, the Department informed that Rs. 159 crores in the BE of 1997-98 was in
accordance with the recommendations of the wérking group on Teachers Education for 1X
Plan. However, the norms for grant of Central Assistance for setting up of DIETs/CTEs/
IASEs and strengthening of SCERTs could not be revised in view of instructions from
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance. The budgetary provision was accordingly


5

reduced from Rs. 159 crores to Rs. 89.50 crores at the RE stage. Expressing its concern over
such drastic cuts, the Committee observes that Teachers Training Progranime is an essential
pre-requisite for achieving the Total Literacy Target by 2005 A.D. Hence, the Committee
recommends that the BE of 1998-99 for this scheme be maintained and no further reduction
under this scheme be brought about.

2.6 Non-Formal Education—The allocation under the schemes for the year 1997-98 was
Rs. 324.86 crores for running 2.90 lakh NFE centres. The Department informed the
Committee that since Ministry of Finance did not allow revision of the scheme as envisaged,
the budgetary allocation for NFE scheme was reduced to Rs. 183.05 crores at the RE stage.
The Department further clarified that the drastic reduction did not: affect the smooth
functioning of NFE centres as grants were released on the existing pattern during 1997-98.
The Committee has made a number of regommendations in its 560 Report for smooth
functioning and effective monitoring mechanism of NFE scheme in general and in U.P.,
Bihar and Rajasthan in particular. The Committee reiterates the same and notes that a draft
report of the evaluation study conducted by the Planning Commission on impact of NFE
scheme is at present under examination of the Department and hopes that remedial steps in
the light of this study would be taken by the Department without delay.

2.7 District Primary Education Programme (DPEP)—There was a provision of Rs.
651.31 crores for DPEP in BE 1997-98 which was reduced to Rs. 560.89 crores at RE stage.
The Department clarified that this was due to slower pace of expenditure in States and
procedural delays in appraisal and approvals to the projects.

2.8 The Department informed the Committee that a new initiative of providing
integrated education to disabled children and distance education for teacher training has also
been incorporated in the DPEP scheme. At present, the scheme is under implementation in
149 low female literacy districts in 14 States. Expansion of the project in another three
districts in U.P. and 19 districts in Rajasthan is in the pipeline. Expansion in another 14
districts in A.P. through IDA assistance has been negotiated as a State sector project. The
increase in BE 1998-99 (Rs. 667 crores) over the last year’s budget is to meet the
requirements of additional districts and DPEP phase III in Bihar, approved for coverage in
1997-98. Budgetary Provisions have also been made to match the expected flow of external
assistance for the project. The Committee hopes, that procedural delays would be removed
so as to fully utilise the funds allocated for DPEP. projects during 1998-99. 85% funding of
DPEP projects by external agencies is a welcome step. But the Committee feels that there
should be no-imposition of their own terms and conditions by these agencies as it may create
problems for its proper functioning.

2.9 The Committee was informed that the first in-depth Review of DPEP conducted in
September/October, 1997 through a mission comprising of representatives from the external
funding agencies and GOI has commended the progress of programme implementatjon. The
Committee notes with satisfaction that there has been a significant increase in enrolment in
the DPEP districts as compared to Non-DPEP districts, gender and social inequities have
been substantially reduced and preliminary signs of increased learning achievements are in
progress. The Committee, however, expects the Department to see that the disparity
between the norms of the external aid agencies and the norms of State Governments in
respect of salaries and other amenities is removed.

2.10 Mid-Day Meal Scheme—The Physical and Financial achievements of Mid-Day Meal
Scheme launched in August, 1995 have been commendable. The number of children covered
under the programme has risen from 3.4 crores in about 3.22 lakh schools in
1995-96 to 9.10 crores in about 6.41 lakh schools in 1998-99. Funds spent have risen from

|
|

6

Rs. 441.21 crores in 1995-96 to Rs. 1070.38 crores in 1997-98. Supply of cooked food in only
5 States and 1 UT due to resource constraint and insufficient cooking arrangements, less
than satisfactory lifting by a few States and inadequate provision of transportation charges,
especially in North-Eastern States were the major. operational problems being faced in
implementation of this programme, the Committee was informed. The Committee is of the
view that only cooked food be served to the students and in order to overcome the
problems of auxiliaries, the employment schemes may be linked with this scheme so as to
provide logistic support to it and to make the scheme successful.

2.11 Against the projected requirement of Rs. 1900 crores for Mid-Day Meal Scheme
for the year 1998-99, only Rs. 1092.15 croreg has been provided. The Department advocated
provision of required funds in 1998-99 so as to prevent delays in release of payments to FCI.
While not disputing the Department’s requirement of funds under this programme for
1998-99, the Committee expresses its deep concern for there being no effective monitoring
mechanism evolved so far. Mere monitoring and review of the implementation of scheme at
regular intervals through various Committees and groups set up at Block, District, State and
national levels would not serve the purpose. As admitted by the Department, monthly data
on enrolment, number of eligible children, number of students benefited, quantity of food-
grains allocated and lifted from FCI outlets and utilised by each school through a
computerised Management Information System (MIS) has not been forthcoming from most
of the States. The Committee recommends that the Department should approach the State
Government for making furnishing of monthly data as a pre-requisite for release of funds to
District Headquarters. Feedback from time to time should also be made available to Centre.
In views of reports of large scale corruption and malpractices in the scheme, the
representatives of people such as MPs, MLAs and Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) should
be involved for effective implementation and monitoring of those schemes. Only then,
positive impact of the Scheme on enrolment and participation of children in primary classes
can be assessed in the real sense.

2.12 Drop-Out Rates—The Department informed that the drop out rates have shown
declining trend during the last five years. The decline is from 42% in 1991-92 to 39% in
1996-97, showing an overall decrease of 3% at the primary level. At the upper primary
Stage, the drop out rate was 58.7% in 1991-92 and it declined to 52.3% in 1996-97, showing
an overall decrease of 6.4% points. Whereas the drop out rate for boys in primary classes
declined by 1%, for girls it declined by 6.0% during the period from 1991-92 to 1996-97. In
upper primary classes, mf é drop out rate has declined by 4.2% for boys and 9.6% for girls
during the same period./However, the Committee was given to understand that this positive
trend is not equally distributed over the various regions and regional disparity remains an
area of great concern. The persistence of high levels of female illiteracy in Bihar, U.P.,
M.P., Rajasthan and Orissa is a matter of great concern. The Committee feels the problem
of drop-outs can be effectively tackled by increased public spending on elementary education
by the State Governments, emphasis on teacher-student ratio, increased parental motivation
and above all a cooperative social environment. Economic and social factors operating are
likely to be different in different regions. Hence a detailed area based study on these aspects
will be necessary before policies for micro intervention can be formulated and implemented.

II]. SECONDARY EDUCATION

3.1 The Department informed the Committee that the number of Secondary and Senior
Secondary Schools has increased from 0.07 lakh in 1950-51 to 1.02 lakh in 1996-97.
Provisional statistics available in the Sixth All India Educational Survey indicate an increase


7

to the extent of 51% in the enrolment in classes IX to X and 54% increase in classes XI to
XII. The demand on senior secondary education is bound to increase during the coming
years because of universalisation of elementary education causing a greater transition to
secondary education. There is a provision of Rs. 922.98 crores in BE 1998-99, for secondary
education as compared to Rs. 684.29 crores in BE 1997-98.

3.2 Kendriya Vidyalayas—The Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan has been facing severe
resource crunch for the last few years as a result of inadequate allocation of budget
estimates, the Committee was informed. The allocation of Rs. 356 crores under Non-Plan
for 1998-99 as against Rs. 543.24 crores projected was so low that additional allocation will
be necessary at the stage of first supplementary itself to take care of additional requirement
due to Sth Pay Commission recommendation. Similarly, there is a meagre proposed
allocation of Rs. 88 crores as against Rs. 180 crores projected under Plan for 1998-99. There
are no funds for on-going construction activities and maintenance and repair of existing
buildings. At present there are 357 Vidyalayas without permanent school buildings. The
Committee recommends that adequate budgetary support be provided to Kendriya
Vidyalayas so as to prevent the decline of Kendriya Vidyalayas which were conceived as
pace-setting institutions. At the same time, the Committee would like the Department to
ensure that school buildings already constructed are provided with infrastructural facilities so
that they can start functioning without delay. The Committee feels that in ordér to get
cooperation of the local people, it will be advisable if certain percentage of local students are
also admitted.

3.3 Vocationalisation of Education—In order to promote vocational education facilities
have been created for diversion of about 9.35 lakh students at the +2 level. The Committee
was given to understand that there was a provision of Rs. 60 crores in BE 1997-98.
However, after the decision of Planning Commission to transfer the Scheme to States, as
well as transfer the salary liability after the 8th Plan period, no funds could be released to
States/UTs. As a result budget provision was brought down to Rs. 20 crores and actual
expenditure was only Rs. 4 crores. Allocation for 1998-99 is Rs. 10 crores. The Department
clarified that pending a final decision regarding the transfer of the scheme to the States, and
assuming that this programme will continue to be implemented as a Centrally-sponsored
Scheme, the NCERT has been requested to constitute a full-fledged working group with
representation from Industry and employer agencies for a complete revamping of the scheme -
for implementation during the 9th Plan. The Committee is however of the view that as
stated earlier this scheme is of special significance and should therefore continue as a
Centrally-sponsored Scheme. :

3.4 In view of increasing number of educated unemployed youths there is a greater need
for Vocational Education. Hence the Committee recommends that enhanced allocations for
Vocational Education in the RE stage must be done. The Committee further recommends
that Vocational Education be properly linked with Industries and Corporate groups. Where
there are no industries focus should be on area specific needs.

3.5 Computer Education in Schools—The Department informed the Committee that for
Computer Education in Schools a provision of Rs. 20 crores under BE 1997-98 was proposed
in anticipation of the approval of the 9th Plan allocations to cover 400 additional Senior
Secondary Schools. However, while preparing the Draft Approach Paper for 9th Plan,
Planning Commission indicated that the Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS)
scheme would no longer be a Centrally-sponsored Scheme and it was proposed to be
transferred to the States during 9th Plan. Besides this scheme was identified by the Ministry

3.6 Integrated Education for Disabled Children (IEDC)—The Committee was given to
understand that the BE of 1997-98 for this scheme was Rs. 13 crores which was reduced to
Rs. 4.70 crores in the RE stage. The Department in its reply stated that the actual
expenditure in 1997-98 was Rs. 9.99 crores and the reduction was due to the guidelines
issued by the Planning Commission to transfer all committed expenditure under the IEDC to
the State Governments in view of the decision taken to transfer this scheme to the States in
a phased manner. In addition, the Ministry of Finance issued instructions that funds under
Centrally Sponsored Scheme be released only after prior clearance for Planning
Commission/Ministry of Finance. However, in December, 1997 the Planning Commission on
reconsideration approved the Department’s proposal for allowing release of funds for
committed expenditure as a very special case. Further, Planning Commission informed that
there was no immediate more to transfer the scheme to States. Expenditure thereafter
picked up and the actual expenditure during 1997-98 was Rs. 9.99 crores. Keeping in view
the noble idea of this scheme which aims at providing educational opportunities to disabled
children with mild to moderate disabilities in the general school system the Committee
recommends that efforts to expand this scheme should not suffer a set back and provision of
Rs. 13.00 crores made in BE 1998-99 should not be reduced at RE stage.

3.7 The Committee in its 56th Report expressed the need for the telecast of syllabus
based programme for the benefit of student. The Department in its reply stated that with the
coming into existence of Prasar Bharati the entire issue of education telecast is being looked
into by a sub-Committee of Prasar Bharati on Educational channel. With the closure of DD
Il, the earlier proposal for seeking slots on Education could not materialise, the
Department clarified. Expressing its concern, the Committee recommends that the decision
on education channel should be expedited so that school children can make use of this
facility without delay.

3.8 Promotion of Science Laboratories—The Committee was given to understand that
the BE of 1997-98 for this scheme was Rs. 19.90 crores which was reduced to a meagre
amount of Rs. 3.25 crores in its RE stage. The Department in its reply stated that as most of
the State Governments except Kerala, H.P. and Pondicherry had unspent balances of the
previous grants under this scheme, it was not considered appropriate to release further
grants. Some general constraints at the level of State Governments were lack of adequate
infrastructure, inadequate science teachers and cumbersome procedure for procurement of
laboratory equipment etc. The Committee expresses its concern over unspent balances lying
with States which could have been utilised for removing the constraints being faced by State

streamlining the procurement procedures and improving infrastructure in schools for
successful implementation of this scheme.

IV. ADULT EDUCATION

The Committee was constrained to note that the Literacy rate as per the 1991 census was
around 52%. If compared with the neighbouring countries such as Myanmar, Sri Lanka,
Thailand, Japan and Singapore our position is poor. Taking a rough estimate for the year
1998 the Literacy rate might have gone up to around 60% which shows that the country still
is having around 40% illiterates. The Department stated that the National Literacy Mission
(NLM) set up in the year 1988 with the target of making 100 million persons in the age
group of 15—35 Literate in a phased manner through its policy of Total Literacy Campaign
(TLC) & Post Literacy Campaign (PLC) has been able to achieve a target of 68.57 million
persons by now of which 60% are Women, 23% SCs and 12% STs which is a very
encouraging achievement. 447 districts are covered under Literacy Campaigns.The
programme of TLC and PLC has been faced with some difficulties in the low Literacy States
mainly due to the absence of Voluntary Organisations and other socio-cultural barriers. At
present 215 districts are under the TLC programme and 173 districts under PLC and another
59 districts under the third stage of Continuing Education where the impetus built up in the
first two stages is sought to be sustained together with elements of skill training. This
programme requires qualitative upgradation in order to make it relevant, contextual and
acceptable, the Department further clarified. Provision of Rs. 127 crores in BE 1997-98 was
reduced to Rs. 81.42 crores due to economy cuts imposed by Ministry of Finance,
uncertainly regarding transfer of the scheme of strengthening of Administrative structures of
States and less number of proposals for TLC projects. Bihar, M.P. and U.P. are some of the
States where the campaigns have lagged behind and thus not able to utilise funds fully. The
Committee feels that concerted efforts are required to make Pr paigns for Total Literacy
and Post Literacy successful in Educationally Backward Statey/The Committee is not fully
satisfied with the implementation of the scheme and the impact ‘it has had on the targetted
group. The Committee therefore recommends that the scheme be evaluated properly and
effectively and its benefit to the masses in real terms should be assessed.

५. UNIVERSITY AND HIGER EDUCATION

5.1 There is a provision of Rs. 1821.78 crores under Non-Plan in BE 1998-99 as
compared to allocation of Rs. 472.47 crores in BE 1997-98. The total increase to the tune of
Rs. 1349.43 crores over 1997-98 is intended to meet claims of salaries and allowances of
teaching staff of Central and State Universities/Deemed to be universities and colleges.
However, the position is totally different under Plan allocation. Allocation under Plan is
Rs. 412.75 crores in BE 1998-99 as against Rs. 403 crores provided in BE 1997-98. The
Department clarified that the modest increase of around Rs. 10 crores has been made for
upgradation of Libraries and Laboratories in selected colleges and universities» No major
additional provisions have been made in keeping with the Government’s policy of ensuring
self supporting institutions by encouraging internal resource generation by the Institutions/
Organisations themselves.

5.2 University Grants Commission (UGC)—The Committee heard the Secretary,
Department of Education and Chairperson, GC on the issue of pay-scales of teachers. The
Chairperson, UGC submitted that the mandate of UGC is to maintain the standards of
Edcuation and to advise the Government. In pursuance of that, the UGC undertook
consideration of the scales of pay of teachers recommended by the Fifth Pay Commission.
The Chairperson also pointed out that UGC is now-a-days finding it difficult to attract talent

\


10

in the field of teaching as other fields are offering more to the puss-outs. It is therefore,
necessary to offer attracting pay scales to the talented persons so as to make them join the
teaching profession. The suggested pay scales are linked with qualifications also. The
Chairperson also added that the revised pay scales were arrived at after a series of meetings
held with all concerned. The suggested pay scales were finally crystallised in consultation
with all Central and other Universities in the meeting held in the month of October, 1997.
The Secretary, Department of Education was also invited in the meetings. The Education
Secretary submitted that what the UGC recommended was wholesale revision of the scales

recommended by the Rastogi Committee for the teachers. This had created an unusual

situation and the Department is finding it difficult to accept the recommendations in toto.
The Committee notes that as per the convention, the scales suggested by the UGC are
usually accepted by the Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should initiate immediate steps to resolve the issue amicably.

5.3 The Committee was informed that the Central Universities and IITs etc. were
expected to undertake their own resource generation, as a result of which they had
generated an amount of Rs. 67 crores during 1991—96. The Department informed that the
institutions were allowed to utilise those funds for developmental purposes. The Committee
recommends that such institutions should be ‘allowed to utilise these funds for developmental
purposes in future also. The Committee also feels that the Universities and other such
institutions which generate resources and make earnings should be provided sufficient
incentives.

5.4 Programme to strengthen Scientific Research—The Committee notes that for
research works a meagre allocation of Rs. 28 crores is‘also a matter of great concern. The
Chairperson UGC further clarified that due to financial constraints research projects were
adversely affected during the 8th Five Year Plan. As without proper research the progress of
a country is handicapped to a great extent. Greater attention must also be given to the
applied and scientific research.

5.5 The Committee was also given to understand that the Government has put higher
education as a non-merit subject and plans the de-subsidisation of higher education from the
present 90 percent to 50 percent in three years and with a further aim of reducing jt to:a
meagre amount of 25 percent in another two years. The Committee feels that the idea that
higher education caters only to upper middle class and rich is quite. a fallacious conclusion.
Sizeable portion of students are drawn from SCs, STs and-Backward classes including rural
youths, many of whom are first generation learners. Pence the Committee is of the view
that a reasonable allocation must be made for UGC in general and for the “Programme to
strengthen Scientific Research” in particular at the RE stage.

5.6 Indian Council of Historical Researeh (ICHR)—The Committee was constrained to
note that the ICHR, which was previously having its composition of eminent historians of
proven calibre was reconstituted. In the reply supplied to the Committee, the Department
stated that ICHR was inaugurated on March 27, 1972. The normal tenure of the
membership is three years. In this way the term of the council, which was constituted on
September 8, 1994 came to an end on September 7, 1997. Hence the कर कस of ICHR
was due and the council has been re-constituted on Junie 1, 1998 for three year; 521 Regarding
the methodology to determine the composition of the council the Department further
clarified that it was governed by Rule 3 of the MOA & rules of. the ICHR. Eighteen
Historians are nominated by the Government of India and an eminent Historian is
nominated as the Chairman of ‘the council. However, the Committee was given to
understand that it is the interpretative scholars and not the ones dealing with documentation |

11

that the ICHR was set up to help. Hence the Committee recommends that keeping the
objectives of ICHR in view, reconstitution in future must be made so that future generations
see a more humanitarian, secular and ‘live and let live’ form of society through history. The
Committee also recommends that all shades of opinion should be given representation on
the Council.

VI. DEVELOPMENT OF LANGUAGES

6. The Committee noted that the BE of 1997-98 for Sanskrit in total was Rs. 32.31
crores which was reduced to Rs. 19.96 crores in its RE stage. However the BE of 1998-99
has increased it to Rs. 37 crores. When enguired about such fluctuations the Department
stated that certain fresh proposals could not be considered during 1997-98 due to the ban
imposed by the Ministry of Finance. However during the BE of 1998-99 those fresh
proposals such as recognition of two new Adarsh Sanskrit Mahavidyalayas, construction of
buildings of Kendriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeths at Sringeri, Lucknow and Puri, opening of new
Kendriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeths at Garali (H.P.), Mumbai, Bhopal and proposal to increase
the amount of honorarium of Shastra Chudamani from Rs. 1000/ to Rs. 2500८ per month
per scholar and above all to increase the existing corpus fund from Rs. 10 crores to Rs. 20
crores during 9th Five Year Plan to provide funds for the construction of building of the
Maharshi Sandipani Rashtriya Ved Vidya Pratishthan, Ujjain got accepted. Hence, the
increase in the BE of 1998-99. The Committee is happy to note that steps for development
of languages are to be taken during 1998-99. The Committee also recommends additional
amount of Rs. 6 crores (Rs. 5.50 crores Plan + Rs. 0.50 Non-Plan) which is required for the
Development of other Languages may also be provided at the RE stage.

VII. TECHNICAL EDUCATION

7.1 The Committee was given to understand that various inadequacies existed in the
technical education. There was necessity to widen the course areas under Polytechnics. The
Committee in this regard heard the views of the Chairperson AICTE who stated that
allocation for AICTE for 1998-99 was totally inadequate, which is only Rs. 79 crores in the
BE stage which shows. around Rs. 8 crores less than the BE of 1997-98. Guidelines for
granting recognition to Technical Institutes have been throughly simplified. There was a grey
area in the field of technical education. Most of the students after completing their studies in
Computer Science, instead of joining teaching profession are drawn towards the corporate
and business groups which offer lucrative salary from the beginning. Unless this is checked
we may face lop sided development in our technical education. In this direction for
attracting the students towards teaching professions after the completion of the 6th semester
from 7th semester onwards an amount of Rs. 10,000/ per month per student is given in
terms of scholarships, the Chairperson clarified. The Committee emphasises the necessity of
motivating the students for teaching profession to meet the long term goal of producing a
qualitative technical education.

7.2 The Department clarified that under the Apprentices Act the spread of apprentices
trained increased to 10000 industrial establishments of the country in 90 technological/
engineering subject in 94 subject fields. In addition apprenticeship training of vocational
students in 94 subjects fields has also been introduced. The Government has extended the
facilities of National Scheme of Apprenticeship Training to graduate Engineers and
Technicians of SAARC Member States. In this regard the Committee recommends that
there should be updated courses in Polytechnics and adequate allocations be made for
AICTE in the RE stage in particular and technical education in general. f


12

VIII. FUND FOR GOLDEN JUBILEE OF INDIA’S INDEPENDENCE

8. The Committee was given to understand that the entire allocation of Rs. 200 crores
made in the BE 1997-98 under the plan side for the Golden Jubilee of India’s Independence
had been taken back by the Ministry of Finance. The Department informed the Committee
that a series of Programmes and activities were chalked out only to be told at the last stage
that provision of Rs. 200 crores was meant for all the Departments of the Government and
not for Department of Education alone. Incidentally, this entire amount has been treated as
surrendered by the Department. The Committee observes that such cuts must not be
effected at the last stage.

IX. NEW INITIATIVES

9. The Department informed the Committee that certain new initiatives have been
taken which are: ‘

(i) Free Education for Girls—Apart from free and compulsory primary education, it is
proposed to launch a new scheme for providing free education for girls up to college level
including professional courses. An amount of Rs. 100.00 crores has been earmarked for this
scheme in the current year.

(ii) Sports Schools—In order to dove-tail, a sports component in the Educational
System, as mentioned in the earlier National Policy on Education, it is proposed to either
upgrade or set up 20 sports schools by suitably adapting the Navodaya Vidyalaya Schemes in
different States. The schools would mainly be geared to physical disciplines and have some
academic subjects in addition. An amount of Rs. 20 crores has been earmarked in the
current year for this purpose and further modalities are being worked out. The Committee
desires that 50% of the allocation should be earmarked for rural areas.

(iii) Strengthening of the Statistical Machinery in States—A new Centrally Sponsored
Scheme of strengthening of statistical machinery in States will be launched to strengthen the
educational data base and to meet the international requirements of the educational statistics
(UNESCO) and also to meet the requirement of the World Education Indicators. 0, notional
provision of Rs. 1 crore has been provided in the current year. The Education Department
collects statistics from: 900,000 institutions from the primary to the tertiary stage, the
Department clarified.

The Committee appreciates those new initiatives taken by the Department and hopes
that those new initiatives would be carried out with a greater enthusiasm in this 50th year of
India’s Independence.

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The main objective of the Department is to ensure qualitative, and quantitative
improvements in Youth Programme’ and also on broad basing and bringing about awareness
of sports and physical fitness amongst school children. and youth. The programmes
undertaken by the Department are mainly Sports and Games and Youth Programme.

1.2 The Department finances various youth welfare programmes ranging from personal-
ity development to vocational training. Most of these programmes are implemented by
reputed institutions, non-governmental organisations as well as State Governments whereby
financial assistance is provided by the Mepartment as per the stipulated norms. The major
schemes for youth development are: National Service Scheme, Nehru Yuva Kendra
Sangathan, National Integration Programmes, Youth Hostels and National Service Volun-
teers Scheme, etc.

1.3 The Department also finances a number of: programmes which aim at promotion of
sports, including creation of sports infrastructure in all parts of the country, grants for laying
of synthetic surfaces, spotting and nurturing of talents through the schemes of Sports
Authority of India, grants to National Sports Federation, National Championships, organis-
ing of tournaments for rural youth, women and in the North-Eastern Region etc.

Il. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION

2. The total outlay, both Plan and Non-Plan taken together, provided to the
Department for the year 1997-98 was Rs. 159.33 crores in BE which was reduced to
Rs.158.39 crores at RE stage. The allocation made for the year 1998-99 is Rs. 214.76 crores
(Plan Rs.179.00 crores and Non-Plan Rs. 35.76 crores). -'

Ill. EIGHTH FIVE YEAR PLAN

: 5
3.1 The total approved outlay of the Department for th¢ Eighth plan was Rs. 435.89
crores. Out of this amount, Sports Division and Youth Division were provided a sum of Rs.
249.86 and 184.78 crores respectively. Coming to the actual expenditure made, the
expenditure of Sports Division and Youth Division has been at the level of Rs.271.30 and
171.51 crores respectively totalling to an amount of Rs. 443.45 crores for the entire
Department. The Committee is constrained to note that the achievements of targets made by
the Youth Wings both in financial and physical terms have been unsatisfactory. As regards
the sports wing, the allocations have been fully utilised by the wing. But the net result is
dismal. The country has not made any improvement in its performance in jnternational .
sports. If we have to make our presence felt in international sports some radifal steps are
required to be taken.

3.2 The Committee holds the same views with regard to running of Youth Schemes.
Inspite of its earlier observations/recommendations since the inception of the Standing
Committee in 1993 for improving the schemes of Youth Wing, schemes are still running in
ineffective and inefficient manner. Impact of the schemes, as desired by the Committee, is
not being felt all over the country.



IV. APPROACH TO THE NINTH FIVE YEAR PLAN

4.1 The Committee has taken note of the approach on Youth Affairs and Sports during
the Ninth Plan period. The contents of relevant paras from the Approach Paper to the Ninth
Five Year Plan are reproduced as -below:—

“The thrust in Youth Affairs will be to consolidate and expand youth activities
by involving youths in the entire gamut of the developmental process as the youth
are a major resource in the task of nation building. Youth activities will focus on
environmental and health programmes such as greening of wastelands, solid waste
management, anti-smoking compaign, prevention of drug-abuse, health education
with emphasis on reproductive health and prevention of AIDS, population control as
well as various adventure activities. Greater access will be given to the rural and
marginalised youth in the vocational training programmes of Nehru Yuva Kendras by
involving the NGOs, self-help groups and community polytechnics in the task.

The thrust in sports will be on providing greater access to sport facilities through
substantial investments in physical education, infrastructure development including
centres of.sport physiology and sports medicine and in creating wide spread
awareness for physical fitness through nutrition, health education and yoga with
special focus on school children. Area specific sports programmes recognising the
traditional sports skills of the inhabitants, specially tribal population, will receive
priority consideration. Rural sports programmes will be revamped in order to tap
vast talents available in the rural areas. Special attention will be given for the
promotion of sports and games among the disabled. the need for a hélistic approach
that will integrate youth and sports activities and programmes within the context of

‘ education is well recognised and will guide all actions”.

Vv. NEHRU YUVA KENDRA SANGATHAN

5.1 Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan is an autonomous organisation under the
Department. It is the largest grass-root level organisation in the Asia and Pacific region,
catering to the needs of:more than 8 million non-student rural youth in the age group of
15—35 years enrolled through 1.82 lakh village-based youth clubs covering education,
training, employment promotion, income generation, self-employment, enterprise creation
etc. Allocation to Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan on plan side has been enhanced from
Rs. 12.00 crores in BE 1997-98 and Rs. 11.40 crores in RE 1997-98 to Rs. 17.35 crores in
BE 1998-99 10 take care of programme funds requirements. According to the Department,
due to financial constraints against proposed release of Rs. 1.00 lakh per Kendra only Rs.
35000/-per Kendra could be released for the regular programmes of NYKS during 1997-98.
The Committee disapproves any reduction in the allocation for NYKS as it would go against
the interests of the rural youth. With the enhanced allocation, it will be possible to give
about Rs. 1.35 lakhs per Kendra for regular programmes during 1998-99. The Department
also informed that in addition to its own programmes, the Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan is
implementing programmes of various other State Governments, Central Government and
other national/nternational agencies.

5.2 The Committee during the course of discussion with the representatives of the
Department expressed the view that activities of NYKS are not being noticed at grass-root
level. Even people’s representatives of the area are not aware of the activities undertaken by
concerned NYKS. The Committee in this connection would like to suggest that efforts
should be made to involve people’s representatives of the concerned areas. It would also. be
in the interest of the programme because it would be conducted in a more democratic,
meaningful and transparent manner. The Committee feels that the Department should look
into the feasibility of forming a task force with a view to identify'any new schemes to be
included under NYKS.


VI. NATIONAL SERVICE SCHEME

6.1 The National Service Scheme launched in Gandhiji’s Birth Centenary Year 1969,
with primary focus on the development of personality of students through community service
has at present over 13.75 Jakh student volunteers on the roll spread over 174 universities/+2
system. Since its inception, more than 1.52 crore students from the Universities, Colleges
and Institutions of higher learning have benefited from NSS activities. Due to its
overwhelming popularity and demand, the scheme was extended to the students of +2 level
in selected institutions.

6.2 The Department informed that the expenditure on programmes of NSS is shared
between the Cent¥e and the State Governments in the ratio of 7:5, except in the case of
Jammu & Kashmir and Union Territories without Legislature, where the entire expenditure
is met by the Central Government.

6.3 According to the information furnished to the Committee, for 1997-98 the target was
to enroll 13.75 lakh student volunteers which was fully achieved. 6764 special camps on
“Youth for Sustainable Development’ and ‘Wasteland and Watershed management” were
conducted. Besides, 6764 villages were adopted for literacy and other developmental
activities. Under AIDS Awareness Programme, 600 teachers and 60,000 peer educators were
trained and 30 lakh students were sensitised towards HIV/AIDS. There is a‘need to
reorganize NSS as third dimension of education. A number of universities have alrédy
integrated NSS into the curriculum. There is tremendous scope for further increase in the
number of NSS volunteers in the country but, due to resource crunch, it has not been found
possible to do so, the Department informed.

6.4 For 1998-99, the target is to enroll 15.13 lakh student volunteers and to conduct
7,500 special camps. Besides, it is also planned to adopt 6000 villages for literacy and other
development activities.

7.1 The scheme is being implemented through Nehru Yuvak Kendra Sangathan and
State Governments/Union Territory Administrations. It aims at assisting newly/set up youth
clubs to enable them to start their activities and\ get established. One time financial
assistance of Rs. 5000/- is given to registered youth clubs. During the year 1996-97, 960
youth clubs were given financial assistance.

7.2 The Committee is happy to note that the working group, constituted for the

scheme for Assistance to Youth Club and steps in this regard have been initiated. The
Committee is also happy to note that as recommended by it earlier, the amount of assistance
to Youth Clubs is proposed to be enhanced from Rs. 5000 to 10,000.

8.1 The National Service Volunteer Scheme, launched in 1977-78, aims at providing
apportunities to youth to involve themselves, .. a voluntary basis, in nation building

, activities for a year or two.

8.2 At Present, 3500 NSVs are deployed with the Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan,
National Service Scheme, Bharat Scouts & Guides, ‘Youth Hostels Association of India,
IDARAs,"etc. The State Governments/Union Territories are also availing the services of
these volunteers.

8.3 Explaining the reason for allocation of Rs. 18 crore in BE 1998-99 compared to Rs.
