Budget Speech of the Finance Minister for creation of a National Reconstruction Cedéps

. which will mobilige youth for community based nation building activities is being formulated

in consultation with concerned Ministries/Departments.

8.4 The Committee is of the view that funds for any new scheme may be allocated only
after completing the exercise of consultation among various Ministries/Departments and
scrutiny by Ministry of Finance. It would have been better if the scheme has been allocated
the required fund at RE stage after completing all rounds of deliberations. The Committee,
however, hopes that the scheme will be formulated and implemented during the current year
itself.

Rs.40 crores, were provided in anticipation of Government's approval to enhance financial
norms. The Department has also informed that since the EFC meeting for the same was
‘held only in May, 1998, the:-same provision has. been kept for 1998-99. The Committee is
however, constrained to point out that things are being done in ad hoc manner and lack of
proper planning continues to plague the department. This is evident from the number of
Anganwadi Workers Training centres opened in different States e.g. where as 42 such
centres have been opened in J & K, there are only one centre in each of the States like
Punjab, West Bengal, Bihar and two centres each in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra. The

equitably to the extent possible. The Committee notes with satisfaction that honorarium of
Anganwadi Workers and Helpers has been revised by 25% to 30% respectively with effect
from 16.5.97.

attention to the task. The Committee hopes that with the given allocation the Department
will be in a position to meet the requirement of working women. In case, more funds are
required the same may be considered at the RE stage.

15. In respect of Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, the Department has submitted that it extends
credit through its partner NGOs to women! below poverty: line to undertake smatfl income
generating activities. The loan ceiling have been revised from Rs. 2500 under short term and
Rs. 5000 under medium term to Rs. 4000 and Rs. 6000 respectively with effect from 16.9.96.

agricultural activities, tailoring, petty shop keeping, small trade and handicrafts. It is
apparent that the sum being given to women under the kosh is a paltry sum and no-
meaningful activity can be undertaken with this nominal amount. The Committee also feels
that @wseas£ 2,17,846 women who have been benefited under the kosh and who have on an

Rs. 60 crores was sanctioned to States/Union Territories under the scheme. The Department
has’ also submitted that the amount provided is inadequate. The Committee feels, that the
scheme can go a long way in bettering the lot of girl child and therefore deserves special

17. The Committee finds that an amount of Rs. 2.50 crores has been earmarked for BE
1998-99 as against Rs. 2 crores for BE 1997-98. The Commission has been given important
mandate as far as prevention of atrocities on women and girl child is concerned. The
Commission is also expected to make recommendations to the Central Government on all
che important issues pertaining to upliftment of women and safeguarding their interests.

During the evidence of the Department a discussion took place as to the efficacy of the ,

Commission in the prevention of atrocities on women. The Commission submitted that
‘hough it makes very useful recommendations every year in the absence of mandatory
power, the Commission finds itself handicapped in enforcing its recommendations. The
Commission desired that it may be legally equipped sufficiently to enforce its
recommendations and decisions. ‘The Committee is inclined to recommend that the
recommendations of the Commission ‘be taken seriously and the Commission be allowed to
play a. greater and meaningful role in the interests of women and girl child. The Committee
is also inclined to recommend that if need be sufficient legal and legislative measures may be
taken to see that the Commissjon plays its role effectively. The Committee feels that the
allocation made for the Commission deserves to be enhanced in order to expect real»
contribution by the Commission in the field assigned to it.

XVII. WELFARE OF TRIBALS

18. Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the unusually high number of deaths
of infants and children in the tribal areas of Maharashtra in recent years. The Committee in
its ealier report had also taken note of the. horrifying reports of a large number of children
dying because of mal-nutrition in tribal areas. During the discussions with the Secretary of
the Department, the Committee enquired about the steps taken by the Government in this
regard. The Department has enumerated a number of steps taken by the Central
Government and the State Government of Maharashtra to alleviate the sufferings of the
people. The Committee, however, finds that 1477 deaths took place in 1996, 1118 in 1997
and 417 in first five months of 1998 in tribal areas of Amravati and Dhule districts. The
Committee apprehends that this might be happening in other parts of the country also, The
Tommittee is not satisfied with the results of the steps taken by the Central Government and
he State Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends that immediate adequate
neasures be taken to control the deaths of children in tribal areas of the country including
Maharashtra.

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The Department of Culture plays a vital role in the promotion and dissemination of art
and culture. The aim of the Department is to develop ways and means for instilling basic values
and perceptions in the minds of the people, particularly the young. The Department also
undertakes the programme of preservation, encouragement and dissemination of various
manifestations of creative activity, both past and present. The Department is engaged in
excavation, conservation and promotion of ancient monuments and historic sites;
administration of libraries, museums and institutions of anthropology; collection, preservation
and ethnology of national character; catering to institutions and organisations in the areas of
Buddhist and Tibetan Studies; promoting literary, visual and performing arts; observing
centenaries and anniversaries of important personalities and entering into cultural agreements
with foreign countries. The Department carries out its various programmes through two
attached offices, six subordinate offices and 26 autonomous organisations.

1.2 During the Ninth Five Year Plan period, the focus would be on a comprehensive plan
for preservation of the archeological heritage and development of the monumental complexes in
the country. Efforts would also be directed towards the preservation of archival heritage and the
promotion of classical, folk and tribal art and crafts and oral traditions which are threatened
with extinction. हे

1.3 The Department had prepared a modest Ninth Five Year Plan of Rs. 1124.40 crores for
effectively funding a variety of activities in Archaeology, Archives, Anthropology, Performing
Art, Buddhist and Tibetan Studies and library sector. As against this proposal of Rs. 1124.40
crores, only Rs. 794.30 crores have been allowed. This.reduction of Rs. 330 crores which is
almost 30% of the proposal means a steep cut in the promotional and support activities in the
field of performing arts (Rs. 97 crores), ASI (Rs. 49 crores), museums (Rs. 58 crores). The
Ninth Five Year Plan allocation for the Department of Culture is Rs. 794.30 crores of the total
plan outlay of Rs. 505161 crores which is only 0.16% of it. Whereas in Eighth Plan it was 0.19%
of the total plan outlay. The Committee feels that against the ongoing onslaught of western
culture through electronic media a greater attention towards cultural activities in general and a
reasonable budgetary allocation in particular in this regard is quite essential.

1.4 The Secretary informed the Committee that the 1998-99 budget provision of the
Department is Rs. 301.2 crores, plan and non-plan put together. Of this as much as Rs. 235
crores or roughly 75% of the total provision has been earmarked for 35 institutions attached to
the Department. If Rs. 22.24 crores, a one time provision for commemoration of 50th
anniversary of India’s Independence is excluded from the current year’s budget, the provision
for these institutions account for 81% of the Department’s outlay, the Committee was
informed.

1.5 During 1998-99, the Department projected a plan outlay of Rs. 200.40 crores.
However, finally the Department's plan allocation come down to Rs. 145 crores of which Rs. 5
crores is earmarked for the Science City, Jallandhar. According to the decision of the CCEA the
allocation for Science City has to be an additionality. Therefore, the annual plan outlay for the
Department is Rs. 140 crores only which is lower than the 1997-98 Revised Estimates of Rs.
143.21 crores. The Committee was given to understand that with the meagre Plan allocation the
Department would be handicapped in carrying out its functions effectively. Keeping in कल
projections made by the Department the Committee recommends that the Plan allocation for
1998-99 should be increased at the RE stage. x

1


1.6 The Secretary informed the Committee that during the current year, attention will
be given to all the sectors under Culture. However, the activities of the Department will be
particularly focussed on conservation and preservation of our Cultural Heritage, Scheme on
the National Culture Fund, Linkage between Education & Culture, Development of a Public
Library Movement, Archives Strengthening of Museums and Art Galleries. It has also been
decided to concentrate on a limited number of sites and bring them up to world standards.
These are Taj Mahal & Khajuraho, Ajartta & Ellora, Konark, Bodh Gaya, Nalanda,
Vaishali & Sarnath and Hampi, the Secretary added. Emphasis will also be there on
improving the Archaeological Museums.

1.7 The Department further informed that it is exploring the possibility of promoting
networking among allied institutions and exchange of professional information and expertise.
The Department is also trying to build strong linkages between the Central Akademies, the
Zonal Cultural Centres, State Governments and State Akademies so that there can be
greater pooling of resources and coordinated programme planning by which the out-reach of
the public sector cultural institutions can be extended.

1.8 Committed Liability:- The Committee in its 58th Report had recommended that the
Department should make a thorough review of the schemes and identify the committed
liability. In this matter, the Committee considered the Report of the Tenth Finance
Commission. The Tenth Finance Commission have observed as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in

deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan scheme,

the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan Scheme
completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The

Commission are, therefore of the view that the Planning Commission may consider

providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the plan itself as was

done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92.”

The Committee in this connection heard the views of the Secretary, Department of
Expenditure last year to clarify the position. He informed the Committee that even though
communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the
committed expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under
Demand No. 31. The Secretary also assured that if required more funds for this purpose will
be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the Departments may approach the
Department of Expenditure for their share.

1.9 The Department in its Action Taken Report has informed that only a certain
portion of the committed liability could be accommodated within the over-all allocation
under Non-Plan due to the sudden increase in Non-Plan requirements on account of the
implementation of the 50 Pay Commission’s recommendations. The Department further
stated that it has 12 schemes. under the Plan Head whose Non-Plan component is not
‘significant. It is meant only to defray the travel expenses of experts, meet the cost of their
sitting fees etc.. Therefore, there is little liability to be transferred from Plan to Non-Plan in
respect of these schemes. However, the budgets of individual organisations are being
reviewed to ensure that all Non-Plan activities which are undertaken with Plan funds are
transferred to Non-Plan. This will be reviewed once again this year when the Revised
Estimates are prepared in September-October, 1998.

The Committee views with concern that the Finance Ministry has not honoured such
clear cut commitment made before the Parliamentary Committee. As the recommendations

of the Tenth Finance Commission have been accepted by the Government, it is the
e


3

commitment of Government too. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department of Culture should get the assurance implemented without any delay.

1.10 National Culture Fund:- The Committee was informed that the National Culture
Fund with the Government contribution of Rs. 19.5 crores was created on 28.11.99. So far,
Rs. 4 crores have been released during 1996-97 and 1997-98 from the plan budget of the
Department. In addition commitment of Rs. 1.61 crores which includes Rs. 1.5 crores from
Indo-British Fiftieth Anniversary Trust have been secured till now.

_ 1.11 The Committee is, however, constrained to note that incentives for contributions to
the NCF are inadequate. The Committee was informed that efforts of the Department for
securing 100% exemption under Section 80G(2) of the Income Tax Act to the donations
made to the National Culture Fund have not met with success so far. There are many other
organisations like the National Defence Fund, National Children’s Fund and National Sports
Fund, Universities etc. which are already having 100% tax exemption. The Committee feels
that a total exemption to the contribution made to NCF will prove to be a much desired
incentive for the possible donors. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
contribution to the NCF be fully exempted from Income Tax.

Il. ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA

2.1 The Committee desired that there should be a Light and Sound Programme at
Ajanta & Ellora. The Department in its reply stated that the Light and Sound
im protected monuments are organised by the Department of Tourism, Government of India
or the State Tourism Department with the permission of the ASI. The Department assured .,
that suggestion of the Committee would be communicated to the Central and State Tourism
Departments.

2.2 The Committee expressed its serious concern over the announcements made by
many archeaologists regarding dates of their findings without proper verification. The
Department clarified that apart from conducting excavations themselves, the ASI also
authorises the State Departments of Archaeology, Universities and Research Institutions for
excavation work. The ASI staff is fully trained to date the findings based on established
scientific methods. However, ASI is not responsible for statements given in this regard by
other agencies conducting excavation.

2.3 The Committee took serious note of the lack of preservation of monuments,
paintings and sculptures. The Department explained that the ASI has 3593 Centrally
protected monuments and complexes in the country. ASI has been taking up about 500
protected monuments for conservation, preservation and environmental development
annually. Besides that, paintings and sculptures in the Centrally protected monuments are
also taken up for chemical treatment. However, funds allocated for the overall conservation
of protected monuments and museums are quite meagre. For 1998-99, despite a projection
of Rs. 48 crores under plan, only Rs. 20 crores have been provided.

2.4 The Committee recommends that additional funds should be provided for ASI at the
RE stage so that ASI can increase the number of. monuments to be taken up annually.

2.5 The issue of creation of 5000 posts of Monument Attendants against an overall
requirement of about 11000 additional posts has been commented upon by the Committee in
its earlier Reports. In its 58th Report, the Committee had strongly recommended that the
Department should take immediate steps for creation of these posts and their subsequent
filling up. The Department in its reply has informed that the proposal, initiated by ASI in
1996 was kept in abeyance in view of Ministry of Finance instructions dated 9.2.1997 putting


4

a ban on creation of new posts. Meanwhile, ASI suggested that a Committee be constituted
with a Member from the SIU to look into the actual requirement of Monument Attendants.
This proposal was not accepted by the Integrated Finance Division and it was processed
further in consultation with the FA and referred to the Planning Commission in November,
1997. Based on their advice, a draft EFC proposal was prepared and sent to the appraising
agencies including the Planning Commission for comments. Comments from all the
appraising agencies have not yet reached and a reminder was last sent by the ASI in early
May, the Department informed.

2.6 The Committee takes serious note of virtually no progress being made in the matter
of filling up of posts of Monument Attendants. The Committee can well imagine the time
that would be taken by when these posts would be finally filled up. It is very surprising that
the proposal for additional Monument Attendants initiated in 1996 has not been finalised
even after a lapse of almost two years. The Committee wonders what would be the state of
3593 centrally protected monuments in the care of only 3443 Attendants till now. Hence the
Committee recommends that steps must be taken in this direction without further delay.

गा. NATIONAL ARCHIVES OF INDIA

3.1 The Committee in its 58th Report has stressed upon the need for improvement of
services provided by the National Archives. The Committee was given to understand that
the plan allocation for NAI was reduced from Rs. 3.50 crores to Rs. 2.65 crores at RE stage
in 1997-98 because the Computerisation Programme was deferred. Also the proposals to
revise the scheme of Financial Assistance for preservation of Archival material did not
materialise. The Department clarified that the allocation for NAI has been restored in BE
1998-99 since NAI has already initiated action to implement the Computerisation
Programme. Preparation of: computerised indices has been taken up with assistance of
ET&T, a public sector undertaking. This would faciliate retrieval of documents needed by
scholars. The Committee hopes that funds earmarked for National Archives in BE 1998-99
would be utilised fully.

3.2 As a result of efforts made by the Department, the officials of the National
Archives, System Specialists, young researchers and senior academicians of the Indian
Council of Historical Research are engaged, at present, in finding out ways and means to
make the Indices more user friendly, the Committee was informed.

3.3 The Committee suggested that as the National Archives was going in for large scale
Computerisation, research scholars visiting NAI should be allowed to use Lap-Top
Computers. The Secretary assured the Committee that the use of Lap-Top Computers by
Research Scholars will be permitted.

IV. MUSEUMS ‘

4.1 Indian Museum, Calcutta—The Committee had expressed its concern over the need
for expansion of space for increasing the range of display in the Indian Museum, Calcutta.
The Department has informed that although some upgradation has been executed during
1997-98, installation of Videogames, audio playback system, interactive display methods and
central air-conditioning of the building depended upon the completion of the new annexe
building. When asked to specify the time by when the proposed annexe building was likely
to be completed, the Department informed the Committee that the plan for constructing the
new Annexe Building of the Indian Museum which was taken up in October 1993 was
estimated to be completed within a span of 3 years from the date of approval by the
Calcutta Municipal Corporation. Unfortunately, work was stalled on account of an


5

injunction passed by the Calcutta High Court in July, 1994 which has since been vacated.
However, the estimate (Rs. 19.50 crores) for the building has still to be approved by the
Expenditure Finance Committee, which is, at present under exantination of the Department.
The Department further informed that the project for construction of the annexe building is
expected to be completed within a span of 5 years from the commencement of the actual
work, subject to availability of necessary funds for this purpose.

4.2 The Committee is constrained to note that no serious efforts have been made by the
Department with regard to construction of new annexe building for the Indian Museum,
Calcutta. Estimate for the building at present under examination of the Department is still
to be approved by EFC. The Committee can foresee that there is no likelihood of
construction of annexe building being started in near future. The Committee strongly
recommends that Department should get cleared all the procedural delays and monitor the
construction work of new annexe building of Indian Museum, Calcutta closely.

4.3 Salarjung Museum, Hyderabad—Expressing its concern over a number of thefts that
had taken place in the Salarjung Museum, the Committee had enquired about details of
action taken by the Government in this regard. The Department informed the Committee
that CBI enquiry in this regard is still continuing and its report is awaited. The Committee
feels that the CBI enquiry be completed at the earliest and appropriate action be taken. The
responsibility for the lapses should also be fixed.

4.4 While giving details about other remedial measures taken by them, the Department
also stated that a “Review Committee” has been set up by the Government to review Salar
jung Museum Act and Rules etc. and to draw up a Perspective Plan for the Museum.
However, the Review Committee was unable to finalise its ‘report due to the resignation of
its Chairman. Approval for the composition of the revised Committee as proposed by the
Salarjung Museum Board in its meeting held on 19.2.98 is awaited. The Committee falls to
understand the reasons for undue delay for approving the Revised Review Committee. The
Committee therefore, recommends that action in this regard should be taken without further
delay.

4.5 The Committee expressed its concern over the slow pace of construction of the new
wing of Salarjung Museum. The Department in its reply has informed that the NBCC were
not able to hand over the completed building by the target date of December, 1995. This
slow progress has been viewed seriously by the Salarjung Museum Board. All pending work
is expected to be completed by the end of August, 1998 and the Eastern and European
galleries made operational by October, 1998. The Committee takes serious note of the very
slow pace of construction work in Salarjung Museum and strongly recommends that the
works must be finished and galleries made operational within the time-schedule.

4.6 The Committee enquired about steps being taken to professionally catalogue the
collections of Salarjung Museum. The Department informed that the work of preparing
Catalogue/Index Cards for each art object has been completed in 1983 itself. However,
some cards were incomplete as far as pasting photographs was concerned. So far, 33,703
cards have been completed leaving a balance of 14,000 cards. The Committee hopes that
remaining work would be completed: by December, 1998.

५. LIBRARIES

5.1 Rural Libraries—The Committee was given to understand that the Rural Library
Scheme was proposed to be implemented through the Raja Rammohan Library Foundation
under the Scheme-of Financial Assistance for setting up Rural Libraries at the Panchayat


level. However, the Department informed that the scheme for establishing Rural Libraries at
the Panchayat level was drafted in consultation with the State Governments and referred to
the Planning Commission for approval. The Planning Commission, after examining the
proposal in detail, communicated in September, 1997 that they were unable to support the
idea in view of the NDC approved policy to transfer all Centrally Sponsored Schemes
(barring exceptional cases) to the States. In view of the NDC decision the Department now
wishes to support the State and local Governments to strengthen existing Rural Libraries.
For this, there is scope within the existing scheme of Raja Rammohan Roy Library
Foundation, the Committee was informed. Close coordination will be maintained with the
National Literacy Mission. The Department further informed that Library legislation has
been enacted in 10 States and action is being taken to persuade other States. The Committee
is of the opinion that steps should be taken to make Rural Library Scheme a reality with the
coordination of the State Governments. Keeping in view the noble objective behind this
scheme, the Committee desires that the Department should again approach the Planning
Commission.

VI. PROMOTION OF ART AND CULTURE

6.1 Centenaries—The Committee desired to ma about
Department in holding various centenary celebrations duri: -98. The Department in its
reply stated that during last year, the birth cente celebrations of Netaji Subhash
Chandra Bose, Zakir Hussain and Shri V.K. Krishna Menon, Enlightenment of Bhagwan
Raman and commemoration of the 400th death anniversary of Maharana Pratap were held.
Besides that the observance of the 50th anniversary of the Martyrdom of Mahatma Gandhi,
125th birth anniversary of Sri Aurobindo and birth bi-centenary of Mirza Ghalib have also
begun; Programmes for the current year are commencement of celebrations of the 600th
birth anniversary of Sant Kabir and the birth centenary of Shri Gulzari Lal Nanda and also
preparations for celebration for the 300th anniversary of the founding of Khalsa. The
Department also intended to attend to a number of unfinished tasks arising from the
decisions of the National and Implementation Committees like the establishment of the
Netaji Foundation, establishment of Netaji Memorial at Cuttack, Moirang and Calcutta, the
full release of the Rs. 3 crores committed for the memorial of Maharana Pratap and so on.

iflitiatives taken by the

6.2 The Committee enquired whether the Department was considering giving assistance
to Sisters of Ramkrishan Mission for organising the centenary of Sister Nivedita’s arrival in
India later this year. It was informed that the Department was in the process of examining
the proposal. The Committee feels that needful must be done in this regard.

6.3 The Committee appreciates the various initiatives taken by the Department in the
celebration of various centenaries and hopes that the Department would be able to attend to
various unfinished tasks during the current year. The Committee desires that the freedom
. fighters such as Kunhali Marikar of Kerala, Pazhassi Raja of Malabar and Veluthambi

-Dalawa of Travancore may be given due place in the programme of the Department.

6.4 Netaji Research Bureau—The Committee was constrained to note that out of
publicly committed grant of Rs. 6.25 crores, only a corpus grant of Rs. 3 crores has been
released to the Netaji Research Bureau by the Department. The Department informed that
the matter was taken up with the Prime Minister’s Office which conveyed on
14th November, 1996, Prime Minister’s directive for release of corpus grant of Rs. 3 crores
to Netaji Research Bureau and accordingly Rs. 3.00 crores was released in March, 1997. The
matter was again discussed in the meeting of the National Committee on 17.1.98 held under
the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister and it was decided that apart from Netaji Research
Bureau, other institutions like Netaji Institute of Asian Studies should also be helped.


7

Further, it was suggested that the Research Bureau, which has now received substantial
funds should be asked to amend its bye-laws to include academicians, on a rotational basis,
so that views and experience are not restricted to a limited group of people. However, in
view of the observations of the Standing Committee the matter would once again be taken
up with the PMO, the Department assured. Taking note of these developments the
Committee would like to emphasize again that the public commitments made by three
former Prime Ministers must be honoured and the balance amount should be released to
Netaji Research Bureau which has proved its worth over forty years and holds great
potential for the future.

6.5 Sahitya Akademi—The Committee was given to understand that about 50% of the
Sahitya Akademi’s publications are lying unsold. The Department clarified that Sahitya
Akademi publishes literary works in all the major Indian languages including less popular
languages such as Kashmiri and Dogri. While it is not always possible to take a very
commerical approach in the matter, the Department has advised the Sahitya Akademi to
plan their publications in such a manner that stocks do not accumulate. The Committee feels
that besides devising means to reduce the inventory of unsold publications of Sahitya
Akademi, steps should also be initiated for creating and increasing the interest of public in
such books so that they do not remain unsold in such large numbers. The Committee also
feels that the unsold publications may be distributed to all the Libraries.

6.6 Sangeet Natak Akademi—The Committee desired to know the various steps being
taken for promotion of the performing arts of India. The Department in its reply stated that
by arranging performances in various parts of the country by renowned veterans as well as
by talented young artists, through training programmes supported by scholarship and
through documentation and dissemination, the Akademi seeks and enhanced public
appreciation of music etc. The Akademi confers Fellowships and Awards to eminent
performers every year. The Committee, while appreciating the activities of Sangeet Natak
Akademi observes that special efforts should be made for nurturing Kathakali which needs
financial support for sustenance.

6.7 Multi Purpose Cultural Complexes—A maximum grant of Rs. 1 crore is given for
setting up Multi-Purpose Cultural Complex to an autonomous body set up by the concerned
State Government. The Committee desires that there shold be a proper monitoring
mechanism for the successful completion of these complexes under construction so as to
make them functional at the earliest. The Committee was informed that a number of sites
have been visited by the Officers of the Department. However sites yet to be inspected are
Manipur, Orissa, Mizoram, Jammu & Kashmir and Haryana. The Committee is perturbed to
note that most of the projects are still in the construction stage, and none of the Multi-
Purpose Cultural Complexes has become operational as yet. The Committee’ therefore,
recommends that special efforts should be made so that these Multi-Cultural Complexes
become operational without further delay.

6.8 Indira Gandhi National Centre for Arts (IGNCA)—The Indira Gandhi National
Centre for Arts (IGNCA) which was launched in November, 1986 was formally established
as an Autonomous Trust in March, 1987. The Committee was given to understand that the
Government’s commitment is to provide Rs. 100 crores for building and Rs. 50 crores
towards the corpus. The entire amount of Rs. 50 crores towards the corpus has been
released. As far as the amount of Rs. 100 crores is concerned, Rs. 80 crores have been
released and Rs. 45 crores have been spent. This amount of Rs. 100 crores is now going to
be increased to Rs. 300 crores. The allocation for the current year is Rs. 1.02 crores (Rs. 1
crore Plan and Rs. 2 lakhs Non-Plan).


8

6.9 It has come to the notice of the Committee that efforts are being made to interfere
in its internal working. It is an autonomous body doing excellent work with the help of
donations received from abroad. The Committee strongly feels that being an autonomous
institution Government should not interfere in its internal working.

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Sixty-eighth Report of the Committee on the
Demands for Grants (Demand No. 42) of the Department of Family Welfare, Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare for the year 1998-99.

2. The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from
the Department of Family Welfare, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and also heard
the Secretary and other Officials of that Department on the said Demands for Grants in its
meeting held on 22nd June, 1998.

3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same on the 2nd July,
1998.

New DELH; S.B. CHAVAN
July 2, 1998 Chairman

REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 One of the most pressing problems that is being faced today by the country is the
alarming rate of growth of population. Population of the country has multiplied by more
than four times during the century. It was 23.8 crore in 1901 Census while it became 84.6
crore in the 1991 Census and is presently expected to be 97.6 crore. India has only 2.4% of
the world land mass while its population constitutes 16% of the present world population.

1.2 The current high population growth rate is mainly due to three major factors as
enumerated below:

1. the large size of the population in the reproductive age group;
2. higher fertility due to unmet need for contraception; and
3. high wanted fertility due to prevailing high Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)

The all India average annual exponential growth rate during the last decade has been of
the order of 2.14% which is marginally lower than 2.22% during the previous decade. As
per the latest 1996 SRS estimates it is 1.85%, but it is still very high when compared with
the developed nations of the world.

1.3. The Committee notes that while there are creditable achievements and hopeful
signs in many States, the overall situation warrants concern. States of Kerala, Tamil Nadu
and Goa have already controlled birth rates and they are now at below the replacement level
of fertility. The situation in many other States like Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and West Bengal holds out hope that they could also control
birth rates sufficiently to reach below the replacement level of fertility. The situation in
regard to other large States is not yet so good as to warrant optimism. The Technical Group
on Population Projections appointed by the Planning Commission, reported in August, 1996
that if the trends indicated by the 1981—1991 Census continued, the country as a whole can
be expected to achieve replacement levels of fertility by the year 2026.

1.4 The Secretary stated that according to the UNFPA Population projections estimate
India would have a population of 162 crore by the year 2050 and it will surpass China as the
most populous country in the world.

1.5 Commenting on the Population Programme, the Department stated that there is
growing awareness in the country about the population situation. It is one among the most
critical issues before the country and unless this is controlled, there will be less scope for
optimism in other sectors. Taking note of this fact during the special sitting of the
Parliament coinciding with the celebrations for 50th anniversary of national independence
the population situation was one of the five themes highlighted in the document placed
before the Parliament for special debate. The resolution adopted by the Parliament, stated:

“that a vigorous national campaign be launched by all political parties to combat

economically unsustainable growth of population, recognising that such growth lies
at the root of most of our human, social and economic problems....”

II. NINTH PLAN PROPOSALS

2.1 The main objectives during the Ninth Plan Period, will be (a) to meet all the felt
needs for contraception and (b) to reduce the infant and maternal morbidity and mortality
so that there is a reduction in the desired level of fertility.

As per the Ninth Plan approach paper for achieving the above objectives, the following
broad strategies will be adopted.

(a) The needs of reproductive and child health care at PHC level will be assessed and
area specific microplanning will be undertaken.

(b) Attempts will be made to provide need based, client centred demand driven high
quality, Integrated Reproductive and Child Health Care.

The goal to be achieved by 2002 A.D. (end of Ninth Five Year Plan):—
1. Reduction of Total Fertility Rate to 2.6-2.9 from. the existing 3.5.

2. Reduction of birth rate to 23-24 per thousand population and infant mortality rate
to 50-56 against the current rate of 72 (1996).

3. Increasing the couple protection rate to 51-60% against the current figure of
45.4% (March, 1997).

2.2 The Committee observes that for the Ninth Plan Period which began in 1997-98, an
outlay of Rs. 16750.36 crore of Domestic Budgetary Support (DBS) and Rs. 5296.58 crore
of External Assistance (EAP) for implementing the Family Welfare Programme was

1432/RS/F-38


proposed to the Planning Commission. Of the DBS of Rs. 16750.36 crore Rs. 10270 crore is
required for the ongoing activities of the Department and Reproductive and Child Health.
Another minimum of Rs. 2000 crore is required for strengthening some of the key
programmes. Thus to achieve the targeted growth rate of population, Rs. 12270 crore is the
minimum requirement of DBS. Against this, the Planning Commission has earmarked a
DBS of Rs. 9100 crore for this Department. The EAP allocated of Rs. 1916.78 crore is also
far less than the amount projected.

Ill. BUDGET ALLOCATION

3.1 The Committee notes that the allocation to the Department has been substantially
increased from Rs. 1844.81 crores, in B.E. 1997-98 to Rs. 2510.51 crores in the current year.
Out of Rs. 2510.51 crores, Rs. 2489.35 crores, forms the plan component and Rs. 21.16
crores is the non-plan component. The Domestic Budgetary Support is Rs. 1726.85 crores
and the Externally Aided component is Rs. 762.50 crores.

3.2 Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, the Secretary stated that
Family Welfare Programme is a 100 per cent centrally funded programme and this time
realising the importance of the programme, the Planning Commission provided Rs. 660
crores more than that of the last year. The Secretary further stated that out of Rs. 660
crores, Rs. 410 crores will be used for infrastructure maintenance which is a welcome sign.
Asked about the settlement of arrears to the State Governments the Department stated that
on the basis of statements received upto 1st April, 1997 Rs. 192 crores was due as arrears
payable to the States and during the year claims worth Rs. 361 crores was received. It was
also stated that only an outlay of Rs. 79 crores was provided in the Budget and another Rs.
187.11 crores was reappropriated towards liquidation of arrears by cutting down on other
programmes and as on 1-4-1998 an amount of Rs. 287.24 crores remains to be settled.

3.3 The Secretary while deposing before the Committee stated that the Department
made lot of efforts to solve the issue and the matter was taken up at the political level also.
An assurance was given that while determining Annual Plan outlay for the Department, the
Planning Commission would take a realistic view of the arrears and actual level of
expenditure, for maintaining infrastructure and provide this as first charge for the
Department. As a result an amount of Rs. 250 crores has been set apart this year for
liquidating the arrears. The Secretary also expressed his hope that although this will help in
the control of the problem of arrears, it will take a minimum of 2-3 years, to overcome it.

3.4 The Committee feels that non-payment of arrears claims of State Governments is
unfair to the State Governments because it is the responsibility of the Central Government
at whose insistance the infrastructure was created. The Committee finds that this long
pendency of dues has resulted in non-filling up of posts of para-medical and medical staff by
some States so as to reduce their financial liabilities which in turn is hurting the Family
Welfare Programme. The Committee is of the opinion that urgent and concrete steps need
to be taken in this regard.

3.5 The Department also submitted that from last year, the Planning Commission
started indicating the Domestic Budgetary Support (DBS) and External Assistance
Programme (EAP) component separately in order to make full use of external assistance.
However, the Domestically Funded Programme which was otherwise also underfunded was
further squeezed.


E 4

3.6 The Committee notes that the NDC Committee on Population had recommended in
1993 that States should meet 10% of expenditure of Family Welfare Programmes and this
recommendation was taken up more than once with the States in the Central Council of
Health and Family Welfare (where Ministers of State Governments are members) but the
States have strongly resisted sharing any burden in this regard.

3.7 The Committee feels that the matter should be discussed at the Prime Minister level
with the Chief Ministers of States at the full-fledged NDC meeting.

IV. RURAL FAMILY WELFARE CENTRES

4.1 Rural Family Welfare Centres are entrusted with the responsibility of implementing
the Family Welfare Programme i.e. Planning, mobilization, monitoring, administration and
supervision in rural areas. 5435 such centres are working at all block level PHCs and the
number has been stagnant at the same level since 1.4.1980. These centres have been marged
with the Primary Health Centres thereafter.

4.2 The budget allocation made to these centres in 1998-99 is Rs. 265 crores which is
slightly higher than that of last year. When the Committee sought to know whether the
increased allocation would be sufficient to maintain the existing centres, the Department
replied in the negative.

4.3 The Committee is of the opinion that it is the duty of the Department to provide
sufficient funds for maintenance of the infrastructure created, as these centres serve the rural
poor and they should not starve for funds.

V. RURAL SUB-CENTRES

5.1 Rural Sub-Centres are the peripheral Health institutions available to the rural
population for the delivery of Health and Family Welfare Services. These centres have been
opened for every 5000 rural population in plain areas and 3000 population in the tribal and
hilly areas. There are at present, 1,31,900 sub-centres functioning in the country out of
which 97757 sub-centres are funded by Government of India as per approved pattern and
the rest are funded under Minimum Needs Programme.

5.2 This year an allocation of Rs. 340 crores has been provided for the centres. When
the Committee sought to know about the opening of new 1500 rural sub-centres as envisaged
during the 1997-98, the Department submitted that the State Governments are not being
assisted for opening new sub-centres during VIII Plan period because there has been no such
scheme and outlay was insufficient to maintain even the existing ones.

5.3 The Committee was informed that from 1997, the Government decided that the
State Governments should be given freedom to use additional Central assistance transferred
to them by the Planning Commission for any item covered by the Basic Minimum Services.
The Committee feels that this is not the correct approach. The Committee apprehends that
there is a possibility of diversion of funds and therefore recommends the revival of the old
pattern. Around 386 sub-centres have been opened by three State Governments during the
year 1997-98.

5.4 The Committee notes that as per 1991 census the shortfall in the sub-centres is
7,727 and by the end of the Ninth Plan it will be 22, 987. The Committee feels that opening
of only 386 sub-centres is not going to serve any purpose. The Committee, therefore, desires
that the Department should urge upon the States to open fixed number of centres each year
and to set apart some provision in their Budget for the purpose.


VI. URBAN FAMILY WELFARE CENTRES/HEALTH POSTS

6.1 Urban Family Welfare Centres provide Family Welfare and Maternity Child Health
Services in urban areas. At present 1499 centres are functioning, of which 208 are run by the
Central sector i.e. Ministry of Railways, Defence, Labour, etc.

6.2 The allocation for the centres has been stepped up from Rs. 50 crores last year to
Rs. 64 crores this year. On the question of methodology adopted for establishment of Health
Posts, the Department stated that the proposed city to be covered under the (Urban
Revamping) scheme should have a slum population of about 40% and the existing staff of
the centres in the area were to be adjusted against the proposed sanctioned posts to be
created under the scheme.

6.3 Asked about the progress made by the Committee to suggest appropriate
programmes to reorganise health posts, the Department stated that the expert group
appointed to formulate MCH and F.W. Services (RCH package) in urban slums has
submitted its recommendations and the Department has formulated the scheme guidelines.

6.4 The scheme broadly envisages establishment of fixed health posts one each for slum
population of 15000, mobile health units for clusters of smaller slums and maternity clinics
run by medical NGOs with a lumpsum grant to the NGOs, to provide all primary health
care and spacing methods of contraception. These facilities will be managed by Municipal
Bodies. The funds for the same would come from the World Bank Project and the scheme
has been given to them for their concurrence.

6.5 The Committee feels that slums are proliferating at a faster pace in the urban areas.
The Committee, therefore, suggests that the Department should get the concurrence of
municipal bodies expeditiously so that the scheme could be implemented at the earliest.

VII. INFORMATION, EDUCATION AND COMMUNICATION (IEC) -

7.1 To provide full and integrated support to the community oriented services for
mother and child health and to encourage adoption of small family norm, IEC activities
were reoriented during the 8th Plan by carrying the Family Welfare Programme towards the
community.

7.2 The allocation for Information, Education and Communication (IEC) has been
reduced from Rs. 61.80 crores in B.E. 1997-98 to Rs. 55.05 crores in R.E. 1997-98 and
further to Rs. 29.70 crores in B.E. 1998-99. The Department contended that the total
allocation for Information, Education and Communication (IEC) in B.E. 1998-99 is Rs.
81.70 crores, which includes Rs. 52.00 crores for IEC under RCH Programme and there is
no reduction in the overall allocation for IEC activities. The reduction from Rs. 61.30 crores
in B.E. 1997-98 to Rs. 55.05 crores in R.E. 1997-98 is mainly due to discontinuation of some
of the ongoing activities like Swasthya Mela, IEC for primary school health check-up
programme etc.

7.3 The Secretary while deposing before the Committee stated that action has been
initiated in consultation with National Literacy Mission and Department of Education to
involve Zilla Saksharata Samities for district specific IEC activities through professionals at
district level, the District Collectors have been requested to formulate the proposals and
forward the same to the Department for approval. The Secretaries, Family Welfare and
Directors, Family Welfare of the States have also been requested to expedite the proposals.
The Department of Education has also advised the State Directorates of Education
accordingly.

(gr. RS


7.4 The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Department in this regard. The
Committee is of the view that the Department should try to involve the local bodies also in the
IEC activities. This in turn will yield fruitful results as the IEC activities will percolate down to
the bottom level.

VIII. TRAINING OF AUXILIARY NURSE MIDWIVES/LADY HEALTH VISITORS

8.1 An allocation of Rs. 25 crores have been provided during the current year. The
amount allocated under the scheme is towards the maintenance of the existing ANM Training
Schools on the basis of approved pattern of assistance. There are at present 509 ANM
(Female Health Workers) Training Schools with an admission capacity of 16000. The
Committee notes that against 1,58,349 sanctioned posts of ANMs, there are 1,33,282 LHVs,
only 18409 LHVs are in position.

8.2 When Committee sought to know the steps taken by Department to fill up the large
vacancies that are existing, the Department stated that the appointment of ANMs and LHVs
is done by the State Governments, and the Department monitors only the health manpower
availability through quarterly reports, review meetings with the State officials and visits to the
States and UTs. From time to time, the State Governments are reminded to fill up the
vacancies to provide quality services at the field levels.

8.3 The auxiliary midwife is the most effective functionary in the system to man the
Primary Health Centres, Rural Family Welfare Centres and Health Posts. The Committee,
therefore, feels that the Department should impress upon the State Governments to fill up the
posts at the earliest. The Committee feels that keeping such an important post vacant for a
long time, will hurt the programme and quality of services may also be effected at the field
level.

IX. VILLAGE HEALTH GUIDE SCHEME

9.1 An allocation of Rs. 10 crores has been made for the scheme this year. When the
Committee sought to know the details about the Expert Committee constituted to suggest
ways for making use of Health Guides more meaningful, the Department submitted that the
expert Committee is expected to submit its report in August, 1998. The Committee hopes that
an early decision on the expert Committee recommendations will be taken by the
Department.

X. STERILISATION BEDS SCHEME

10.1 For providing facility for tubectomy operation in hospitals run by Government, local
bodies and Voluntary Organisations where such cases could not be admitted due to non-
availability of beds, a maintenance grant of Rs. 4500 per bed per annum is paid to each
institution subject to the condition that a minimum 75/60 tubectomy operations per bed are
achieved. At present, 3170 beds are functioning.

10.2 An allocation of Rs. 1.7 crore has been made this year, against a provision of Rs.2
crore made last year. The Committee notes that around 16,45,367 tubectomy operations,
4,62,274 laproscopic female sterilisation, 2514 No-scalpel Vasectomy have been performed
during 1997-98.

10.3 The Department submitted to the Committee that with a view to increase the male
acceptance of family planning Government of India has recently launched a programme for
popularising the new method of vasectomy known as the No-scalpel Vasectomy. This project
consists of training of 1,500 doctors in different parts of the country in the conduct of the No-
scalpel Vasectomy.


7

10.4 As the training programme requires case-load, funds are provided for organising
publicity in advance. The project, is funded by UNEPA and was launched in the last quarter
of 1997-98, 19 training courses were organised in thé States of Andhra Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana. 2514 men underwent the No-scalpel Vasectomy in
these training camps and 71 doctors were trained. The maximum response to this scheme has
come from Andhra Pradesh where 14 training courses were organised.

10.5 The Committee feels that for popularising the No-scalpel Vasectomy and for
healthy implementation of the programmes training course should be organised in all the
States. A massive IEC campaign through AIR/DD stating the merits of No-scalpel
Vasectomy may also be undertaken.

XI. SOCIAL MARKETING OF NIRODH

11.1 For social marketing, a provision of Rs. 80 crore has been made in B.E.
1998-99 as against a provision of Rs. 54.05 crores in 8.8. 1997-98.

11.2 The Department contended that the actual expenditure incurred under the head
during the last year was Rs. 65.36 crore, that is why higher provision has been made this
year. The Department also informed that with the increased allocation steps are being taken
to strengthen the social marketing where availability of contraceptives is a problem.

11.3 On the question of strengthening the social marketing through small companies and
NGOs, to ensure reliable and regular supply of contraceptives upto Panchayat level, the
Department stated that a proposal in this regard has been submitted to the EFC for
approval.

11.4 The Committee desires that EFC approval may be obtained at the earliest to
enable the NGOs and small companies to supply the contraceptives in the rural areas where
there is much need in view of the threatening AIDS scenario.

XII. REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROJECT

12.1 “Reproductive and Child Health” programme was launched in 1997-98. The main
objectives of the programme are (a) improve the performance of the Family Welfare system
in implementing policy change; (b) strengthen the quality and effectives of a defined
essential package of services, and improve project implementation through the application of
performance based criteria for continued funding.

12.2 There has been a steep hike in the budget provision for ‘Maternal and Child
Health’ from Rs.450.10 crores in B.E. 1997-98 to Rs. 758 crores in B.E. 1998-99, justifying
the increase for the programme to achieve the objectives of the Reproductive and Child
Health (RCH) Programme the Department submitted that all interventions of Fertility
regulation and Material and Child Health (MCH) have been integrated. Under the ongoing
Child Survival and Safe Motherhood (CSSM) Programme, the focus was on integrated MCH
services and establishment of First Referral Units (FRUs) for providing emergency obstetric
care services at sub-district level health facilities. The input provided under CSSM
Programme was the equipment kits. However, under the RCH Programme the focus will be
on strengthening maternal care at all levels by:

(i) strengthening essential obstetric care by providing contractual staff viz. additional
ANMs in the remote/tribal/backward areas specially in the backward States of
Assam, Bihar, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Nagaland, Rajasthan and Uttar
Pradesh, Staff Nurse:at PHC level etc.


8

(ii). enhancement of RCH facilities in PHCs by providing of infrastructure upgradation,
drugs support and contractual trained manpower.

(iii) facilities of MTP and IUD insertions are also strengthened in PHCs and Sub-
centres.

(iv) strengthening and enhancing of essential obstetric care at FRU level by provision of
Lab. Technician, Anaesthetist, drug support and provision of equipment in
remaining sub-district hospitals.

(v) assisting States in conducting ‘diploma Courses’ in Anaesthesia.
(vi) strengthening 24 hour delivery services in PHCs.
(vii) strengthening the new born care service by providing equipments.

(viii) a special programme for detection and treatment of Reproductive Tract infection
and STDs at FRU level.

12.3 The department further submitted that the Programme also aims at improving the
outreach of services primarily for the vulnerable groups of population who have till now
been left out of the planning process e.g. urban slums, tribal population and adolescents.
The Committee approves the idea. However, the Committee feels that there should be a
monitoring Committee comprising of representatives of Central/State/Local bodies and
people’s representatives of the concerned area for effective implementation of the
programme. The Programme also envisages enhanced role and participation of NGOs and
Voluntary Organisations, practitioners of Indian System of Medicine. Panchayati Raj system
will have a greater role in planning, implementation and assessment of client satisfaction.

12.4 The additional amount under the Programme will be utilised for the additional
inputs brought under the RCH Programme like drugs, equipments, NGO participation, ISM.
Special Project on urban slums, tribal areas and adolescents, referral services, upgradation of
infrastructure, contractual staff and strengthening facilities under Local Capacity
enhancement component of the programme.

12.5 The Committee observes that out of the total budget of the department, 1/3rd of
the budget has been allocated to this programme. The Committee hopes that the department
would be able to achieve the objectives as envisioned in the programmes when sufficient
allocation has been made.

XIII. THE CONSTITUTION (SEVENTY-NINTH) AMENDMENT BILL, 1992

13.1 The Bill seeks to amend the Directive Principles of State Policy to provide that the
State shall endeavour to promote population control and to include to the Fundamental
Duties a commitment to promote and adopt the small family norm. The Bill also proposes
that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as and for being a Member of either
House of Parliament or the Legislature of a State, if he has more than two children. The Bill
will, however, have prospective effects.

13.2 On the steps being taken by the Government to ensure an early passage of 79th
Constitutional Amendment Bill, the department stated that the Minister of State for Health
and Family Welfare (Independent Charge) desires that the Constitution (Seventy-ninth
Amendment) Bill needs to be reconsidered by the Government. The matter is accordingly
being submitted to Cabinet for directions.


9

13.3 The Committee is constrained to note that despite the Committee submitting its
report on the matter in 1995, no decision has been taken so far. The Committee is deeply
anguished to note that the bill is being reconsidered.

XIV. NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY

14.1 The Draft National Population Policy prepared by the Swaminathan Committee,
was presented to the Parliament in June, 1994. However, the final document has not yet
been finalised.

14.2 Asked about the latest position, the Department stated that the National
Population Policy was approved by Cabinet on 20th November, 1997, with directions to
table the Policy in both Houses of Parliament. On account of the two Houses of Parliament
being adjourned sine-die on the date on which tabling of this Policy document was scheduled
in the business of two Houses, followed by the dissolution of Eleventh Lok Sabha, the
Policy could not be tabled in Parliament. The Direction of the new Government have been
sought on the contents of the National Population Policy. The Minister of State, Health and
Family Welfare desires to consult experts before a view is taken.

14.3 The Committee notes that it is quite a long time since the draft policy has been
submitted to the Government. The Committee feels that necessary consultation with the
experts may be completed soon to enable the department to table the policy in the next
session of Parliament.

14.4 In view of the total neglect of Family Planning and population control, the
Committee feels that it deserves urgent attention, and the policy is a step in the right
direction. The Committee desires that all the political parties should evolve a consensus
approach in the matter.

XV. FREE DISTRIBUTION OF CONVENTIONAL CONTRACEPTIVES

15.1 An allocation of Rs. 92 crores has been made for the current year, as against
Rs. 109.90 crores in B.E. 1997-98. When asked to explain the reasons for reduction, the
Department stated that the actual expenditure incurred during the year was
Rs. 80.66 crore, this was due to the measures taken to avoid unnecessary wastage of
condoms. The Department also stated users of oral pill increased by 20.6% whereas the
condom users remained the same.

15.2 The Committee was also informed that a new scheme for allowing the field level
workers for charging service fee of Re. 1/- for packet of 10 condoms from the beneficiaries
and allowing the field level workers to retain the proceeds is proposed to be implemented
throughout the country.

15.3 The Committee feels that the scheme should be implemented in the-current year
itself, as it will not only promote the use of condom at the field level but in turn reduce
wastage.

XVI. INVOLVEMENT OF VOLUNTARY ORGANISATIONS

16.1 The allocation for involvement of other Departments and Voluntary Organisations,

: etc., on the plan side has been reduced from Rs. 8.50 crores in B.E. and R.E. 1997-98 to

Rs. 6.00 crores in 1998-99. When the Committee sought to know about decrease, the
Department stated that actually against a provision of Rs.8.50 crores in 1997-98, provision in
1998-99 is Rs. 31 crores. The NGO Programme will actually be strengthened in 1998-99. The
Committee fails to understand how the allocation suddenly jumped when only Rs.8.50 crores
has been shown in the expenditure budget. The Committee feels that something is wrong in
the reported figures.


10

XVII. ACCURACY AND AUTHENTICITY OF DATA

17.1 The Committee was informed by the Secretary that the rate of Growth of
Population in 1996 as per (SRS) estimates is 1.85. On being questioned about the accuracy
of the figures, the Secretary stated that from 1996 a National Family Health Survey have
been started at the District Levels and figures are obtained from that survey which is
authentic. The Secretary also stated that this will be done every year. The Committee
welcomes this idea.

XVIH. COMMITTED LIABILITY

18.1 The Committee in its 60th Report had recommended that the department should
make a thorough review of the schemes and identify the committed liability. In this matter,
the Committee considered the Report of the Tenth Finance Commission. The Tenth Finance
Commission have observed as under:

“Although the Tenth Finance Commission have gone by their terms of reference in
deciding the cut-off date for transfer of committed liability on account of plan scheme,
the incremental liabilities that would arise in 1997-98 on account of 8th Plan scheme
completed in the next two financial years would have to be provided for. The
Commission are, therefore, of the view that the Planning Commission may consider
providing for the maintenance of such schemes till 1999-2000 in the Plan itself as was
done for the schemes of the two Annual Plans of 1990-91 and 1991-92.”

18.2 The Committee in this connection heard the views of the Secretary, Department of
Expenditure last year to clarify the position. He informed the Committee that even though
communications were sent to various Ministries, the Ministries could not identify the
committed expenditure on time. Accordingly a lumpsum amount has been provided under
Demand No. 31. The Secretary also assured that if required more funds for this purpose will
be provided at the RE stage. He also stated that the Departments may approach the
Department of Expenditure for their share.

18.3 The Department submitted that a proposal to shift the committed expenditure
under Family Welfare Programme to the Non-Plan budget was moved to Ministry of Finance
in February, 1997. In response, Ministry of Finance suggested that instead of transferring to
Non-Plan budget, the maintenance expenditure be transferred to the State Government’s
budget in consultation with the Planning Commission. Accordingly, a letter was addressed to
the Planning Commission seeking their advice on the issue in July, 1997 but no response has
been received from them so far. The issue of transfer of committed liabilities to the State
budget was included in the agenda for the fifth meeting of the Central Council of Health and
Family Welfare. The Council felt that the time then was not opportune to transfer the
liabilities to States.

18.4 The Committee views with concern that the Finance Ministry has not honoured
such clear cut commitment made before the Parliamentary Committee. As the
recommendations of the Tenth Finance Commission have been accepted by the
Government, it is the commitment of Government too. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department of Family Welfare should get the assurance implemented
without any delay.

REPORT

I. INTRODUCTION

1.1 The Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is instrumental and responsible
for implementation of various programmes of national importance like family welfare,
primary health care, prevention, control and eradication of major diseases which form the
main plank of our development efforts. Apart from these, the Ministry also takes special
care for preventing the spread of diseases assuming the dimension of epidemic. The
Department of Health, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is
committed to achieve the goal of health for all by the year 2000 A.D. is responsible for |
evolving broad policies for the health sector and provides financial and technical assistance
to State Governments in critical areas through the implementation of important health
programmes.

1.2 Broadly, the objectives of the Department are to undertake National Health
Programmes, to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to
prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs, to provide primary health care at the door
steps of the people, to take steps for better implementation of health care programmes for
tribal and other weaker sections of the society and also to collaborate with member countries
of United Nations and international agencies like WHO, UNICEF, etc. in matters relating
to health promotion and development.

1.3 The Department finances the State and Union Territory Administrations for
Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being implemented by them and includes national
programmes for prevention control and eradication of diseases. Some of the schemes which
are financed to the tune of 100% by the Central Government are National Schemes for
Prevention of Visual Impairment and Blindness including ‘Trachoma, National Leprosy
Eradication Programme, National Guinea Worm Eradication Programme and National
AIDS Control Programme. While for some other programmes like National Malaria
Eradication Programme (Rural and Urban), National Sexually Transmitted Diseases Control
Programme, National 1.8. Control Programme, Kala-Azar Control Programme it is on a
50:50 basis by the Central and State Governments.

1.4 The Department also finances, wholly or substantially,the following autonomous
institutions engaged in patient care andor research; All India Institute of Medical Sciences
and Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences, New Delhi, Post-Graduate
Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh, All India Institute of Speech and
Hearing, Mysore., Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi.

II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

2.1. The Department of Health has been allocated Rs. 1122.16 crores on the Plan side
and Rs. 654.52 crores on the Non-Plan side, for the year 1998-99.

2.2 As compared to total outlay of Rs. 920.20 crores in 1997-98 outlay of Rs. 1122.16
crores for medical and public health for 1998-99 shows a quantum jump. Major portion of
the outlay is meant for National Programmes for control of Communicable Diseases and
other diseases implemented through State Governments on the health side. Maximum
allocation has been made for National Malaria Eradication Programme (Rs. 287.00 crores),

Programme, National Trachoma and Blindness Control Programme, National Leprosy
Eradication Programme, National TB Control Programme and Kala-Azar Control Prog-
ramme. On the medical side the emphasis is on the development of medical sciences
including medical education, training and research for which an outlay of Rs. 254.01 crores
have been provided during 1998-99.

2.3 Commenting on the budget allocation, the Secretary stated that when compared
with the Eighth Plan figure of Rs. 2,825 crores, the Ninth Plan figure of Rs. 4,995.59 crores
including a foreign aid component of Rs. 1,497 crores, signifies a 75% increase. However, in
real terms, it has increased by 35 per cent only.

2.4 The Secretary informed the Committee that the allocation made to the Department
is insufficient to ¢arry“Oi its activities: With this allocation,” the Secretary stated that the
Department’ may ot be~ able 10 start the programme for testing -hepatitis, for which the
Department would be short by Rs. 68 crores. The Committee feels that testing hepatitis
should be started in a big way and necessary funds may be provided at the RE stage.
Another area which needs immediate attention and the Department may not be able to
attend to, is immunisation for Hepatitis-B as part of immunisation programme for which
there is a need for Rs. 600 crores. The Committee is of thé opinion that immunisation for
Hepatitis-B should be started in a phased manner in view of paucity of funds. Funds will not
be sufficient for setting up a trauma Centre at AIIMS, for which a minimum of Rs. 100
crores is required. The Committee was also informed that there is shortage of funds for
construction of quarters for the faculty of AIIMS.

2.5 The Committee feels that the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance
should take a realistic view of the needs of the Department and try to provide more funds to
attain the goal of Health for All by 2000 A.D.

गा, CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME

3.1 The Plan allocation for CGHS was reduced from Rs. 9 crores in BE 1997-98 to
Rs. 5 crores in RE 1997-98. However, it has been stepped up to Rs. 9 crores in BE 1998-99.

stated that the increase is for expansion of CGHS to new cities and for opening of new

caters to about 44 lakh beneficiaries in 18 cities of the country. The Secretary assured the

study of CGHS dispensaries from Ministry of Finance by July, 1998. The Committee
recommends that the expansion of CGHS as envisaged during the year be undertaken.

privatise. some of the services. This was duly approved by the Expenditure Finance
Committee in February, 1998. However, there has been a lot of resistance from the Group
‘C’ and ‘D’ Unions against these efforts of privatisation or for even having contract labour.

9.3, Considering the fact that a large number of new cases occur in the country every
year and the facilities at the grass root level are not available at all, the Committee
recommends that the Department should take necessary steps to providé requisite funds for
establishing regional cancer centres. The Committee also feel that the departments should
take steps to establish Diagnositic Centres for preliminary screening of caricer at the district
hospitals. है

X. NATIONAL T.B. CONTROL PROGRAMME

10.1 T.B. continues to be a major health problem in the country. It affects mainly
people in their most productive years of life and is commonly associated with poverty,
overcrowding and malnutrition. Lack of education, environmental pollution and poor
sanitation compound the problem. The Secretary informed the Committee that the
Department is seized of the magnitude of the problem of T.B. morbidity and mortality in
the country. The Committee was informed that the Prevalence rate of T.B. is around 1.5.%
i.e. about 1.5 crores T.B. patients are presently there in the whole of the country. Control of
’T.B. has become all the more important due to the emerging dangers from HIV/TB co-
- infection. The Secretary further informed that the department is presently adopting revised
DOT Strategy (Directly Observed Treatment Short-Course Chemotherapy) to fight against
T.B. under a World Bank funded project which has been implemented in 102 districts in the
Country and already 42,741 cases have been treated under the project till 31st March, 1998.
Apart from this; support from World Bank to 203 other districts is also being given for
strengthening of State T.B. Cells/Training and Demonstration Centres/Labs as well as
training and for IEC. For the remaining 154 district of the country, the project intervention
is in the form of strengthening of State TRB Cell/Training and Demonstration Centre and
supply of conventional drugs.

10.2 This year the allocation for the programme has been substantially raised :
Rs. 90 crores BE 1997-98 to Rs. 125 crores in BE 1998-99. However, the Committee would
like to point out, that inspite of a well planned strategy for control of T.B., financial targets
could not be achieved in the entire Eighth Plan period. Not only this, in 1997-98, only
Rs.32.05 crores could be utilised against the allocation of Rs.90 crores in BE 1997-98. This
has been mainly due to delay in the delivery services as a result of lengthy World Bank
procedures. All these procedures have now been streamlined and also supply of drugs ‘has
also been decentralised, the Department clarified. The Committee recommends that th
Department should take effective steps for full utilisation of allocated funds.

XI. NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME

11.1 This programme is implemented with the aim to achieve elimination of leprosy by
the year 2000 A.D. The Committee was informed by the Secretary that it is one of the most
successful programme and it is due to the effect of the recent drugs which have entered in

1483/RS/F—-A


the market. States like U.P, Bihar and Orissa where the Prevalence rate is high also took active
part in the programme. Recently, Tamil Nadu has launched a new programme, the modified
Leprosy Programme, where identification squads are sent to bring out the hidden cases which
are not reported due to several reasons. The same procedure was followed in the States of U.P.,
Bihar and Orissa and about 3,70,000 hidden cases were identified, the Secretary added.
However, some States like West Bengal, Rajasthan have so far not followed this procedure.

1 While appreciating the steps taken by the Department so far, the Committee is constrained to

note that out of Rs. 75 crores allocated for this programme in 1997-98, only Rs.57.60 crores
could be utilised. Not only this, there was shortfall in the achievement of physical targets as well
during 1997-98. The Committee feels that Identification squads should be made compulsory for
all the States. The Committee also desires that programme should be implemented with greater
vigour so as to achieve elimination of leprosy by the year 2000 A.D.

XII. NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS

12.1 The Programme.was launched by the Government in 1976 to reduce the blindness

“from 1.4% to.0.3%. by-2000-A.D. The Committee was informed by the Secretary that a World

Bank Assisted Cataract Blindness Control Project is being implemented since April 1994 in
seven States where prevalence rate is very high (i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh,
Maharashtra, Orissa and Rajasthan). The Secretary informed that in the last four years
6.6 million cataract operations have been performed against the target of 11 million operations
over a period of seven years.

12.2 Delay in creation of posts in the various eye-care facilities, slow progress of civil

constructions work in District hospitals, PHCs etc., delay in procurement of drugs/consumables,

of stock level in the States funded under the World Bank Project were the main reasons cited by
the Department for under utilisation of funds under the Programme. The Committee
recommends that the Departni€at should take effective steps for streamlining the procedural
delays.

12.3 The Committee was also informed that the stress is now on 101, surgeries and there is

a shortage of surgeons to perform this surgery. The Committee feels that when the stress is on ~

quality more number of surgeons should be given training for performing IOL surgery.

12.4 The Committee also notes that in 1997-98 against the target of 30,18,000, cataract
operations, upto November, 1997, 11,76,000 cataract operations have been performed but by
March, 1998 the number has risen to 30,11,000. (Provisional). The Committee wonders how so
many operations have been performed within the short span of time when the stress is on
quality. The Committee desires that the reported figures be. verified thoroughly.

XIII. NATIONAL MALARIA ERADICATION PROGRAMME

13.1 Out of the total allocation of Rs. 297 crores for Malaria Control in BE 1998-99, Rs.137
crores have been earmarked for National Malaria Eradication Programme. The allocation for
Kala-azar Control is Rs. 10 crores and under Externally Aided Component (EAC) for the
Enhanced Malaria Control Project with World Bank support, Rs.150 crores have been
allocated. Thus, it would be seen that as against Rs.140 crores in 1997-98, during the current
year, allocation for NMEP has been reduced by Rs.3 crores, While the provision for Kala-azar
Control Programme has been retained at the same level as in 1997-98 there has been substantial
increase in the budgetary allocations under Enhanced Malaria Control Project with World Bank
support from Rs.50 crores in 1997-98 to Rs.150 crores, in 1998-99. Out of this, the Committee
was told, Rs.105 crores have been kept for Insecticides, Larvicidés, Drugs Material and
Equipments.

13.2 Keeping in view the rising incidence.of Malaria and focal outbreaks in some parts of

the country as well as the vectors of malaria to the conventional insecticides, integrated
approach of Malaria Control under the National Programme has been taken up.

13.3 The Department further informed the Committee that in order to intensify the
Malaria Control activities, an Enhanced Malaria Control Project with World Bank support
to essentially cover 100 Districts in 7 Peninsular States namely Andhra Pradesh, Bihar,
Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and Rajasthan as well as 19 Towns/cities has
been launched during 1997-98. The Committee desires that the Department should explore
the possibility of including Terai areas of U.P. under the World Bank Project.

13.4, The Committee is happy to note that the Department has initiated a programme
for observance of Anti-Malaria Month in June every year from 1997 for creating public
awareness and involving the community in the prevention and control of Malaria. However,
the Committee finds that targets for spray coverage of population could not be achieved
during the last two years :—
