4736/ RS/ F—4-B


5

Since no regular maintenance could be taken up due to paucity of resources, now in addition to regular
maintenance, SAI needs Rs. 16.00 crores for special repairs of various stadia at Delhi and Rs. 2.52 crores for
infrastructure at SAI Regional Centres. The entire special repair programme can be taken up immediately provided
funds are available.

The non plan budget of SAI has been reduced from Rs. 11.63 crores in 1994-95 to Rs. 6.00 crores in 1997-98.
Ministry of Finance has opined that SAI should generate its own resources to take care of the Non Plan expenditure.
The generation of resources by SAI, though, has gradually increased from Rs. 1.83 crore in 1992-93 to Rs. 6.18
crores in 1995-96 to approximately Rs. 8 crore in 1996-97, is not enough to take care of the maintenance requirement.
As such a planned programme of maintenance cannot be taken up unless suitable budgetary support is provided to
SAI under Non-Plan. However, whatever is possible within the existing resources is being done after prioritising
the works.

As regards monitoring and inspections of these buildings, SAI and the Department are taking necessary action.
Further Comments

The Secretary stated that all the five stadia in Delhi are maintained by different organisations but the Department
has very little resources and within that they have to meet the expenditure. The maintenance agencies do not pay
for the maintenance and only SAI provides funds for this purpose, it was clarified. While agreeing that the
maintenance is not properly done, the Secretary informed the Committee that alteast Rs. 16 to 20 crores are
required for bringing these stadia up to the required level. The Secretary stated that sufficient funds should be
made available to the Department for major repairs since for the last twenty years there had been no proper
maintenance of these stadia for want of money. The Secretary further informed the Committee that for the last two
and a half years, all new schemes have been put on hold so that all the funds could be spent in completing the
unfinished stadia.

On the question as to whether the stadia should be handed over to local bodies for maintenance or not, the
Secretary agreed that they should be handed over to the local bodies.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is very constrained to note the pathetic condition in which the stadia are existing now. The
Committee strongly feels that the Department should approach the Ministry of Finance and the Planning Commission
without delay for providing a one time grant for immediate and necessary maintenance of all the stadia. The
Committee is of the view that new schemes should also be initiated side by side. The Committee feels that efforts
should be made to transfer all the stadia to the local bodies for their regular maintenance.

The Committee is of the view that a big stadium instead of being used only for the event for which it was built,
may be divided into 4 or 5 sub-divisions so that it can be used for different events. Not only this, infrastructure
available in big stadium can be made available to nearby schools, sports clubs, sports bodies etc.

Recommendation No. 15

The Government has erected huge and massive sports infrastrucutre in the metro cities and big towns. These
structures are used only when national or international tournaments take place. For the rest of the period, they are
just lying idle or under-utilised. Some of them are rented out for cultural programmes and other shows. There is
a problem of their maintenance as well. A plan should be drawn up for utilisation of the infrastructure.

Action Taken

The stadia which were built by the Central Government directly are under the management control of SAI.
Sports Authority of India, after its coming into existence, had also undertaken construction of several facilities of
very high standards. As has already been pointed out that due to budgetary cut of SAI and the insistance that SAI
should raise resources for its survival, increasingly the facilitiés will have to be rented out for raising resources.
The Department agrees that playing facilities should primarily be used for sports and games only. In fact the SAI
has already initiated a dialogue with the Govt of NCT Delhi for using the playing facilities for school children.
Renting out for other activities will, however, have to be continued for generating resources.

Recommendation No. 16

The Committee feels that instead of organising the games at the State Capitals, many of the games could be
held in other places in the State so that the sports infrasturcutre is not concentrated in one particular area.


Action Taken

National tournaments as also the international ones need to be held in such places, where good facilities are
available. At the same time, such facilities, once created, need to be utilised on a regular basis. In many small
places, such facilities of international quality are nor available, nor are they required. In fact, in small places what
is needed is decent playing facilities.

The matter has already been taken up with the Indian Olympic Association. In fact the latest trends are also in
favour of holding tournaments in places other than State Capitals. In the last national games events took place
both in Pune and Bombay. In the Karnataka National Games also, some of the events are taking place in Mysore.

Further Comments:

The Secretary further stated that school education being a state subject, the State Governments were primarily
responsible for starting sports activities right from the beginning or at the local level. Although attention of State
Governments had been repeatedly drawn by the Department they did not have suffcient funds for doing that. The
situation was so bad that a large number of schools in the States were continuing without adequate play grounds.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is pained to note that a large number of schools in the country do not have adequate playgrounds.
Immediate action is required to be taken for improving the situation and Department should impress upon all the
State Governments to make efforts for providing adequate playground for every school. The Committee feels that
sports appears to be a neglected subject. For the youth of the country, it is necessary that sports facilities are
provided everywhere. International meets come once in a while. If we do not start from the beginning, the
performance of our sports-persons is not going to improve. The Department should formulate schemes whereunder
sports activities can be started by the State Governments in every school of the country.

Recommendation No. 21

The Committee desires that, as an incentive, sportspersons who have participated in the state, national and
international events should be allotted houses or plots by Housing Boards and Urban Development Authorities on
priority basis at concessional rates. They may also be given house building loans by Banks and other Financial
institutions at low interest. Eminent sportspersons, who, after retirement, intend to start their own industry/
business, etc. may be given licenses for purpose, alongwith bank loans and land, if necessary.

Action Taken

The recommendation of the Committee has been brought to the notice of the concerned agencies like State
Governments etc.Although, there are cases in which individuals, companies, State Governments have given cash
awards or awards in other forms to a few sportspoersons, who have achieved excellence in international arena, till
today, no formal scheme or even a pattern has emerged. In certain games like cricket or tennis, the achievers have
been given gifts or cash awards. However, in other games, which do not have high spectator value or have not been
able to catch the imagination of the people in a big way, the lot of even international achievers is quite dismal.
However, as has been mentioned, the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports have been giving cash awards to those
who win medals in World level tournaments.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is constrained to note that no formal scheme has emerged so far to provide for loans, financial
incentives to the sports persons. The Department’s acceding to this fact is not going to take away its responsibility.
The Committee strongly feels that even though no other agency or State Government has evolved any such
scheme it is for the Department to take an initiative in this direction.

Recommendation No. 29

The Committee recommends that one of the outstanding sportpersons may be nominated to the Rajya Sahba in
recognition of his/her distinguished service to country.
Action Taken

The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs, who in turn took it up with the Ministry of
Home Affairs. No final decision has been communicated to the Department in this regard.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee desires that the Department may pursue the matter with both the Ministries of Parliamentary
Affairs and Home Affairs for an early decision in the matter.


Recommendation No. 33

The Commitee feels that kits should be provided: to players and teams well in advance before they leave for
international meets.

Action Taken

DYAS has already forwarded the Committee's recommendations to the National Sports Federation and IOA for
necessary action. It is the responsibility of the National Federations to provide kits to the players and teams well
in advance before they leave for international meets.
Comments of the Committee

The Committee feels that mere forwarding its recommendation to the National Sports Federations and IOA will
not be sufficient. Since the Federations do not feel accountable to any agency including the Department, it would
be a futile exercise. The Department should, therefore, insist upon the Sports Federations to adhere to this procedure
and in case of any complaint, strict action should be taken against them.

Recommendation No. 34

Efforts should be made to ensure that the diet available to sportsmen and women has the nutritional value
necessary to meet the specific requirements of different games and sports in which they participate. The Committee
is of the firm opinion that the Government should immediately raise the amount of diet allowance substantially so
that players can get a rich and nutritious diet.

Action Taken

The dietary requirements for Power and Non-Power disciplines have been worked out in consultation with the
National Institute of Nutrition (NIN), Hyderabad.

Boarding charges are enhanced from time to time to meet the cost of menu suggested by NIN. The rates of menu
for the coaching camps were last revised in March’96 and the existing rates for Non-Power and Power disciplines
are Rs. 90/- and Rs. 100/- per person respectively. The catering is being done at SAI Centres departmentally. Howerver,
in Delhi, it is being done by a private caterer.

Due to paucity of resources the rates for Board & Lodging of the sportspersons under SAI schemes like NSTC,
SPDA and ABSC have been Rs. 35 and for SAG and Sports Hostel, the same is Rs 40, even though the amount
required for providing diet according to the NIN norm is higher. In case the rates are enhanced considerably the
number of sports persons under the schemes will have to be proportionately reduced.

A Clarification was sought by the Committee as to what efforts have been made to increase the rates and the
response of the Finance Ministry, in this regard. The Secretary deposed before the Committee that the rates have
been revised recently from Rs. 35/- to Rs. 42/-. When the Committee sought to know as to whether it would meet the
requirement, he stated that it would meet the requirement, at the very basic level and there was a case for increasing
it.

Comments of the committee

The Committee is of the view that even the revised rates are very insufficient and the charges should be increased
sufficiently in order to enable the sports-persons to have adequate nourishment.

Recommendatiog Wo. 42

The Committee feels that Government should make arrangements to provide personal coaches to those
sportspersons who have adequate potential and hope of winning medals at international level. Thesé persons coaches
should also accompany the sportspersons whenever they go abroad to participate in international tournaments.

Action Taken

Personal coaches are also being allowed to train their wards (sportspersons) even in the national camps, in cases
where the sportspersons have extraordinary potential. Some of the eminent coaches who have continued to train the
sportspersons have been in the National camps and have accompanied the sportspersons abroad are- (i) Shri O.M.
Namibiar, Athletics and (ii) Shri Hargobind Singh, Athletics.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee finds that even though, there are a few instances of personal coaches being provided to some of
the sportspersons this is not being followed as 4 general rule even in the case of all the sportspersons going for

4736/ RS/ F—S-A


international events. The Committee, therefore, desires that once a sportsperson is decided to be sent for an
international event such a person should be provided a personal coach.

Recommendation No. 43

A comprehensive plan to upgrade the skills and qualifications of technical officials, referees and judges in the
identified disciplines needs to be taken up as quickly as possible.

Action Taken

Technical Officials, referees and judges are the reponsibility of the national sports federations. They have been
asked to prepare a comprehensive plan for upgrading the skills and qualifications of technical officials, referees
and judges as part of their Long Term Development Plans.

Comments of the Committee

The reply given is not acceptable to the Committee. The Department cannot be absolved of its responsibility
particularly in view of the shabby working of the National Sports Federations and their ineffective and inefficient
handling of their respective fields. The Committee would like to be informed of the action taken by the federations.
The Departments may give its compliance report at the earliest.

Recommendation No. 44.

The various federations/associations in the country are alleged to be the weakest link in the chain of sports
management and their functioning has been described as perfunctory. The selection of teams and players by them
is also stated to be lopsided, based on favouratism, nepotism and arbitrariness. There is no democratic functioning
at all in most of them. It is also stated that huge amounts of money are spent on the election of office bearers.
Many federations/associations are being headed by people who have nothing to do with sports.

Action Taken

The national sports federations/associations vary in terms of strengths and weaknesses. The management of
some of these federations/associations is satisfactory or even very good whereas in case of some others, indications
are that things are not satisfactory. As per the guidelines of the Department for selection of teams, the national
sports federations constitute the selection committees which include representatives of the Government and SAI
and the selection is supposed to be done by them on merit. However, sometimes, complaints do appear that
selections are not done entirely on merit.

As for the nature of functioning of the federations, they are not accountable to the Department. About spending
of huge amounts of money on election of office bearers, the Department has no authentic information. Many
federations/associations are being headed by people having background in sports, while it may not be true in case
of some others. As stated above, while the Department has no control over federations/associations as such, in
connection with giving up grants, the Department seeks to exercise some accountability. A set of guidelines exists
for this purpose.

The guidelines are proposed to be revised, defining the roles and responsibilities of national sports federations
more clearly, making them more professional and even incorporating provisions for de-recognition of federation.

Recommendation No. 45

Federations must hold their elections regularly and democratically. The first and the most important task
before each national federation is to mobilise its energies and efforts for obtaining sponsorship and financial
support from various sources.

Action Taken

This recommendation has been brought to the notice of the IOA and the National Sports Federations. As per
information available, many federations are holding their elections regularly. The IOA and national sports federations
have also been advised to mobilise its energies and efforts for obtaining sponsorship and having suppurt from
various sources. It is seen that financial sponsors have been mobilised by few federations, such as, cricket, tennis,
golf, hockey etc. The Department has also held series of meetings with organisations like CII, requesting them to
sponsor various sports projects and disciplines.

4736/ RS / F—S-B


Further Comments

The Department was asked to clarify whether there existed any mechanism whereby proper implementation of
guidelines defining the roles and responsibilities of national sports federations could be ensured. In response, the
Secretary explained that some of the federations, besides getting Central funds, were having their own source of
income by way of Doordarshan or TV rights, sponsorships etc. However, no accounts of money thus generated
were being made available to the Department. Not only this, no statements of accounts were being published by
these federations, it was clarified. So far as implementation mechanism was concerned, it was smooth in majority
of the cases. Only those federations which were not in receipt of any Government funds, did not feel bound by the
Department guidelines, it was informed.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee expresses its serious concern at this state of affairs prevailing in the sports federations. The
Committee feels that these sports federations, registered under the Societies Act, are duty-bound to file their
actounts. The money they spend is the money collected from the public. Therefore, it is obligatory on their part to
publish their accounts. The Committee is of the view that the annual statement of accounts filed by these federations
should not only reflect the funds released to them by the Centre but also the money received from other sources.

Recommendation No. 46

It is essential that the national federations organise competitions, tournaments and championships on a regular
basis throughout the sporting season: This can be achieved by monitoring, guiding and motivating their State/
district units.

Action Taken

This recommendation has been brought to the notice of the national sports federations. It is true that some of
the federations have been deficient in holding national championships regularly, particularly under various age
categories. The holding of national championships regularly is discussed at the time of reyiew of LTDPs.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee strongly feels that the Department should take action against those federations which do not
hold championships regularly. The Committée is of the firm view that non-holding of regular tournaments in the
mofussil areas, rural areas and small towns has been one of the most important factors contributing to the present
dismal scenario in sports. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should make concerted
efforts to motivate the State Governments for taking up tournaments in a major way in the rural areas starting from
block level onwards.

Recommendation No. 49

Aj important area of resource mobilisation in whcih the Government can help the federations greatly is by way
of transferring the remaining sum of the advertising revenues earned by Doordarshan from showing sports
programmes to the concerned federations after deducting its costs.

Action Taken

The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and Doordarshan. Some of
the federations have entered into arrangements with Doordarshan in this regard.

Further Comments

The Committee wanted to know the reaction of the Ministry of information and Broadcasting in the matter.
The Secretary informed that they had not received any further information from the Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting who have again been approached. Normally views from each federation and Ministry of Information
and Broadcasting were taken by the Department. Only then, agreements were entered into between Doordarshan
and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and the federations, the Committee was informed

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is of the view that if the federations are to be encouraged, sufficient revenues should be
allowed to them, The Department should, therefore, pursue the matter with the Ministry of Information and
Broadcasting.


Recommendation No. 51
» There is no coordination or. cooperation between various agencies engaged in promotion of sports. There is no
accountability and responsiblity for poor performance in sports in international events. The Committee emphasises

the need for clearly demarcating the duties and responsibilities of each one of the agencies so that the accountability
could be fixed for their lapses.

Action Taken

For having propoer coordination and cooperation on structured ‘and orgat ised lines, it is felt that-suitable
legislation and rules and regulations under such legislation is necessary. While by and large, attempts at effective
coordination and cooperation are being made by the Department constantly with the IOA, national sports federations
and the State Governments, the results are not always commensurate with the efforts. Accountability and
responsiblity for performance in sports in international events can also be appropriately apportioned if there is
legislation, rules and regulations. However, it may be pointed out that in matters such as sports, where international
standards are constantly changing, normally upwards, and many other factors such as the state of development of
infrastructure, scientific and medical support available including the pharamacological factors, the effort put in
and the output by way of medals etc. cannot be determined with a reasonable degree of precision. It is not easy,
therefore, to fix accountability for lapses.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee does not agree with the contention of the Department that it is not easy to fix accountability for
lapses. If the Department cannot fix responsibility for poor performance and for lapses in the international events:
without any chance of winning any medal, it should find a via media to locate the lacunae in the system and to
provide for accountability for poor performance.

Recommendation No. 52

It is often seen that teams are selected virtually almost on the last day and at times had reported after the events
had already started. The Committee feels that this state of affairs is highly deplorable and has to be stopped forthwith
if we really intend to achieve medals in the international sports arena. The Committee feels that there is a need for
a long-term planning and selection of teams has to be made much in advance so that players are aware of their
selection and they could concentrate more on sports rather than running around till the last moment for various
clearances. The Committee also desires that once the teams are selected they should be sent to places of training and
also sufficiently in advance to the venue of the event for proper exposure and acclimatisation to the foreign
environment.

Action Taken

The recommendation has been brought to the notice of the national federations. The primary responsibility of
selecting the team well in time lies with the federations only. On the part of the Government, the procedure for
clearance of teams has been simplified whereby each proposal is considered even before the selection and an
approval in principle is conveyed to the federation and air seats are blocked. However, it is not possible for the
Government to actually issue the sanction as long the names of the persons are intimated to the Government.

teams.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is constrained to note the Department’s acceptance that sometimes due to various factors, selection
of team is done at a late stage which delays the final clearnace of teams. The Committee is of the firm view that if the
federations make advance preparations and select the teams sufficiently in advance then this problem will not arise.
The Government should, therefore, not clear the teams which are not selected sufficiently in advance. Unless this
condition is made mandatory by the Government, the federations will never fall in line.

The recommendation has been brought to the notice of the rational federations. The annual calender for each

The Committee desires to know as to whether all the National Federations are adhering to the procedure and

The Committee noticed that neither the sports psychology nor the sports medicine was being given any priority

Action Taken

In India, only SAI has made a beginning in setting up facilities for sports sciences support. Practichlly no

SAI’s efforts to upgrade the scientific labs and the scientists have been limited due to availability of scarce

The Committee finds that the Department has not mentioned about the efforts being made by the sports federations

Recommendation No. 66

The Committee desires that the Department should prepare a comprehensive scheme indicating the overall
requirement for development of sports in the country and bring it before the Committee and before the Parliament

The Committee feels that the Government alone cannot deliver the goods. Public and private sectors’ involvement

The Department is in agreement with the recommendation of the Committee. The Department has already taken

The Committee feels that the efforts being made are too negligible to tap the vast sports talent available in

Recommendation No. 75

The Committee feels that unless sports is also brought under the “Concurrent List” of the Constitution, sports
activities in the country cannot be uniformly regulated in an effective and coordinated manner.

Action Taken

In 1988 the Government approved a proposal to bring sports on to the councurrent list of the Constitution and a
bill was introduced accordingly, in the Rajya Sabha 24th November’88. However, it was decided that further
consultation with the States be undertaken.

The Prime Minister addressed a letter to all Chief Ministers on 3rd November’90. This resulted in 12 States
agreeing to the proposal and 12 opposed with no response from Manipur. Subsequently, letters were addressed by
the MOS/HRM to these 13 States. Out of these States, 4 have further conveyed their concurrence to the proposal.
Thus, 16 States have now agreed to the proposal. Out of the remaining 9 States, the State Governments of Rajasthan,
» & 8, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu have not agreed to the proposal which State Governments of Karnataka,
Gujarat and West Bengal have stated that they are examining the proposal. Comments from Assam and Punjab are
yet to come.

This matter was again placed before the Cabinet and it was decided that this should be discussed under the
Chairmanship of Minister of Parliamentary Affairs with leaders of all political parties in the Parliament. Accordingly,
a meeting was held on 28th November 1996 to consider the proposal.

The matter was also discussed with the State Secretaries in the Conference held in October ’96 and with the
State Ministers in the Conference held in February’ 97. It was mentioned clearly that the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on HRD had also made recommendation that sports should be brought under Concurrent list of the
Constitution and a comprehensive legislation enacted by the Central Government. However it was seen that the
States which have not given their agreement to the proposal are still opposed to bringing the sports on to the
conurrent list of the Constitution even though the Department has very clearly stated that the proposal will not in”
any way affect the autonomy of the States. It has also been clarified that it was only an enabling provision which
will allow the Central Government to legislate so as to define the role and responsbilities of the various agencies,
especially in the context of our performance in important international events. It has also been mentioned that our
experience with regard to other sectors which figure on the concurrent list has been that the Central Government
and State Governments have worked in unison to achieve better results.

Further Comments

conference of all the State Ministers of Sports, State Government of West Bengal which has been opposed all

The Committee desires that discussions should be continued with the States that have not agreed with the
proposal. The Committee however feels that merely bringing Sports under the jurisdiction of Concurrent List

CHAPTER II

RECOMMENDATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation No. 1

The Committee feels it should be our objective to see that every child takes part in sports and games that every
Parent encourages the child to do so. It should also be our endeavour to see that as children grow, they do not lose
their enthusiasm for sports, nor does the pressure of studies towards a bright career diminish their interest. for
Participating in Sports and Games.

Action taken

To promote sports and games amongst children a decision has already been taken to integrate physical education
and sports with the educational curriculum. The Central Advisory Board on Education (CABE) had recommended
to make sports and physical education a compulsory subject in schools and colleges. Followng are the salient
recommedations of the CABE:-

(i) Physical education and sports should be made a compulsory part of curriculum and assigned at least 40
minutes everyday for all school going children;
(ii) Mass participation activities and sports competitions may be organised by the State Government regularly
for schools and colleges;
(iii) Subject teacher may be trained as physical education teachers through pre-service and in-servce training
courses;
(iv) Special weightage may be considered to be given to sportspersons who have excelled in school and
college admission; and
(v) State Government may identify at least one school per district as a sports school for nurturing of
talented sportspersons.

These recommendations of the Sub-Committee have been accepted by the CABE, Deptt. of Education
and Deptt. of Youth Affairs and Sports. All the State Governments have been advised to implement the
recommendations. The progress of the implementation of the report was also discussed during the meeting of State
Secretaries held during October’ 96, Conference of Ministers and Secretaries of North East States held at Guwahati in
November "96 and Conference of Ministers of State for Youth Affairs and Sports held in February '97.

The Education Department has also set up a Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri A.K. Pandya, ex-
Secretary, Deptt. of Youth Affairs and Sports, Government of India, to review the progress of implémentation of
the Sub-Commitiee Report in the Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodya Vidyalayas and the States. During the course of
these meetings it is seen that the Committee’s report has been accepted by the managements of Kendriya
Vidyalayas\Navodaya Vidyalayas and these are being implemented in schools administered directly by the
Government of India. Also many of States have already initiated action on implementation of recommendations
of the Committee.

Apart from the above, to provide encouragment to sportspersons at early stages of their career, the Department
provides monthly scholarship of Rs. 500 to talented children. The Department has also recently revised the scheme
of Promotion of Sports and Games in Schools which aims at encouraging effective participation in competitions
at inter-school, district, State and National levels. The scheme will provide an opportunity to a large number of
school children to participate in school level tournaments and will thereby give impetus to sports activities amongst
school children.

The Department has also proposed a new scheme as part of the IXth Plan proposals called “National Schools
Fitness Programme.” It is proposed to formulate a battery of test to judge the fitness level of school children in
High\Higher Secondary Schools and based on that stars and certificates will be provided to the students passing
the tests.

In 1988 the Government approved a proposal to bring sports on to the concurrent list of the Constituion and a
bill was introduced accordingly, in the Rajya Sabha, on 24th November, 1988. However, it was decided that futher
consultation, with the States be undertaken.

The Prime Minister addressed a letter to all Chief Ministers on 3rd November 1990. This resulted in 12 States
agreeing to the proposal and 12 opposed with no response from Manipur. Subsequently, letters were addressed by
the MOS/HRM to these 13 States. Out of these States, 4 have further conveyed their concurrence to the proposal.
Thus, 16 States have now agreed to the proposal. Out of the remaining 9 States, the State Governments of Rajasthan,
J&K, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu have not agreed to the proposal while the State Governments of Karnataka,
Gujarat and West Bengal have stated that they are examining the proposal. Comments from Assam and Punjab are
yet to come,

This matter was again placed before the Cabinet and it was decided that this should be discussed under the
Chairmanship of Minister of Parliamentary Affairs with leaders of all political parties in the Parliament. Accordingly,
a meeting was held on 28th November, 1996 to consider the proposal.

The matter was also discussed with the State Secretaries in the Conference held in October’96 and with the
State Ministers in the Conference held in February’97. It was mentioned clearly that the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on HRD had also made recommendation that sports should be brought under consucrrent list of the
Constitution and a comprehensive legislation enacted by the Central Government. However, it was seen that the
States which have not given their agreement to the proposal are still opposed to bringing the sports on to the
concurrent list of the Constitution even though the Department has very clearly stated that the proposal willl not
in any way affect the autonomy of the States. It has also been clarified that it was only an enabling provision
which will allow the Central Government to legislate so as to define the role and responsibilities of the various
agencies, especially in the context of our performance in important international events. It has also been mentioned
that our experience with regard to other sectors which figure on the concurrent list has been that the Central
Government and State Governments have worked in unison to achieve better results.

coaching camps, equipment support, participation in international competition selection ‘Committee procedures,
instructions for preparation of long term development plans and for handling of players’ grievances etc.

Recommendation No. 77

The Committee has come to the conclusion that the bureaucratic functioning of the SAI is proving to be a
major obstacle in the free and smooth operation of the regional centres. The Committee feels that unles these
Centres are strengthened, we cannot expect better results from them. The SAI office in Delhi could be just a
coordinating authority and should concentrate on policy, planning and monitoring. There should be a Sub-regional
centre of SAI in each State, with a Director in charge of it.

Action Taken

The Regional Director of SAI enjoy full autonomy and authority so far as administration of and expenditure on
approved schemes/projects is concerned. However, in the last two years due to paucity of funds, the RDs have to
frequently refer the matter to Corporate Office for release of funds. This apart, the Regional Directors are vested
with full powers for scouting and selecting the young talent and weeding them out where necessary as per the laid
down norms and their recommendations in this regard are submitted to DG for formal ratification.

Further, the Regional Directors have been authorised to transfer the Asstt. Directors and coaches within their
region from one Unit to another.

The opening of a sub-centre of SAI in each State with a Director level officer in charge can be considered only
if adequate funds/infrastructure is available. Further with some States developing their own structures and
investments in this area, it may be better to supplement their effort.

Recommendation No. 78

At present, there are six Regional Centres at Chandigarh, Delhi, Bangalore, Calcutta, Imphal and Gandhinagar.
The Central Region, which is at present located in Delhi, should be shifted to Lucknow, as originally contemplated.
The North-Eastern region, comprising eight States including Sikkim, should have two centres, one located Imphal
and the other at Guwahati/Shillong. The Committee desires that each one of the Regional Centres should be
headed by a Regional Director, with almost full powers. Two Executive Directors in Delhi could look after the
administrative and coordinating works of the organisation, as well as matters relating to teams. The Secretary,
Department of Youth Affairs and Sports, should not be the Director-General of SAI. Instead, a full-time Chairman-
cum-MD, with good sports background or interest in sports, should be appointed by the Government.

Action Taken

The recommendation of the Committee to have a full time Director-General, SAI separate from Secretary,
Department of Youth Affairs and Sports has already been implemented. It is felt that the present structure of SAI
gives enough autonomy to Director-General vis-a-vis the Department and as such there is no need to redesignate
the 0. 0, as Chairman-cum-Managing Director.

The Central Centre will be shifted to Lucknow only when the infrastructure for the Regional Centre is developed.
For the time being due to financial crunch, the proposal has been kept in abeyance. The Regional Centre at Imphal
and Sub-Centre at Guwahati are already functioning. The SAI Sub-Centre at Guwahati can be strengthened only
if funds are available. Most of the Regional Centres are already, headed by Regional Directors who have adequate
administrative and financial powers.

(Committee’s comments on this reply may be seen in Chapter-1)
Recommendation No. 79

The SAI governing body shall consist of fifteen members, including the Chairman-cum-MD, two Executive
Directors, seven Regional Directors, one Financial Advisor and four non-official Members elected by the. General
Council. The General Council of SAI, headed by the Minister of Human Resource Development, shall consist of
the Minister of Sports, the Secretary, Department of Youth Affairs and Sports, the Chairman-cum-MD of SAI, the

Financial Advisor, the Executive Directors, Regional Directors and Directors of SAI sub-centre: ee meas
of the State Sports Authorities/Sports Council, Joint Secretary in the Ministry of HRD, five thd Awardees/

olympians, three coaches, Secretary General, IOA, five representatives of national sports federations, two
representatives of public sector sports control boards, five sports experts such as sports journalists and commentators
and three Members of Parliament. The number shall not exceed 100. am


30

Action Taken

The recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee will be placed for consideration before the
next meeting of the general body of SAI.

Recommendation No. 81

Out of 78 SPDA Centres proposed to be set up, only 33 centres have started functioning so far. The Committee
expresses its displeasure over such a tardy progress of the scheme and strongly urges upon the central as well as
the State Governments to work in close tandem with each other in the larger interest of development of sports. As
regards the suggestion of Tata Consultancy Services to phase out the SPDA scheme, the Committee is of the view
that it is not based on a sound proposition. To wind up the scheme simply on the pretext of States’ failure is not
sound, The SPDA centres should be converted into SAI Sub-regional centres in course of time, with additional
inputs.

Action Taken

The Governing Body of SAI has decided that SPDAs and Sports Hostels would be known by new name as SAI
Training Centes and there would be a total of 78 SAI Training Centres. It has also been decided that where living
accommodation is not upto the mark, SAI would take action to provide the same. The new SAI Training Centres
will be opened only when proper accommodation and sports infrastructure is available. :

Recommendation No. 82

Although the Committee expresses its overall satisfaction with the functioning and performance of the Speical
Area Games Scheme as far as archery, hockey and watersports are concerned, it is constrained to observe that the
achievements in other disciplines, particularly gymnastics and athletics, have not been upto the mark. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that based on the population/concentration of tribal and other communities,
Government should try to expand this scheme in the rural and tribal areas and take all necessary measures to
streamline and revamp the scheme.

Action Taken

The Governing Body of SAI has decided that the scheme of SAG will be continued and the existing Centres
will be further improved upon by providing sports infrastructure and best possible coaches. Regarding opening of
new SAG Centres it will depend upon the availability of resources.

Recommendation No. 83

The Committee recommends that Government should review the National Coaching Scheme to set right
shortcomings and streamline the functioning of the scheme at the earliest. The concept of sports hostel should be
reoriented and focussed towards achievement of excellence at the international level.
Action Taken

The observations of the Committee have been noted for compliance. As far as Sports Hostels are concerned, as
already mentioned in reply to Recommednation No. 81, it has been decided to call the sports hostels as well as
SPDAs, as SAI Training Centres and focus them towards achievement of excellence.
Recommendation No. 84

The Committee is also of the view that it is imperative to prioritise disciplines for sports hostel scheme and
select only those games in which India has the potentiality of achieving results in the international arena.

Action Taken

The Committee’s recommendations for prioritising of disciplines under the SAI Schemes have been accepted
and action is being taken accordingly. As a result of this decision, Basketball and Volleyball which has no scope
in the North-Eastern Region have already been discontinued.

Recommendation No. 85

The Committee found that the Army Boys Sports Company Scheme is functioning very efficiently because the
overall atmosphere of discipline in the Regimental Centres is quite conducive for the development of sporting
skills amongst children. The Committee is of the opinion that the amount of Rs. 35 being given for diet per head
under this scheme is quite inadequate and should be increased substantially. During the course of their interaction
with the Committee, representative of the Services Sports Control Board expressed a desire to have one school in


31

each Regiment. SAI may have to enlarge the scheme, accordingly, as it is likely to pay better dividends. The
Committee recommends that apart from extending the scheme to other regiments of the army, the scheme should
be extended to the central para-military forces also who are keen to run schools on the same lines as by army
regiments.

Action Taken

The Governing Body of SAI has decided to continue with the Army Boys Sports Companies (ABSC). The
scheme has shown some creditable performance at the national level. The money under the scheme is comparatively
inadequate, However, the increase for this scheme will depend upon the availability of resources. Regarding opening
of one school in each regiment and extending the scheme to other regiments of the Army, the matter can only be
considered provided funds are available for such extension,


CHAPTER III

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE
TO PURSUE

Recommendation No. 3

The Committee emphasises that physical education and sports should be made an essential and integral of
educational activity in schools and colleges. There is need for reducing academic burden on the children, particularly
at the primary stage, so that they can spare enough time for sports.

Action Taken

Action Taken note against Recommendation no. 1 has already brought out that the CABE, Department of
Education and Youth Affairs and Sports have already accepted recommendation. The Department has advised the
State Governments to implement it. The progress is also being monitored through meetings with State Governments.
Regarding reduction of academic burden on the children, particularly at primary stage, the Department has taken
up the matter with NCERT and the Department of Education.

Recommendation No. 4

Ideally all the schools and colleges must have physical education teachers/coaches. Until it is possible, physical
education teacher may be provided in each secondary school and one in a group of primary schools. The Committee
feels that unless some financial support is provided to the schools and colleges specifically for this purpose and
fdr purchase of simple and basic sports equipment and consumable sports items, this objective would not be
achieved.

Action Taken

While provision of Physical Education Teachers in every School is the most desirable thing, it has been the
experience that this will entail huge expenditure on the part of the State Governments. The Central Government is
also not in a position to share this burden in view of the resource constraint. The matter was discussed in the
recent Conference of the State Secretaries and also that of the Sports Ministers. Most of the State Governments
expressed their inability to bear this additional burden. It is in this context that the strategy of equipping the
existing subject teachers with the skills required for Physical Training appears to be a sound one.

One of the recommendations of CABE was that the subject teachers may be trained as physical education
teachers through pre-service and in-service training courses. We have already written to all the State Governments
to implement the recommendations.

The Working Group for the Ninth Plan had suggested that a scheme for training of teachers be taken up. This

* proposal has been included in the Ninth Plan, but is yet to be approved by Planning Commission. Also, the matter

has been taken up with Education Department to make changes in the curriculum for B.Ed. and other Teacher’s

training courses so as to make it compulsory for all teachers to have physical education and sports as a subject
during training. The use of DIETs for pre-service and in-service training of teachers has also been suggested.

For development of infrastructure and provision of sports equipment, the Department through its various schemes
have been giving financial assistance to Secondary/Sr. Secondary Schools located in rural areas as well as to
colleges including engineering/medical/agricultural colleges.

Recommendation No. 7

The Committee strongly recommends that the functioning of the Association of Indian Universities should be
revamped to increase sports activities in the Universities and improving thereby their contribution to sports. The
inter-university sports, board, which existed before the independence, should be revived, so as to supervise sports
activities in our universities and their affiliated colleges.

Action Taken

This matter has been taken up with the Association of Indian Universities (410) which has stated that since the
functioning of AIU covers diverse areas including sports, culture, research, equivalence of degrees and international
cooperation in higher education, the recommendations of the Committee would require careful consideration and
the concurrence of the General Body.

a2


33

Further AIU has informed that the inter-university sports board is already in operation and it oversees all sports
activities of the Universities. The Board is quite active and it has organised inter-university competitions in 14
games for men, 10 games for women and 14 games for both men and women at 66 University centres.
Recommendation No. 10

The Committee feels that Government should plan the development of sports in a phased manner so that
necessary infrastructure is built up over a period of time and scarce resources earmarked for the purpose are
optimally utilised.

Action Taken

While the Department agrees with the above observations of the Committee, it may also be submitted that the
demand in the area of sports vastly outstrips the resources made available to the Department of Sports of the
Central Government and also to the sports departments of the State Governments. It may also be appreciated that
training for excellence would need international class infrastructural facilities as also equipment of the same
class. All these are costly and need increasing investment over a period of time.

The Department of Youth Affairs and Sports have tried to use the limited resources more effectively. For
instance, during 1996-97, no large infrastructure has been sanctioned and most of the resources have been utilised
for completing the construction of the infrastructure that have been initiated in earlier years.

Recommendation No. 22

The Committee was shocked to learn that till March, 1995 only 25 persons were recruited as sportspersons in
the 25 Ministries/Departments of the Government of India (except in Railways and Defence) and that too in the
Group “C” category.

Recommendation No. 23

The Committee feels that there is a lack of will and determination also in implementing the existing guidelines
in employing sportspersons by the Government. There is no provision for promotion of outstanding sportspersons
or giving them adequate cash awards after they win medals and bring laurels to the country.

Action Taken on Recommendations No. 22 and 23

While no precise data is available regarding employment of sportspersons in Government Departments, many
of the Departments in addition to Defence and Railways have been employing sportspersons on a regular basis.
Some of these organisations are Indian Airlines, Air India, Postal Department, Audit Department, Food Corporation
of India. Most of the State Governments are also employing sportspersons on regular basis. However, the problem
appears to be that most of these sportspersons are appointed at very low levels with very meagre pay, which do not
act as a suitable incentive. The Department, therefore, has been trying for suitable reservations in the higher cadre
also.

Recommendation No. 24

The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should have (i) a definite policy for recruiting
sportspersons in various ministries/departments and public sector undertakings; (ii) effective monitoring to get
regular feedback and to ensure proper implementation of the provisions of the policy, which is virtually non-
existed as on date; (iii) the Department of Sports and Youth Affairs should act as a nodal agency for this purpose;
(iv) the Government should also issue clear-cut guidelines to the Union Public Service Commission for recruiting
sportspersons in Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ services also as there are many sportspersons of international standard having
adequate educational qualifications for these categories of posts.

Action Taken

The observations of the Committee have been noted. The policy with regard to personnel are decided by the
Department of Personnel and the matter has been taken up with the Department of Personnel & Training (DOPT)
and the Chief Secretaries of various State Governments for implementing the recommendations made by the
Committee.

As per the existing provisions, 5% of the vacancies in Group ‘C’ and ‘D’ posts can be filled up from amongst
sportspersons. However, such appointments can be made only when other requirements in terms of age and
educational qualifications are fulfilled. Sportspersons are also eligible for advance increments on the basis of their
performance in National and International events. The total number of increments to be awarded to a sportsperson
during his career should not exceed five. Certain Departments such as the Police Organisations also give out of
turn promotions to sportspersons excelling in major sports events.

The Department of Youth Affairs and Sports is implementing a number of schemes under which outstanding
sportspersons are given awards such as Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna Award, Arjuna Award in recognition of their
outstanding achievements in the field of sports. There also exists specific scheme entitled ‘Special Award’ to


34

Winners in International Sports events and their coaches under which awards ranging from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. 5
lakh is given to the medal winners at international events.

On a specific issue of filling up of 5% posts of Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ posts a meeting was held with DOPT on
29.10.96. The DOPT was of the view that the proposal may be examined in the context of public sector under
takings but the DOPT was not very encouraging about earmarking Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ posts in the Government for
sportspersons.

Recommendation No. 25

The Committee does realise the sportspersons’ concern about not getting adequate time for practice due to
pressure of work in their jobs. In such a situation, the Committee feels, it is the duty, both of the sportspersons and
their employers, to give top most priority to sports so long as the person is in full form and is in a position to win
medals.

Action Taken

While this is true in some cases, utilisation of sportspersons properly and giving them right opportunities will
depend largely on the sports consciousness of the employers. However, the Department is writing to all Departments
bring to their notice, the recommendation of the Committee.

Recommendation No. 27

The amount of cash awards and pension being given to sportspersons by the Government should be increased
substantially so as to make sports more attractive and lucrative. The Committee recommends that the Mini
Railways and the airlines operating in the country, both private and the Government, should provide free/concessi
tickets to eminent sportspersons.

Action Taken

The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Ministry of Railways. Ministry of Railways
have agreed to provide concession to the Arjuna Award winners. Discussions have also taken place between the
officials of the Department and those of the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The latter, however, have not agreed to the
proposal.

Recommendation No. 30

The Committee suggests that the Government should ensure that no player or team is sent abroad for participation
in international tournaments unless they are accompanied by qualified sports medicine doctors alongwith the
necessary kits and other aids.

Action Taken

For teams/sportspersons, who may be needing doctors during the tournaments abroad, a doctor is normally sent
at Govt. expense. In addition, for all major international sporting events like Asiad and Olympics, doctor is
invariably sent alongwith the team. For other international tournaments, normally a doctor is sent with the
contact sports teams.

Recommendation No. 31

The Committee was informed that, in some cases, the Government is paying only 90% of fare and the remaining
10% is to be borne by the player himself or herself. The Government should investigate as to why part payment of
air fare is being made to players attending international meets and ensure that such a thing is not repeated in
future.

Action Taken

Generally, the air tickets are provided to the players through the travel agent of the Department, M/s Balmer
Lawrie, which is a Government of India undertaking. The Department makes 100% payment directly to the travel
agent and therefore, there is no question of making the players pay 10% of the fare.

Recommendation No. 38

The Committee suggests that either the entire control of the SAI coaches should be given to the State Governments
who have comparatively better mach: sche for their close monitoring or they may be completely withdrawn. The
State Governments should be given full authority for all the service matters of SAI coaches, including their
postings and transfers.


35

Action Taken

As regards handing over the entire control of SAI coaches by the State Governments, the Department is of
considered view that services of the SAI coaches may be placed at the disposal of the State Governments with full
control provided the States bear the cost of SAI coaches. In a meeting of Secretaries and Directors of Sports of
States/UTs held on 24-25 October, 1996 at Delhi, the general opinion of the States was not in favour of taking SAI
coaches due to various administrative problems, particularly with reference to their pay scales etc.

Recommendation No. 39

One of the problems raised by the coaches deployed in the schools was that they did not have accommodation
either in the school premises or anywhere near the school. The Committee feels that it is a genuine problem which
needs to be looked into sympathetically and Government should try to give residential accommodation to these
coaches either in the school premises itself, or just near to their working place so that they could reach the ground
early in the morning.

Action Taken

SAI coaches working at SAI Centres i.e. Patiala, Chandigarh, Bangalore, Calcutta, Imphal and Gandhinagar
have been provided with residential accommodation. Few coaches working in the Delhi have also been provided
accommodation by the SAI.

As far as schools under NSTC are concerned, accommodation is provided to coaches in only such school which
are 100% residential. In semi-residential schools, the States/private managements do not have residential
accommodation available with them which can be provided to the coaches. In such cases like other SAI coaches,
these coaches are being provided house rent allowance. The managements of the schools assist the coaches to find
accommodation near the school premises.

Recommendation No. 61

The Committee finds that so far neither the Department of YouthA ffairs & Sports nor the Federations have taken
any particular interest in the development of sports among the Indian women and whatever distinction women have
achieved so far is largely due to their individual efforts.

Recommendation No. 62

The Committee feels that there is a need to give good incentives in the form of cash awards and medals so as to
attract mass participation by women. Many parents would like to send their daughters to play games but they are
hesitant to do so because of security and safety reasons. The Committee noticed that out of 18 sports hostels of SAI,
there is only one sports hostel for women and there is no exclusive SPDA hostel for girls. Therefore, the Committee
feels, there is a need for proper planning to develop sports amongst women by opening more sports hostels and
adopting more sports-oriented girls’ schools.

Action Taken on Recommendations No. 61 and 62

It is submitted that Government with its limited resources have taken steps to encourage women to participate in
sports. As a result of such efforts, Indian women have done comparatively well in Athletics and weightlifting.
Women sportspersons are also getting scholarships under the scheme of sports talent search scholarship. Generally
50% of the recipients of the scholarship are women. In recent years, some of the women have also won impressive
cash awards from the Department.

Unfortunately, due to serious resource crunch, it is becoming increasingly difficult for Sports Authority of India
to run the existing Hostels. Any new Hostel only for women sportspersons, therefore, cannot be considered at this
stage.

On receipt of information regarding banning of drugs in some countries abroad, Drugs
Controller General (India) invariably consults medical experts and expert bodies like Indian

The WHO has so far reported withdrawal of 44 drugs by some countries. Out of these,

from the Indian market has already been taken in consultation with the experts.

stated that though these drugs are withdrawn in some countries, yet are still being marketed

Power of Central Government for banning drugs

Before 1982, Central Government did not have any power under the Drugs and
Cosmetics Act to prohibit manufacture and sale of a drug licensed by the Licensing
Authorities appointed by the State Governments. The Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment)
Act, 1982 empowers the: Central Government to prohibit import (Section 10A) and
manufacture, sale and distribution (Section 26A) of a drug which is considered by experts to
be ineffective or irrational or the possible risk of administering the drug outweighs the
benefits due to administration. As such there is no necessity to make any amendment in the
Drugs and Cosmetics Act to achieve this objective. However, some of the affected
manufacturers moved to the various High Courts against the alleged infringement of
Fundamental Rights granted by Article 19 of the Constitution of India. In some cases they
have been successful in obtaining stay from different High Courts. In such cases, the Central
Government initiates action for vacating the stay.


19

In the past, all over the world a drug used to be registered on the evidence of safety
and efficacy data generated in laboratory studies and animal models and based on clinical
trials on patients. The concept of rationality for a combination drug is relatively recent in
origin. What appears to be rational once upon a time may not stand the scrutiny of modern
tests for evaluation. As a result, the necessity was. left globally to examine formulation
moving in the market not only from the angle of safety and efficacy but also from the angle
of rationality. For example in the United States, Food and Drugs Administration have
delegated this task of screening formulations moving in the market to National Academy of
Sciences (NAS). The NAS, from time to time, advises Food and Drugs Administration on
the continued marketing of certain formulation which are under question.

The relative benefit—risk ration of a drug is also influenced by the disease pattern in a
country, the ethnic group of a selected population which may react differently to a particular
drug, the availability of safer substitution for the treatment of a particular disease and cost
factor for the management of a disease. All these factors are taken into consideration by
Indian experts before recommending a drug (which may be indicated for a disease not
prevalent in that country), many other countries would recommend continued marketing of
the same drug keeping in view that administration of any drug is not absolutely free from
side effects or adverse reactions in a statistically insignificant minority population. Because
of this, it may appear paradoxical at a point of time that some drugs may be banned in some
countries, yet continued to be marketed in many other countries.

The Committee, however feels that the first judgement of the Supreme Court is absolutely

the consumption except for medicinal purposes of intoxicating drinks and of drugs
which are injurious to health.

The Committee feels that by no stretch of imagination this kind of an interpretation of the

Transfer Policy

The Committee sought to know the normal tenure of the doctors in the CGHS
dispensaries, details of Chief Medical Officers due for transfer and whether they had been
transferred and if not the reasons therefor. The Department in the note submitted as under:

“According to the Transfer Policy of CGHS, Medical Officers posted in the different
allopathic dispensaries, are required to be rotated within the zone after completion of three
years of service at one dispensary in a phased manner, by the Zonal Heads taking into
account administrative exigencies so that services of the dispensaries are not hampered.
Incharge of dispensaries are required to be) rotated after four years.

Generally more than 80% transfers have been effected expect, at Patna, Chennai,
Allahabad, Pune, Jabalpur, Meerut, and Nagpur where the Orders are being implemented in
a phased manner. In Ahmedabad and Calcutta, the transfers have been 100% while at Delhi
and Luknow, they are to the extent of 96%.”

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is constrained to note that at Patna and Allahabad, even 50% transfers
have not been effected. In fact the worst performance is at Patna where it is 20% only. The
situation should change immediately. Unless the transfer are done on rotation as per the
guidelines laid down, nepotism and indiscipline will creep into the system. The Department
should seriously consider the matter and take necessary action.

Protection of CGHS Beneficiaries

The Committee noted that the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissioner,
New Delhi has taken a view that a Government servant under the Central Government
Health Scheme is not a consumer within the meaning of Consumer Protection Act, 1986 as


43

defined in Section 2(1) (d) of the Act and the services rendered to him under the CGHS do
hot constitute service as defined under Section 2(1) (0) of the Act. The Supreme Court in a
recent decision in Indian Medical Association vs. V.P. Shantha & others dated 13th Nov. 95
has ruled that service rendered at a Government Hospital/health centre/dispensary where
no charge whatsoever is made from any person availing the services and all patients (rich
and poor) are given free service—is outside the purview of the expression ‘service’ as
defined in Section 2(1) (0) of the Act. The payment of a token amount for registration
purpose only at hospital/nursing home would not alter the position.

- The Secretary clarified that it was in 1994 that the Consumer Protection Act sought to
cover all categories of services given in hospitals, including the Government hospitals, When
the matter came up before the Cabinet, agitations took place at several quarters and the
then Health Minister took the view that Government hospitals are not able to give quality
service for lack of certain factors that are beyond their control, nemely, overcrowding,
infrastructure, support of the para medical staff and overall conditions prevailing in the
hospitals. Therefore, it was decided that it would be kept out of the purview of the
Consumer Protection Act. Nonetheless, when the matter went to the Supreme Court, it was
mandated that anything which is a free service will be kept out of its purview.

The Secretary, however, admitted that there ougth to be a forum where people who are
aggrieved about negligence, both in Government as well as private hospitals, can seek
redressal.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee is of the view that in the light of Article 21 of the ‘Constitution it is
obligatory on the State to see to it that proper service is given to all patients, it is irrelevant
whether he is charged or not. Merely because it is a free service, this kind of negligence,
cannot be tolerated. Therefore, the Committee strongly feels that efforts should be made to
amend Section 2(1)(0) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. Thereafter, the Department
after consulting the Ministry of Law may approach a larger bench of the Supreme Court in
the matter.

Introduction

The Central Government Health Scheme
(CGHS) was started in 1954, with the
objective of providing comprehensive
medical care to the Central Government
employees and their family members so as
to avoid the cuimbersome system of
medical reimbursement.

Besides Central Government employees the
scheme also provides services to Members
and former Members of Parliament, Judges
of Supreme Court and Delhi High Court
(sitting and retired), freedom fighters,
Central Government pensioners; employees
of a few autonomous bodies and semi-

PREFACE

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Human Resource Development, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the
report on its behalf, do hereby present this Seventy-ninth Report of the Committee on
Action Taken by the Government on the Recommendations contained in its Fifty-first
Report on National Institute of Homoeopathy, Calcutta.

2. The Fifty-first Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Human Resource Development was presented to Rajya Sabha on 3rd December, 1996
and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on 3rd December, 1996. Replies of the Government on
the recommendations contained in the Report, received from the Department of Indian
Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy were considered by the Committee. Clarifications
were also sought by the Committee from the Secretary and other Officials of the
Department.

3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same on the 27th

August, 1997. The Committee at its meeting held on 19th November, 1998 decided to
present the Action Taken Report in the House during the Winter Session of Parliament.

facilitated the day to day functioning of the Institute to some extent. Giving details about

Comments of the Committee

The Committee, is not convinced by this kind of arrangements. The reason for making the
Minister the President of the Governing Body seems to be that no reference should be called
for and there should be some one in a position to take decisions immediately. The
Committee wonders as to how the Executive Committee which has been constituted by the
Governing Body has all the powers of the Governing Body. The Committee is, however, not
interested as to which body should exist but whichever body exists should have all the
powers to take immediate decisions to enable the Institute to work properly and regularly.
There should not be any delay in taking decisions. The Committee is of the view that‘ since
the National Institute of Homoeopathy is an autonomous body, the proposal for making the
pensionary scheme applicable to the Institute will not be agreed to by the Ministry of
Finance. The Committee feels that adoption of LIC Pension Scheme will prove
disadvantageous to the employees of the Institute. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the autonomous character of the Institute be done away and it should be brought at par
with other Government departments.

Further Comments

Commenting about the vacancy position in the Institute, the Secretary during her
evidence before the Committee on 17th August, 1998 stated that out of the 42 sanctioned
teaching posts, 20 posts have been filled so far. On being asked to specify the reasons for
delay in filling up of the posts, the Secretary informed the Committee that the Central

uncil of Homoeopathy have rationalised the norms and have accordingly fixed the norms
of 42 teaching posts as against 63 posts earlier, out of which at least 28 should be full time
teachers. The Secretary further clarified that these norms have not been incorporated in the
rules so far which has resulted in delay in filling up of the teaching posts.

Comments of the Committee

The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Department in filling up the vacant
posts. However, the Committee emphasises that the norms fixed by the CCIH should be
incorporated in the rules without further delay. If that is not done, the Committee
apprehends that the students of the Institute will be the sufferers as 50% posts are still lying
vacant.

4.1 The Committee also feels that unless adequate pay-scales are given to the teaching
faculty or made at least at par with the other Central /State Government organisations, the
Institute will not be able to attract well qualified candidates, leaving the posts vacant as is
the case today. The Committee feels that the qualification required for the various teaching
posts should not be reduced in an attempt to fill up the vacant posts. However, the Institute
should take steps to immediately revise the pay-scales of the faculty members bringing them
at par with the Central /State Governments. The representatives from the Department of
ISM&H informed the Committee that they are awaiting the recommendations of the Sth Pay
Commission and as soon as the recommendations are made public, the Department will
revise the pay-scales of their faculty members on the lines of recommendations made by the
Pay Commission. The Committee did not agree with this plea as NIH, Calcutta is an
autonomous organisation and has no relevance with the recommendations of the Sth Pay
Commission set up by the Government. The pay scales of the teaching and non-teaching
staff have not been referred to the Sth Pay Commission at all. Therefore, the Department of
ISM&H should take immediate steps for revising the pay-scales of their teaching staff
without waiting for the recommendations of the Pay Commission.

5250/RS/F—4-B


Action Taken

4.1 Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance has decided not to entertain any
proposals pertaining to revision of pay scales, allowances, creation/ upgradation of posts,
Cadre Review/Cadre restructuring in all Ministries / Departments including autonomous
bodies pending decision on the recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission.

Further Comments

The Secretary, during the course of oral evidence before the Committee on 15th
September, 1997 explained that the pay scales in the Institute were definitely lower. The
reasons was that there were very few post gradutes because post graduation in Homoeopathy
started late. Since they have Post Graduate Degree as the minimum qualification, for the
post of Director, the scale cannot be at par. The moment they raise the standard of Post
Graduation they will be able to give higher pay scales. On being asked as to whether any
reference was made to the Fifth Pay Commission for revision of pay scales etc., the
Secretary informed that they had not made any reference. She further stated that even
though they had not made any reference, they would be adopting the recommendations of
the Fifth Pay Commission because all Central Government rules were applicable. As regards
the pay scales of Director also she said that whatever is recommended by the Pay
Commission for the post of Director, it shall be applicable here. She further stated that a
decision had been taken recently in the Executive Committee to take steps for upgradation
of the post of Director, NIH from Rs. 3700—5000 to Rs. 5900—6700, but the Ministry of
Finance had not agreed for it and the proposal was turned down. The Secretary while
appearing before the Committee on 17th September, 1998 stated that efforts were now being
made to fill up the Post of Director on a regular basis. A few applications in response to an
advertisement in this regard have been received which will be processed shortly.

Comments of the Committee:

The Committee is not convinced by the replies given by Department and the Secretary
of the Department. The Committee is in total disagreement, that the pay scales of the
teaching staff could be revised only after a final decision of the recommendation of the Pay
Commission. Upgradation of the pay scales is different from the Pay Commission’s
recommendations. In this case the Deptt. and the Institute have committed a mistake of not
getting the pay scales revised for so long. The Committee recommends that the pay scales
should be upgraded without any further delay. As regards prescribing higher qualifications
for the teaching posts is concerned, necessary steps may also be taken immediately so that
higher pay scales could be prescribed. As regards the reference of the institute to Pay
Commission, the Committee feels that there is a total confusion. Nobody seems to be
interested in taking any decison. Either the Pay scales of the staff of the Institute should
have been referred to the Pay Commission and in case it has not been referred, independent
decision should be taken for upgradation of the pay scales of the staff. The Ministry of
Finance should also keep this in mind while taking decision in regard to the pay scales of the
teaching posts.

4.2 The Committee also feels that the Government may either consider allowing private
Practice to the Doctors or paying adequate non-practising allowances in order to attract well
qualified and competent doctors to join the Institute. The Committee also desires that
besides filling up the vacant posts, the Govt. should also sanction the 24 additional posts as
required. The Committee also feels that the Government should provide good promotional
avenues to the teachers to avoid stagnation in promotion. The Committee again reiterates
that the Government should not wait for the outcome of the Sth Pay Commission and take
immediate decisions on these long pending issues.


Action Taken

4.2 Govt of India’s decisions regarding private practice and the quantum of NPA are
applicable in the NIH, Calcutta and all other autonomous bodies working under the Deptt.
of ISM&H. Departure from these norms would create problems both within and outside the
Department of ISM&H.

The short-term goal of the Deptt. is to try and fill up all vacancies in the teaching
faculty. Regarding posts which have already been created some progress has been made in
this regard. The long term goal of the Department is to create and fill up all posts as per
Central Council of Homoeopathy norms

Further Comments

The Secretary further informed that the Department had made a reference to the
Ministry of Finance for reviving the posts in writing. On a query made by the Committee as
to whether the ban on filling up all the posts which remain vacant for more than one year
applies to teaching institutions or not, she stated that it was necessary to go to the Ministry
of Finance for reviving the posts.

Comments of the Committee:

The Committee feels that such a ban would put hurdles in the smooth functioning of the
teaching institutions. Teaching institutions should be made an exception from such a ban
because from the time post fall vacant till they are filled up, sometimes it might take very
long time and meanwhile the one year period may lapse. Therefore, the Ministry of Finance
should amend its rules and exempt the teaching institutions from applying such a ban.
