XIV. REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH PROGRAMME
14.1. For improving the effectiveness of Family Welfare Programme, the programme for mother and child care was
reorganized in 1997 in the form of Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme. The programme aims to meet
the unmet needs of Family Welfare Programme by improving health status of women and children, especially the poor
and undeserved, by reducing Infant, Child and Maternal mortality and morbidity through:-
a. Sustaining and strengthening the ongoing Child Survival and Safe Motherhood Programme to ensure the
essential services as per package of services;
b. Improve the performance of the Family Welfare system in implementing policy change;
c. Strengthen the quality and effectiveness of the services under essential package of Reproductive and Child
Health Services; and
d. Improve project implementation through the application of performance-based criteria for continued
funding.
14.2. The Department stated that the allocation for the project in BE 1998-99 was Rs.758 crore which was decreased
to Rs.603 crore at RE stage. It has been raised to Rs.676.80 crore in BE 1999-2000. On being asked, how the
provision will be utilised, the Secretary stated that even though RCH was launched in October, 1997 it could be

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/87repfw.htm[01-07-2016 15:10:52]
started in full pace only from April, 1998. The key strategy of the programme is to weld the vertical services into a
unified programme, covering the family welfare sector and also to establish linkages with other allied sectors so as to
achieve proper inter-sectoral coordination for bringing about a sustained improvement in primary health care, the
Committee was informed.
14.3. Further elaborating on the programme, the Secretary stated that MMR in the country is 437 per 100,000 live
births which is unacceptably high and the main thrust of the programme is, therefore, towards expanding the scope
and improving the quality and availability of services in the area of women’s health. Under the programme, a number
of programmes and schemes have been formulated and operationalised for tackling the specific causes for high
maternal mortality and morbidity in the country. The outlines of the various RCH schemes were circulated among the
States, seeking specific proposals. A number of proposals in every State have already been sanctioned. Particular
mention must be made of such schemes as Referral transportation through panchayat level institutions; facilitating
round the clock delivery services by providing additional inputs and facilities to the rural hospitals; for engaging
doctors on a contractual basis in PHCs for conducting MTPs, the services of private anaesthesiasts in emergency
obstetric care, etc.
14.4. The Secretary further stated that the low state of institutional delivery (less than 30 per cent according to the
NFHS survey 1992) has been one of the major causes for high maternal mortality. So developing and equipping PHCs
for handling deliveries on a larger scale and the FRUs for handling complicated deliveries is a major task under the
RCH. Apart from training and contractual appointments, Government is also providing drug and equipment support to
both the FRUs, primary health centres and the sub-centre on a wide scale.
14.5. No doubt, the goals set to be achieved are laudable but the Committee feels apprehensive about the
achievement level if the programme is not monitored properly. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that
a Monitoring Committee consisting of the Central and State Government officials be set up for better
implementation of the programme.
XV. PULSE POLIO
15.1. Briefing the Committee about Pulse Polio campaign, the Secretary stated that in 1998-99, in order to
achieve the WHO mandated global goal of reaching polio eradication by 2000 A.D., the Government has
intensified the Pulse Polio Immunisation Programme. Even though more than 100 per cent was reported
coverage every year, it was found that about 8% of children were still left out. Therefore, the Government made
special efforts by supplementing the booth immunisation with house to house search and also through
surveillance efforts. The Cabinet has also approved a proposal for launching additional rounds covering the
whole States of U.P., Bihar, M.P. and Rajasthan as the performance of these States had come down
considerably, the Department informed.
15.2. The Committee hopes that by these measures the Department will be able to achieve zero incidence
of poliomyelitis by the end of the millennium.

setting up drug storage centres on a regional basis in all major States and to improve the logistics of supply from the

Commission and UNFPA is currently under circulation for consideration in the EFC. The Committee hopes the EFC
will clear the project at the earliest.

elimination of Neo Natal Tetanus has been also launched in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. The Government proposes
to intensify these campaigns in the coming year. The Committee hopes these initiatives will yield the desired
results.

XVII. COLD CHAIN EQUIPMENTS
17.1. A large cold chain system has been established under the immunisation programme since its inception which
consists of a series of transportation and storage facilities for carrying vaccines from the manufacturers to the
beneficiaries. The equipments being used for storage, distribution and transportation of the vaccines are walk-in-

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
1.1. The National Health Policy  of  1983 visualised the importance of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy
and its role in the national health care system.    People of our Country have faith in the traditional systems especially
when the services provided are cheaper and available in  very  small  place  and rural areas.  Moreover, the remedies are
free from side-effects.  India has  a  large resource  of ISM&H practitioners of Homoepathy whose services need to be
fully utilised in the national health care delivery  system.    For this  purpose,  a  new  Department  of  Indian Systems of
Medicine and  Homoeopathy (ISM&H) has been set up to promote and develop the  Indian systems of Medicine
(Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and drugless Therapies like  Yoga  and  Naturopathy). 
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
2.1. The total allocation, both Plan and Non-Plan  taken  together, provided to  the Department for the year 1998-99 was
Rs.  85.60 crores  in BE which was enhanced to 89.12 crores at RE stage.    The  Committee  has  observed  that  the 
increase at the RE stage in 1998-99 was made only in Non-Plan head i.e.  from Rs.  36.60  crores  to  40.12 crores. 
2.2. On a specific query regarding amount sought by the Department for 1999-2000, the Committee was informed that
an  amount of Rs.  106.88 crores (Rs.   63.45  crores Plan  + Rs.  43.43 crores Non-Plan) was sought and the approved
amount was Rs.  100.96 crores (Rs.  59.13 crores Plan  +  Rs.    41.83 crores  Non Plan).  Thus there is an increase of
Rs. 15.36 crores in 1999-2000 as compared to the allocation made in BE 1998-99. 
2.3 The Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 260 crores for the Department for Ninth Plan is at a considerably
enhanced level when compared to Eighth Plan allocation of Rs. 104.44 crores.  However, the fact remains that it is
much below the projected requirements of the Department.    The Department of ISM&H’s share of Plan allocation has
remained about 3.4% of the total health sector allocation.  If various systems under ISM&H have to develop properly,
there is a need for substantial higher allocation of funds for the Department.   Reduction  of  amount particularly  under 
plan head could severely affect the activities of the Department aimed at development of the ISM&H. The Committee
therefore recommends that Plan allocation made for the  year 1999-2000 should be increased at RE stage. 
 
III. AYURVEDA
3.1. The allocation  for  Ayurveda under Plan in BE 1998-99 was Rs. 10.54 crores which was enhanced to Rs. 13.16
crores at RE stage and again reduced to Rs. 12.09 crores in 1999-2000.    Explaining  the  reason for the uneven
increase/decrease in the plan allocation for Ayurveda,  the  Department  submitted  that  it  was  mainly due  to  
payment of arrears of salary and allowances  caused by implementation of Vth Pay Commission recommendations 
to      Ayurvedic Physicians  and  personnel.    The Department also submitted  that this additional liability was not
required to be   paid  during  1999-2000, hence the less provision. 
3.2 The Committee has noticed that there is a growing demand of Ayurveda treatment in the Western countries.  Some
private parties are reported to have shown interest in starting Ayurveda Health Care Centres so as to attract foreign
tourists.  The Committee is of the view that the Department should draw an action plan in this regard which will
popularise the Ayurvedic System of treatment in and outside India in due course  which in turn will attract more tourists.
3.3 Committee’s attention has also been drawn to a lot of misleading advertisements regarding some Ayurvedic
medicines which are not scientifically tested.   On a specific query as to what preventive action has been taken in this
regard, the Secretary informed that all the State Govts. have been requested to take stringent action in this regard. 
Action was also being taken for bringing about necessary amendments in the Magic Remedies Objectionable
Advertisements Act.  However, the Secretary admitted that there was a need for strengthening the drug control
administration at the state level.  The Committee is of the view that there is a need for building up a mechanism for
taking preventive action so that public at large is not misled. 
3.4 The Committee is aware that there are a number of persons who are doing some good work in the Ayurvedic system
of treatment.  However, due support for their achievements seems to be lacking.  The Committee strongly feels that the

Department should make all concerted efforts to give due recognition and provide financial support to deserving
practitioners.
IV. UNANI
4.1   Under  the allocation for the Unani System, Plan provision was reduced from Rs.  8.55 crores in BE 1998-99 to
Rs.  6.98 crores in the RE.  However,  an allocation  of Rs.  8.55 crores  has been made  in  BE  1999-2000. 
4.2. The Committee was informed that additional funds were allocated in 1998-99 for construction of buildings for
Regional  Research Institute of Unani Medicine at Srinagar and Karimganj and also for strengthening of RRIUM,
Hyderabad.  However, as these projects could not be started, amount of allocation had to be reduced at RE stage in
1998-99.  The Committee finds that approval of the appropriate authority is awaited for RRIUM, Srinagar.  For
RRIUM, Hyderabad and Karimganj, estimates are being obtained from the concerned authorities.  The Committee
hopes that necessary formalities will be completed at the earliest and the projects will not be delayed further. 
4.3. The Committee has been informed  that in view of the change in the  objective and the funding pattern, fresh
approval of EFC has become necessary for National Institute of Unani Medicine, Bangalore.  The Committee would like
to impress upon the Department to expedite the procedural requirements so that construction work of the main building
of  NIUM, Bangalore is started without any further delay.
V. HOMOEOPATHY
5.1. For Homoeopathy, the  plan provision was Rs. 6.77 crores in BE 1998-99 which was increased to Rs. 7.02 crores at
RE stage.  In BE of 1999-2000 it has been reduced to the level of Rs. 6.27 crores.  When the Department was asked to
explain the reason for these variations, it was informed that in the RE 1998-99, a provision of Rs. 7.02 crores was made
primarily to meet the arrears on amount of salary and allowances  to Homoeopathy physicians/personnel.   Since this
additional  liability is not to be paid during 1999-2000,  less provision has been made. 
5.2. The Committee notes that the increase of bed capacity for in-patient department of National Institute of
Homoeopathy, Calcutta has been linked up with the introduction of post graduate course in homoepathy which  is going
to commence from Feb, 1999. Last year, the Committee had suggested that research on detoxication  of arsenic
poisoning being conducted by NIH, Calcutta should be intensified as this problem had severely affected West Bengal. 
The Committee is happy to note that NIH has submitted a project costing Rs. 14.04 lakhs under the Department’s extra
mural research scheme and an amount of Rs. 6 lakhs has already been sanctioned during 1998-99 for this research.  The
Committee hopes that the research will be completed within the stipulated time.
VI. YOGA AND NATUROPATHY
6.1. For Yoga and Naturopathy the BE for 1998-99 on the plan side was Rs. 3.95 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 3.63
crores at the RE stage.  However, it has been increased substantially to Rs. 6.20 crores in  BE 1999-2000.  When asked
to justify the same, the Department explained that enhanced allocation is on account of construction of building  for
Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga (MDNIY).  During 1999-2000, an amount of Rs. 325.00 lakhs has been
earmarked to accelerate the construction work. 
6.2. The Committee, however, notes  that in the year 1998-99, the provision of Rs. 170.00 lakh for the purpose could not
be utilised resulting in no expenditure upto to Feb, 1999.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that effective action
should be taken for completion of construction work of the building of the Institute. 
6.3. The Committee has been given to understand that the Institute propose to undertake experimental study on the
effect of yoga in alcohol intake and the research project in this regard has been submitted for seeking grant in aid from
W.H.O.  The Committee desires that the project should be cleared as early as possible. 
6.4. Last year the Committee recommended that Yoga be taught in schools right from the primary level.  The
Committee finds that the response of the Department of Education is awaited. The Committee recommends that the
Department should pursue the matter with the Department of Education. 
6.5. The Committee was informed last year that comprehensive project report for the establishment of the National
Institute of Naturopathy, Pune will be placed before EFC.  However the Committee is pained to note that the approval
of the EFC is yet to be obtained.  The Committee in this connection has also noted that an expenditure of Rs. 36.50
lakhs could be made  against provision of Rs. 75 lakhs.  The Committee feels that this is not a happy situation and there
is a need to expedite the matter to avoid under-utilisation of the provision made for the year 1999-2000.

General 
6.6. The Committee has been given to understand that certain positive achievements have been made in the treatment of 
Cancer by some ISM&H practitioners specially in Homoeopathy and Ayurveda.  The Committee feels that the
department should provide due patronage to the deserving cases. 
VII. MEDICAL EDUCATION 
7.1. At present, there are 311 undergraduate and 47 postgraduate ISMH colleges  in the country.  In order to improve the
standard of education in these institutions, the Department has  adopted multi pronged strategy:- 
i) To set up model ISM&H Educational Institutes under the Department with the modern facilities and to maintain very
high standard of Education;
ii) To provide financial assistance to improve UG & PG ISM&H colleges run by State Govts./NGOs/Semi Govt.
organisations; and 
 
iii) To establish statutory regulatory bodies to regulate the education by laying down the minimum standards of
education and curriculum and register the practitioner of these systems.
7.2. Last year, the Committee was informed that views of the State Govts. have been sought by the Central Council of
Indian Medicine on norms for establishing a new Ayurveda  college/prescribing the minimum standard for the existing
colleges.  However, the Committee is constrained to note that the views of the State Govts. are yet to be received. 
Position with regard to Homoeopathy education is more worrying as no action seems to be initiated by the Central
Council of Homoeopathy so far.  The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation that speedy action is
called for checking the growth of sub-standard colleges and also for having the minimum standard of education in the
existing colleges. 
7.3. Regarding para- medical education in pharmacy and Nursing, the Department informed the Committee that they
have proposed to introduce a scheme as an add-on component to the existing schemes of improving and strengthening
of the existing UG colleges of ISMH for  financial assistance for setting up of pharmacy/nursing education.  Pharmacy
Council of India and Nursing Council of India were approached for making suitable modifications/amendments in their
Acts for facilitating introduction of pharmacy and nursing education in Ayurveda, Homoeopathy, Unani and Siddha
systems.  Though the response from the Nursing Council was encouraging, the Pharmacy Council has shown their
inability.  Setting up of a separate Pharmacy Council is therefore under-examination, the Committee was informed.  The
Committee hopes that these issues would be decided without further delay. 
7.4. So far as  teaching of yoga and naturopathy is concerned, the Department informed that the task of regulating
education in Yoga and Naturopathy has not yet been entrusted to the Central Council for Research in Yoga and
Naturopathy.  Setting up of a regulatory body for education in Yoga and Naturopathy was under active examination of
the Department.  The Committee therefore, recommends that a separate regulatory body be formed at the earliest so that
research activities in yoga and Naturopathy are fostered. 
7.5. Regarding need to check huge amounts of donation/capitation fee being taken by some colleges under ISM&H, the
Committee was informed that a fee structure to be charged by private colleges as per guidelines of Supreme Court
Orders is being finalised actively and the schemes submitted by the respective Councils on fee-structures in Private
Professional ISM&H colleges have been returned to the Councils for taking opinion from the State Governments.  The
Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the matter with State Govts. so as to finalise this issue at the
earliest. 
7.6 The Committee was informed that 30 institutions have been identified to impart training under RCH programme of
Department of Family Welfare to ISM&H physicians and Para- Medics and Director ISM&H of State Governments and
other personnel.  During the year 1997-98, 2310 professionals have been trained and during 1998-99, 1450 professionals
have been trained upto February, 1999.    The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by the Department.
VIII. POOR QUALITY OF DRUGS 
8.1. In view of the Committee it is necessary to prescribe standards for ensuring efficacy of ISM&H drugs  and also for
checking their  genuineness and purity in the market  as there is general skepticism about the quality of ISM&H drugs. 
The Committee was informed that the Department was giving higher priority for standardization of drugs.  It has been
resolved that the standardisation work on drug may be completed during the Ninth Plan period.  On a specific query as
to what progress has been made so far, the Department informed as under :-

(i) The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia Committee has approved 78 monographs on single drugs titled as  Ayurvedic
Pharmacopoeia of India (Part I, Volume II) which is expected to be published during 1999-2000. 
A further 100 monographs have been approved for inclusion in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (Part I, Volume III) 
(ii) 32 laboratories/institutions are engaged for developing Pharmacopoeial standards of ISM drugs and out of the  387
single drugs allocated to them, data on 100 drugs has been generated.
(iii) Drug standardisation work on 915 homoeopathic single drugs have been finalised.  Standards on 710 homoeopathic
drugs have already been published.
8.2. The Committee has also noted that at present two drug testing laboratories are providing the technical back up to
these Pharmacopoeial Committees and it is proposed to strengthen these laboratories.  There is also a need for setting up
of Regional Drug Testing Laboratories.  In order to accelerate the work of  evolving of standards, 31 Research

VIII. NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS 
9.1 80 % of ISMH drugs are based on medicinal plants.  However, due to over exploitation, unscrupulous collection and
denuding of forests, which are the source of medicinal plants, supplies have been dwindling.  The Department informed
the Committee that it has initiated various steps to enhance the supplies of medicinal plants. These are conservation and
preservation of medicinal plants through in situ and ex-situ cultivation, developing tissue culture, storage in gene banks,
developing large-scale gardens of medicinal plants in coordination with concerned Ministries/Departments. A special
scheme to provide assistance to research organizations for development of agro-techniques has also been introduced.  26

REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION    
1.1              The main objectives of the Department of Health are:-
 
(i)         to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention, control and
eradication of communicable diseases;
(ii)        to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the medical
colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas;
(iii)       to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs;
(iv)       to provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people and to train the required number of
personnel for this purpose;
(v)        to take steps for better implementation of Health Care Programmes for tribal and other weaker sections
of the Society; and
(vi)       to collaborate with  member countries of United Nations and International Agencies like WHO,
UNICEF in matters relating to health promotion.
1.2       The Department of Health incurs expenditure either directly or through various institutions and establishments
run by it and by way of grants given to autonomous and voluntary organisations.  Grants to States and Union Territory
Administrations are mainly for Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being implemented through the State Governments
and Union Territory Administrations.  They include national programmes for prevention, control and eradication of
diseases.
1.3       The Department finances, wholly or substantially, the following autonomous institutions engaged in patient care
and/ or research:
 
(i)         All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Dr. Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences,  New
Delhi;
(ii)        Post-Graduate Institute of Medical Education and Research, Chandigarh; 
(iii)       All India Institute of Speech and Hearing Sciences, Mysore; and
            (iv)       Indian Council of Medical Research, New Delhi.

II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       A Budgetary provision of Rs. 2167.86 crores has been made for the Department of Health for 2000-2001.  Rs.
1277.86 crores is the Plan component and Rs. 890.00 crores have been provided under Non-Plan.
2.2       On a specific query as to the projected requirements of the Department for 2000-2001, the Department submitted
that as against the original projected demand of Rs. 1350 crores, the amount finally approved is Rs. 1300 crores
(including a component of Rs. 22.14 crores  under Capital Works). The requirements originally proposed for Annual
Plan 2000-2001  were keeping in view the Ninth  Plan priorities and likely  expenditure.   The major programmes/
institutions where outlays have been reduced following reduction by the Planning Commission are Malaria, TB, AIDS,
Cancer and the National Institute of Biologicals (NIB).
2.3       The Committee has been given to understand that there has been no substantial increase in the allocation for
health sector.   The Committee notes that out of the total investment of 6% of GDP for the health sector, 1.3% is
contributed by the State sector, i.e. the State Governments and the Central Government.   However, due to the
constraint-ridden financial position of majority of the States, there has not been any major addition to the Plan outlay of
the State Governments.   The Committee is of the opinion that  in view of the weak financial position of majority of the
States the  Central Government has no other alternative but to bear the main responsibility in this regard.
2.4       The Committee, at the same time, is also distressed to note that the Department has not been able to utilise the
funds allocated to it for the past few years.   The Committee finds that allocations made are invariably being reduced at
the RE stage and even this reduced allocation is not fully utilised.   Provision of Rs. 2361.69 crores was made in 1998-
99 which was reduced to Rs. 2067.56 crores.   Actual  expenditure is  only Rs. 1901.69 crores.   Similarly, provision of
Rs. 2449.23 crores in BE 1999-2000 has been reduced to Rs. 2231.88 crores at the RE stage.   Details of actual
expenditure  when made available would again indicate under-utilisation of allocations.   The Committee finds that
maximum saving is due to surrender of funds under EAC component of various National Health Programmes in 1997-
98 and 1998-99.   The Committee takes a serious view of this.
2.5       In fact, it is an irony that on one hand we have funds constraint and on the other whatever allocation is made,
despite funds constraint, is not fully utilised.   The Committee is of the considered view that this is one of the reasons for
non-effective and improper implementation of most of the schemes in our country.  Last year, the Committee had
extensively dwelt on this issue and had observed that the Department of Health, being the nodal agency, has to take
remedial steps.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the measures  taken by the Department. The Committee
would also like to know about the utilization of fund under EAC component of various National Health   Programes
during 1999-2000. 
2.6       The Committee has been informed that foreign direct investment  (FDI) upto 10%  is allowed in health sector.  
FDI policy has been further liberalised thereby putting almost all items/activities except a small negative list under the
automatic route.   Further, a special Subject Group to look into the policy framework for private investment in
Education, Health and Rural Development has been recently re-constituted by the Prime Minister.   The Committee

2.7       Performance Budget should clearly reflect both the financial provision and corresponding physical achievements
of different schemes/programmes during the financial year.  The Committee, however, observes that Performance
Budgets of almost all the Departments are prepared in such a manner that one does not get a clear  idea in this regard. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the department should take corrective steps in this regard, if the

III.      CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME(CGHS)
3.1       Rs. 10  crores have been provided under Plan for CGHS for  2000-2001 against an allocation of Rs. 9 crores in
BE 1999-2000 reduced to Rs. 8 crores at the RE stage.  To a question as to  in what manner  this enhancement in budget
allocation is proposed to be utilized, the Department replied that the allocation is proposed to be utilized for the new
schemes based on the proposals contained in the Ninth Plan which included extension of CGHS to new cities and also
opening of dispensaries/polyclinics/ Labs. etc. in the existing CGHS cities.
3.2       The Committee observes  that during the Ninth Plan, it was targetted  to extend the CGHS  network  by covering
seven new cities.   However, the Committee is constrained to note that no achievement could be made during the first
three years of the Ninth Plan as the  SIU Report of the Department of Expenditure on the Norms study of CGHS
(Allopathic)  dispensaries submitted on 2.11.99 stated that creation of additional/new posts under CGHS can be done
only on completion of six months from the date on which action as given in, the SIU Report has been completed.  The
Committee finds that as the SIU Report  is, at present under examination of the CGHS ,  it will take some more time for
the CGHS to implement the recommendations contained in the report.  It is doubtful whether the creation of additional
new posts under CGHS would be taken up during 2000-2001.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department  should make concerted efforts to expedite all the formalities,   so that Ninth Plan target for upgrading
CGHS network is achieved.
3.3       Apart from expansion of CGHS, the Committee is of the view that there is a need for improvement in the quality
of services provided by the  CGHS Dispensaries.   The Department should take effective measures  in this regard.
3.4       The Department has informed that the report given by a Review Committee constituted on 17
th February, 1999
for formulating lists of Patent Proprietary drugs for inclusion in the combined formulary for CGHS/VMS is yet to be
approved.   To a query by when  this exercise is likely to be completed, the Department has stated that initially a
Committee under the Chairmanship of Dr. P. Das Gupta, the then DCG (I) was constituted to prepare a combined drug
formulary of CGHS and MSO.  The formulary recommended by this Committee excluded drugs where purchases were
less than Rs. 5 lakhs.  The report of the second committee headed by Dr. Ranjit Roy Choudhary was not found feasible
as it excluded most of the old drugs finding place in the earlier formulary.   It was also observed that small and medium
scale manufacturers would be hit if this formulary was accepted.  The reports of both the above Committees were
reviewed by a Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS and  after going through all the  reports a fresh Committee
for formulating a single comprehensive formulary for CGHS and MSO is under consideration of the Department.   The
Committee expresses deep anguish over the delay in finalising the combined formulary due to contradictory
recommendations of the various committees appointed by the Department and recommends that the formulary be
finalised without any further loss of time and the Committee be apprised thereof.

V.        SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL
5.1       The allocation for Safdarjung Hospital  for the year 2000-2001 is Rs. 86.80 crores which shows a marginal
increase in comparison to  RE allocation of Rs. 84.35 crores for 1999-2000.
5.2       The Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 25.93 crores for Safdarjung Hospital in 1999-2000 was
enhanced to Rs. 26.54 crores at the RE stage.  However, the Committee is constrained to observe, that against this
enhanced allocation, expenditure reported upto 10.3.2000 is only Rs. 19.27 crores.  What is more disturbing is that
against a provision of Rs. 8 crores for Machinery and equipment, there has been expenditure of only Rs. 1.13 crores
upto 10.3.2000.  The Committee has been pursuing the progress made in the purchase of equipments required for
upgradation of the Burns and Plastic Surgery Department of the Hospital.  Equipments worth Rs. 90.30 lakhs against a
sanction for procurement of equipment worth Rs. 115.86 lakhs have been purchased upto 1999-2000.  The Committee
hopes that the process of procurement of the remaining equipments would be completed during 2000-2001.
5.3       Safdarjung Hospital,  the largest hospital under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, provides  medical
services in all basic specialties including super specialties  and also provides round the clock casualty and emergency
services.  The number of indoor patients is more than the capacity of the hospital, almost at any point of time. 
Furthermore, the Hospital is run with the policy of not denying  admission to any one who comes to it for treatment. 
The Committee is, however, constrained to observe that most of the services provided by the Hospital are 
unsatisfactory, there is total lack of cleanliness and behaviour of the  staff  is  wanting.   This is true about other
Government Hospitals too.  Some drastic measures need to be taken at the earliest.   The Committee understands that at
one stage, the Department had decided to entrust the work of maintaining cleanliness at least in the emergency wards to
private agencies.   The Committee fails to understand the reasons for non-implementation of this decision.   The
Committee is of the view that the Department should find out ways and means of maintaining cleanliness in all
Government Hospitals.
VI.       DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHIA HOSPITAL
6.1       Plan allocation for the Dr. RML hospital, New Delhi has been substantially increased from Rs. 12.47 crores in
1999-2000 to Rs. 24.50  crores in 2000-2001.  To a question as to in what manner this allocation of additional funds is
proposed to be utilised, the Department submitted that the enhanced allocation is meant for payment of salary for newly
created posts in various Departments, purchase of equipments and new schemes like Nephrology, Hematology and
Pediatric Surgery. 
6.2       To a query as to by when the task of building of a Trauma Centre is likely to be completed, the Department
replied that the work of building a Trauma Centre has been entrusted to the Hospital Services Consultancy Corporation. 
A draft E.F.C. proposal is likely to be submitted shortly. After the E.F.C. proposal is approved by the competent
authority and no objection/approvals are received from the various authorities, the construction work will start.  The
project is likely to take five years to complete.   The Committee feels that considerable time has already been taken at
the proposal stage.  The Committee is, therefore, of the view that the Department should expedite the completion of all
procedural formalities so that the construction work can start at the earliest.   The Committee feels  that all preliminary
exercise should be completed  before provision for any scheme is made.
6.3       The Committee understands that Nursing Home facilities are available only in Dr. Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital
at Delhi which are meant for Central Govt. employees drawing certain level of salary and other VIPs.  However, certain
constraints are being faced in availing of this facility.   It has been reported that upkeep of the rooms is also generally
lacking.   At present, rooms in the Nursing Home are being allotted only during specific time on recommendation of the
doctors authorised to do so.  The Committee fails to understand the rationale behind this procedure as the illness does
not come with an advance notice.  The Committee would like to be apprised about the rules/guidelines governing the
allotment of rooms.  The Committee is of the view that a proper chart displaying the availability of rooms should be
displayed at the Nursing Home.   The Committee also recommends that in the event of a room not being available, on
the basis of recommendation of the doctor on duty, the patient should be free to go to one of the CGHS recognised
private hospitals.

VII.      CENTRAL INSTITUTE OF PSYCHIATRY, RANCHI
7.1       The Plan allocation for this Institute in BE 1999-2000 was Rs. 3.80 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 2.71 crores
in the RE.  For 2000-2001, the Plan allocation is Rs. 3.00 crores.
7.2       Last year, the Committee was informed that the allocation of Rs. 2.80 crores in 1998-99 for the Institute was
enhanced to Rs. 3.80 crores in 1999-2000 for filling up 260 vacant posts.  However, the Committee finds that  posts
could not be created on account of ban orders issued by the Department of Expenditure.  This issue has been continuing
for a considerable time as  an IWSU study conducted for the Institute had recommended creation of 260 posts on
16.1.97, i.e. about three years ago.  The Committee is of the view that given the nature of the ailment, the patients of this
Institute need special treatment.  Doctors and para-medicals with specialized skills should be appointed to treat the
patients more efficiently.  It is an undesirable situation specially in view of that CIP, Ranchi is a teaching institute of a
national level.  The Committee is,  therefore, of the view that creation of additional posts is a necessity which cannot be
avoided.
7.3       To a query as to  the latest position in respect of the Draft Cabinet Note conferring autonomous status to the CIP,
Ranchi , the Department replied that  the Note  was circulated to the concerned Ministries and their comments received
are being examined. The Department of Expenditure vide their O.M.  dated 5.3.99 desired to clearly bring out the
financial implications on the upgradation and to come up with a proposal for rationalization of the manpower in the
Institute.  Some information has been received from the Institute which is being examined.  The Committee is of the
view that the issue of granting autonomous status to CIP, Ranchi has been unduly delayed.  The response of the
concerned Ministries/Departments has also not been quick and encouraging.  The Committee recommends that a
decision may be taken without any further delay.
VIII.     ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIIMS)
8.1       The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi is a premier medical institution of the country.  The Plan
allocation for the Institute in BE 1999-2000 was Rs. 81 crores, which was reduced to Rs. 70 crores in RE.  The plan
allocation for 2000-2001 is Rs. 91.30 crores.  Asked about the reasons for reduction in RE, the Department stated that
the EFC memo relating to the setting up of an Organ Bank, procurement of PET Scan, and setting up of Trauma Centre
at AIIMS could not be cleared during 1999-2000 and hence the reduction in RE.
8.2       The Committee is worried to note that despite its earlier recommendation, no progress seems to have been made
in respect of setting up a Trauma Centre.  The workshop on Trauma Centre was held in the Institute on 9-10 July, 1999. 
The Committee, however, finds that recommendations made at the workshop are still in the process of examination. 
The Committee recommends that the Department should make concerted efforts for completion of all the procedural
formalities prior to setting up the Trauma Centre.  It should be ensured that allocation made for this purpose should not
be left under utilised in 2000-2001 like the previous year.
8.3       It came to the notice of the Committee that Dr. R.C. Anand, Medical   Superintendent of the Institute who had
earlier been suspended on corruption charges was reinstated pending inquiry.  The Committee has come to know that
the reinstatement of Dr. Anand has not been approved by the Governing Body of the Institute.  The Committee fails to
understand as to why Dr. Anand was reinstated before the outcome of the inquiry instituted against him.  The
Committee feels that an institute of repute like AIIMS should avoid such controversy.

9.2       The Committee has been informed that against 3003 sanctioned posts as on 31.3.99, 2707 staff members

X.        NATIONAL MALARIA ERADICATION PROGRAMME
10.1     In the case of National Malaria Eradication Programme, the plan provision of Rs.240.00 crores in BE 1999-2000

10.2     The Committee notes that to protect the population from transmission of malaria, every year target for spraying

Pradesh, Chnadigarh and Daman & Diu.  168.04 million population were targetted to be covered by residual insecticidal
spray in 1998-99, but only 79.26 million population could be covered.  The Committee is of the view that corrective
measures need to be taken in this regard.
10.3     The Committee has been informed that the major constraints affecting the effective implementation of the
National Malaria Eradication Programme, such as vacancies in key positions, inadequacy of vehicles, frequent transfer
of officials even at the supervisory and grass root level were taken up with the State Govts.  from time to time.  States of
Rajasthan and Maharashtra have initiated action for recruitment of Multi-Purpose Workers/Surveillance Workers. 
Other States are also being advised to remove the constraints. The Committee is of the view that besides a regular
channel of interaction with the State Governments for removal of constraints, the Department should also closely
monitor the implementation of the National Malaria Eradication Programme.
10.4     To a question as to which states are covered by the National Dengu Control Programme,  the Department

Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and West Bengal have been considered to be endemic as reports of more
than 10 cases of Dengue Fever and Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever have been received from these States in the past.  The
Directorate of National Anti Malaria Programme propose to intensify the Dengue Control measures in these endemic
States in the first phase although the Programme would ultimately cover all the States/UTs.
10.5     The Department further informed that the endemic States were requested to convey their formal concurrence for
implementation of the programme on 50.50 cost sharing basis.   However, response have been received only from the
States of Haryana, Rajasthan, U.P. and Chandigarh and the remaining States have been  reminded to expedite their
views/comments.  The Committee recommends that the Department should pursue this matter with the remaining States.
XI.       NATIONAL LEPROSY ERDICATION PROGRAMME

the year 2000 AD by reducing the case load to less than 1/10,000 population. This objective is likely to be achieved by
19 States by the end of 2000 AD.   In case of the rest of the States, the target is likely to be achieved in different stages
between 2000 and 2005. Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaign, which was implemented in 21 States/UTs. till June,
1998, has been extended to 6 more States/UTs during the year. H.P., Manipur, Rajasthan and Delhi have  been included

2001 has been further reduced to Rs. 74 crore.  The Committee has been informed that the decrease at the RE stage was
due to lesser requirement of anti-leprosy drugs by the States, as some of the States already have balance of drugs.

11.3     The Committee is constrained to note that about 70% of the country’s Leprosy caseload is recorded in 5 States of

Practitioners and other functionaries.  Besides that, a special publicity drive was also launched through Doordarshan
/AIR.  The Committee finds that as a result of these actions the number of hidden cases detected in the above States has
decreased in comparison to cases detected under the Ist Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaign.
11.4     The Committee notes that the World Bank funded Project, National Leprosy Elimination Programme with an
outlay of Rs. 302 crore has been extended upto September, 2000.  Extension of the project for three years in the high
disease burdened States (MP, Bihar, UP, Orissa and W. Bengal) is proposed.
11.5     The Committee appreciates the efforts of 9.35 lakh General Health care staff and volunteers engaged  in creating
public awareness and integration of Leprosy activities with general Health Care.    The Committee feels that special care
need to be taken for leprosy patients of infectious category.   Post treatment rehabilitation measures for the needy
patients should be taken by the Department.
XII.      NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS
12.1     The aim of the National Programme for Control of Blindness launched  in 1976 is to reduce the blindness rate
from 1.49% to 0.3% by 2000 A.D. Besides, a World Bank Assisted Cataract Blindness Control Project is being
implemented since April, 1994 in  seven States i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan,
Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu,  where prevalence rate is very high.  Physical achievements have been – Cataract
Surgery – 100%, training – 80%, OTs – 70%, IOL – 133%.
12.2     The Committee is  constrained to note that in the States of Goa, J&K, M.P., Nagaland, Orissa, Rajasthan and
Chandigarh, the prevalence rate of blindness is much more than the national average.  The Committee, therefore, feels
that special efforts should be made for the above mentioned States.
12.3     The Committee notes that  Epidemiological Blindness Survey has been conducted on a pilot basis  in the two
districts i.e. Bharatpur in Rajasthan and Sivaganga in Tamil Nadu in 1998-99 to assess the prevalence of blindness. 
Prevalence of blindness in illiterates is as high as 14.90% in Bharatpur District of Rajasthan.  Major cause of blindness
is cataract with 57.3% and 53.4% rate of prevalence in the two districts. The Committee feels that given the vastness of
the country such surveys should be conducted in more districts.
12.4     The Committee is constrained to note that  under the National Trachoma and Blindness Control Programme as
against a provision of Rs. 700 lakhs as grant-in-aid to State Governments during 1997-98, actual expenditure amounted
to only Rs. 110.48 lakhs due to the poor performance of the States in developing the service units.  During 1998-99 
also, the position was somewhat similar. States of MP, Orissa, UP, Assam, Delhi, Gujarat, Haryana, HP,  J&K,
Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, Punjab were having unspent  balances lying with them.  The main reason for unspent
balances is the reluctance on the part of the State Govts. to create the posts due to the liability at the end of the plan
period.  Situation is more worrying in the case of Orissa as funds  were not released by the Finance Department of the
State Govt. to the executing Agencies.  The Committee recommends that the implementation of the Programme in the
States should be closely monitored  and in the event of any problem, the matter should be taken up with the concerned
State Government. 
XIII.     NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME
13.1     The Plan allocation for the Programme has been increased from Rs. 139.50 crores in BE & RE 1999-2000 to Rs.
145.00 crores in BE 1999-2000.   There has been a constant increase in number of individuals infected with HIV and
number of cases of AIDS.   The  cumulative number of HIV and AIDS cases up to the end of December, 1999 are
92312 (out of 3572144 screened) and 9966 respectively.   The highest number of HIV infections have been reported in

89th Report On Committee On HRD

Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu and  among Injectable Drug Users (IVDUS) in Manipur.  Males account for 78.6% and
females 21.4% out of the reported AIDS cases and are in the age group of 15-49 years.  Trends indicate that HIV
infection is spreading in two ways from urban areas to rural areas and from individuals pratising risk  behaviours to the
general population.  The major opportunistic infection in AIDS patients is TB.  Thus, it may emerge as dual epidemic of
TB and AIDS in future.
13.2     The Committee was informed that the National AIDS Control Programme Phase II launched from 9 th
November, 1999 has the following objectives:-
 
a)         to keep HIV prevalence rate below 5% of adult population in Maharashtra, below 3% in Andhra Pradesh,
Karnataka, Manipur and  TN and below 1% in remaining states;
b)         to reduce blood borne transmission of HIV to less than 1%;
c)         to attain awareness level of not less than 90% among the youth and others in the reproductive age group;
and
d)         to achieve condom use of not less than 90% among high risk categories like Commercial Sex Workers.
 
13.3     The Committee feels that identification of target population and providing peer counselling and increasing
public awareness and community support are the two most vital objectives, which if implemented as per the strategy
chalked out under NACP II, can result in arresting the increasing spread of AIDS.
13.4     The Committee finds that on various issues related to HIV/AIDS prevention and control in the country, a
comprehensive draft policy document has been formulated.  Similarly, a draft national Blood Policy has also been
formulated.  The Committee also notes that setting up of new modern blood banks and upgrading of 20 existing major
blood banks and setting up of 80 new districts level blood banks is also envisaged under NACP II.  The Committee
appreciates all the new initiatives.  The Committee, however, feels that effective monitoring of all the activities with an
element of random inspections/surveys is very essential for making the programme a success in the real sense.

1993-94, about 130 million people were covered in 61 districts as of mid-1999.   Service delivery has started in about 70

15.1     Hospital Waste is one of the biggest health hazards that is being faced by every citizen of this country.  This
subject has been extensively dealt with by the Committee in its earlier Reports.   In pursuance of Supreme Court`s
judgement given on 1.3.1996 on writ petition No. 286 of 1994 filed by Dr. B.L. Wadhera  the Bio-Medical Wastes

constituted Advisory Committees for implementation of Bio-Medical Waste (Management & Handling) Rules,  1998. 
The Committee would like to be apprised about the feedback, if received regarding  implementation of these rules in the
States.   Remaining States/UTs should also be approached for constituting Advisory Committees under these Rules.

Government Hospitals functioning in Delhi is made known to it.

patients who receive  free treatment at Government hospitals.   As you are aware, Civil Courts are already for
seeking redressal of such grievances but this procedure entails delay.   We are of the view that instead of the
Consumer Protection Act, it would be better that the Ministry of Health, being the administrative Ministry

OVERVIEW 
1. The National Health Policy (1983) has reiterated India's commitment to attain "Health for 
All (H.F .A.) by 2000 A.D.". The Eighth Plan envisages that health facilities must reach the 
entire population by the end of the Plan period. The B.F.A. paradigm, according to the 8th 
Plan, must take into account not only the high risk vulnerable groups i.e. mothers and children, 
but must also focus sharply on the underprivileged segments within the vulnerable groups. Health 
for under privileged will be the key strategy for the HFA, by the year 2000 A.D., a declaration 
to which India is a signatory. This can only be achieved by associating the pre-defined segments 
of population with not only the health planning process but also with the method for the 
, evaluation of programmes. 
2. India is facing highly complex and challenging health problems. There are health hazards 
of communicable diseases like leprosy, T.B. and malaria, besides challenges of post-transitional 
diseases like cardio-vascular and cancer. Above all these, we are also faced with horrendous 
threat of AIDS. These health problems are further aggravated by wide spread poverty, which 
leads to malnutrition, unhygienic sanitation, illiteracy and ignorance. Population growth is playing 
further havoc on the availability and quality of health services. 
3. Department of Health deals with the health administration of the country, including drugs 
control and prevention of food adulteration . 
4. The main functions of the Deparment of Health are to undertake national programmes of 
health for the prevention and eradication of communicable diseases; to promote education 
research and training in various medical disciplines; to prevent adulteration of food as well as 
drugs; to promote research and treatment on scientific lines in Indian Systems of Medicine; to 
provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people; to implement better health care 
programme for tribals, and to collaborate with WHO and other international agencies. 
5. For the financial year 1994-95, Budgetary allocation of the Department of Health is Rs. 
1255 crores, this is 18.34 per cent more than the previous year's allocation. This increase, as 
stated by the Department, is due to steep escalation in the prices of consumable items, machinery 
and equipments, publications, raiVair traffic fares, etc. Grant s of additional instalment of D.A., 
Interim Relief, increased number of patients in Government hospitals and increase in cost of 
insecticides, anti-leprosy and anti-T.B. drugs, etc. 
6. According to the Ministry's documents, the major thrust of Budg~t provisions in 1994-95 is 
on National Leprosy Eradication Programme, National Programme for Control of Blindness, 
National Tuberculosis Control Programme and National AIDS Control Programme. It also 
emphasised on setting up of a separate Directorate of Indian System of Medicine and 
Homoeopathy. 
7. The public expenditure in the health sector, both at the Centre and the States put 
together, has been a little over 1.5 per cent of G.D.P. The WHO had recommended that public 
health care expenditure should cross at least 5 per cent of GDP, if equity and universal coverage 
are to be realised. The Committee hopes that concerted efforts will be made to increase health 
expenditure upto 5 per cent of GDP in the next year's budget. 
8. However, the Budget for 1994-95 does not reflect that the Department is heading towards 
Health for All by 2000 A.D. It is noted that more funds are allocated for curative functions 
rather than for prevention of diseases. Programmes of health are uneven in States which may be 
corrected by the efforts of the Department. State should also participate actively in achieving the 
goal of Health for All. However, Department should also provide help to States by releasing 
money on time.

43. The basic objectives of the proposal is to strengthen the organistional set-up for ISM & 
H so as to effectively initiate organised measures to enable each of the systems of Indian 
Medicines , i.e., Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani, to devel op, in accordance with its genius and 
enable each of these systems to play its due role in the overall health care delivery system, to 
achieve the goal of "Health for All" by 2000 A.D. In addition, Yoga and Naturopathy, which are 
time-tes ted drugless therapies and Homoeopathy should also be promoted and strengthened to 
realise their potential in promot ing the public heal th. The Committee recommends that this 
Directorate should be set up expeditiously. 
44. On the question of increase in allocation from Rs. 20 lakhs in 1993-94 (RE) to Rs. 100 
lakhs for National Institute of Siddha, the Department explained that the proposal for setting up 
NIS in Tamil Nadu had been pend ing fl want of concrete proposal from the Government of 
Tamil Nadu. This year Tamil Nadu Government is in the process of getting land for the institute 
of Siddha. The Committee was also informed that the state Government is also willing to 
participate financially in the institute. Therefore, the Department is hopeful of starting the work 
on the institute during 1994-95. 
45. In the Eighth Plan Rs. 500 lakhs has been kept as assistance for upgrading ISM, PG 
Departments. However, in 1993-94 Rs. 25 lakhs was allocated anu in the Revised Estimates it 
was reduced to Rs. 20 lakhs. For 1994-95 also Budget allocatio n is Rs. 20 lakhs. 
Ayurveda 
46. Budgetary allocation for many of the institutes of Ayurveda for 1994-95 has been reduced 
in -:omparison to last year 's. For example, funds for Central Council for Research in Ayurveda 
and Siddha, New Delhi, have been red~ced from Rs. 346 lakhs to Rs. 330 lakhs. In the case of 
National Institute of Ayurveda, Jaipur, it has been reduced from Rs. 190 lakhs to Rs. 180 lakhs 
and for Gujarat Ayurveda University, Jamnagar, funds have been reduced from Rs. 130 lakhs to 
Rs. 127 lakhs. In case of Pharmacopoeil Labo ra tory for Indian Medicin e, Ghaziabad, there is a 
drastic reduction from Rs. 195 lakhs to Rs. 35 lakhs. 
47. The Committee expresses its displeasure over this decrease and recommends that 
increased funds should be provided to the institutions of Ayurveda. 
48. The Committee has also taken a serious note of the fact that there is not sufficient 
infrastructure to check and regulate the quality of Ayurvedic medicines. The Committee, in the 
discussions, also named some of the famous products of Ayurveda which have been found 
1m pure. 
49. The Committee recommends that standards for Ayurved ic med icine should be fixed and 

nonitored. The Secretary Deptt. of Health had stated in its oral evidence, had stated that 
;tandard of Ayurvedic medicines can be checked only at the stage of manufacturing and after 
:hat it is very difficult. The Committee recommends to take appropriate measures for this. 
50. The Committee also notes that the Department had proposed to establish a National 
Institute of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani Medicine, Homoeopathy and Naturopathy on the lines 
of All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi. But, till now all these institutes are in 
very bad condition and they are nowhere near to the standards of AIIMS, in any sense. 
The Committee feels that scientific research in Indian Systems of Medicines is not done 
properly. It shows sleekness on the part of the Department. 
Unani Medicine 
51. The Central Council for Research in Unan i Medicine (CCRUM) was established in 
1979 to initiate, aid, develop and co-ordinate scientific research in different aspects, fundam en­
tal and applied, of Unani Medicine and to promote and assist institutions of research for the 
disease, their prevention, caution and remedies. 
52. In 1993-94, CCRUM was provided Rs. 371 lakhs (Revised Estimates). For 1994-95, it 
is further increased to Rs. 507 lakhs. 
53. The Committee, while satisfied with the allocatiOn made for the development of 
Unani Medicine, however, recommends that the Department should ensure that the funds are 
utilised properly and achievements are evaluat~d regularly and effectively. 
Development & Cultivation of Medicinal PJants 
54. To meet the shortage of plants for manufacture of quality ISM & H drugs, a scheme 
for central assistance for development and cultivation of medicinal plants in the ISM & H hBs 
been initiated. Under the scheme, financial assistance is provided to eligible Government/ 
semi-government or~anisations, including the ISM & H institutions and pharmacies for non­
recuning expenditure i.e., fencing. land shaping, irrigation, equipments and construction of 
sheds etc. for cultivation and development of identified species of medicinal plants: 
55. The Department has taken steps for production of medicinal plants. This will save 
some of the im~,...,rtant medicinal plants from extinction, and also ensure the availability of 
these plants iu the market. However, the Committee feels that these efforts should be 
continued. 
Excise Duty 
56. The union Budget for 1994-95 has propo sed 10 per cent E;"cise Duty on •he 
Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani medicines, alongwith Homeopathic medicines and the med icines 
of alternative sy:.tems. 
57 The Cou.rnittee feels that i.1 the cootempo,.ary scenerio of globalisation of the science 
of Ayurveda, the proposed levy of 10 per cent Excise Duty adversely affects the exc-,lft of 
Ayurveda Siddha and Unani Medicines. which is sti11 in the ptimitive stage of growth. 
58. The Committee also feels that at home , where Aymvedic medicines have always been 
a common man \ alternate remedy, the proposed levy would lead tc price enhancem ent in 
Ayurveda , Siddhc.. and Unani medicines. 
59. The Committee recommends that the Depar tment should take necessary steps to 
remove Excise Duty. 

Yoga 
60. Budgetary allocation for Central Council for Research in Yoga and Naturopathy has 
been increased by Rs. 10 lakhs from Rs. 30 lakhs in 1993-94 to Rs. 40 lakhs in 1994-95. For 
Central Research Institute for Yoga, .New Delhi (CRIY) also, budgetary allocation for 1994-95 
is Rs. 20 lakhs which is 10 lakhs more than previous year's allocation. 
61. The Committee is satisfied that allocation for Yoga has been increased during this 
year's budget, but feels that more attention should be paid for popularisation of Yoga in 
schools and colleges as well as residential areas. Media should also be used effectively. Proper 
monitoring of the utilisation of funds should also be done. 
III 
HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES 
Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) 
62. The Committee takes serious note of the continuous decrease in the budget provision 
of CGHS. In 1993-94 a provision of Rs. 95.72 crores (BE) was made for CGHS. However, in 
the Revised Estimates it was enhanced to Rs. 117.72 crores . In 1994-95 Budget Estimates it 
has been provided Rs. 104 crores. In the 8th Plan CGHS has been allocated Rs. 15 crores for 
planned expenditure. 
63. The Secretary, Department of Health, explained to the Committee that there is no 
large-scale reduction in outlays for hospitals and CGHS Dispensaries. In some hospitals, 
where larger outlays were provided in 1993-94 for procurement of specific machinery and 
equipment, corresponding reduction has been made in the budget provision for 1994-95. 
However, provision for essential services, which is covered under non-plan expenditure, has 
been raised in all cases. 
64. He further stated that in CGHS due to rise in the cost of drugs it is expected that 
higher outlay will be necessary during the current year. Additional funds will have to be 
provided at the R.E. stage to meet these liabilities. 
65. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons <tdduced by the Department for 
decrease in the allocations. It feels that Central Government Employees are not served well 
by CGHS. There are complaints from C.G.H.S. beneficiaries in regard to non availability of 
required medicines, delay in supply, insistence for pre-payment by private recognised hospitals 
etc. The Committee recommends that the Department should look into this matter and take 
remedial measures. The Committee also recommends for increase in funds of C.G.H.S. and 
the Department should see that quality of services improves to the satisfaction of be­
neficiaries. 
Central Institute of Psychiatry, Ranchi 
66. In 1993-94 this institute was allocated Rs. 4.16 crores but it spent Rs. 4 crores. For 
1994-95 it is again allocated Rs. 4.51 crores. 
67. The Committee is concerned at the bad state of Central Institute of Psychiatry , (CIP) 
Ranchi. The Committee feels that a review of the functioning of this institute is made. 
All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
68. The Secretary, Department of Health , in his oral evidence had stated that the Vlllth 
Plan outlay for AIIMS is Rs. 100.00 crores. In the B.E. 1993-94 a sum of Rs. 73.48 crores 
(Rs. 26.23 crores Plan+Rs. 47.25 crores in Non Plan) had been provided which was enhanced 

to Rs. 82.63 crores (Rs. 32.23 crores in Plan + Rs. 50.40 crores in Non-Plan) in the Revised 
Estimates, 1993-94. Though the provisions of Rs. 82.05 crores (Rs. 29.05 crores in Plan+ Rs. 
53.00 crores in Non- Plan) in B.E. 1994-95 is marginally low with reference to R.E. 1993-94, it is 
substantially more with reference to B.E. 1993-94. 
69. The Committee feels that there is no increase in the allocations for AIIMS in real terms. 
The Committee recommends that it should be provided with sufficient funds to carry out its 
increasing responsibilities. It is one of the premier institutions in the field of medical education, 
research and treatment. The Committee feels that it should maintain its supremacy and speciality 
with up-to-date equipments and highly qualified doctors. The Committee also recommends that 
functioning and achievments of AIIMS may be reviewed periodically by an experts Committee. 
Para Medical Personnel 
70. The Department informed the Committee that shortage of para medical personnel of 
certain categories is there. In order to overcome this problem the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development, in cooperation with the Ministry of Health, have started vocational courses in 
various para-medical disciplines in a number of institutions. 
71. There is also a proposal for establishing a National Institute of Nursing Education and 
Research in Kerala which was examined in this Deptt. It is felt that the objectives of the 
proposed Institute are being largely fulfilled by the Nursing Council of India and the Deptt. of 
Health. Thus, the proposed institute may duplicate the functions of professional bodies like the 
Nursing Council. However, upgradation of nursing services, both qualitatively and quantitatively 
have been engaging the attention of the Department, and the different possibilities for achieving 
this have been under active consideration. It is, however, premature to make an allocation for 
the proposed National Institute. 
72. The Deptt. is also promoting various Health Related Vocational Courses (HRVC) for 
which the nodal department is the Department of Education in the Ministry of Human Resource 
Developm ent. The courses ident ified so far relate s to Medical Laboratory Technology, X-R ay 
technician , Ophthalmic techniques and A.N.M.'s training. 
73. The Committee notes that the Department has accepted the fact that there is a serious 
shortage of para-medical personnel. The Committee is concerned to note that the num ber of 
nurses is less thaa the number of doctors in many cases. The Committee hopes that this shortage 
is a short-term iJhenomenon and very soon it will be overcome. It recommends open ing of more 
institutions for tra ining of para-medical personnel, creation of additional p::>sts and strP.amlining of 
the recruitment process to achieve these goals. It also recommends for increase in the allocat ion 
for para-medical training institution·s.

74. The Committee notes that a large amount of external aid remains unutilised, and as the 
aid increases, unutilised portion is also increasing. Therefore, it recommends that reasons for 
non-utilisation of funds should be looked into and rectified. It also recommends that before going 
for external assistance the Department should ensure full utilisation of the funds. 
Indian Council of Medical Research 
75. The non-plan Budget Estimate of ICMR, for 1994-95 is Rs. 2238 lakhs, consisting of 
grants in aid of Rs. 1860 lakhs and Mi,scellaneous Receipts of the Council of Rs. 378 lakhs. The 
plan Budget Estimate for 1994-95 is Rs. 28 crores. This amount is to be utilised for intra-mural 
. projects (Rs. 190 lakhs) as well as extra-mural projects (Rs. 880 lakhs). 
76. The Committee recommends that proper system of evaluation of research activities 
should be developed~ to assess the working of the Council. 
Serologist and Chemical Examiner. 
77. In 1993-94, Serologist and Chemical Examiner (SCE) spent Rs. 54 lakhs (Re.vised 
Estimate) and it is allocated the same amount of Rs. 54 lakhs in 1994-95 (Budget Estimate). 
78. On the question of abolition of posts in SCE, the Department informed the Committee 
that the abolition would take place not through retrenchment, but by not filling up the posts as 
and when they fall vacant/placement in the surplus cell. The decision to abolish the posts is on 
account of the fact that most of the States have established their own Forensic Science Institute 
Laboratories. 
79. The Committee feels that the reason given for abolition of technical posts is not 
plausible. As per the report of the Department number of medico-legal cases in forensic serology 
coming form the states has not gone down, showing that the demand for such services continues 
to be there. Also, this is not the only work done by the Department. The Department is the only 
indigenous producer of VDRL antigen and different antisera of internationally recognized 
standard; they are earning revenue and saving foreign exchange. Before the decision is 
implemented the Committee feels that assessment of the work done by the Department must be 
undertaken to see whether a massive curtailment of posts would not hamper this work. 
North Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health and Medical Sciences, Shillong 
80. A sum of Rs. 100.00 lakhs was provided in BE 93-94. During the year 1993-94, the 
institute made a demand for sanction of funds to meet the cost of land acquisition and fencing 
work, to be reimbursed to the Govt. of Meghalaya. Accordingly, a sum of Rs. 110.00 lakhs was 
released to NEIGRI towards the grant-in-aid for the year 1993-94. However, a sum of Rs. 500.00 
lakhs was sought in BE 94-95 as provision to meet the cost of civil works etc. 
81. On the question of low grants, the Department had stated that the preparation of site 
plan, detailed plans and estimates of building, statutory clearance, invitation of tender etc. Take 
substantial ~e ~nd it cannot be said with certainty that substantial expenditure on actual 
construction ca~ achieved during the year 1994-95. Therefore, a small provision is made. 
However, if the progress can be speeded up, the additional requirements can be attended to at 
the R.E stage. 
82. The Committee is not satisfied with the progress of NEIGRI, as it is behind schedule. 
Therefore, the Committee reco'iltmena that, a time schedule should be fixed for the completi o11 
of the work and the Department should make every efforts to complete it on time. 

IV 
MISCELLANEOUS 
I 
83. The Committee is disappointed to know that there is no scheme for starting and running 
mobile dispensaries/clinics, particularly in rural areas. It recommends start of such schemes to 
cover rural and for off-places in hills and tribal areas so that people in these areas could get 
urgently needed medical facilities at their doorstep, instead of running to hospitals in towns and 
cities. 
84. The Committee also feels that D.G.H.S. Scholarship Scheme is providing very small 
amount for scholarships in the context of the present price situation. The Committee recommends 
that stipends/scholarships should be raised keeping in view the present rate of inflation and rising 
costs. 
85. The Committee is happy to note that Health Education has been started in about 50,000 
schools. However , it recommends that this should be made compulsory in schools and necessary 
steps be taken in this direction.

PREFACE
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this
Ninetieth Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants (Demand No.44) of the Department of Family Welfare, 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for the year 2000-2001.
 
2.         The Committee considered the various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of Family
Welfare and also heard the Secretary and other Officials of that Department   on the said Demands for Grants in its
meeting held on 27
th   March, 2000.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 15th  April, 2000.
NEW DELHI;
 April  15, 2000 Chaitra  25,   1922 (Saka)
S.B. CHAVAN
Chairman
Department-related Parliamentary

REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population.  The census of 1991
had indicated the population of India as 846.3 million.  In the decade of 1981-91, 163 million persons were added to the
population of India.  On 11th May, 2000, India is projected to have 1 billion (100 crore) population.  If the present rate
of annual growth of population  of 1.74% continues, India may overtake China in 2045 to become the most populous
country in the world.
1.2      With a view to check the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was taken up with the
introduction of Planning in the country.  The objective of the Family Welfare Programme for the country has been to
stabilise population at a level consistent with the needs of national development.  To achieve this goal the Department
continues to implement the three-pronged strategy of :
(i)         improvement in the health status of women and children;
(ii)        fulfillment of the unmet needs of contraception with a special focus on widening the range of choice
available to the people; and
(iii)       professionalising and broad-basing the Information, Education    and Communication Campaign on
Family Welfare, by not only using the mass media, but also involving the community, NGOs, women’s
organisations in the local specific IEC work at the district, sub-district and village level.

II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee notes that the allocation for the Department has been substantially enhanced from Rs. 2940.60
crores in  BE 1999-2000 to Rs. 3541.47 crores in 2000-2001.  Out of  Rs. 3541.47 crores, Rs. 3520.00 crores form the
Plan component and Rs. 21.47 crores is the non-Plan component.
Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, the Secretary stated that in the Annual Plan proposal for the
year 2000-2001 sent to the Planning Commission, a requirement of Rs. 6056.78 crores was projected.   However, an
outlay of only Rs. 3520 crores  for 2000-2001 has been fixed by the Planning Commission, which is grossly insufficient
and is far below of even the Department’s minimum requirement. 
2.2       The Committee was further informed that the annual plan allocations, though increasing each year, have not
been adequate to meet the existing cost of maintenance of infrastructure.  There has been no increase in the
infrastructure since 1980s.  Besides that, huge arrears on account of committed expenditure of salary etc. have been
building up over the years.  During 1999-2000, additional funds by re-appropriation and supplementary grants of the
order of Rs.400 crore had to be provided to clear the arrears certified on the basis of audit till 1996-97 and 1997-98 in
most of the cases.  The statements of 1998-99 are yet to be received.  Projected requirement for this specific purpose is
Rs.900 crores for 2000-2001.
2.3       Adverse impact of non-settlement of arrear claims of state govts. on the Family Welfare Programme, which is a
100 per cent centrally funded programme has been engaging the attention of the Committee for considerable period. 
Last year, the Committee had recommended that the Planning Commission may be approached for one time grant.   In
response, the Department has informed that a Committee has been set up to solve this problem.   As per the latest
information, recommendations of the aforesaid Committee are yet to be finalised in consultation with the States.   The
Committee feels that setting  up a Committee and then awaiting its recommendations is indirectly an effort to evade the
issue.   Settlement of arrear claims of State Governments  is a long-standing problem which needs a  solution at the
earliest. The Committee reiterates that the Planning Commission should be approached for one-time grant.
2.5       The Committee is not in agreement with the proposal placed by the Department before the XI Finance
Commission in September, 1998 for transfer of liability of maintaining the health infrastructure set up in the States over 
the earlier Plan periods to the State Governments’ budget.  The Committee  fails to understand as to how majority of the
states, being already in a very bad shape so far as mobilisation of resources is concerned, would be able to bear this

8.1       The Information, Education and Communication (IEC) component of  National Family Welfare Programme is
mainly to create an effective communication strategy to inform the masses about the  means and measures of Family
Welfare programme, educate them about the perils of over population and motivate and persuade them to adopt small
family norm, using all possible channels of media.  A multi-pronged strategy to carry out IEC activities is being

units of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.   The activities listed  are –
i)          RCH-IEC activities through Zila Saksharata Samitis
ii)         Mahila Swasthya Sanghs
iii)         Sensitisation of Opinion Leaders Scheme.
iv)        Preparation of IEC Print material
v)         Production of Audio-Visual Software
vi)        Intensification of IEC activities in 135 demographically weak districts etc.
 
Allocation of Rs. 30.00 crores is proposed in BE 2000-2001 for this scheme.   This is in addition to the provision made
in RCH of Rs. 130.00 crores for IEC activities.
8.2       The Committee  finds that a number of activities are being carried out for awareness generation in the masses
about Family Welfare measures. Local agencies are also being actively involved and 135 demographically weak
districts have also been specifically focussed  in this regard. There is no dearth of funds also for this purpose.   The
Committee however, fails to understand that inspite of so many measures, effect of IEC activities is still not reaching the
targetted sector.   The  Committee is of the view  that  in states where level of health and population indicators is much
below the average level, there is a need of having  area specific IEC activities.   In weak pockets and remote,
inaccessible and tribal areas of such states, intensive  campaigns in local dialect and based on local perspectives in
active cooperation with local agencies should be taken.  Mere initiation/launching of such activities would not be
sufficient. Follow up action with modifications and corrective measures as and when necessary would also be required. 
The Committee feels that in states where there is lack of initiative on the part of administration at whatever level,
Department can take steps to associate the local MPs/MLAs in the family welfare measures.   Another effective measure
can be convergence of IEC activities of all the concerned Departments at the Centre.   The Committee feels that in states
also, this kind of exercise would lead to better achievements in family welfare measures.  The Committee recommends
that the Department should take necessary measures in this regard.
