The Committee takes strong exception to the failure of the Department and recommends that 
henceforth budget allocations given to the Department should be fully utilised and appropriated. The 
Committee also notes that the distribution of available funds is also not need-based. While on the one 
hand, funds are being blocked by allocating them to such scheme where appropriation is less and are 
~ing surrendered on the other, some schemes where appropriation is cent percent and more grant is 
required, suffer from lack of resources. Therefore, the Committee recommends that instead of 
surrendering the untllised funds the Deptt. should reallocate them for the needy schemes in time. 
7. The Secretary, Deptt. of Culture, during the course of his oral evideqce tendered before the 
Committee stated that this year the major thrust of the Deptt. are on the Scheme of setting up of 
rural libraries assistance to private museums, documentation and promotion of folk and tribal arts, 
attracting private sector in the field of arts and culture by according them tax exemptions etc., 
encouraging people's initiative and participation in the process of cultural development and organising 
festivals of India abroad. 
8. In order to give fillip to the culture and to restore and refurbish its dying facets, Govt. has 
drafted an Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture. Views/comments received from Members 
of Parliament, eminent person in the field of literature, arts and culture, critics and administrators, 
etc. on the Policy Paper have been discussed in the meetings of the Consultative Committee of the 
Department. Presently, by the Draft Approach Paper on National Policy on Culture is under 
consideration of this Standing Committee and it proposes to submit its report to the Parliament soon. 
REPORT 
9. The Committee, taking note of the revolutionary changes taking place in communications and 
mass media and threat to the Indian culture from outside, emphasises that culture should be seen in 
right perspective and stresses the need of countering cultural invasion from outside. The Secretary, 
during the course of his oral evidence before the Committee, while taking note of the concern of the 
Committee stated that efforts are being made to have parleys with the Secretaries of Ministry of 
Information and Broadcasting and Department of Tourism in order to ensure better coordination 
between them in this regard. The Commmittee urges upon the Government to make all-out efforts to 
contain cultural invasion and to restore our cultural ethos, ideals and values. 
10. The Committee expresses its concern over the neglect of the rural areas due to the 
centralisation of programmes in the urban areas by the Department of Culture. More and more 
programmes of the department are concentrated in the major cities and the rural areas are being 
neglected in the process . It was admitted by the department that in our cultural programmes priority 
is being given to the urban areas due to reason that major cultural institutions arc located in the cities 
and there are better transport and other facilities available in cities for the foreign delegates and 
dignatries visiting these centres. The situation c~n improve only when more and more such facilities 
are provided in the rural areas to facilitate the establishment of cultural centres in villages or semi­
urban areas. 
The Committee was also informed that there is a provision with the Department to extend 
building grant of Rs. 10 lakhs to any organisation for setting up of auditorium at any place including 
the rural areas, if it has a piece of land and is ready to spend matching amount. During the year 1993-
94, fifty nine such institutions/organisations were given building grants to the tunc of Rs. 1.38 crores. 
But the logic of the Department does not appear to be sound enough in the sense that if the semi­
urban, under-developed and rural areas are neglected and rejected on this pretext, how the cultural 
needs of the vast majority of people living in these areas would be met. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the programmes and resources of the Department be considerably decentralised and 

taken to the backward, rural and und erdeve loped urban areas where ancient cultural heritage still 
holds appeal and requires to be galvanised by the centre. 
Archaeological Survey of Indi a (ASI) 
11. Archaeological Survey· of India, set up way back in 1861, is engaged in several activities, 
prominent among which arc conservation and preservation of ancient monuments, exploration and 
excavation of ancient sites, study of inscriptions, research and training in different areas of 
archaeology. etc. Povisions made for this head during the last two years arc given in the table.

12. There has been an increase of Rs. 1.90 crorcs this year, as against the revised estimates of the 
last year, which, in view of price esclation, is negligible. Therefore, the Committee feels that allocation 
for ASI should be adeq uately increase d because a large number of monument s are in dilapidated 
conditions and need urg ent repairs and a great number of monument s and sites remain unidentified 
and unprotected. Out of arou nd 8,000 monuments, about 3,500 are cent rally protecte d. The Committee 
expresses its concern over the fact that even the centrally prot ected monuments do not have proper 
maintenance and foolpr oof protectioq. Cases of larcen y of artefacts, idols etc. have been occuring from 
time to time. During the course of evidence the Committee came to know that the number of staff 
engaged in preservations and maintenance of monuments is so small that the ratio works out to 11h 
staff per monument. Therefore, the Committee recommen ds that staff st rength of the ASI engage d for 
protection and preservation of monuments be adequa tely increased and all other necessary measures be 
taken to check the increasing menace of pilferage. Some amount from the proposed National Cultural 
Fund may also be utilised for the purpo se. 
The Committee is also of the view that, as envisaged in the Eigh th Plan documen t related to the 
Department of Cultur e, volunta ry organ isations should be attracted and encouraged to take up the task 
of preservation and protection of monu.ments. 
13. Even after one hundred and twenty five years of its existence, ASI has not been able to cover 
all parts of the country as far as excavation and exploration of ancient historical sites are concerned. 
Nor it has been able to decipher all the inscriptions. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
network of ASI sho uld ha ve been extensively expanded and enlarged. It should also be well equipped. 
The scheme of village to village survev should also be undertaken and expanded. 
Anthropological Survey of India 
14. Researches in anthropology and allied disciplines and study of customs and traditions are 
some of the major functions undertaken by the Anthropological Survey of India. In the Eighth Five 
Year Plan document it was proposed to salvage and document those specimens of the tribal and folk 
art which face the threat of extinction. It was also proposed to study inherent socio-religious 
disabilities of the tribals, nature of transformation and mobilisation of their special skills in arts, dance 
and music and mastery over musical instruments. But, no follow-up action on these lines is found in 
the Annual Plans of the Department. Therefore, the Committee urges upon the Government to pursue 
vigorously those objectives. Reasons for decrease in the plan allocation of Rs. 140.00 lakhs from Rs. 
150.00 lakhs (Plan Expenditure Revised) of the year 1993;94 arc not tenable . Hence the Committee 
recommends that the provision shou ld be incr eased. Study and research in the field of conservation of 
environment, welfare of women and children, nutritional status of Indian population, etc. have also 
been added to its activ~ties, recently. 

15. In keeping with its aims and objectives, the Anthropological Survey of India took up a 
national project called 'People of Indi a' to analyse Indian population on the basis of bio-cultural 
variables and socio-cultural determinents like marriage, kinship, region, language etc. Out of the 
proposed 43 volumes of the prestigious National Project 'People of India'- three under national and 
two under State ser ies have so far been published. The remaining work should be expedited. 
Museums 
16. Museums play a vital role in the preservation of documents and objects of cultural antiquity. 
In this field, at present, there are ten premier institutions under Govt. of India, including the 
National Reserach Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural property located at Lucknow. Out of the 
ten institutions, three each are located at New Delhi and Calcutta and one each at Lucknow, 
Allahabad, Hyderabad and Bombay, all situated in major cities. To provide representation to cultural 
aspects of other states of Indian Union, a new scheme for Promotion and Strengthening of Regional 
and Local Museums has been mooted and is envisaged to be operationlised during the Eighth Five 
Year Plan period. Govt. is also providing assistance for opening private museums. Govt. proposes to 
intensify this scheme through a Committee which will look after them. But for this well conceived 
scheme a meagre amount of Rs. 10 lakhs has been provided for the year 1994-95. There has been no 
change in the allocations for the last three years. In such a situation the Committee wonders how the 
scheme contemplated for the Eighth Plan could be implemented within the time-frame with this 
insignificant budget allocation. As the Eighth Five Year Plan is left with only two financial years, the 
Committee strongly recommends enhancement of financial allocation to speed up the implementation of 
the scheme. 
National Council of Science Museums (NCSM), Calcutta 
17. It is an autonomous organisation engaged primarily in the task of popularising science and 
technology among the students in particular and the mas~es in general through a variety of interactive 
and innovative programmes and activities like science exhibitions, school centres, portable 
planetarium and national science seminars etc. and setting up of a Science City in Calcutta, is the 
highlight of the activities of the National Council of Science Museums. In the Eighth Plan document it 
was proposed to create 1000 science centres to reach the common man, five new regional centres, 20 
district science centres and 203 school science centres in the under privileged rural schools, 20 new 
mobile science exhibition buses, a science train, etc. The total out lay for the 8th Plan period of Rs. 
4500.00 lakhs for these ambitious proposals is too littfe. Slight increase in the allocation for this year, 
as against the last year's Budget Estimates, of around Rs. 161 lakhs and of Rs. 111 lakhs in Revised 
Estimates may not be said to be adequate in view of the rising prices. The implementation of the 
scheme has made very little progress and should be speeded up. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that additional grant be given for this scheme to increase scientific temper among the people. 
National Museum, New Delhi 
18. During 1994-95, the National Museum, New Delhi, proposes to organise exhibitions of 
Persian manuscripts in Teheran, an exhibition of Indian Art at Singapore and of miniature paintings 
at Tashkent. Apart from this, it is also proposed to introduce such new programmes as developing 
software for physically handicapped persons, lending consultancy services to the State and other 
museums, introduction of disc system for documentation of its huge collection, microfilming of 
manuscripts and computerisation of its library, etc. 
19. The provisions made for this year, as against last year, remain more or less the same. Plan 
provision has fallen from Rs. 200.00 lakhs to Rs. 190.00 lakhs and Non-Plan provisions has increased 
by only Rs. 7 lakhs in comparison to the Revised Estimates of the last year. Thus, there has been a 
decrease of Rs. 3 lakhs this year. The Committee is surprised to know as to how with this small 
allocation. It would be possible to achieve the targets set for this year. The Committee therefore, 
recomm ends that the allocation for National Museum be increased appropriately. 
Indian Museum, Calcutta 
20. The total provisions made this year for Indian Museum, Calcutta, arc less by 1.45 lakhs as 
agianst the Revised Estimates (both Plan and Non-Plan) of the last year. In this situation, apart from 

carrying out on-going functions the proposal to construct a new building for display of valuable 
artefacts may find itself in rough weather. It was also envisaged in the Eighth Plan document to set 
up new galler ies on textiles, folk arts, gems and jewelleries. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that sufficient grant should be provided to the Museum so that these schemes are completed. 
Institutes and Organisations of Tibetan and Buddhist studies 
21. There are. four autonomous institutes, namely, the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan 
Studies, VaranasC the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, Leh; the Sikkim Research Institute of 
Tibetology and the Library of Tibetan Works & Archives, Dharamsala, which are engaged in 
preservation and propagations of Tibetan culture and tradition, restoration of ancient Indian literature 
preserved in Tibetan language, imparting higher education in Buddhist philosophy and literature, etc. 
The Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Varanasi, enjoys the status of a 'Deemed 
University'. The Committee while expressing its satisfaction over the encouragement given to these 
institutes feels that they should be allowed to pursue their academic interest without any extraneous 
influences. 
22. The Committee feels that due attention is not being paid in these institutes to promotion and 
development of Pali, one of ancient language of India and, therefore, recommends suitable steps in this 
regard. 
Libraries 
23. The Committee feels that the reading habi!s of the general masses are on the wane, partly 
owing to revolutionary changes in electronic media, partly due to the shift in social values titled more 
to materialism, and partly because of high prices of books. In this situation, libraries have to be 
opened on a large scale with even distribution in urban and rural areas. 
24. There arc six major libraries under the Department of Culture. The total budgetary provision 
(lOth Plan and Non -Plan) for the year 1994-95 under this .head is Rs. 13.36 crores a total increase of 
Rs. 2.38 crores in comparison to the Revised Estimates (Both Plan & Non Plan) of the last year. In 
view of the rising prices of books and other allied items, maintenance cost of buildings etc. this 
increase of Rs. 2.38 crores in not enough. 
25. The tendency of centralisation is perceptible in the scheme of libraries also. The Committee 
feels that suitable scheme be devised to spread the network of libraries to District Headquarters and 
small towns. There is also a need to Interlink the major libraries with computer network. It will 
facilitate the research scholars and other persons desiring any information sitting in one library to 
gather additional information from all the connected libraries. 
26. The Delhi Public Library, established in 1951 with the assistance of UNESCO to provide free 
library service to the citizens of Delhi , has also now developed into a Metropolitan Public Library. A 
major portion of its activities is located in the affluent localities of Delhi and the rural and 
underdeveloped areas are being neglected . Therefore, -the Committee, recommends that Govt. should 
take adequate steps to spread it~ network of libraries and reading rooms in the slum and 
underdeveloped ar~as of the National Capital. More and more mobile library vans should also be made 
available. In view of all these, the Committee recommends that the budget allocation for Delhi Public 
Library be enhanced appropriately. 
Raja Ram Mohan Roy Library Foundation, Calcutta 
27. Established in 1972, it is an autonomous organisation fully funded by the Deptt: of Culture. 
The · main aim of the library is to support and promote library services in the country. 
28. Increase in its budget provision this year is welcome. However, some Irregularities in the 
fuQctioning of the lib_rary have come to the notice of the Committee. Guidelines on book purchasing are 
not being adhered to and books are allegedly being purchased at higher r~tes than the market rates. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that these matters be looked Into. 

Rural Library Scheme 
29. The Committee is happy to note that the Department of Culture has decided to focus its 
attention on the rural populace by deciding to set up rural libraries in villages. A teacher from the 
local school is proposed to be made in-charge of the library which will, in the incipient,have around 
300 books. The Committee "is of the view that these libraries should also ~ave such books which may be 
used by neo-literates in the post-literacy stage. It is, undoubtedly a well conceived scheme and generous 
funds should be provided for it. The Committee recommends that this scheme be made a pilot project 
so that about five and half lakh villages could be covered within a stipulated time-frame. The 
Committee also recommends that separate allocation be made for individual states. In consultation with 
the Ministry of Rural Development, the assistance of Panchayats may be sought to ensure speedy and 
effective implementation of this scheme. The Committee also recommends that the modalities for the 
implementation of this scheme be worked out as early as possible so that the scheme implemented in 
right earnest. 
Akademies and National School of Drama 
I. Sahitya Akademi 
30. The Sahitya Akademi was inaugurated in 1954 and registered as an autonomous society in 
1956 with the objective of working actively for development of literature and to foster and coordinate 
literary activities in all the Indian languages and to promote through them the cultural unity of the· 
country. To achieve these objectives, the Akademi is running programmes such as granting literary 
awards, translation and publication of books in different languages, etc. The Akademi also provides 
assistance to State Akademies. 
31. The Committee is not happy with the budgetary allocation made for the Akademi this year, 
which is only Rs. 57 lakhs more than the Revised Estimates of the last year :-

32. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that a premier literary institution like the 
Sahitya Akademi is made ·to curtail its activities due to lack of funds. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends strongly that more resources be made available to the Sahitya Akademi and the arrear 
payments, if any, should also be released forthwith. The Akademi should bestow more attention on the 
development of regional languages, in addition to Hindi. 
II. Sangeet Natak Akademi 
33. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, which come into being in 1953, is a national institution engaged 
in promotion and preservation of performing arts, extending financial assistance to cultural institution 
for training and production, undertaking inter-state cultural exchange programmes etc. Although 
there is an increase of around Rs. 27 lakhs this year, as compared to the last year's Revised Estimates 
(both Plan and Non-Plan) this is negligible in view of the price escalation. The Committee is of the 
view that the outlay for the Akademi may be appropriately increased. 
III. Lalit Kala Akademi 
34. The Lalit Kala Akademi an apex institution in the field of art was established in 1954 for the 
promotion and development of paintings, graphics, sculpture, ceramics, etc. in the country. The major 
activities of the Akademi are to organise exhibitions (in and outside the country), artists' camps, 
bringing out art publications, and implementing cultural exchange programmes. 
35. The allocation for the Akademi this year has come down from Rs. 2.85 crores (Revised 
estimates) of the year 1993-94 to Rs. 2.40 crores. The Committee urges upon the Govt. to increase the 
allocation appropriately. 

National School of Drama 
36. The National School of Drama, established in 1959, is a premier institution devoted to 
imparting training in the field of theatre and to propagate dramatics in the country. Increase in this 
year's budgetary provisions for the institution from Rs. 266.65 lakhs to Rs. 285.00 lakhs is welcome. 
The National School of Drama proposes to set up regional centres, which is a welcome step, and the 
Committee desires that these regional centres should enjoy due autonomy in their functioning and not 
made mere branches of the National School of Drama, New Delhi. 
Promotion of Art & Culture 
37. A number of organisations and institutions are active in promoting and disseminating 
different types of art and cultural activities in various regions and zones of the country. A brief sketch 
of their activities, objectives vis-a-vis provisions thereof is given below:-
/. Centre for Cultural Resources & Training 
38. The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, set up in 1979 with its headquarter in New 
Delhi, is doing a commendable job in the propagation of culture, especially among college and school 
students. One of the major activities of the Centre is to train inservice school teachers in the area of 
linkage between education and culture and to provide a cultural component in the curricula. The 
Centre also prepares audio-visuals and printed materials to be used in schools for cultural education. 
The centre also took over the scheme 'Cultural Talent Search Scholarship' from the Deptt. of Culture 
in 1982 under which 300 children in the age group of 10-14 years are awarded scholarships each year 
in various fields. 
39. The Centre has been entrusted with the task of interlinking culture with education, mass 
media and the scheme of the Deptt., bearing an identical nomenclature, has since been merged with 
the centre's scheme. 
40. The Committee is of the view that it is not practically feasible to cover whole country by the 
one and only Centre in New Delhi and hence feels the need to decentralise the activities of the Centre 
by opening sub-centres in various zones and regions. 
41. The provisions made for the Centre are not in consonance with the multifarious activities of the 
Centre. A comparative analysis of the allocation suggests that there has been a meagre increase of 
Rs. 20 lakhs in Plan and 0.65 lakhs in Non-Plan expenditure, as against the revised estimates of the last 
year. Since this is the only institution which is taking culture down to the general masses, students and 
teachers, the Committee recommends that more .resources should be allocated to the Centre, 
particularly keeping in view the Committee's recommendation for opening sub-Centres at various 
places. 
Zonal Cultural Centres 
42. At present, there are seven Zonal Cultural Centres which cover the entire country. The main 
functions of the Zonal Cultural Centres are to provide facilities for the creative development in the 
entire spectrum of culture, particularly in that of folk and tribal art. These centres are also 
implementing National Cultural Exchange Programmes, Republic Day folk dance festival and setting 
up Shilpgrams etc. For the year 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 200 lakhs has been earmarked for zonal cultural 
centres. During the year 1992-93 there was an under-utilisation of the approved outlay to the tune of 
about Rs. 175 lakhs, mainly because of the delay in allotment of land by Sta~ Government for setting 
up of Shilpgrams. The Committee, however, feels that such delays should be avoided so that funds are 
utilised in time. The Committee recommends that speedy progress be made in setting up Shilpgrams at 
the remaining six zonal cultural centres, particularly the one being set up at Thanjavur. The 
Committee also feels that centrewise allocation should also be reflected in the documents of the 
Department. 
43. Documentation and propagation of folk art constitute one of the main functions of Zonal 
Cultural Centres and as stated by the Secretary, Department of Culture, it is also one of the major 
thrust areas during this year. But the work being done in this regard cannot be said to be satisfactory. 
There is no indication as to how much money each Zonal Cultur al Centre spends on the propagation of 
the Jjving folk art forms at the grassroot level in villages where they are actually performed. Therefore, 

~he Committee is of the view that due emphasis of the Zonal .Cultural Centres should be on folk arts 
and necessary financial assistance should also be provided for the same. 
44. The Committee is constrained to note that the hopes generated at the time of establishment of 
Zonal Cultural Centres have not been fulfilled and realised. Because these centres are not pursuing the 
programmes and schemes fop which they were set up, therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
time has come for a high-powered Review Committee to be constituted to look into the working of the 
Zonal Cultural Centres. 
Dissemination of Tribal Folk Art & Culture 
45. Under this scheme, financial support is given to voluntary cultural organisations, institutions 
and individuals-both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small duration projects of around one year 
for preservation and development of tribal folk art and culture, conduct of tribal cultural activities, 
including their festivals and festivities. This year, there has been an increase of Rs. 10 lakhs for this 
scheme. But the Committee is not happy with the working of the voluntary organisations/institutions 
in this field because it is found that the assistance does not percolate down to the folk artistes, 
although the Secretary, Department of Culture, has submitted before the Committee that Gqvern­
ment is taking necessary steps to ensure that the artistes get the desired benefit. The Committee 
recommends the pro_gressive establishment of a network of organisations to ensure that folk artistes in 
villages are enabled to derive full advantage of the scheme meant for them. Assistance should also be 
given for opening performance centres or auditoria at the village and block level so that artistes could 
perform and interact with each other to improve their particular art forms. 
Multipurpo se cultural complexes at States & National Cultural Complex in Delhi 
46. Under this scheme, financial assistance is proposed to be extended to autonomous bodies for 
settmg up art complexes in the States to improve the quality of life among youth and students and to 
sensitize them to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society and also to expose them to the 
finest forms of creative expressions. 
47. The Committee is not happy with the progress made in the scheme and expresses its serious 
concern over the fact that almost two financial years have elapsed and the projects have not been 
finalised yet. The Committee is also not happy with the idea of creating more and more cultural 
infrastructure in big cities and towns at the cost of rural areas. However, the Committee is satisfied to 
note that multi-purpose complexes, are being set up in smaller towns, rural and backward areas and 
recommends that other schemes being formulated by the Deptt. should also be located in sucn art!aS. 
The Committee also recommends that the National Cultural Complex (Parisar), proposed to be set up 
in Delhi, be established in the trans-Yamuna or outer Delhi areas. 
48. The Committee is also of the view that instead of concentrating only on huge cultural 
complexes, Govt. should set up smaller units where the deprived, under privileged and unprivileged 
may have access to all forms of culture as well as to practice and promote their arts. The Committee 
also holds that the Department may construct multi-purpose stadia in smaller towns and cities which 
could be utilised for sports during the day and for cultural purposes in the evening and night. 
Asia'tic Society, Calcutta 
49. The Asiatic Society, Calcutta, is an institution of national importance involved mainly in 
oriental studies and research, research in humanities and science, publication of periodicals, books 
and other literature. At present, there are around 12 senior fellows and 30 junior research scholars 
attached to the Society. 
50. The Committee is surprised to note that a drastic cut has been resorted to in this year's budget 
allocation for the society. The plan provision has been reduced from Rs. 341.00 lakhs (Revised 
Estimates) during the year 1993-94 to Rs. 200.00 lakhs for the year 1994-95. The provision is 
understood to have been reduced in view of the opening of the Asiatic Society, Bombay. The Committee 
desires that the activities of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta should not suffer pending opening of Asiatic 
Society, Bombay. 

51. No financial assistance has been provided to the Asiatic Society, Bombay, during the Eighth 
Five Year plan. The reason behind this is stated to be that the Planning Commission has earmarked a 
provision of Rs. 200.00 lakhs to be given to the Society as corpus fund. But this fund also has not 
reached the Society so far as it is pending approval from the Ministry of Finance. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that government shotJd expedite the matter and release the amount without 
any further delay. 
Assistance to Cultural Organisations 
52. For promotion and dissemination of Cultur¢ the Department extends financial assistance to 
voluntary organisations under various schemes such as Scheme for Building grants to voluntary 
organisations, Scheme for financial Assistance to Dance, Drama and Theatre Ensembles, Financial 
Assistance for Research Support to voluntary organisations· engaged in Cultural Activities, Grants to 
Institutions I Individuals engaged in literary Activities. 
There' has been only marginal increase in allocations for these schemes and the Committee 
recommends that they should be enhanced adequately. 
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Centre for Asian Studies 
53. This centre, proposed to be set up in the wake of the centenary celebrations of Maulana Abul 
Kalam Azad, is still not complete. The Committee is surprised to note that this ·year budget provision 
for the Centre has been reduced by Rs. 5 lakhs, for the reasons not acceptable to the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that tLere should be no further delay in the setting up of this Centre. 
Indira Gandhi National Centn: for Arts 
54. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts was established in 1985 as an autonomous 
Trust. The Government had contributed to its Corpus Fund Rs. 46.75 crores between 1987-88 and 
1993-94. The balance of Rs. 3.25 crores of the Committed amount has been provided in this year's 
Budget. For the building fund, the Government has so far allocated Rs. 32.35 crores and in this year 
Rs. 16.75 crores have been provided. The Committee regrets to note that even after eight years or 
establishment of the Centre, its main projects including the building are yet to be completed, though 
requisite allocations are being made by the Government. The Committee has been told that work on 
the construction of the building has started in the real sense only in March, 1994. The other activities 
of the Centre like microfilming of unpublished manuscripts and creation and updating of data base are, 
however, in progress. The Committee feels that ~teps should be taken to utilise the funds fully and 
speedily so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
Memorials and Centenaries 
55. The Department of Culture proposes to commemorate this year the 125th birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi through Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti. But the allocation earmarked for the 
purpose is most inadequate. Also, in 'this year, the country will observe the 75th Anniversary of the 
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre but no budgetary provision has been made for this purpose. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the budget provision for celebration of the 12Sth birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi be increased and adequate funds be allocated for the observance of the 7S.th 
Anniversary of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.

I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population.  The census of 1991
had indicated the population of India as 846.3 million.  In the decade of 1981-91, 163 million persons were added to the
population of India.  On 11 th May, 2000, the population of India has already crossed 1 billion mark.   If the present rate
of annual growth of population  of 1.74% continues, India may overtake China in 2045 to become the most populous
country in the world.
1.2      With a view to check  the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was taken up with the
introduction of Planning in the country.  The objective of the Family Welfare Programme for the country has been to
stabilise population at a level consistent with the needs of national development.  To achieve this goal the Department
continues to implement the three-pronged strategy of :
(i)         improvement in the health status of women and children;
(ii)        fulfillment of the unmet needs of contraception with a special focus on widening the range of choice
available to the people; and
(iii)       professionalising and broad-basing the Information, Education     and Communication Campaign (IEC)
on Family Welfare, by not only using the mass media, but also involving the community, NGOs,
women’s organisations in the local specific IEC work at the district, sub-district and village level.

1.6.      The Committee notes that though there is a continuous decline in various demographic indicators over the years,
they are still very high in comparison to other developing countries like Sri Lanka, Indonesia, China and Cuba.  The
Committee, therefore, feels that rural and inaccessible areas are still outside the reach of Family Welfare Programme 
and unless these  areas are covered by the various Family Welfare Programmes, there cannot be any significant decline
in the abovementioned indicators and the growth of population will remain unabated.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee notes that the allocation for the Department has been reduced from Rs. 3541.47 crores in  BE
2000-2001 to Rs. 3221.37 crores at the RE stage.  However, a provision of Rs. 4232.28 crores has been made in BE
2001-2002 which represents an increase of Rs. 690.81 crores over the previous year.  
2.2       Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, it has been stated that in the Annual Plan proposal for
the year 2001-2002 sent to the Planning Commission, a requirement of Rs. 5922.72 crores was projected.   However, an
allocation of only Rs. 4210 crores  for 2001-2002 has been made by the Planning Commission.  As a result of the cut in
the Plan proposal, there is likely to be an accumulation of arrears and inadequate funding on infrastructure side of
various programmes and activities like RCH Programme, contraceptive supplies and maintenance of expenditure on
Rural Family Welfare Centres, etc.  
2.3       The Department has further informed that in the case of Rural Family Welfare Centres  the outlay proposed by it
was Rs. 700.00 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 430.00 crores.  In the case of Sub-Centres the outlay proposed
was Rs. 1237.00 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 675.00 crores.  In the case of maintenance of Urban Family
Welfare Centres, outlay proposed was Rs. 53.33 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 35.00 crores. 
2.4       The Committee notes that the Eleventh Finance Commission agreed with the views of the Committee that the
transfer of cost of maintenance of infrastructure under Family Welfare Programme to the States would impose
enormous liability on them and weaken their resources and also there is no guarantee that the transferred funds would be
used for Family Welfare Programme.   The Committee, therefore, reiterates  its earlier recommendation that status quo
in this regard should be maintained.

3.7.      The Committee was informed that a Consultative Committee was set up by the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare on the recommendation of the Planning Commission to examine the revision of Schemes on maintenance of
infrastructure and manpower.  Among other recommendations, one pertained to the proposal of Government of India
accepting the responsibility of funding all the existing sub-centres in exchange for the States accepting the financial
liability for supporting the Rural Family Welfare  Centres.  It was observed that out of the existing 1,37,271 sub-centres,
only 97,757 were being funded by the Central Government and the rest were being funded by the respective State
Govts. from their own resources. The Consultative Committee reasoned that the additional liability of the Central
Government in accepting the recurring expenditure of the remaining Sub-Centres would be Rs. 421 crore whereas it was
already spending Rs. 439 crore in maintenance of the RFWCs. Therefore, the Consultative Committee  recommended a
swap of these responsibilities between the Central Government and  the States.  The Committee feels that the issue 
needs to be discussed with the State Governments/UT Administrations before any decision is taken in this regard for
effective implementation of the scheme.

IV.       URBAN FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
4.1       Urban Family Welfare Centres are on the ground since 1950s to provide Family Welfare Services in the urban
areas. There are three types of Urban Family Welfare Centres viz. Type I, Type II and Type III, depending upon the
staff sanctioned and the population covered by them. In all, there are 1083 Urban Family Welfare Centres functioning in
the country.
4.2       The total budget allocation at all India level including allocation for NE States is  Rs. 60.00 crores and Rs. 75.00

4.3.      In order to improve outreach service delivery system in Urban Slums, Urban Revamping Scheme was
introduced, under which 871 Health Posts and 10 City Family Welfare Bureaux have been sanctioned so far.  The
Committee has been informed that the proposal of Department to rationalize the structure of Urban Family Welfare
Centres by reducing the number of levels was considered by Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC). However, owing
to resources constraints the EFC advised the Department not to pursue it.  These centres will be taken up for
reorganization as and when the cities are taken up under Urban  RCH Programme separately.   The Committee feels that
for improving outreach service delivery system in urban slums, the revamping of the  scheme should be undertaken in
right-earnest so that the structure of the Urban Family Welfare Centres is rationalized.  Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the reorgnisation of the Urban Family Welfare Centres should be taken separately and not under 
Urban RCH Programme.
V.           REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH  PROGRAMME (RCH)
5.1.         The concept of RCH Programme is to provide need-based, client-oriented, demand-driven, high quality and
integrated RCH services to the beneficiaries. The RCH programme is a composite programme incorporating the inputs
of the Government of India as well as funding support from external donor agencies including the  World Bank and the
European Commission. 
5.2.         The Programme aims at meeting the unmet needs of Family Welfare Programme by improving health status of
women and children, especially the poor and underserved, by reducing infant, child and maternal mortality and
morbidity through:-
 
(a)
          Sustaining and strengthening the ongoing Child Survival and Safe Motherhood Programme to ensure the
essential services as per package of services;
(b)         Improving the performance of the Family Welfare System in implementing policy change;
(c)          Strengthening  the quality and effectiveness of the services under essential package of Reproductive and
Child Health Services;
(d)         Improving project implementation through the application of performance based criteria for continued
funding; and
(e)          implementing and managing project activities by following certain fixed benchmarks.
5.3.         Allocation of Rs.951.00 crores was made in BE 2000-2001 which was reduced to Rs.801.00 crores at the RE
stage. Allocation in BE 2001-2002 has been substantially enhanced to Rs.1126.95 crores. On being asked as to how the
additional allocation will be utilized, the Department informed that the additional allocation is because of release of
funds direct to SCOVA Committees formed in the States to avoid delay while routing funds through the State Finance
Departments. The increase is proposed to be utilized in the following components.
(A)
        RCH Other interventions-
(i)                  RCH Camps – Presently  undertaken in 102 districts;  proposed to be conducted in  all the
category C districts.
(ii)                Dais Training
(iii)               Out-reach Services – Presently being implemented in 50 districts, proposed to be extended to
another 100 districts covering thereby 150 districts in all.
(iv)              Hepatitis-B Project – A new Pilot Project on Hepatitis B at a cost of Rs.9.27 crores proposed to
be taken up during 2001-2002.
(v)                Financial Envelope – Currently, provided to 4 States only, proposed to extend it to 2 more
States during the next year.

5.4.         Reproductive and Child Health Programme is the flagship programme of the Department on which around
25% percent of the allocation is spent. The Committee notes that the restructuring of the World Bank aided component
of the Programme was undertaken during October-November, 2000 in order to further tailor it  to the needs and capacity
of the States.  Also, focused attention was paid on initiatives of Dais’ Training, Border District Charter Project, RCH
Camps and RCH out-reach services.
5.5.         The Department has informed that in order to remove the difficulties in transmitting RCH funds to the
implementing agencies in the States, the mechanism of fund flow through specifically created society known as SCOVA
was adopted by all the States and UTs except Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The Committee notes that the
SCOVA societies have been vested with decision making powers for implementation of the RCH Programme in the
State and for this purpose, the Society is headed by Chief Secretary of the State/UT and has representatives from
Departments of Finance, Planning etc.  The Committee, is of the view that the Chief Secretaries of the States due to
their innumerable other engagements may not be able to devote the kind of attention these societies deserve for effective
implementation of RCH Programmes in the States. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department may
examine whether these Societies could be headed by the Secretary,  Department of Family Welfare of the respective
States.
5.6.         The Committee observes that situation in the States of Assam, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Nagaland, Orissa,
Rajasthan and U.P. continues to be a cause of concern as more than 75% deliveries  are still conducted at home and as a
consequence MMR in these States is high. The Committees notes that following initiatives have been taken to
encourage institution delivery:-
               -        Scheme of Referral Transport to Pregnant women belonging to Indigent Families through Panchayats.
               -        Provision of additional honorarium to the staff to encourage round the clock delivery  System of PHCs
and CHCs.
               The Committee is, however, constrained to observe that although Rs.326.30 lakhs have been released to 12
States under the first initiative, feedback from the States suggests that funds are not being utilised by Panchayats.
Similarly, against a release of Rs.959.15 lakhs to States till now under the second initiative, an expenditure of only
Rs.33.80 lakhs has been reported. The Committee feels that proper awareness seems to be lacking at the level of
Panchayats and PHC/CHC functionaries about such initiatives. Wide publicity, therefore, needs to be given to make
optimum use of such initiatives.
5.7.         The Department has also informed that the Government of India and World Bank has reviewed the programme
in the year 2000 and based on the performance and capacity to implement and manage project activities, certain
benchmarks were fixed and are being followed vigorously. The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department in
overcoming the deficiencies noticed in the RCH Programme. The Committee, however,  notes that  no surveys which
track the movement of access and reach of health services are conducted on a year to year basis. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that such surveys should be made a regular phenomenon for effective implementation of the
programme.

VIII.     COMPENSATION      
8.1.     Allocation under the head ‘Compensation’ is meant to compensate acceptors of terminal methods (sterilization)
of Family Planning against loss of wages and to meet the costs of diet, dressing, drugs, transport etc.   The States/UTs
have the flexibility to apportion the amount of compensation among various heads of expenses subject to guidelines
given by  Government of India.   An allocation of Rs. 120.00 crores was made in BE 2000-2001 which has been
increased to Rs. 125.00 crore in BE 2001-2002. 
8.2      The proposal to revise norms of compensation was under consideration of the Department of Family Welfare
since 1996.  The Committee has been informed that the reason for delay in the matter is late receipt of the proposal to
revise norms of compensation from States/UTs.  The CCEA in its meeting held on 7
th February, 2001 approved the
proposal for increasing the amount of compensation for loss of wages for undergoing Tubectomy from Rs. 200 to Rs.
300 from Rs. 180 to Rs. 200 for vasectomy and from Rs 16 to Rs. 20 for IUD insertion. The same is  applicable from
1.4.2001.  The Committee notes that though there is an increase in the amount of Compensation the increase is not
sufficient.   The increase should be adequate enough to inspire people to accept family planning methods/norms.

X            POST PARTUM PROGRAMME
10.1.    Post Partum Programme is a maternity centered hospital based approach to Family Welfare Programme covering
550 Post Partum Centres at district level and 1012 Post Partum Centres at sub-district level hospitals. The objective of
the programme is to provide antenatal, natal and post-natal services to expectant mothers and also to provide Family
Planning Services, besides diagnosing early cases of cervical cancer.  An allocation of Rs.111.00 crores was made for
Post Partum Programme in BE 2000-2001 which has been increased to Rs.135.00 crores in BE 2001-2002.
10.2.       To a query as to  whether any review of the programme has been undertaken during the last three years, the
Department has replied that besides monitoring of the programme, no study has been done during the last three years.
However, an evaluation of the programme is under consideration during 2001-2002. The Committee is of the opinion

101st Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/101streport.htm[01-07-2016 15:13:15]
that  evaluation of any programme is the natural corollary of effective monitoring of that programme.   The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department should undertake evaluation of the Scheme during 2001-2002 and take
necessary remedial measures, if any, for effective implementation of the Scheme.
XI        DISTRIBUTION OF CONTRACEPTIVES
11.1.    An allocation of Rs. 108.71 crores was made under the head ‘Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptives’
in BE in 2000-01 which was reduced to Rs. 95.71 crores at the RE stage.  However, allocation in BE 2001-2002 has
been increased to Rs. 117.00 crores.  Explaining the reasons for this variation, the Department has informed that
reduction at RE 2000-2001 was mainly due to unexpected less expenditure in the procurement of Copper T, less
procurement of  Mala N on account of less demand from the States, and limited number of Laparoscopes procured. 
However, allocation in BE 2001-2002 has been increased mainly due to more demand of free supply of Nirodh from the
State Governments. The increase in allocation in 2001-2002 is also due to the fact that cost of raw material has been
added in the proposed BE as UNFPA  has discontinued the supply of  raw material as commodity assistance for
manufacturing  of Oral Contraceptive pills.
11.2.   The Committee has been informed that according to the studies conducted by the International Institute of
Population Studies, Mumbai in Haryana, Maharashtra and UP revealed that around sixty percent of condoms under free
distribution system was unused and wasted.  Hence, in order to minimize wastage and promote distribution of
comdoms, a scheme of service charge of ten paise per condom, to be retained by the health worker, was introduced
during 1997-98.  However, subsequent survey revealed that this new incentive did not reach most of the doctors and
health workers in PHC/ Sub Centres.
11.3.    The Committee feels that the scheme of service charge of ten paise per condom to be retained by the health
worker is  good except for the fact that ten paise per condom is too meagre an amount to attract the enthusiasm of the
health workers.  The Committee is also disturbed to know that this new scheme did not reach most of the doctors and
health workers in the sub centres.  This means that the funds  earmarked for the purpose are being squandered by the
middlemen instead of reaching the health workers.  The Committee views this as a serious lapse in monitoring the
utilization of funds by the Department and recommends that  corrective measures may be taken in this regard.
XII.         STERILISATION BEDS
12.1.       Under this Scheme, maintenance grant @ Rs.4500/- per annum is paid to each institution subject to a condition
that a minimum of 75/60 tubectomics per bed per annum are achieved by the Government/Voluntary Agencies
respectively. At present 3115 beds are functioning which is 58 below the last year’s figure of 3173.
12.2.       The Committee notes that the allocation under ‘Sterilisation Beds’ for 2000-2001 was Rs.1.70 crores.   The
Department has informed that a proposal to enhance the maintenance grant to Rs.6500 has not been implemented, so, far
and once they are revised the requirement shall be around Rs.2.02 crores.  The Committee  observes that since 1998-99
same level of allocation is being made under this scheme which indicates that there has been no increase in the numbers
of Sterlisation Beds during this period.   What is more disturbing that during 2001-2002, a reduced provision of Rs. 1.35
crores is proposed.
12.3.
              The Committee has been given to understand that after vigorously pursuing with the State Governments  for
augmentation of Sterlisation Beds, proposals from 16 NGOs for 54 Beds have been received from Tamil Nadu, West
Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Kerala in 2000-2001 which  have been sanctioned by the
Department.
12.4.              The Committee recommends that the Department should take necessary steps to  increase the number of
sterlization beds, particularly in the more populated states of the country.   The Committee also recommends that the
proposal of revision of maintenance grant from Rs. 4500/- per bed per annum for   Rs.6500/-  per bed annum which is
under consideration for long may be expedited.
XIII.        NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY
13.1.       The Committee notes that after many years of deliberation and consultation, the National Population Policy,
was presented to Parliament last year.  The Committee has been informed that the immediate objective of the National
Population Policy is to address the unmet needs of contraception, health infrastructure, health personnel and to provide
integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care.  The medium term objective is to bring the total
fertility rates to replacement level by 2010 through vigorous implementation of intersectoral operational strategies. The
long term objective is to achieve a stable population by 2045, at a level consistent with the requirement of sustainable
economic growth, social development and environmental protection.

13.2.       The Committee has been given to understand that a number of new structures, i.e. National Commission on
Population, State/UT Commissions on Population, Coordination Cell within the Planning Commission and a
Technology Mission are proposed.  The Committee has been informed that the First meeting of the National
Commission of Population was held  on 22
nd July, 2000 under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister where the following
policy  decisions were taken:
1.                   Setting up a National Population Stabilisation Fund with seed money of Rs.100 crores to support project
contributing to population stabilization. It is expected that trade, industry, corporate sector as also individuals
will contribute to this fund.
2.                   Setting up an Empowered Action Group presided by Minister of Health & Family Welfare     for area
specific programmes with special emphasis on States that have been lagging behind  in containing population
growth.
3.
                  The National Commission on Population decided to constitute Working Groups on the following
subjects:-
                       -           Unmet needs for contraception, material and child health.
-           Unmet needs of other social sectors like health, women’s development, nutrition, water supply and
sanitation.
           -           Primary and Secondary Education in relation to population stablization.
-           Registration of births, deaths and marriages.
           -           Media for IEC and motivation.
-           Mainstreaming of Indian System of Medicines and Homoeopathy.
            -         Adolescents
            -         Mechanism for monitoring by the Commission.
            -         Involvement of civil society, including industry, labour and NGOs.
13.3.       The Committee feels that there should be a consensus at the political level as to how to implement the
population policy. The political parties have to consciously take a decision in this regard and rise above their electoral
considerations. The Committee has also noted  that where there is  higher literacy particularly amongst women, the rate
of growth of population is on the decline. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should focus
more and more on education of women in its IEC activities.
XIV        TRAINING, RESEARCH AND EVALUATION
14.1.       A provision of Rs.93.35 cores in BE 2000-2001 for ‘Training, Research and Evaluation’ was reduced to
Rs.90.25 crores at the RE stage.   BE for 2001-2002 has been increased to Rs.122.61 crores.  To a query as to in what
manner the additional fund is proposed to be utilized, the Department has replied that the additional funds are provided
mainly for staff salaries, contingencies, POL, rent for training schools/hostel buildings and training of medical and para-
medical staff and enhancing research activities.
14.2.       The Committee has been given to understand that based on 1998-99 survey, there are 142 districts in the
country where the cases of safe delivery is below 30%. Most of these districts are in U.P., Bihar, M.P., Rajasthan and
Orissa. The Department also informed that in order to facilitate safe delivery,  it has been decided to give theoretical and
practical training to one Dai in each revenue village. These Dais are to be given medical kits and training so that they
use these kits effectively. They are also to be taught as to how to identify difficult delivery cases so that such difficult
cases are referred to the ANMs or Lady Health Visitors.
14.3.       The Committee is deeply distressed to know that the percentage of safe delivery in some States is below 30%.
The Committee though appreciates the efforts made by the Department to train Dais in this regard but feels that the
gravity of the problem is too big to be tackled by a few trained Dais.   The Department would have to give a serious
thought to this situation, particularly with reference to comparatively vulnerable States where the position of safe
delivery is really grim.

I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H)  was set up by the Government of
India as an independent Department in March, 1995 under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.  The main
objective of the Department is to develop and promote Indian Systems of medicine, namely, Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani,
Homoeopathy, Yoga and Naturopathy in an organized and scientific manner in the country.
1.2       For the 9
th Five Year Plan, the Department identified the following six thrust areas for the development and
growth of systems.
Improvement and upgradation of standards of education in ISM&H
Standardisation of drugs and quality control
Research and Development
Ensuring sustained availability of raw materials, ie.. medicinal plants, metals, minerals and materials of animal origin
etc.
Participation of ISM&H in the National Health Programme and Family Welfare Programmes
Information, Education and Communication (Publicity)

IV        HOMOEOPATHY
4.1       For Homoeopathy the plan allocation was Rs. 8.20 crores in BE 2000-2001 which was raised to Rs. 8.49 crores
at the RE stage.  The allocation for 2001-2002 has been reduced to Rs. 8.27 crores.  Commenting on the reduced
allocation, the Department submitted that the increase at RE stage from Rs. 8.20 crores to Rs. 8.49 crores was mainly on
account of additional allocation to NIH, Calcutta for renovation of existing building and the allocation for 2001-2002
reflects its normal spending pattern.  The Committee observes that BE 2001-2002 has been kept almost at the same level
of BE 2000-2001 and there is no increase at all.
4.2       In the National Institute of Homoeopathy, Calcutta there was a proposal for creation of additional posts for a 100
bed hospital as per the norms prescribed by the Central Council of Homoeopathy (CCH).  The Department last year
stated that the matter would be taken up with the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance for getting the posts
sanctioned as required .  Asked about the progress made in this regard,  the Department informed that as per the norms
prescribed for a 100 bed hospital by CCH, National Institute of Homoeopathy submitted a proposal for creation of posts.
However, on examination of the proposal it was found that it was different from the one suggested by the Cadre Review
Committee and as such NIH was asked to submit a revised proposal for NIH as a whole including the hospital.  The
clarifications are still awaited from NIH.
4.3       The Department further informed that separately CCH considered modifications of the norms for the Colleges to
make them more realistic.  One of the proposals pertained to the minimum number of beds, according to which a
hospital attached to a College must have at least 25 beds for indoor patients.  The Department considered this  proposal
to amend this regulation after taking into consideration the Central Council of Homoeopathy submissions that bed
requirement should be confined to 25 only with a rider that there should be one peripheral clinic for 10 admissions. 
Thus, a college having 50 admissions will be required to have a hospital of 25 beds and about 5 peripheral dispensaries
which the college has to set up for community service.
4.4       The Committee recommends that the CCH should amend the regulations without any further delay and NIH take
steps to establish the peripheral dispensaries at the earliest so that effective patient care can be provided.

VII       SIDDHA
7.1       The Department has  informed that the State Govt. of Tamil Nadu has given 14 acres of land for the Institute and
an OSD has also been appointed to look after it. The drawings are ready and the concept has to be agreed upon.  The
Committee was also given to understand that financial clearance for it would be obtained soon.  A feeling has somehow
developed that the Central Government should not fund autonomous institutions anymore and  the States should take the
responsibility of meeting the recurring cost at least to the extent of 20 percent.
7.2       The Committee is of the view that as far as the National Institutes are concerned, it is the primary responsibility
of the Government of India and not that of State Government and the Committee strongly feels that the present approach
needs to be changed.
7.3       The Committee had in one of its recommendations recommended last year that the Department should take
necessary action to popularize the Siddha system in North India, as presently the system is concentrated in South India,
particularly Tamil Nadu only.  The Department has informed the Committee that the matter was taken up with the
Director-General, Health Services, who has informed that at present there is one Siddha unit each at Delhi and Chennai
and no proposal has been received from any of the CGHS unit to strengthen and popularize the existing Siddha unit in
North India.  The Committee expresses is dismay over the fact that Department has no policy regarding Siddha system
of medicine.  It does not also appear to have the will or initiative to popularize and strengthen the system in other parts
of the country.  The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that the Department should have a clear policy on
Siddha whether to confine the system in a limited area/state or to popularize it in the whole country.  In case, it decides
to spread the system throughout the country, the Committee would like to be informed about the Department’s strategy
in this regard.

IX        MEDICAL EDUCATION
9.1       At present, there are 311 Undergraduate and 47 Postgraduate ISM&H colleges in the country.  However,
standard of education in some of the institutions is far from satisfactory and they are nowhere near the norms fixed by
Statutory Bodies. The Committee was  informed that high priority was given to this area.  The number of colleges
assisted and budget provision made during the year has been increased.  About 55 colleges were assisted all over the
country particularly for teaching equipment, books, Journals and access to computers.  The Department further released
funds for teaching assistance, hospital services, patient services, and for the first time patient care in medical colleges
was also assisted.
9.2       Regarding the recognition part and mushrooming growth of  large number of colleges, the Department informed
that the power for recognition to increase the capacity lies with the Central Council of Indian Medicines, and there has
been a proliferation  in the intake of colleges. The problem is more acute in the States of Karnataka and Maharashtra. To
discuss this problem threadbare, the Department requested the CCIM to call a meeting of the  Vice-Chancellors of the
universities and representatives of State Govts. Even though the response was not overwhelming, the major States were
represented and deficiencies in mushrooming of colleges were pointed out to them.
9.3       The Department also informed that in order to check the mushroom growth of colleges legislative changes are
required and instead of establishing new colleges emphasis should be on  establishing new centres of excellence.
9.4       The Committee feels that  legislative changes, as required, may be made at the earliest to check the mushroom
growth of colleges coming up without adequate infrastructure.  The Committee also desires that whenever a centre of
excellence is opened, it may be opened in an area  where the level of acceptance of the system is high, so that
effectiveness of the system could be popularized in a standardized  manner.
9.5       The Committee was also informed that there is a growing feeling among the students that those who could not
get seats in Allopathic Medical Colleges get relegated into Ayurvedic, Unani and other Colleges in the Common
Entrance examination.   The Committee was further informed that  in view this scenario, the Department has plans to
have a separate entrance examination for admission into Ayurvedic and Unani Colleges so that students who are really
interested in this field could join.  This issue has been thoroughly debated in the Central Council and the decision on it is
likely to be taken soon.
9.6       The Committee wonders whether this could be achieved through the common entrance examination itself by
making compulsory a fixed number of questions for students who seek admission to Ayurveda/Unani Colleges instead
of having a separate entrance examination.  The Committee would like this to be examined.
X         QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS
10.1     Laying down the pharmacopoeial standards and quality control of ISM&H drugs is one of the priority areas of
the Department.  The Committee was informed that the Pharmacopicial Laboratories at Ghaziabad both for
Homoeopathy and for Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha are working at a very low ebb for the last so many years.  It was
also informed that the number of tests they were conducting was so low that it is really questionable whether there is a
need to have this kind of Institution, if at all any impact has to be made. 
10.2     The Department further informed that the proposal to strengthen the two Laboratories is under way. EFC
clearance for the project has since been obtained. The funds are available with the Department and the construction
work for the building of PLIM and HPL, Ghaziabad has been entrusted to Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA). 
The Department also informed that it had consulted CSIR, the Department of Biotechnology and the ICMR on the
matter and the number of posts in laboratories is likely to go up.  The Committee hopes that the entire process would be
hastened up.
10.3     The Committee was informed that the Department plans to recognize Private laboratories for quality
certification.  Before any private lab is recognized, inspection  by the Central Government and State Government
officials will be made.  Testing in these labs would be accorded high priority and  a draft rule in this regard has already
been notified which will soon become  law for the privatelaboratories.  The Committee while appreciating the steps
taken by the Department feels that after the job of recognition of Private Laboratories is undertaken, some type of
monitoring mechanism on them should also be evolved.
10.4     A scheme for assisting State Drug Testing Laboratories of ISM&H has been announced by the Finance Minister
in his Budget speech for 2001-2002.  The scheme is meant primarily for renovation and modernization of state
laboratories  of Indian Systems of Medicines and Drugs which would enable them to fulfil the statutory responsibility
under the Drugs and Cosmetics, Act.  Under the scheme devised,  equipments  would be supplied and funds for
modernization of facilities would also be given apart from training for giving standard treatment to the patients.

XI        NON-AVAILABILITY OF HERBS AND MEDICINAL PLANTS
11.1     The efficacy of  most of the ISMH drugs is dependent upon the use of pure and genuine raw material obtained
from medicinal plants.  However, due to over exploitation, unscrupulous collection and denuding of forests, supplies
have been dwindling.   The Department informed the Committee that it has initiated various steps to enhance the supply
of medicinal plants.  A special scheme to provide assistance to research organisations for development of agro-
techniques has  been introduced and a  component of R&D has also been included under the scheme to achieve better
results.  The Department further informed that National Board on Medicinal Plants as a statutory body has been set up
under the Cabinet order on 2
nd  November, 2000.   The Board has been constituted by official members and has been
notified. Non-official members are in the process of being notified.   The Committee was also informed that based on
Cabinet order,  6 special committees for demand and supply of medicinal plants have been set up to look into the aspect
of intellectual property, cultivation and conservation of medicinal plants and the committees have started functioning.  
About 6 to 8 Deptts. including ICAR, CSIR have been roped in to have a co-ordinated plan.
11.2     The Committee appreciates the steps taken and desires that regular monitoring of the Committees constituted
should also be there to study their effectiveness.  The Committee also reiterates its recommendation made last year that
the study to conduct the collection of authentic data on the demand, consumption and availability of medicinal plants be
entrusted to the National Board of Medicinal Plants.
 
XII       PUBLICITY
12.1     Forthis purpose, the Department took several steps during the year both within the country and outside.  For
popularizing the systems abroad, the Department participated for five months at Hanouver in Exp-2000 by putting a
stall and the response was overwhelming.  Keen interest was shown in the areas of yoga and pulse diagnosis.  The
Department also informed that a conference of Ayurveda in  New York was inaugurated by PM and six areas where
ayurveda is extremely strong were presented before a mixed crowd of Americans and  non-resident Indians.  The
industries in the field were also encouraged to display their products.  The research publications, drug list and research
done on plants were also displayed.   The Department, however, informed that the difficulty there was that USA
recognizes Ayurvedic items as  food supplements only.   Apart from the above measures, the Department informed that
it presented its case before the House of Lords Sub-Committee on alternative and complementary systems of medicines
because the Sub-Committee earlier concluded that Ayurveda and Unani lacked scientific  evidence.
12.2     The Department also informed that it took several steps to popularise the Indian  systems within the country. 
Health Melas were  held at five places in the country, where medicines were given under the three systems and
presentations were made on Yoga and natural food and diet therapy through Naturopathy.  The basic idea of Health
Melas was that the public should be given  access to the highest quality of both primary health care as well as secondary
and tertiary level care.  The response to the health melas  was reported to be encouraging.
12.3     The Committee appreciates the holding of  Health Melas outside the country  for popularizing the Indian systems
of medicines as the people outside don’t know much about them.  But such melas in the country do not serve much
useful purpose . The Committee is of the view that positive achievements made in all the systems of Indian medicine
should be given wide publicity through print and electronic media so that people at large would come to know about
them.  The Committee observes that the Department has not taken any effective steps to remove the prejudices of the
system.  The Committee feels that this grey area should be included in the IEC component, which the Department
prepares in future.

XIV     INTRA MURAL AND EXTRA MURAL RESEARCH
14.1     The Committee was informed that in the area of intra-mural research  the Council has been able to work in
coordination with the Indian Council of Medical Research.   An operational research study of using 11 ayurvedic
medicines and approaches dealing with women’s and children’s problems would  be started in the next three months. 
10 blocks are being taken in the country in five States to work on ayurvedic medicines in specific areas like anemia, etc.
and work   on unani and homoeopathy will also be taken in due course.   By  these measures, the Department stated,  the
Council would be able to test the efficacy  more than what has been done in the past in the case of Indian systems. 
14.2     The other measure which the Department proposes to take not through Budgetary support, but through the
support of World Health Organisation is identification of  five  areas in ayurveda like prostate, menopause,  preventive 
cardiology, arthritis  and Rasayan where ayurveda and  unani are very strong, and where it could be subjected to clinical
trials and testing the efficacy.   The Department stated that at least in two  areas the work will start soon.
14.3     The Committee was also informed that the  research councils have been given direction that they must look for
priority areas where ayurveda, unani, homoeopathy can work in tandem with allopathy.
14.4     As far as the extra-mural research was concerned, the Committee was informed that the scheme is being
reworked as people were applying in areas for  working in animals which   even the ICMR does not require it now.  
The need ofthe hour is  to identify some good institutions which could take up cases of ayurvedic, unani and
homoeopathic medicines through pre-determined ones.   A new scheme has been drawn up and applications  would be
invited by June, 2001.
14.5     The Committee hopes that the new scheme on extra-mural research work will start by June, 2001.  However, the
Committee feels that at the time of selection of institutions for research  purposes, institutions which are already
working in the area and well-established in Ayurveda may be identified and assisted so that better and fruitful results
could be achieved.

15.1     Patent Cell (ISM)  was created in the Department on 22.4.97 to look after the work relating to :-
To keep track of patents being filed in India or other parts of the world with respect to Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani
Drugs and Patent proprietary medicines.
To extend professional assistance to organizations and scientists in the ISMH Sector in connection with the filing of
Patents by providing information contained in ancient texts.       
15.2     The Department has informed that after observing the work  of the Cell and after visiting the World  Intellectual
Property Organisation it was realized that there is not much scope  for such a Cell.  By establishing a Traditional
Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), the need of a legal expert will not be there.  Whenever there is any controversy  it
can be effectively countered by effective use of knowledge and advanced technology.   The Director, NISCOM was also
of the  view that after establishment of TKDL, the patent cell would become redundant because patents are valid only
within a country and patents are generally published only after they are granted and not before.   Moreover, the Patent
Cell of the Department would not be able to access any information at the time of filing  patents, and the cell   would be
useful only for filing of patents by Research Councils working under the Department.
15.3     The Department further informed that with the help of TKDL, the accessibility of information would  become
easier and nobody can claim to have innovated or discovered on 14 items mentioned in the TKDL.  Ayurveda Experts
would also be recruited for giving expertise in regard to plants and other things and this would also find place side by
side in the 14  TKDL texts  which would be completed within eight to ten months.   Unani and Siddha experts would
also be encouraged  to do a similar exercise.
15.4     The Department also informed that the research councils have already documented 4,500 items of traditional
knowledge of which people have been taking help since a very long time.  One monograph of this knowledge has
already been published.

sensitive  and important issue.   The Committee would like that the matter should be examined afresh in consultation
with the concerned Departments and an early decision may be taken in this regard. TKDL cannot be a substitute for
patent cell.  The Committee, therefore, feels that Patent Cell  should also co-exist with TKDL.
